summary: The Food Inspector, P.W. 4, took a sample of Lal mirchi powder from the grocery shop of the respondent. The Public Analyst found that the sample contained nine living meal worms. There was no other evidence in support of the case of the prosecution that the Lal mirch powder was adulterated. It was contended before the High Court that the evidence by way of the Public Analyst had failed to prove that thelal mirchi was adulterated and he accordingly acquitted the respondent, but convicted the respondent under section 7 read with section 16 of the . On appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that in the case where the Food Inspector had found that a proportion of percentage of the article not being a proportion or percentage as would be covered by the rule, de minimis non curat lex is putrid, filthy, disgusting, decomposed or diseased and that the Public analyst was not competent to say as to what extent of insect infestation would make the article "adulterated" within the meaning of section 2(1)(f) of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The word "otherwise" in sub clause (f) Of cl. (l) of section2 does suggest that all the adjectives used earlier refer to the quality of the Article being unfit for human consumption. [473F] 2.1 In the instant case, the Public Food Inspector was competent to opine and testify about this fact. The prosecution has not established by any satisfactory evidence the requirement of section (2) of Act. [474G] Dhanraj 's case is largely based on the circumstances that the standard of quality and purity was not prescribed in respect of cashew nuts. Now that r. 48 B of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955 has been framed, the decision in Kacheroo Mal 's Case (supra) is rendered inapplicable. [475B] 2:2. The evidence led by the prosecution is inadequate to warrant interference with the judgment of acquittal passed by the trying Magistrate and upheld by the High court. [476D] Dhan Raj vs Delhi Administration, ; , referred to.

The appellant was convicted under section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act for violation of cl. 3(2) of the order. He was acquitted by the Magistrate but on appeal, the Sessions Judge acquitted him. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the presumption under para. 3 (2) could not be drawn against him because the presumption in his case cannot be drawn from proof of storage only. HELD: The appellant produced a number of lease deeds in which leases of various parcels of land were shown to have been granted to him. He also produced receipts of payment of lease money and he cited witnesses who deposed on oath that he and his brother cultivated 80 90 bighas of land. No doubt, the lease deeds are not registered but for the purpose of a criminal prosecution, it is easy to see that the evidence which wasbrought for ward of witnesses deposing orally was not concocted to set up a false defence. Indeed no adequate reasons were given for rejecting the testimony of witnesses. [90 D E] Manipur Administration vs M. Nila Chandra Singh, ; , followed. The appellant could successfully prove that he is an agriculturist and the presumption thereunder cannot be raised against him. That paragraph expressly excludes bona fide consumers and agriculturists from the presumption to be drawn under section 49 of the Registration Act. If that be so, then he is not entitled to the benefit of article 14 of the Constitution. [92 F G] Manipur Adminis trative consumers are in fact carrying on agricultural operations. They were in possession of 80 90 bits of land on which Paddy and other foodgrains found in their pos session were grown. No evidence was given for this purpose. The High Court rightly rejected the testimony.

The appellant was the lessee of a certain land in respect of which a lease of Rs. 100 was granted to him by the Receiver. The lease was for one year each year and the rent was paid in the succeeding year. The respondent instituted a suit against the appellant for ejectment on the ground that he had acquired permanent right from month to month under section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act, which was decreed by the trial court but the High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the lease was not a monthly tenancy and therefore the defendant could not be ejected in contravention of its terms. The appellant contended that the suit was barred by limitation under article 139 of the Limitation Act and that the respondent had no authority to settle the lands in question as he was a monthly tenant under section 106 of the Act, and that by reason of the payment and acceptance of rent there were two tenancies for one period each for one years each. Held, that the appellant was not entitled to a decree for ejectment against him on the grounds that he was in possession of the land as a trespasser all along and thus acquired a right to be ejected from the land under section 117 of the Indian Transfer of property Act. The suit was therefore time barred by article 139 Of the Limitation act. Held further, that it is one thing to say that in the absence of a valid agreement, the rights of the parties would be regulat ed by law in the same manner as if no agreement existed at all; it is quite another thing to substitute a new agreement for the parties which is palpably contradicted by the admit ted facts of the case.

The appellant assessee, who was a firm of manufacturers and dealers in textile products, filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 1,39,722/86 from the defendants, M/s. D.N. Sharma & Co., for the assessment years 1964 65 onwards. The Income Tax officer, to whom summons were issued, sent the record relating to the income tax assessment of the defendants under section 137 of the 1961 Act, and after making an enquiry, passed a notice to produce the Income Tax records relating to income tax returns, which was followed by a further notice dated November 1, 1972. The assessee also applied for and obtained summons requiring the Income tax Officer to produce certain documents in respect of assessment years, 1964 65 and 1963 66. The appellant also applied under section 138(1)(b) of the Act for summoning the IncomeTax Officer to prove that the said documents were not produced by him. The application was rejected on the ground that no disclosure of information regarding income tax return was made by the assessee or any other person, as required by section 137(1). The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeal and the Tribunal confirmed the order of the Income Tex Tax officer. In the reference to the High Court, it was contended for the appellant that after the repeal of section 137, the jurisdiction of the court to summon the documents, after April 1, 1964, for the said assessment years had been taken away for all times to come, notwithstanding the repeal by Act V of 1964, and that the finality attached to an order of assessment under section 139(1) was not affected by the repeal. The High Court held that the omission of Section 137 did not make any difference and that it was not open to the IncomeT Tax Officer to take advantage of the provisions of section 138 (1). In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellant it was submitted that after repeal of the 1922 Act by Act VI of 1964 and after its repeal by the 1962 Act, there was no longer any impediment left in the way of a court to summoning the production of documents filed after April I, 1964 relating to assessment proceedings for 1964 65. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.

The plaintiff appellant filed a suit for partition and possession of the property which was claimed as an heir under Muhammadan Law. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in second appeal reversed that decision. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Mujtzal is not the guardian of the person in whose charge he is at the time of gift. He can exercise only the power of a husband to take possession of any thing given to his wife and by the father to his minor child. [553 B] (ii) In the present case there was no evidence that Mammotty was living at the age of her father if the girl was unarmed or absent, and the gift in question was not a valid gift. The donee must not leave behind even a straw belonging to him to show his ownership and possession. [554 C] (iii) In any case, the gift was a valid one. [555 E F] Nabi Sab vs Papiah & Ors., ; , followed. (iv) The gift in the present ease was a validly gift. Mammottty was lived at the relevant time of the gift. In such cases the benefit to the minor and the completion of the gifted for his benefit is the sole consideration. As the donee must depart from it and the donee should enter upon possession, he must enter upon the possession. The strict rule of Muhammadan law about giving possession to one of the stated guardians of the Property of the minor is not a condition of its validity in certain cases. One such case is gift by the husband to his daughter but to her mother, the father.

The Madras Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951 (Act 19 of 1951) was enacted to provide for the better administration and governance of Hindu Religious and charitable institutions and endowments in the State. The Act provided for the establishment of a fund called the "State Public Fund" and the management of such funds and the collection of contributions from religious endowments. Section 76(1) provided that the Commissioner shall keep regular accounts of all receipts and disbursements. of the receipts of the temple. The Commissioner of Hindu Endowments, Madras, issued notices to the respondents under section 76(2) calling upon them to pay the arrears of contribution and audit fee under the Commissioner 's order. The respondents moved a petition in the High Court for an order restraining the Commissioner from enforcing the provisions of the Act. The High Court held that sections 21, 30(2), 31, 55, 56 and 63 of the Madras Religious & Charitable Endowments (Amendment) Act, 1954 were ultra vires the Constitution as they infringed the guarantee of fundamental rights under articles 19(1)(f), 25 and 26 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts had no power to issue writs for enforcing the Act which imposed a duty upon the administration of temples governed by the Act, and that the power to make rules was not restricted nor were the rules framed by the Government rendering invalid. HELD : The High Courts erred in holding that appropriate rules were not in existence at the time when the demand was made and on that account the demand for payment of a sum of Rs. 1, 1, 62 8 3 nP. towards the audit of accounts of the religious institutions. [923 B C] The Commissioner could not under section 77(2)(a) impose a flat rate of audit fee on the religious institution governed by section 76 (1) of the . He has to determine the fee for meeting the cost of auditing the accounts as a per centage of the income of each religious institution. [936 D E] The High court erred in not determining whether there was a reasonable relation between the expenditure incurred by the government for providing services and the amounts intended to be collected from the religious institu tions for whose benefit the services were to be rendered. Since the High court had proceeded upon the ground of ab sence of determination by the Commissioner, which was never pleaded, and the High has not determined whether the audit fee demanded was in truth for meeting expenditure or meeting the expenses incurred for rendering the service, the contribution would still be recoverable.

The appellant, a contemner under section 19(1) of the , was served with a notice in accordance with the procedure prescribed under section 17 of the Act to show cause why he should not be proceeded against for committing contempt. The respondent filed an application before the High Court under section 20 of the . The High Court dismissed it holding that the proceeding is not barred by section 20. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) Section 19(2) of 'the Act provides "No Court shall initiate any proceedings for contempt either on its own motion or otherwise after the expiry of a period of one year from the date on which the contempt is alleged to have been committed". The order or the decision must be such that it decides some bone of contention raised before the Court affecting the right of the party aggrieved. Mere initiation of a proceeding for contempt by issuance of notice on the prima facie view that the case is a fit one for drawing up the proceeding does not decide any question. This Court, therefore, cannot be asked in such an appeal to decide whether the person proceeded against has committed contempt of the High Courts or not. [512 D E] (2) The order of the decision of the Supreme Court is set aside and the High court holds that the proceedings are not barred under section20 of the Contempt Act from proceeding as nothing else except a matter of right under section19. [511 G H] Baradakanta Mishra vs Orissa High Court, ; , referred to. (3) The present appeal filed by the appellant against the order of dismissal of the alleged contemner for non compliance with section 20 is not maintainable.

The appellant was prosecuted and convicted for possessing a wireless transmitter in contravention of the provisions of section 3 of the , and was sentenced to six months rigorous imprisonment. The conviction and sentence were confirmed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : Section 4 of the Repealing and Amending Act of 1952 applied to a case of repeal of an earlier Act which had been repealed by the repealing Act. But the present Act did not give it any legislative effect but only extended the new provisions in an earlier enactment for, where an earlier act was amended by a later Act, it could not be said that the earlier Act applied, incorporates or refers to the amending Act. The earlier Act cannot incorporate the later Act but can only be amended by it. [760 B C] The repealing Act does not affect the continuance of the amendment made by the enactment so repealed. It is clear from section 4 of this Act that the repeal of the earlier statute does not effect the subsequent Act. Section 6 A of the Act was designed to provide for a different situation, namely, the repeal or amendment of an existing law which had previously been applied, incorporated or referred to in a later enactment. Under that section the repeal by this Act did, notwithstanding the repeal, affect the operation of the previous law in which the repealed enactment had been applied. [761 C D] The present case was not covered by the provisions Of section 6 A. The word " text" in its dictionary meaning means " subject or theme". When an enactment amends the text of another, it amends the subject or feature of it, though sometimes it may expunge unnecessary words without altering the subject.

The appellant, who was the managing Shebait of a deities in the family of R, instituted two suits against the respondents for recovery of money due to them on the ground that the properties mentioned in Schedule Ka and Kha were not his benamidars for another person. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court affirmed it. In appeal to this Court by special leave: Held, that the appellant was a mere benamidar for R and as such she could not be regarded as a person other than the decreeholder acquiring rights bona fide as contemplated by cl. (b) of section 36(2). The court had no power or jurisdiction to entertain an application for setting aside the decrees on the grounds provided for in the Act, namely, that it was not open to the court to go behind the decree and launch an enquiry as to whether the ostensible purchaser at the execution sale, or the person who purports to have acquired an interest therein under a subsequent transfer from the decree holder purchaser, had bonafide acquired such rights within the meaning of cl. 2(b) Of section 36 (2). Renula vs Manmatha, , applied. The court could not enter into the question as to the validity of the decree in respect of the properties sold, because, it was a fictitious transaction and the husband of the appellant who really advanced the money upon which the decrees were obtained, had been held by both the courts below to be a fictitious one. Renula v Manmathas, , followed. The fact that the purchaser at a execution sale was a benamidar in the case of a decree holder does not make any difference in the matter as to who is the real purchaser for the decree.

The respondent, who was the owner of certain properties in Bombay, instituted a suit against the appellant for recovery of Rs. 7113 7 0 as arrears of land revenue and interest on the ground that the latter had been transferred by assignment in writing within the meaning of Order XXI Rule 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure to the respondent. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed it on the view that the appellant could not apply under Order XXI, rule 16 of that Code for that rule could not be applied to a case where there was no decree at the date of the assignment of the property and the term "decree holder" could not cover a party who had become entitled to the benefits of the decree. The High Court also held that the respondent could not claim to be transferees of the said decree by an assignment in the writing of the transferor in writing executed before the decree came into existence and that the application for execution was maintainable under Order 21, rule 15 of the Civil Procedure Code. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the transfer of or an agreement to transfer a decree that may be passed in future could not affect the rights of the actual decree holder in the decree and (ii) the respondent had not become a transferee of the execution of the original decree by assignment within the mean time prescribed by Order XXI rule 16. HELD : (i)(a) The words "decreeholder" must be construed as meaning decree holder who has been granted an assignment, notice of such application being given to him and the matter resting merely in a contract to be performed in the future which may be specifically enforced as soon as the decree was passed. [1423 B] (b) The word "decree" is not defined in Order XXI of the C.P.C. but it has been used in the sense of execution proceedings and has been understood by this Court as a means of execution to transfer the decree to be passed at any time before the date on which it was passed, or to take effect immediately.

The respondent, a manufacturer of glass and door leaves, entered into an agreement with the Executive Engineer, Ajmer Central Division, for the supply and maintenance of certain sizes of windows. The price was fixed by the Government in consultation with the Superintending Engineer, and were to be fixed within six months from the date of its acceptance "to the building". The respondent paid the price but not the charge for service. The Sales Tax Officer held that the contract was one of sale of goods and the respondent had with a view to promote sales of goods manufactured by it "carries" undertaken to fix the windows without demanding any charge for that service, and accordingly levied tax on the price for materials only. The Deputy Commissioner of Excise, who tried the respondent 's case, held that from the acceptance of the tender, two contracts resulted one for providing doors and windows and another for laying and fixing those doors and window in cut stone work. The High Court also held that there was a stipulation by the respondent to supply and deliver the fittings and the price was not taxable. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the contract entered into by the Respondent was one for sale of material and the contract did not acquire the character of a contract of service, (ii) in undertaking to install or fix these units or articles the sellers do not enter into a works contract merely because they undertake to install and sell them all steel work etc; and (iii) the price of the supplied but not its charge for services was taxable. HELD: (i)(a) The contract in question is of the second variety, and the window leaves did not pass to the Union of India under the terms of the contact as window leaves. Only on the fixing of the windows as stipulated in the contract the property in the materials passed under the contract. [510 B C] (b) The object of the respondent was to enter into contracts for sale and only upon the fixing, of the window, leaves and window, the property would not be complete, and that the respondent could not claim the amount agreed to be paid to it. [511 E F] (c) The construction of the contract by the appellant was a works con tract which was one entire and indivisible, there was no sale of the goods. In the absence of an agreement to the contrary, the materials in the construction of a building became the property of the other party to the contract only on the theory of accretion. [ 512 E F; 512 A] (d) The High court was right in holding that it was only upon a "fixing" of the walls as stipulated for special technical skill and labour by the experienced engineers and mechanics of the assessees. This Court agreed with the High Court that it Was only upon these "fix" of windows that the property was transferred to the buyer. [612 G H] (e) The specifications of the roads to be constructed were set out in the contracts. The primary undertaking of the Respondent, was not merely to supply the windows but to "firel" the walls. The service is not rendered under a separate contract nor is the service shown to be rendered customarily or normally as incidental to the sale by the person who supplies window leaves.[511 E] (f) The respondent 'could not claim that it agreed to sell and deliver to it, [512 A B] (g) The agreement was one composite price of mild steel billets, and when the window leave had become a part of the building construction that the premises in the goods passed under tho terms of contract.

The prosecution case was that the appellant and his brother were charged with offences under sections 420, 468 and 471 Indian Penal Code read with section 120B of the Indian Penal code. The trial court convicted the respondent and sentenced him to pay a fine of Rs. 38/ . On appeal by the State, the High Court set aside the conviction and sentence on the ground that so far as Raj Kumar was concerned no case had been made out against him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since Raj Kumar had not filed any charge sheet on the basis of which he could be discharged, his acquittal by the High court was bad in law and that the report lodged by Ram Avtar was not a forged one. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The report lodged with the police against the respondent did not disclose the name of Raj Kumar Agarwalla respondent because it was the case of the prosecution itself that Raj Kumar appeared on the scene only subsequent to the lodging of the report. [280 D] In the instant case, there is no cogent ground for interference with the judgment of the High Courts as might induce us to interfere. The report which was lodged by R was lodged after his arrest and was accepted by the trial court. Therefore, there was no cogent reason for interference. [281 E F] The report was lodged only after the order of acquittal was passed. It could not be said that Raj had been a party to any conspiracy to defraud or cheat Ram Avtar. There is no infirmity in the judgment as might lead to interfere with the judgments of the courts below.

The petitioner, an allopathic doctor by profession, had himself prepared and filed a petition under article 32 of the Constitution in this Court for implementing the reports of the Medical Officers of the Railways. The petitioner alleged that the Railways had violated the fundamental rights guaranteed to the citizens under articles 19 and 21 of the constitution. He further alleged that there were nearly 12 years old unmanned level crossings on the Railways and that he was mentally unsound, unmaned and financially weak and finalisation of schemes for over bridgeing the right of way is of great importance. The respondent Union of India filed a counter affidavit stating that the petitioner had violated fundamental rights under Articles 19 and 20 of the Constitu tion. It was further stated that the guidelines issued by the Railway Board were not in conformity with the accepted position that at least 50% of the bridges would be constructed on roads where the volume of road and train traffic is low, and that the total life of 80 years for steel work and 100 years for masonry structure would be necessary and similarly an annual recurring expenditure of Rs.22 crores would be incurred. The Union Government had also filed a rejoinder denying the assertion in the counter affidavit that no accident has taken place on account of defective bridges and that it was not possible to provide for such level crossing of the road and that there was no necessity of rebuilding a bridge. It further stated in the rejoinder that the cost of construction would be borne by the Railways, that the price it charges for the services should correspond to relative costs. The Court, HELD: 1.1 The Union of india has failed to establish its case. The Railways are a public utility service run on monopoly basis. Since it is a public sector undertaking, the petitioner has attempted to voice the grievances of the community availing the services of the Indian Railways. [723D] 1.2 It is not in dispute that the Railway Administration had evolved the Railways which provide the link and make working out of both these rights possible. The Railway Administration has been following the pattern of the growth of the railways. The growth of these Railways is a serious concern, and there are many other features which have to be taken into account. [700G H] 1:3 It is this class of passengers which is a menace to the system. Strikes in the rolling stock and the Railway that have passed away all are a warning that no nation founded upon injustice can stand. The railway has been a public welfare organisation, and it has been established as the main viable and stable means of transport and was providing the lifeline and link throughout the length and breadth of the country. [623D E] 1 :4 It is the paramount obligation of the State to ensure availability of situations, circumstances and environments in which every citizen can effectively exercise and enjoy those rights. If these rights of the citizens are to be ensured, it is undoubtedly the obligation of a Union of States and its instrumentalities to improve the established means of communication in this country. It is of paramount importance that the services to be efficient should not be delayed or unduly prolonged. [750H; 751A] 1 5. The responsibility of the Union of Indian for ensuring availability of situation, circumstances, and enimities in which each citizen can successfully exercise and enjoyed those rights cannot be doubted. If this right based on any monopoly based public utility should ever be a commercial venture geared to support the general revenue of the state but there is not an iota of hesitation in this regard to say that the common man 's mode of transport closely connected with the free play of this fundamental right should not he. [751C D] 1 6. The Ministry of Home Affairs has issued guidelines for the implementation of the National Policy and the Financial Rules. The guidelines are given in a letter, which is evidence of every State Government.

The appellants applied for compensation to the Jagir Abolition Officer, Baroda under section 13 of the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953. The application was rejected by the Tribunal on May 6, 1961. In appeal to this Court it was contended that since the orders passed dismissing the appeals were received by them on April 9 and April 20, 1961, the restitution applications filed on May6, 1961 were within 30 days of the receipt of the order of dismissal and hence the application for restoration should be allowed as they were prevented for sufficient cause from appearing at the hearing of the appeals. HELD: (i) The Tribunal had no power to dismiss an appeal for non prosecution but it was obligatory on its part to decide the appeal on merits even though there is default in appearance of the appellants and to record its decision regarding the merits of the appeal. If an appeal is dismissed for want of prosecution, it cannot be said that the Tribunal has decided the appeal and recorded its decision even though no sufficient cause had been shown from the appellant to appear in the appeal.[144 C D] (ii) The language of section 17(1) of the Jagirs Abolition Act makes a decision of the Tribunal in appeal as final and conclusive and not to be questioned in any suit or proceeding in any court. In the context of section 20 and in view of the express language of that section, it is obligatory on the part of the tribunal to decide an appeal on merit even though the appeal has been dismissed for lack of prosecution under Regulation 19(1). [144 E F] (iii) The words "decide it on merits" occurring in Regulation 20(1), are wide enough to take in its scope and ambit an application for restoring an appeal dismissed for non Prosecution as also an application of restoration of appeal decided on merits under Regulation 20.

The appellant was the owner of a village Telibandha in Madhya Pradesh. The respondent 's father died in 1857 leaving behind his two sons, one daughter and another son. The appellant filed a suit for partition of certain lands of Mouza Teligana by metes and bounds. The trial court held that there had been a valid dedication in respect of the village Teliabandha to the temple and that consequently it was a public religious trust. On appeal the High Court set aside the decree holding that the dedication was made in favour of the temple for the temple of Shri Ramchandra Swamy, and that by the use of the words "Mouza Telia Dasi" in the will the witness meant "the time of the partition in the village". The High Court also held that the respondent ' had not been given a right to succeed to the property because by the shrubs she was given possession of it as the manager and trustee of the public trust. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High court was wrong in holding that there was no absolute dedication of the Village Teli Dasi in favour the temple. [422 D] (ii) The mere use of word "Malik" so wide enough that examination of the context was not necessary. The intention was not to make Ramsaran Lal the absolute owner of the property but give him possession and management of the same. [427 G] (iii) The fact that the suit was stated to be dismissed as compromised and the compromise appears to have been in accordance with the terms of the will, gives the property to the members of the family with only a charge on it for the expenses of the Temple and did not make an absolute dedication to the deity. [527 B] (iv) The conduct of the parties is of no consequence as the intention was to give an absolute and full ownership of the properties to the respondent. [321 D E] (v) The document (the Panch Faisla Award of 1896) clearly and unambiguously showed anabsolute dedication of village to Shri Ramchandra Swami temple, and it unnecessary to examine the oral or documentary evidence as to how the property or income of Teli riparian was dealt with. [416 G H] (vi) The respondent had no right over the village. He had not only a right of ownership but also a charge thereon.

The appellants were convicted by the High Court under section 5(1) of the U.P. High Court 's Act, 1953. The High Court discharged them on the ground that they committed contempt of court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Courts had not properly construed the resolution and the High court erred in holding that since the resolution was passed under the Presidentship of the first appellant described as contemner No. 1, he is as much guilty of having committed contempt as contemner NO. 2 was. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Courts were right in discharging their notices. [602 D] There is no gainsaying that the members of the Bar did not act with dignity in regard to the resolu tion. The language used by them was unfortunate. [600 E F] The High court was wrong in holding the contempt as not proper and it should have punished the appellants. [ 602 C D] The resolution passed under section 14 of the Act was not challenged before the High 'Court. There is nothing to show that the judgment of the High. Court was erroneous. [ 603 G] The matter becomes clear when the High, said "we do not propose to punish contemners Nos. 1 & 2 for the contumacious conduct of which we have adjudged them guilty though we express our disapproval of that conduct and hope that the indiscretion will not be repeated". [603 A B] In view of the fact that the notices were discharged, the appeal is disposed of with the above observation.

The appellants and their eldest brother respondent No. 1 filed an application under section 14 of the , before the Sub Judge, Hooghly for a direction on the arbitrator to file the award in the Court in Misc. Case No. 28 of 1977. The Sub Judge fixed the hearing of the arbitrators ' application to return the award to them. On 26th July, 1978 the appellants filed an applica tion under section 151 C.P.C., before the Subordinate Judge Hoolighly praying for a direc tor to file it in the court in Misc Case No 28 of1977. The sub judge fixed the date of hearing of arbitrators ' applications on or about 1st December, 1977. On 14th August, 1978, the arbitrators made an application before the sub Registrar under section 15 of the . The Sub Registrar fixed the hear ings of the parties on 26th November, 1983 and made an order returning the award. On 25th November 1983 the appellants ' applications were heard and the learned Sub Judge ordered return of the award by the arbitrators to enable them to present the same before the court for registration. On 2nd September, 1978 a non compliance report was filed by the Sub Registrar to the effect that the award was presented within time as the period during which the judicial proceedings were pending namely 28th January, 1978 to 24th November. 1983 should be excluded in view of the principle laid down under section15 of the Act. On 19th June, 1986 the arbitrators applied to return back the award and on 2nd Septem ber, 1978 they filed an objection before the learned Subordinate Judge stating that during the subsistence of the interim injunction order on the arbitrators, to maintain status quo till the disposal of Misc. case No. 74 of 1977 initiated by the appellant No. l. The appellants contended that the order made by the sub judge was not complied with and that the limitation for registration of the Award had already expired. The Subordinate Judge ordered the return of award to the arbitrators holding that it was presented beyond time. It was also held that the Registrar 's application before him was heard and he should have returned the award for registration within the period of limitation. On appeal, the Sub judge held that during subsistence of interim injunction on the Arbitrators to maintain Status quo till disposal of the Misc. Cases No.74 of 1977 filed by appellants No. I to 4, the award had been presented within a time as stipulated in section 25 read with section 23 of the and any registration beyond such period would be void. The High Court also ordered that the arbitrators should return the Award to the Arbitrators holding that the Limitation for registration was four months from the date when the judicial proceeding were pending. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 An award affecting immovable properties as in the instant case should be registered. It is therefore not necessary to discuss in detail the ratio of A the decision of the Full Bench of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in M. Venkataratnam vs M. Chelamayya, A.I.R. 1967 Andhra Pradesh In the aforesaid view of matter the judgment and order of the High Court cannot be sustained and are set aside. [123B C] 1.2 The limitation period for registration is four months. The award was made on 28th of January 1978 and it was filed within time. The Registrar ' s application before Sub Registrar, Arambagh on 28.1.1978 was heard by the Subordinate Registrar on 25th December, 1982.

The appellant was the owner of a building in which the respondent had been using it for storing its sub let property. The respondent filed a suit for ejectment on the ground that he had sublet the premises to the appellant and that the sub letting was not bona fide as the sub let was not for occupation by the tenant. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court confirmed the decree holding that section 15 of the Bombay Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947, did not apply to contracts between the landlord and the tenant and that section 13(1)(e) of the Act was applicable only to agreements entered into with the tenant by the landlord. The appellant came up in appeal to this Court by special leave. Held, that the respondent was entitled to a decree for ejectment under section 13 (1)(a) of Bombay Hotel & Lodging Houses Act, 1948, on the grounds of non compliance with the provisions of section 15(1) of that Act and section 23 Of the Contract Act. The agreement between the appellant landlord and tenant was not one for possession but only for licensees. A stipulation in the most solemn form to waive the objection would be tainted with the vice of the original contract, and void for the same reasons. The doctrine of waiver is a rule of law and has been held by this Court in P. D. Jain vs Delhi Administration, ; , not applicable. The principle that a stipulation of the strongest form to waived an estoppel is not a pure question of law but one which is mixed question of fact and law. It is only when there is a provision in the contract that the court will refuse to permit either party to the contract or to those cases where the Court was called upon to assist the plaintiff in enforcing an agreement the object of which was to do an illegal act. P.D. Jain V. Delhi Administration [1945] 1 K.B. 65, referred to.

The appellant, a candidate for the post of Junior Engineer in the respondent University, was selected and appointed as Junior Engineer. The Board issued a notification on July 30, 1990, stating that the candidates were prepared by the examiners of the answer sheets in each subject and that the random counter check by the evaluators was to be conducted at the final examination conducted under the Act. The appellant challenged the validity of the notification before the High Court contending that the Standing Committee of the concerned Divisional Board had no power under the provisions of the Act and Regulations to enquire into the use of unfair means at the stage of inspection, and that it was vitiated for the reasons that the standing committee did not apply its mind to the facts and the decision of the Divisional Board to which they were members. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the finding of the Committee that the fabrication was done at the behest of either the candidate or the parents or guardians was based on records, and quashed the cancellation of the results. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the regulation itself postulates that if the committee disagrees with the Inquiry Officer then only it is obligatory to record reasons. On behalf of the respondent Board it was submitted that the procedure followed by the Divisional Boards in dealing with use of undue means at final examination including fabrication of documents issued by the Board as an integral part of the power of the Division and the powers were exercised by the Committee and recommended to the State Government to rescind the cancellation orders. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Examination Standing Committee was not a delegate of the Divl. Board. It is only a statutory body functioning in conducting the examinations and dealing with the use or training of unfair mean at the examination. [799B] 1.2 In the instant case, the Standing Commit tee did not record any reason in support of its conclusion that the examinees or the parent or guardian were parties to the fabrication. The Standing Committee did not examine the witnesses on behalf of Board and the Board had presumed that the examination was done by either the student or the guardians or the guardian or guardian. It was his contention that all the students admitted, the factum of fabrication and it was to their advantage and that they would be permitted to appear in the examinations conducted by the University. The finding of this Court is based on no evidence and there is no room for a distinction between what is found by inference from the evidence and what is held as a positive face. [899C D] 1:3. It depends on the nature and gravity of the misconduct to be dealt with by the disciplinary authority. The enquiry Standing Committee to record the finding that the parents, or guardians were parties, to the fabricated, would not be entitled to appear at the examinations. [901D E] 1 :4. In the light of the admitted facts and above circumstances, the necessary conclusion that could unerringly be drawn would be that either the examinee o r the parent, or guardian obviously was a privy to the forgery and that he was a signatory to the examination conducted by any other body of persons. [900F G] 1 5. The conclusion reached by the Standing committee that the appellant, his parents or guardian was not parties to fabrication cannot be sustained. It would not therefore be reasonable to exclude from consideration the circumstances on which the whole enquiry came to be held and the general background of the atmosphere in the examination hall. [ 900F G; 901A] 1 6. The findings arrived at by the committee that parents, parents or their guardian were parsided at the instance of either of the students or parents or parents were not permitted to participate in the inquiry cannot be upheld. [800G H] 7.

The appellants were charged with the offence of criminal conspiracy to cause the murder of a person. The prosecution case was that the appellants and two others had gone to the house of one of the accused persons, who had been suspected of exporting potatoes at concessional rates on false declarations or certificates that they were seed potatoes. The appellants were tried for offences under section 120 B Indian Penal Code and section 5(2) read with section 116 of the Indian Penal code for abetting the commission of criminal misconduct by paying a sum of Rs. 2,000 to one Madan Lal who had accepted the bribe. The Special judge acquitted both the accused but convicted them under section 5 (2) Of the Prevention of Corruption Act. On appeal the High Court reduced the sentence on the ground that the prosecution case against the appellants was not dangerous and that the offence was punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years or with fine or with both. The State appealed to this Court by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) section 5 of the Prevention Of Corruption Act, 1947, had no application to the facts of the case and (ii) the offence as defined in cl. (d) did not come within the meaning of bribery. Held, that the offences committed in the course of traps were less grave and call only for lenient or nominal sentences. The offence was of four kinds and categories. The first class of cases might arise where corrupt or illegal means are adopted or pursued by the public servant to gain for himself a pecuniary advantage; secondly, it is enough if by abusing his position as a public servant a man obtains for himself any pecuniary advantage, entirely irrespective of motive or reward for showing favour or disfavour. The second class of case might arise when there is no offer to give an d acceptance of a bribe by a public Servant. In the present case the appellants were not charged with any offence under section 161 of the Penal Code but were convicted under section 3(1) readwith section 5 Of the Act.

The appellant Bank, a bank incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, was decreed by the trial court and the decree was confirmed in appeal by the High Court. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the surety had agreed to become surety on the principal debtor, and (ii) the Bank had discharged the surety under the guarantee. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The surety had made an application that in compliance with the decree made by the Trial Court he had paid the entire amount and he should not be exposed to second round of litigation for restitution of the amount and that this Court would not interfere with the order of the High court dismissing the suit against him. [923D] 2. The appellant Bank was entitled to restitution. It is not a case of granting time or indulgence to the principal debtors or variation of its credit in substitution of some other security or release of any security. [ 925F] 3. In an almost identical situation with regard to an identical clauses in Amrit Lal Goverdhan Lalan vs State Bank of Travancore and Ors., this Court held that subject to certain variations section 141 comprehends a situation where the debtor has offered more than one security one of which is the personal guarantee of the surety. Even if the surety of personal guarantee is not aware of any other security offered by the principal, yet once the right of the creditor against the principal is impaired by any action or inaction which implies negligence appearing from lack of supervision undertaken in the contract, the surety would be discharged under the combined operation of sections 139 and 141 of the Act. [810G H; 911A] 4. The High Court was wrong in holding that the surety having failed to exercise the care of a prudent man, the appellant Bank could not be discharged from its liability under the guarantees. [1210B] 5. In view of clauses 5, 7 and 13 of the letter of guarantee, the sureties would be relieved from their liability as surety if the creditors have put it out of their power to hand over to the surety the means of recouping himself by the security given by the Principal. The Bank 's utter disregard of its responsibility or to use the words of the principal in clause 5 of the said letter and on paying the guaranteed debt, the Bank would be absolved from its obligation under the letter dated February 14, 1961. [936C D] 6. The guarantee given by a surety against proper performance of the contract evidencing advance of loan and methods of its repayment or taking one set of security in substitution Of some other guarantee or release the debtor is not valid. [980F G] 7. The respondent surety has made an applica tion that in complying with the terms of the decree, he had made a sum of Rs. 84,828.07P. inclusive of costs and interest on the Principal amount decreed. The principal amount was lost and therefore the surety could not claim second round the Bank 'S ' to the extent of the value of security and that as in this case the entire security was lost, the respondent would be discharge from his liability under clause 5. [981G H] 8. The Court of first instance has held that the Bank was utterly negligent in discharging its obligation to pay the surety even if it is found that a creditor had taken more than two security on the basis of which advance was made and the surety gave personal guarantee on the good faith of other security being offered by him, which itself may be a consideration for the surety offering his personal guarantee and the creditor by its own negligence lost one of the securities.

The appellant was the holder of a "patelki inam" and the respondent No. 1 was the proprietor of certain village in the State of Madhya Pradesh. The appellant claimed that he had been given certain lands as emoluments for his office to the working patel from the date of the jagir, but the claim was rejected by the Government on the ground that the lands were not "poli" and that the grant was made by the jagirdar of Nawabag in 1853 and section 9 of the Patels and Patwaris Law 1900, which provided for remuneration for services rendered by patel. The respondent No 1 contended that the appellant had no right to resume the lands as he had a share in them and that his claim could not be considered. Held, that the land was given to the jagirdar on behalf of the Government and the grant made by him was valid. The grant was not a service grant but it was made for the maintenance of patel 's office and the appellant was entitled to his share in the "patels" lands as remuneration for the office. The order of the government dated August 28, 1922, did not confer any new right on the patel who had been granted by the British Government. The fact that the patels were given certain land as emoluments in 1927 and the Government was informed by letter dated April 27, 1922 that the village was reserved for the Patel was immaterial because the appellant 's claim to a share was not based on any decision of the revenue authorities. The High Court was right in holding that the grants were made by way of remuneration for service rendered by the pawaldar and not by the sovereign authority and that as the grant had been made by an order of Government, it was open to the Government to resume lands in 1941 and regrant them to respondent No, 1.

The respondents, who were the father of two respondents, claimed that the deceased and his daughter were Hindus residing in Sind. The respondents claimed that on the death of their father as well as on behalf of the appellants, the deceased was governed by the Mitakshara law and the rule of devolution applicable to them or the said properties having been adopted some three or four hundred years ago, but had retained a large part of it and its devolution by survivorship. The trial court held that neither the respondents nor the other respondents had acquired any interest by birth in the property inherited by their father from his ancestors, and that the adoption was valid under section 3 of the , as it stood at the relevant time. On appeal, the High Court reversed this decision holding that the rule applicable to the case having regard to the provisions of the Hindu law as well the rules of Hindu Law, including the rules as to joint family property and its succession, including its principle of devolution of property by survivorship, was not applicable to it or the aforesaid properties. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The rule of succession is applicable only to matters of inheritance and succession in respect of immovable property by birth and the devolution thereof by survivorship is governed by Hindu law. [190 G] (2) The High Court had rightly held that the respondents were entitled to succeed to the estate as they had settled down in Madras, and the High Courts had record findings which were binding on the parties. [189 B C] (3) The question whether the Bombay view was correct or not was a mixed question of law and fact. It was not necessary for the High court to decide whether the Madras view was erroneous. [188 E F] (4) The rules of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, were consistent with the Hindu Law as regards succession and inheritance. They did not make the Mahomedan Law applicable in all matters relating to Muslims nor did they abrogate the custom or usage in respect thereof. [187 B C; 188 D] (5) The fact that the Madras Memons who proceeded either from Cutch or from Bombay to Madras and who, it apears, settled down amongst Hindus, Hindu surroundings and traditions, there was nothing strange that they retained the rules relating to joint families. [186 E F]. (6) The law of succession as applied to the facts of the present case is clear from the fact that in Madras there were no reported decisions on the position of the Cutchi Memons which had been accepted by them as customary law and usage.

The appellants are manufacturers of different types of fabrics. The yarn so obtained at an intermediate stage in the mill of the appellants and subjected to the integrated process of weaving the same into fabrics, will be liable to payment of excise duty. The appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the circular dated September 24, 1980 issued by the Board of Excise under Rule 9 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944. The High Court held that the retrospective effect given by section S(1) will be subject to the provisions of sections 11A and 11B of the Act and directed the subordinate excise authorities to levy and collect duty of excise in accordance with sections 11 A and 11 B of the . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) since the commodity which is produced at an intermediary stage in mill of appellants and subject to a integrated process, is not actually removed from the factory premises, there is no question of payment of duty on the goods; (ii) the notification dated September 23, 1980 which amended rules 9 and 49 of the Rules by adding an Explanation thereto as "place of removal" does not contain any definition of "place" in Rule 9(1); (iii) the Board has wrongly issued a circular dated October 22, 1982 indicating that so long as the goods which are manufactured in the factory are not removed, there was no question or liability to pay excise duty on such intermediate product; and (iv) even assuming that there can be fictional removal as provided in rule 9(2), there cannot be such deemed removal without the specification of the place where the excisable goods are produced, cured or manufactured or any premises appurtenant thereto. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The language of Rule 9 (1) admits of only one interpretation and that is that the specification that has to be made by the Collector is of any premises ancillary to the place of manufacture or production of the excisable good. [717D] 2. The expression "place ' in Rule 3 of the Excise Rules is not required to be given effect to. It is manifestly clear from rule 9 that it contemplates not only removal from the place, where the goods are manufactured, but also removal within such place or premises for captive consumption, as it is called.

The petitioner, a holder of a permit issued under Chapter IV of the Act to ply a stage carriage on Bulandshahr Siana Garh Bugrasi Brijghat Bhasians Shambhaoli Babugarh Jadol Jahangirabad route in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The petitioner filed his objections to the scheme and the State Transport Undertaking submitted its report along with several others. After a number of adjournments, the hearing authority empowered under section 68 D of the , passed an order on April 26, 1979 directing that the scheme published under section 69 C of the was not in force. Before the hearing could be given, the petitioner filed original suit No. 145 of 1979 on the file of the Civil Judge, Bulandshahr for a declaration that the said scheme published was illegal, void and ultra vires and for an injunction restraining the defendants from finalising and approving the scheme. The trial court declined to grant the request of the petitioner and fixed the suit for arguments on November 8, 1985. On November 8th, 1985, the trial court refused to grant its consent to the Scheme under section68 D of Act, but fixed the same day as the suit was not filed in the Court of Civil Judge. The revision petition filed by the petitioner against the order of the trial Court was dismissed by the Additional District Judge, Meerut. In the special leave petition to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondents that the suit is not maintainable for an interim injunction restraining respondent No. 1 from proceeding with the hearing and approving of the scheme either with or without modification. Dismissing the special Leave Petition, ^ HELD: The jurisdiction of the State Government (the Hearing Authority under section 67 D of 'the Act) is exclusive in character and it is not open to a civil court to issue an order of injunction restraining hearing Authority from proceeding further with the hear ings of the case and exercising its statutory functions. Whenever statute uses the expression that a decision of an authority shall be final, the jurisdiction of a civil Court to go into the correctness or otherwise of the decision is taken away. [544C D] H. C. Narayanappa & Ors. vs The State of Mysore & Ors., ; at page 753; H.C. Narayanaappa and Ors. v The State Of Mysore and Ors., , at page 754, referred to.

The appellant was a public servant. He used to live in 1962 with his father at Fazilka. The appellant went to Ambala to bring about illicit connection with someone and became pregnant. In April 1963 the appellant went there to get the child because he wanted to reprimand her. On August 25, 1963 the child was handed over to Roshan Lal who took it with him. The girl was handed back to Roshan Lai. The wife of Roshan Lal made a written complaint to the police that she had illicit connection and asked for something to be done by Roshan Lal. The police registered a case against the appellant under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and section 161 Indian Penal Code. The Special Judge accepted the prosecution case as correct and convicted the appellant. On appeal the High Court maintained the conviction but reduced the sentence to one of rigorous imprisonment for two years. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the concealment of the birth of an illegitimate child was not an offence under the Indian Penal code or any other criminal statute and if the appellant had obtained money from Russel Nathaniel, it could not be said that he had obtained a gratification for doing or forbearing to do any official act or for showing or forbidding to show in exercise of his official functions favour or disfavour to any per son. HELD : The order of sanction was bad in law as all the relevant papers and materials were not placed before the D.I.G. Police. [186 B] In the instant case, the appellant grossly abused his position as a police officer and extorted money from him to the appellant and he had also committed an offence punishable under section 161 of the Indian penal Code. Therefore, the sentence imposed was not excessive. [187 C D] Mahesh Prasad vs The State of Uttar Pradesh, ; , followed.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for three months and to pay a fine of Rs. 500 in default to suffer further rigorous imprisonment. The prosecution case was that on May 12, 1952, the Deputy Superintendent of Police, Special Police Establishment, Calcutta, acting under instructions from the Chief Commercial Superintendent of the Eastern Railway, Calcutta informed the appellant that a sum of Rs 100 was paid as illegal gratification for securing an official act and showing in the exercise of his official functions favour to handcuff him. The appellant was charged with having accepted the bribe and tried for offences under section 161 Indian Penal Code and section 5 (2) Of the Prevention Act. The trial court convicted the appellant but the High Court, on appeal, confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the sanction accorded in this case was not a valid sanction as the sanction had been granted by the Chief Superintendent of Eastern Railway who had applied his mind to the facts and circumstances of the case and was satisfied that in the interests of justice the appellant should be prosecuted. Held, that the sanctioning authority was competent to grant the sanction under section 6(c) of Prevention of Criminal Corruption Act. It is well settled that a sanction granted by a competent authority must be based on sound principles and not on mere suspicions or assumptions. The sanction in this instant case was a valid sanctioned by the Magistrate who had jurisdiction to try the appellant. The sanctioning authority had to consider the facts of each case and circumstances, the circumstances and circumstances in the present case, the motive for the appellant 's action being dishonest it could not be said that he acted mala fide. Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka vs The King, , approved.

The appellant was the holder of life interest in the property. He had two other properties, one for residential purpose and the other for non residential purposes. The first respondent filed a suit against the appellant for eviction on the ground that the building was bona fide required by him for demolition and reconstruction. The trial court held that the requirement of the landlord bona fide and ordered eviction of the tenants. On appeal the High Court set aside the order of the appellate authority holding that the landlord had no right to evict the respondents on the grounds of demolition and re construction, and allowed the appeals filed by the tenants against the orders of eviction. Allowing the appeals by special leave, ^ HELD: The rights between section M. Gopalakrishna and the remainder man with regard to the terms of the Deed of Settlement win have to be worked out in appropriate proceedings if necessary and the general law win govern the matter if any occasion arises. [275E] In a litigation between a landlord and others who are not his tenants under the Act, is outside the ken of this Act. Even a possible dispute imaginary or real, between the landlord and the rest man cannot affect adjudication of the claim of the landlords against his tenants. [276G H] The Act with which section 14(1)(b) is a self contained and complete code for regulation of the rights between landlord and tenants as defined in the Act (See M/s Raval and Co. vs K. G. 276 Ramachandra and others, ; , followed. In the instant case, when the objection on the score of the respondent being a holder of the life interest and hence incapable of invoking section 14 (1) (b), fails the suit must be decreed.

The respondent decree holder obtained a decree against the appellant in respect of certain trees standing on the land. The decree holder filed execution proceedings and obtained an order from the executing court that certain trees, which were deemed to be part of 'land ' under section 6(a)(i) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, vested in the State free from all encumbrances. The executing court held that after vesting of all the rights mentioned in section 6 of the Act in the state of Uttar Pradesh, new bhumidhari rights came into existence under section 18 of the , and therefore, the respondent 's right in trees of groves as these contin ued to vest in the intermediary was vested in State. The High Court dismissed the execution petition holding that after the coming into force of the Abolition Act, what could still be sold in execution of the decree was the right in timber which vested in a free from encumbrances. Dismissing the appeal by certificate, HELD: (1) The respondent decreeholder 's rights in trees were deemed as part of bhumidhari right. After vesting of the Bhumidhari rights in the U P. Zamindari Act, the new bhumidar 's interest came into being under section 3(13) of that Act read with section 73 of the . [582B] (2) The only way in which a mortgagee could enforce his right against the mortgage or after the Act came into force is provided in section 18(1)(a) of Act, read with Section 73 of , so that nothing more than the compensation awarded to the intermediary could be proceeded against by the mortgagee.

The appellants, who were charged with offences punishable under Sections 143, 147, 148, 341, 323, 324, 326 and 302 read with Section 149 IPC, were convicted for an offence under Section 302 IPC. The High Court acquitted two of them and convicted the remaining four only. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) all the six accused persons were charged by the investigating agency for offences punishable u/s 302 IPC; (ii) all other accused except the first accused caused injuries with a chopper, iron rod, cycle chain and lathis; and (iii) all of them were convicted under Section 326/149 I.P.C. and each one of them was sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for three years. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The effect of acquittal of the two accused persons by the High Court and without the High court finding that some other known or unknown persons were also involved in the assault, would be that for all intent and purposes the two acquitted accused persons are not members of the unlawful assembly. Thus only four accused could be said to have been the members of a assembly but such an assembly which comprises of less than five members is not an unlawful assembly within the meaning of Section 141 IPC. [92B C] 1.2 In the instant case, all the four appellants were charged for offences u/ss 143, 148 and 341, 324 and 326 read with section 149 I. P.C., and put on trial. The trial court convicted accused 2 to 6 under section 326 IPC and each of them sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment ranging from three years to six months. Accused 1 to 4 were also convicted for offences under sections 143, 323 and 324 read with 149 I P.P., and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 2000 (two thousand) and in default of payment of fine suffer further rigorous imprisonment. The conviction and sentence passed against all the appellants u/S 326/34 IPC are set aside. [93G H] 1:3. The intention to cause murder of Suku was not proved by the prosecution for the substantive offence of murder under section 302 I.p.C.[94A B] 1 :4. There were other known and unknown persons who had also been a party to the commission of the crime. It is in this case, that all the accused except one of the four accused caused grievous hurt to the deceased with a knife. His offence would, therefore, fall under section 300 I.e. Section 300 IPC punishable u /s 302/149 IPC.

The assessee, a non resident company, entered into a collaboration agreement with the Standard Motor Products of India Ltd. (Indian Company) in November 1939 whereunder it was entitled to royalty of five per cent on all sales effected by the Indian Company. The agreement provided that the assessee was maintaining its accounts on mercantile basis and again for the two subsequent years it stated that it did not receive any income in all these four years, no tax was payable by it. In the accounting year 1967 68, the assessee claimed that it was maintaining their accounts on cash basis and not on mercantile system. The Income Tax Officer completed the assessment for the first two assessment years and assessed the assessee to income tax. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeals holding that the method of accounting adopted by the assessee must be examined afresh and for that purpose allowed the appeals and remanded the matters to the Income Tax officer. In appeal, the Tribunal held that even though the Indian company made a credit entry in the account books of the Indian Companies, it did so on cash receipt basis and therefore it was not open to it to change its accounts with respect to the assessment years 1967 68 and 1968 69. The High Court answered the question against the assessee. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that (i) since the Indian Co operative Bank was maintaining accounts on the mercantile system, it could not be said that until it was so remitted to and received in U.K., the assessee had not received the income; (ii) the mere entry in its account books did not amount to receipt of income by the asses see. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The assessee was assessed as the statutory agent of the non resident Company. [106E] 2.1 The assessee company was maintaining a accounts pertaining to the assessee in its Books.

The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death. The High Court on appeal found corroboration in material particulars from the evidence of an accomplice, and that the conviction was unsustainable. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the statement of the approver was not corroborated in material details and qua each accused, the High Court had no reason to believe that his evidence was corroborated in materials particulars and qua the appellant. HELD : (i) The evidence of the accomplice was sufficiently corroborated for the conviction of the first accused upon which there was no corroboration of the story of the appellant 's story. [835 B] (ii) Under section 133 of the Evidence Act a conviction based merely on the uncorroborated testimony of an approver may not be illegal, but it deserves to have all the reverence of the law. This rule of guidance is to be found in illustration (b) to section 114 of the Indian Penal Code which is as follows : "The Court may presume that an accomplice is unworthy of credit unless he is corroborated in some material particulars". Both sections are part of one subject and have to be considered together. The Privy Council in Bhuboni Sahu vs The King, , held that there should be corroboration of a approver 's version because the knife was got prepared by accused No. 1 and the appellant nine weeks before the murder and that fact by itself will not corroborate the charge under section 302 read with section 34 of the Penal Code against him. [873 B] Bhubani Sahu vs King, A.I.R. , re Rajagopal, , approved.

The appellant was a licensee of the respondent mill. He paid a visit to the Government Hospital and deposited a sum of Rs. 180/ for being taken by him as a public servant. The respondent demanded a bribe from the appellant on the morning of July 6, 1961. On July 8, 1961 he received a bribe. The Deputy Superintendent of Police who was the Head Clerk of the meter and the Assistant Sub Inspector of Police, P.W. 1, visited the office of the Executive Engineer, P & W, 1, and gave him a complaint against the appellant. The appellant was charged with having committed offences under section 5(2) read with section 5 (1) (d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The trial court accepted the prosecution case as true and convicted the appellant under section 161 I.P.C. and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years. On appeal by the respondent the High Court dismissed his appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) since the appellant was not a public officer within the meaning of section 21, Indian Penal Code in view of the language of section 81 of the Act, he was performing only routine clerical duties and could not be treated as an officer within that meaning; (ii) the appellant having been given a notice to show cause why he should not be dismissed from service by giving him one month 's pay for the period of his suspension; and (iii) the High court having found that the appellant had been performing only regular clerical duties, could not treat him as public servant within the mean ing of section 2(1) of Prevention of the Corruption Act. HELD: The appeal must be dismissed. (i)(a) The officers and servants of the Board are deemed to be public servants only when acting or purporting to act in pursuance of any of the provisions of the . The appellant, though he was not acting or purported to act, in pursuance thereof, was not performing the duties of a public Officer within the terms of section 1, I. P.C., and therefore, the appellant could not have been deemed to have been a public servants within the definition of section 3(1)(d) in view Of the language used in section 81. [688 B C] (b) The word 'officer ' in section 21 cl. (12), Indian Penal code, means some person employed to exercise, to some extent, and in certain circumstances, a delegated function of Government.

The appellant was convicted under section 3 of the Maharashtra Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1962. He was convicted and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months and fine of Rs. 500/ in default further rigorous imprisonment. The High Court modified the sentences passed on him by reducing the sentence to one of rigorous imprisonment and fine. In appeal to this Court it was contended that r. 141(2) was ultra vires as it laid down a rule of evidence contrary to the law contained in section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act. HELD: Rule 141(1) is within the powers conferred by section 3 (1). The fact that the rule is contrary to an existing act does not matter because section 43 of the Defence of India Act provides that the rules may be inconsistent with existing legislation but by virtue of section 43, if otherwise valid, they would have effect notwithstanding that they are inconsistent with the existing legislation. [273 G] In the instant case the order of the High Court maintaining the forfeiture was allegations and liable to be set aside. The order of High Court upholding the forfeiture is one under section 114(2). Rule 141 (2) is in the following terms: "Where any person contravenes any provision of this rule, he shall be punisha ble with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years or with fine, or with both". [273 A B] In view of the provisions contained in s 114(3), r.141 (2), is within powers conferred on the Court by section 43(1).

The two appellants were tried by the Sessions Judge, Fatehgarh Court for murder of one Kunwar Singh. The prosecution case was that on the day following the date of occurrence, the deceased Kunwar Singh was a practising lawyer and after finishing his work for the day he left the Fatehgarh court along with the brother lawyers, who had been carrying hockey sticks. The two appellants attacked the deceased with guns while the other two were carrying hoc hardwood sticks. They were tried under section 302 read with section 109 of the Indian Penal Code. The Sessions Judge convicted Sia Ram under section302 read with Section 109 and sentenced him to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of Sia. The State appealed against the acquittal of S, who was also convicted under section 307 read with s 109. Allowing the appeal of S and acquitting S, this Court, HELD : (1) The High court erred in holding that S was not known to the witnesses and therefore he should be put up for being identified in an identification parade. [626 B] (2) The evidence of identification is itself a weak type of evidence. But the point of the matter is that the court which acquitted S, was justifiably influenced by the consideration that though at the earliest stage he had asked that an identification particulari would be opposed to facilitate the murder of the invite. But unless the invitation was extended with intent to facilitate commission of the crime, the person inviting cannot be said to have abetted the murder. It is not enough that an act on the part of the alleged abettor happens to facilitate his murder. [625 E F] (3) The mere proof that the crime charged could not have been committed without the interposition of the actual accused is not sufficient compliance with the requirements of section 107. A person may, for example, invite another casually or for a friendly purpose and that may facilitate the death of the inviting. But, unless the requisite conditions are satisfied, it cannot be used to have the interse relation of the offence. [613 E F; 614 G] (4) The court which convicted S was justifiably supported by consideration of the evidence of witnesses even if not tested by holding an identification in a parade but was denied that opportunity was an important point in his favour.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed his conviction under section 307, read with sections 149 and 147, but acquitted him on the ground that he was not identified by the eye witnesses. In appeal to this Court it was contended that when three of the four named accused were acquitted they could not be convicted under s. 302 readwith section 34, as there was no basis for their plea of private defence. HELD : (i) The High court had rightly held that though accused 1, 3 and 4 were acquitted, they did not take part in the offence. [684 E] Mohan Singh vs State of Punjab, ; , followed. (ii) In the first instance, the High Court convicted accused 2 under section 304, read along with section 149, of the Penal Code, for having committed the murder of the deceased jointly with the acquitted persons. The Sessions judge acquitted all the accused. The State preferred an appeal against acquittal under s, 302, read together with section34, of that Code. But no appeal was filed against the order of acquittal under section 2(1) of the Act. [685 G H] Mohan singh vs State, A.I.R. 1962 S.C. 1348, followed. Mohan Singh v State of Bihar, ; and Mohan Singh V. State of U.P., ; , referred to. (iii) In a case where the trial names only named persons but not mentioned or unnamed, other than those charged or deposed to by the prosecution witnesses, and the court on the basis of that evidence may come to the conclusion that others named or unnaded, acted conjointly along with one of the accused charged. But such a conclusion is really based on evidence.

The petitioner firm, a manufacturer of sheets, filed bills of entry for home consumption and also the goods arrived at Bombay Port on 12th June, 1984. The goods arrived in three consignments and the goods came to be delivered with the remark that "please obtain no objection from the income tax authorities". The goods were again cleared on various dates between September 1, 1966 and February 20, 1967. The bills of Entry were returned with the remarks that "no objection from Income tax" was received. The petitioner 's agent filed six bills of entries for home Consumption or sale of goods arrived on 12.6.1984. The bill of entry was returned with remark that 'please obtained no objection ' from the Income tax authorities under section 102(1) of the . The petitioner claimed rebate alleging that since the consignments had been re ceived, stored and assessed to duty much before the promul gation of the Ordinance, they were liable to pay duty at the rate prevailing on the date of ware house. The Assistant Collector of Customs rejected the claim holding that the goods could not be released. The revision petition filed by the petitioner was dismissed by the Central Government. In the writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution it was contended for the petitioner that in view of the language used in section 15(1)(b) of Act, it would not be possible for the peti tioner to clear the goods on payment of duty on the dates when the goods crossed the customs barrier and were in the process of being cleared, but could not he cleared because of the prohibitory orders of the Income Tax Department under section 103 of the , which was applicable to any imported goods. Dismissing the writ Petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The relief under Article 226 of the Constitu tion is wholly inappropriate in the facts and circumstances of the case.
