[626C] 1.2 In the instant case, the petitioner as such has no fundamental right to clear any goods imported without payment at that rate or without having the matter determined by the procedure envisaged and enjoined by law for that determination. The peti tion is accordingly dismissed. [625D E] Prakash Cotton Mills (P) Ltd. vs B. Sen & Ors., ; , referred to. 1.3 In the facts of this case, such clear ance can only be made on payment Of duty as enjoined by the . [628F] 2.1 Article 32 guarantees the right to a constitutional remedy and relates only to the enforcement of the rights conferred by Part 111 of the constitution.

The appellant who was the managing director of a company which went into liquidation, applied for a declaration that the sale of the whole estate including the share of the sons was not binding on the joint family as it was not liable to pay the debt of the father. The Deputy Registrar of Co operative Societies held that the purchase by the appellant of the bungalow was not valid and that the property in execution of the payment order could not be sold for illegal and immoral purposes. The High Court, however, allowed the appeal holding that the debt was not avyavaharika as there was no evidence to support it and that what passed under the sale did not become any different kind from the moveable obligation imposed on the sons by the partition deed. Held, that the liability of the appellants to discharge the debts of the deceased father which were not tainted with immorality or illegality was based on the pious obligation of the son to discharge his debt and that it was a question of fact in each case depending upon the circumstances of each case as to what passed to the auction purchaser. The liability of a father who is a managing director and who draws a salary or remuneration, incurred as a result of negligence in the discharge of his duties is not an avyava debt as it cannot be termed as "repudiation" within the meaning of section 155 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code. Held further, that where the pious duty of the family to pay and to discharge debts of a deceased father are not discharged by the sons who are legal heirs, such obligation is sufficient to sustain the sale and defeat the sons ' claim in appropriate proceedings taken by them for the same purpose as if they were the estate put up for auction. Held also, that in the present case the liability was not dependent upon the father 's power to alienate the share but on the principle of pious obligation imposed upon the sons under the Mitakshara law. The legal position is that where a joint ancestral property including the shares of the two sons has been sold as such, the remedy of the heirs would be to prove in appropriate proceeding taken by the parties the illegal or immoral purpose of the debt and in the absence of any such proof the sale will be screened from the sons. The personal liability of an sons to discharge a debts of their father which are not tainted by immority or illegality is based on pious obligation. Held therefore, that it is well settled that even after partition the joint ancestral properties including the interest of the minors have been sold and there also it was held that in execution proceedings it is not necessary to implead the sons or to bring another suit if severance of status takes place pending the execution proceedings because the pious responsibility of the brothers continues and consequently there is merely a difference in the mode of enjoyment of the property. Held accordingly, that on the facts of each particular case as well as the circumstances in each particular ease the liability for discharge of the debts cannot be questioned except on proof by the son of immoral or illegal purpose of debt and partition cannot relieve the sons of their pious obligation to discharge their debts.

The petitioners, who were the officials of the Delhi Administration and whose names had been included in the list published by the Committee under section 8 B of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, filed a complaint against them before the Metropolitan Magistrate pursuant to an order dated 23rd February, 1988. The Court passed an interim order on 29th June, 1988 directing that the complaints and criminal proceedings initiated against either of the petitioners for an offence punishable under section 178 I.P.C. shall be quashed and the same shall not be proceeded with in accordance with law. In the meantime, the Delhi Adminis tration and its police officers were also directed to file a complaint before the Committee in the Court. The Committee submitted its report on 9th April, 1988 stating that the petitioners were persons who fall under section 2(8 B of I. P.C., and had to be dealt with accordingly. The petitioners filed an application for quashing the proceedings and the criminal proceedings against them. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that since the petitioners did not either wish to delay the proceedings or to show disrespect to the Committee, it was open to them to get into the witness box for being cross examined. In this appeal by special leave, it is contended on behalf of the appellants that the Delhi administration and its officers will fully cooperate with the Committee so that the Committee may complete its work as early as possible. Dismissing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The orders of the Committee directing the filing of complaints and the Criminal proceedings initiated by the Metropolitan Magis trate pursuant to the complaints filed on behalf the Committee should be quashed. [519D] 2. The Delhi Administration has to examine first all its witnesses as required by Rule 5(5)(a) of the Commissions of Inquiry (Central) Rules, 1972 framed under the Act and if three persons referred to above to whom notices under section 9 of the Act are issued have to be examined even according to the committee at the end of the inquiry there is no justifiable reason to deny the same treatment to the petitioners. [525F G] 3. The action of the committee in asking them to be cross examined at the beginning of the enquiry appears to be discriminatory. Mere non issue of notices to them under section8 B ought not to make any difference if they otherwise satisfy the conditions mentioned in section 8B. The issue of such a notice is not contemplated under section eight B of Act. It is enough if at any stage the Commission considers it necessary to inquire into the conduct of any person. Such person would thereafter be governed by section 8 C of the , Act. [500G H] 4. The committee should have considered whether the petitioners are entitled to be treated as persons governed by Section 8 B before asking them for a declaration and/or to produce evidence in their defence. If the Committee had found that the Petitioners were covered under section 7B then perhaps they would not have been asked to get the witness examined at their end of inquiry. [419A] 5. The procedure prescribed by Rule 4(5) of Commission of Inquiry Rules, 1973 is followed and it is obvious from the order of the Commis sioner that the inquiry of the Chairman of the Board is in great respect and that they never intended to show any kind of discourtsey to the Com missioner. [ 523B C] 6.

The petitioners were the partners of a firm carrying on business in Rajasthan. The firm was assessed to tax for the whole of Rajasthan in respect of all passengers carried by road and goods carried by motor vehicles. The petitioners challenged the Act as unconstitutional and ultra vires the State Legislature on the ground that it contravened articles 301 and 304 of the Constitution. Held, that the Act is valid and does not contravene articles 301 or 304 of Part States. The tax imposed under section 3 of the Rajasthan Passengers and Goods Taxation Act, 1959, is not a tax on passengers and goods. The expression " freights and freights" in article 301 means the amount of freight incurred by the person who pays it but does not include the amount paid for the transport of the goods or at reduced rates. The word "pay" has been used to denote the payment of the price of goods and not upon passengers and the tax is not leviable on passengers. A tax which is imposed ex facie on passengers, and goods, though the amount is not so good as to be more than less than what is good, must be held to contravene articles 304 and 304. The levy of tax cannot be said to offend articles 301, and 304, as a result of which the petitioners are liable to pay tax actually chargeable. The Act and the Rules must be read harmoniously and reading them so, it is plain that the Legislature intended that the rules upon income and not on passengers should be made by competent authority under the , and that the levy of a lump sum payment per year was justified on the assumption of a return in the shape of conveniences.

The appellant company was engaged in the manufacture of a manufacturing process. The raw material for its manufacturing process was tin plates. The appellant was asked to produce a certificate of fitness from the Company which it had obtained under section 4 K of the U.P. , that the workmen were not available for being retrenched. The Company replied that the retrenchment was not bona fide and that the non availability of raw materials or recurrent power shedding and lack of profitability was sufficient to make the undertaking economically viable. The company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the Award contending that the workers who were sought to be retrenched were entitled to the relief of reinstatement effective from the day on which they were sought lo be retrenched. It was contended that the Labour Court had no jurisdiction to award full back wages since the retrenchment of the workmen was not bonafide and that retrenchment was invalid for the reasons found by the Labour court and the workman were entitled for reinstatement effective retrospectively or the back wages. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the respondents who were seeking to be retrenched from the company were entitled only to full back Wages, that they had no opportunity of explaining why their services should not be terminated and that they were entitled also to the benefit of reinstatement with continuity of service. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The Labour Court has exercised its discretion keeping in view all the facts and circumstances of this case. [571F] 2.1 The Labour court is directed to pay all the workmen as back wages for the work rendered by them since the date of retrenchment. [572A B] 2(a) The High Courts order directing reinstatement with full backwages is not sustainable in view of mounting losses and falling production for want of raw material on itself. If the services were not terminated the workmen ordinarily would have continued to get employment, there must be come sacrifice on the part of workmen. [573F] (b) The Labour Courts are directed to make a just con clusion of back wages with some sacrifice on management 's part too. An amount of Rs. 74,587.26 was paid to these 36 workmen for the period rendered by the respondents since the dates of retrenchment and adjustment of the retrenchment compensation towards the amount found due and pay able. [574F G] (c) The appellant wants us to give something less than full back wage in this case which the Labour Courts have awarded. There is nothing to show whether the Managing Director has made any sacrifice; whether his salary and perks have been adversely affected; whether the managerial coterie has reduced some expenses on itself; whether he has paid the retrenchment compiles for the labour or equity shareholders, and if so, what they affording of the weaker segment of the society, to make them eligible for full back. [575F G; 576A B C] (d) The award shall stand accordingly modified to the effect that the retrenched workmen who are now reinstated shall be paid 75% of the back Wages after deducting the retrenchment compensa tion already paid and the retrenchment Compensation towards retrenchment compensation for the remaining period.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the confessional statement of the accused recorded by a second class magistrate (PW 10) was inadmissible in evidence as no such statement was admissible in evidence, and that the confession made by him to PW 10 was not admissible in law. HELD: The appellant had been rightly convicted. The confession was recorded at a stage prior to the commencement of investigation, there would be no bar to the admissibility of such a confession. [434 B] (1) The statement made by the accused to PW10 was recorded during the investigation of the case and as it was not recorded in the manner prescribed by section 164 Cr. P.C. the same is inadmissible in any evidence. [416 C D] Nazir Ahmad vs State of Delhi, ; , referred to. (2) The confession made to a magistrate under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was admissible under section 157 of the Evidence Act. [414 E] (3) The appellant was not entitled to the benefit of doubt. He had been given a chance to make a statement by the police and that he was not examined as a witness. The evidence on record establishes beyond any manner of doubt that the dead body of the deceased was recovered after the accused had visited the house of Shri Mahajan. [413 G] (4) The conduct of the appellant in neither raising hue and cry nor going to the police even though his wife was murdered in his house is hardly consistent with his innocence. [411 D] (5) The evidence established that it was the accused who had caused injuries to the deceased and that there was no reason for him to falsely implicate the accused. [420 E] Nazir Ahmed vs State, ; and King Emperor vs Lalit Mohan, A.I.R.

The plaintiff sued the defendant for a declaration that the properties in suit were divided as follows: (1) Bejoy and Tarakram obtained Chittaranj an Avenue, (2) Be joy and (3) In the alternative claimed a declaration of charge on the properties. The defendants pleaded that the property was liable to contribute in equal shares and that the plaintiff had incurred costs amounting to Rs. 80,507 7 8. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed it holding that the agreement was proved. Held, that the whole law of mortgage in India including the law of contribution arising out of a transaction of mort gage is now statutory and is embodied in the Transfer of Property Act read with section 82 of the Transferof Property Act. The whole law is statutory and the plaintiff has to prove his case by evidence as to the figures, and if he fails to do so, the suit would be liable to be dismissed. The fact that a person who has purchased the property on the basis of a mortgage deed does not in terms say that he has to pay the amount due under it at the date of the decree is immaterial. The rule regarding the weight to be given to the estimate of the judge who saw and heard a witness is superfluous although Order XXXIV, r. 2 (1), does require that the decree in a mortgage suit shall be drawn up in usual way affording either party the right to redeem the whole of the property or to give him any other relief as it deems just to the same extent as if it had been asked for, provided that occasions no prejudice to the other side beyond what can be compensated for in costs.

The appellant No. 1 secured 69.96% marks out of 50 marks in the interview and the 2nd appellant secured 66.40 marks in all 99.46 marks out Of 150. The 2nd Appellant secured 29.50 marks in All India, and secured 66 marks in interview. The appellant No 1 secured 29 marks out from 150.21 marks out oth respondent. The appellants filed a petition before the Karnataka Administrative Tribunal challenging the Rules on the ground that the percentage of marks for viva voce as 33.3% of the total marks was excessive and in violation of the decision of this Court in Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors., [1988] Suppl. S.C.R. 657, the Tribunal dismissed the petitions. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Rules are clearly in violation o f the decisions of this court. However, the Rules are clear that a large number of candidates have been selected though they had secured much lesser marks than the appellants in the qualifying examination but had secured very high marks in their viva voce out of 100. [497E] 1.2 The Rules were clearly in contravention of the decisions laid down by this Court. In case the marks for interview were kept say at 15% of total marks, the appellants before this Court were bound to be selected and a large numbers of selected candidates would have gone much lower in the merit list than the appellant. [498F] 1:3 The Rules being clearly in viola tion of the said decision, the rules under which the present selection was made as they are no longer in existence. No order as to costs. [500B C] Ashok Kumar Jha & Ors vs State Of Haryana & Anr., J.T. on 24th May, 1990 and Mohinder Sain Garg vs State, of Punjab & Ors, J. T. On a direction given by this court on 4th September, 1991 the record of the Selection Committee was produced before this court at the time of hearing. From a perusal of the marks awarded to the selected candidates it is clear that the result of the impugned selections was declared in 1987 and the selected candidate have already joined the posts. Thus it is an admitted position that if the marks of interview were keep even at 15%, of the aggregate marks, then both the appellants were bound by the Rules. [501C D] Ashok Yadav & ors. vs The State of Punjab and Ors., J .T.

The appellants were charged with murder and were convicted under section 302 read with section 120B of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on 14th July, 1982, the deceased came to his house and told him that he had seen God and if they followed him and his preachings, they too could see God. Soon thereafter, he picked up a bombs from the bag which he held and threw it at the Collector. The deceased fell down after being apprehended by the mob soon after the bomb burst. He was chased and caught hold of, but he was caught hold by the villagers. The appellants were convicted for murder under section 307 read with Section 120B I.P.C. and sentenced to ten years ' rigorous imprisonment. Two other accused persons were acquitted by the trial court. The High Court dismissed the appeal preferred by the appellants. In the appeals before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the prosecution evidence on record should be rejected as when on 10th July 1982 Sadanand had continuously been detained in jail till the Collector 's murder on 11th April, 1983, he must have been anxious to ensure that the assault stopped. His plea in such a situation would neither be voluntary nor natural. It would not be proper to rely upon the same for any purpose. Dismissing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1.1 The confession of a co accused is not substantive evidence against other co accused persons in the same trial. As this court pointed out in Kashmira Singh vs State of Madhya Pradesh, ; the confes sion of a Co accused is neither substantive evidence nor substantive evidence. [408B] 1.2 In the instant case, the prosecution has failed to prove that the appellants were responsible for the murder of the Collector through Yadav. The defence was not able to support the charge of conspiracy with direct evidence in every case but if the prosecution relies upon circumstantial evidence, a clear link has to be established and the chain has to he completed, otherwise it would indeed be hazardous to accept a part of the link as a complete one and on the basis of such incomplete evidence, the allegation of conspiracy cannot be accepted. [413D E] Kashmira singh vs State, ; , followed. 1.3 The confession is not a substantive evidence in the case. As the jail records did not show that P.W.4 had an interview with his wife that day, the story of bribing the jail officials has been introduced. It is true as argued by Mr.

The appellants were the workmen of a manufacturing concern known as Crompton Parkinson Private Limited and its main activity was to manufacture high grade interstranded ropes for the textile industry. The last of these companies was governed by the Industrial Tribunal 's award on various dates between April 1, 1959 and January 1959. In respect of the six companies before the Tribunal, the appellants contended that the industry cum region formula which is the basis for fixing wages and dearness allowance had not been properly applied by the Tribunal and it had been carried away by the recommendations of the tripartite conference which suggested need based minimum wages. The Tribunal rejected this contention and held that the usual pattern of having unskilled, semi skilled and skilled grades should be followed and the various workmen, though they should be known by their designation and not by the class in which they were being placed, should be fitted in these categories. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Tribunal was right in following the trend that has begun in this region and in fixing the same scale of dearness allowance for subordinate staff and factory workmen as in the case of clerical and subordinate staff. [368 E] (ii) The award relating to wages and Dearness allowance is based on the region aspect of industry cum Region formula. In the present case, the Tribunal had not specifically considered what the total wage packet would be on the basis of the scales of wages and the dearness allowance fixed by it as it should have done. [369 E] The Tribunal has not specifically examined the region aspects of the industry and awarded the award in respect of factory workmen. It has also not taken into account the trend in that region which was in the same region. [370 G H] (iii) The Industrial Tribunal had rightly fixed the wage scale for subordinate employees and factory workers as in this case. The fact that the Tribunal has relied on the geographical area of the region cum region would not affect its correctness. [371 A B] (iv) The revision of wages made by the tribunal was a week before the change in the wage scales, dear ness allowance and adjustment, the employees of the appellants ' concerns will stand comparison with some of the best concerns in that regions. But considering that there is no question of want of financial capacity and that Greaves Cotton & Co. which is their main company concerned in these appeals, has a high standing in that Region, it would be desirable to put down the pattern of the Tribunal for fixing the wage structure including basic wage and dearness allowances and for granting adjustments in light of the observations made by this Court in the earlier decisions. [372 B C] (v) The new award pursuant to this remand will also come into force from the same date, namely, April 1. 1959. [373 A B].

The appellants filed a suit against the mortgagees for redemption of certain mortgaged property. The mortgagees resisted the suit on the ground that the mortgagor had sold the mortgaged property to the mortgagees and therefore, they were bound to pay the amount also under the simple mortgage and that on taking accounts the mortgages had redeemed themselves. The trial court held that the Rajinama executed by the mortgagees did not extinguish the title of the mortgagors in the mortgaged properties but only created a new tenancy and amounted to a relinquishment of the rights of both the brothers, as they were the manager and karta of the joint family and that the appellants could not claim redemption of the mortgage property. On appeal the District Court held that by virtue of section 74 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, as Shiddappa did not purport to file the same on behalf of the Raj in his capacity as the manager, he had acted in that capacity and therefore the RajInfendants were entitled to redeem the mortgage properties. The High Court dismissed the appeal. Held, that the suit was barred by limitation under section 74 Of the Bombay Revenue Code as Shridappa didnot purport to filed the same, on behalf o of the appellants. Section 74 of Bombay Land revenue Code as it stood at all material times ran as follows: " An occupant may, by giving written notice to the Mamlatdar or Mahalkari, relinquish his occupancy either absolutely or in favour of a specified person". The section does not mean that the other persons in whose favour the occupancy is relinquished cease to have any right. That their right as occupants remains is clearly recognised by the opening paragraph of the section which gives an occupant a right to relinquish his occupation either absolutely, or in respect of a certain land survey numbers.

The respondent company was a manufacturer of carbon paper, typewriter and stepler pins despatches the said goods from its head office at Bombay to its branch office at Kanpur. During the course of assessment proceedings for the assessment year 1956 57, the respondent claimed that carbon paper not being paper falling within the ambit of Entry 2 of the Schedule to the Act, but a specialised article used for copying purposes, its turnover had to be assessed at the rate of 2 per cent prescribed for unclassi fied goods and not at the rates specified in the said Schedule. The Sales Tax Officer held that carbon papers did not fall within the purview of Entry 42 in the First Schedule to Act, 1966 and taxed the turnover of carbon papers for the period commencing from July 1, 1966 to June 30, 1966. The validity and correctness of this order was challenged by the respondent by means of a writ petition before the High Court which allowed the same and quashed the levy. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that carbon Paper is paper falling under Entry 2 in the first schedule to the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948 and not as such liable to sales tax at the point of sale and that ribbon is not an accessory or a part of the typewriter. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The mere fact that the word 'paper ' forms part of a denomination of a specialised Article is not decisive of the question whether the article is paper as generally understood. The word ' paper ' in the common parlance or in the com plete means paper which is used for printing, writing or packing pur poses. [839C] In the instant case carbon paper which was manu factured by coating the tissue paper with a thermo setting ink (made to a liquid consistency) based mainly on wax, non drying oils, pigments and dyes by means Of a suitable coat ing roller and equalising rod and then passing it through chilled rolls cannot be used for the aforesaid purposes but is used. according to 'the Randon House Dictionary of the English Language ' between two sheets of plain paper in order to reproduce on the lower sheet that which is written or typed on the upper sheet i.e., making replicas or carbon copies cannot properly be described as paper. [ 840E F] In Kilburn & Co. Ltd. vs Commissioner of Sales Tax U. P., Lucknow, ; , it was held that the mere fact of a word in the Notification did not constitute a paper as defined by the entry 2 of Notification No. ST 3124/X 1012(4) dated 1st July 1966 issued under section 3 A of the U .P. sales Tax Act 1948. [881B] In re: Strawboard and Co. (India) Ltd., ; , referred to.

The respondents were employed by the appellant as seasonal masons in 1946. They were employed in the factory of the appellant at Bulandshahr, but they were not proprietors of the Sugar Mills at Bulandshahr. The respondents filed a suit for damages against the appellant on the ground that they had disobeyed their orders and thereby committed misconduct under Standing Order No. L(a) of the U. P. Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950. The Labour Appellate Tribunal held that the management was within its rights in terminating the services of the respondents and dismissed them. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the appellant had no right to transfer the respondents from one concern to another because the workmen at Amroha were not employees of the respondent company. The appellant had also no such right as the respondents had been employed in a business or concern and the question whether in the circumstances of each case the transfer from one branch to another was valid or amounted to victimization, could not be decided by the Labour Appellate Court. The workmen at Pilibhit were employed under the Sugar Mill at Bulandshahr in the previous season during the next season also. The dispute between the appellant and the respondents was one relating to the mills at Amroha and the dispute was one of law. It was well within the powers of the Labour Tribunal to entertain the appeal. Mary (Anamalai Plantation) Workman, U.P., vs Ali Hasan, A.I.R. 1950 All. 816, approved. The question whether a person employed in another concern can be trans ferred to some other independent concern started by the same employer at a stage subsequent to the date of his employment was not a condition of service of employment of the respond ents either express or implied that the employer had the right to transferred them to a new concern stared by him subsequent to that date. The respondent had no such rights and it was well open to him to go back on the terms of his appointment.

The appellant company which was formed in 1965 and went into production, the same year, was exempted from the provisions of Chapter V A of the , by a notification issued under section 73 of the Employees ' State Insurance Act, 1948. The employees ' State insurance fund was created in 1948. In 1951, the appellant company was exempted under Chapter VA of the Act until the provisions were enforced in the area where the appellant 's factory was situated. However, this exemption was withdrawn with effect from May 31, 1969 by a Notification of the Government. The appellant company challenged its liability to pay special contribution under Chapter IV A of that Act on the ground that the contribution payable under Chapter VI A was a fee and its levy was illegal as the Act did not contemplate the rendering of any service or the conferment of any benefit to the appellant or its employees as quid pro quo for the payment. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the contributions payable under Ch. V A were a fee, and its imposition was illegal because the Act does not contemplate rendering of service or conferment of an benefit to a person or its employee as quid por. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The object of the amendment was to make an equitable distribution of contributions by all employers. It was not considered fair that only employers of these regions to which the benefit provisions were extended should alone make contribution and thereby help to set up a corporation. [1094C] 2.1 The object is that the benefits which it provides should become available to the employees in all factories through out India as soon as circumstances make it practicable. Statutory bodies have to be set up, various officers have to he appointed and arrangements have to to be made for providing medical help. All contributions will be made under Chapter VII of the Indian Medical Council Act, 1951. [ 1094D] 2:2 The object was to provide a fee which was necessary for the maintenance of medical aid in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement, and in other cases of any undeserved want, to make provision for securing just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief and to secure by suitable legislation or economic organisation or in any other way, to all workers agricultural, industrial or otherwise, work, a living wage, conditions of service ensuring a decent standard of life and full enjoyment of leisure and social and cultural opportunities. It is in pursuance of these Directive Principles that the State has enacted the . The Act also provides for the establishment of an insurance fund in respect of certain factories, in which the provisions may be made by the Parliament, by the Legislature of any State and by both. Entry 23 List III enables Parliament to legislate in respect Of any other matter not enumerated in List I or List III including any tax not mentioned in either of those lists. Entry 97 is a residuary clause which enables Parliament and the legislature of a State to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in Lists II and 24. [1004C D] 2 :3 The Act is analogous to a deferred insurance policy which parents often take out on the lives of their children, but which are to be effective only from a future date after the children attain a certain age, though premium is liable to be paid right from the start. Merely because the benefits to be received are postponed, it cannot be said that there is no quid pro viso for the payments made. [1014E F] 2 .4 The Act doesnot contemplate rendering any service of the conferment or whatever name is given to it should also make their contributions though at a lesser rate.

The petitioners demand regularisation of their services as daily rated workmen for a long time in the mines of the National Mineral Development Corporation Ltd. The management has throughout denied the petition ers ' claim and alleged that they have been continued on humanitarian grounds for several years even though there was no work for them; and that the workers are surplus to the establishment of the Project. Dismissing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The principle of regularisation of a daily rated workman and payment to him of the pay equal to that of a regular workman arises only when the daily rated worker is doing the same work as the regular workman and there being a vacancy available for him, he is not absorbed against it or not even paid the equal pay for the period during which the same worked is taken from him. [620B C] 1.2 The principle is not the position. This Court in spite of its conclusion that there are no vacancies or work available in the establishment for absorption of the petitioners and that for quite some time they have already been continued, has been continued by the respondents. [625C D] 2.1 In view of the offer made on behalf of respondent No. 2 in the counter affidavit together with Annexure R V thereto which was reiterated at the hearing before this Court it is directed that all the petitioners be given the benefit of the voluntary retirement scheme framed by respondent No, 2 and they be paid the specified amounts in addition to their all other dues. [720D E] 2:2 The principles of regularisation are not the same as laid down in the judgment delivered by this Court in Union of India vs M/s. D.K.M.P.No. 3308 of 1985 dated 2.9.1987.

The plaintiffs claimed that the suit properties were purchased by them from the National Agency Co operative Bank Ltd., who had been impleaded as defendants. The National Agency Cooperative Bank Ltd. was a limited company and even if it was not the true owner, the entire interest in the property could not be disputed. The plaintiffs claimed to have purchased the entire property as transferees of the property from the Native Bank Ltd.; but the suit was decreed by the trial court on various grounds including those relating to the transfer of title to the Natives. The High Court dismissed the appeal and confirmed the decree of the trial Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The plaintiffs were entitled to a decree for declaration that in addition to the 8 pies share granted to them by the High Court they would be entitled to the further 2 as Sen 's submission was that the defendants had no right to convey the full 16 annas share of the properties. [211 G] (ii) The fact that the plaintiffs did not raise any specific issue at all in their written statement or in the evidence led before the trial Judge, could not affect the validity of the mortgage of the entire interests effected by them under section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act and the question whether the suit property was a part of the share of Native bank or not must depend on the facts alleged in the plaint. [212 C] (iii) The High Courts have held that the provisions of the Crown Grants Act, 1895, were applicable to the case as they had been made out in the pleadings and the evidence adduced by them was sufficient to establish that the necessary averments were proved or that this point was urged with any seriousness at any stage of the proceedings until in this Court. [213 D] (iv) The question whether a particular property is a part or share of an undivided family property must depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case and the circumstances of the case. In the present case, the plaintiffs had not raised any specific ground touching their right to this share nor were they urged that the claim under the head "share" was not pressed before the courts below. [214 E] (v) The suit was based on title as Native and not on title. The fact of the purchase by Native executed the sale deed in favour of Nantran, the father of Nance, did not affect their right. In any event the claim could not therefore be accepted without careful scrutiny of facts.

The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Judge of Karimnagar under section 302 read with section 34, I.P.C., for murder and sentenced to death. His appeal against his conviction and sentence having been dismissed by the High Court, he appealed to this Court by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the omission in the F.I.R. did not vitiate the entire proceedings and consequently ipso facto a fresh trial became necessary irrespective of whether or not the accused had shown any prejudice; and (2) the failure to comply with the provisions of section 162(4) of the Code was fatal as it resulted in miscarriage of justice. Held, that the omission by the police officer to carry out the provisions Of section 173(4), I. P. C., did not render the entire proceeding and the trial null and void; but the omission complained of in the instant case should not have been cured by the provisions contained in section 537(a) of Code of Criminal Procedure, as no case had been made out for interference with it. Abdul Rahman vs The King Emperor (A.I,R. , referred to. Held further, that even if the omission was an irregularity which could be cured under section 537, Cr. P C., the Court may reopen the proceedings by insisting upon full compliance with the provi sions of the code and that it would not be necessary for the accused to show any prejudice in his defence by any omission on the part of police officers concerned to supply the necessary copies. Abdul Rauf vs The Queen Emperor (I.L.R, referred to and distinguished.

The appellant, a chemical works discharged effluent in the surrounding area of Cuttack. The respondent Municipality filed an application under section 153A(1) of the Bombay District Municipal Act, 1901, for the discharge of the effluent from the factory of the respondent Municipality. The appellant contended that the discharge was not bona fide and that the permission to discharge the effluent was granted without the respondent municipality sufficient opportunity to meet the objections raised by the appellant. The Special Officer decided issue against the appellant and directed the Municipality to arrange for the discharged discharge of its effluent in accordance with the provisions of section 153 A(3) of Act. The Municipality thereupon filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order passed by the Special Officer on the ground that the failure to give an opportunity to the respondent to show cause against the proposed discharge was one for the subjective satisfaction of the Municipality and beyond the scope of his enquiry. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant had failed to establish that the nuisance in question existed. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The power conferred on the Municipality under section153A(3), is not a protection to the party objecting to the requisition. The Legislature intended that the party to whom the notice has been issued should not be the victim of exercise of any power vested in the Municipality in a capricious manner. The provision for appointment of assessors was clearly intended to enable the party aggrieved to establish his right to have the effluent discharged in the manner specified by the notice. (ii)The provisions of s 153A are mandatory and the failure of the requisition contained therein is an irregularity which does not vitiate the proceedings. In the present case, the Special officer had wrongly decided that lie could not go into the question whether the nuisance existed his order must be set aside. The procedure under section 154A is to leave it to the subjective satis faction of the municipality as to the existence of a nuisance before a notice is issued to the parties concerned. If the person to whom notice has already been issued objects to the notice and the requisition contains therein absolutely the objection is in substance to the issue of the notice itself, which means he objects to tile declaration of the public shall be made within the period specified in the notice, and not to the direction as to manner in which the effluent should be discharged.

The appellant was found to be in possession of railway stores which were used for the purpose of carrying goods. The Magistrate convicted him under section 3 of the Railway Stores (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1955 and sentenced him to two years ' rigorous imprisonment. On appeal by special leave, the High Court held that the prosecution had failed to prove that the articles seized were railway stores within the meaning of section 2(b). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The prosecution must first adduce evidence to show that the goods were being actually used or were intended to be used for by the railway. [188 D] (a) In most cases the burden of proof in this respect may be discharged by leading evidence about the identifying marks on the goods or some peculiarity of the goods not to be found in cases of non railway property. [189 E F] (b) The mere description of the articles as new would not fulfil the requirements of section2(b), and the question whether the articles were Railway stores within section 2 of the Act must be answered in the negative. [190 G H] (c) In all cases the onus of proof is on the prosecution to establish that the article were the property of a railway administration but which has been discarded or rejected for further use would be outside the definition of railway administration. [191 B C] (d) The fact that the seized stolen railway property was being sent out of Lucknow through a motor transport agency, a sub inspector of police and another Sub Inspector of Police to the Railway Protection Force along with another Sub Inspcct. of Police is not sufficient to show the existence of railway Stores within the definition in section 2 (b).

The respondent landlord terminated the lease by a notice under section 106 of Transfer of Property Act, but she was not given an opportunity to show cause against the termination. The appellants filed a suit for ejectment against the respondent on the ground that she paid and accepted the rent after determination of the lease. The Trial Court dismissed the suit holding that the respondent had no right to continue in occupation of the demised premises. The first appellate court affirmed the decree of the trial court. In second appeal, the High Court held that as the appellants had not carried on the business with her as family business in the 11 demised premises, they were entitled to the continuance of the tenancy. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The respondent landlord after termination of the contractual tenancy of the tenant is not heritable and the heirs of the deceased tenant are entitled to enjoy the protection under the Act. [16G] 2.1 In case of commercial premises governed by the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1961, the Legislature has not thought it fit in the light of the situation at Delhi to place any kind of restriction on the ordinary law of inheritance with regard to succession. It may also be borne in mind that in case of a commercial premises, the heirs and legal representatives of the original tenant are not entitled to enjoyment of the protection of the Act, an irreparably mischief which the Legislature would never have intended is likely to be caused. [17H; 18A] 2:2.

The appellant Board is willing to extend the benefits of the Contributory Provident Fund Scheme to all its workers except the Government servants who are on deputation and those to whom the Employees Provident Fund Act applies. The employees of the Board are liable to be transferred from one establishment to another both which may not be covered by the same scheme under the Act and therefore it will bring about serious injustice if they are deprived of their benefits under the Provident Fund. The appellant Board has made no effort at all to analyse the balance sheet of the respondent Board to show the actual results of its working. It has made a report that it has not been explained by the management how the depreciation had been calculated. That report was submitted to the Tribunal and it was pointed out that it had not been examined by the Management how the deprecia tion had been taken into account while deciding matters regarding benefits to be made available to its employees. The Tribunal considered the balance matter in a very perfunctory manner. It directed that the contribution should be 6.25 per cent but not on the basic wages but on the total wages. The Board 's contention was that this would impose additional financial liabilities which the Board would not be able to bear. Therefore, the main question for consideration by the Tribunal was whether there should be a contributory provident fund scheme on the basis of basic wage or total wages and whether the employees of Board were liable to pay bonus. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Provident Fund Commissioner has made an observation that the position at present is not worse than what it was earlier and that therefore the Board should extend the benefit of the contributory provident Fund to all workmen other than those who are covered by Act. [47D] 2.1 The Tribunal has dealt with the matter in the very perfunctory way. It should be directed to dispose of the matter afresh in the light of the observations made in this judgment. [46E] Gramophone Co operative Agricultural Credit Society vs Its Workmen, ; , referred to. 2.2 In a perfunctory manner it should be direct ed to dispose the matter finally in the absence of a detailed examination of the finances of the board. That is why the Tribunal has dealing with the matters in a perfunctory way and directed the management to dispose it afresh in accordance with the observations in this Judgment. [48F] 2:3 The Tribunal had dealt with all the matters relating to benefits to the employees and was deducted from the total wage. The contribution to the depreciation reserve is a statutory obligation and is a definite proportion whereas it is open to an ordinary commercial concern to credit any amount to the deprecations reserve. These and other matters cannot be properly decided in the presence of a proper examination of finances of Board. [49B] 2 :4 In the instant case, the Tribunal had treated the whole matter in one way as between the appellant Board and its employees and awarded the contribution to all the workers except those who were covered by it. The management has made the contributory Provident Fund contributions to the Board for the purposes of the Act. Section 68 of the Electricity Supply Act, 1948 provides that as far as practicable and after taking credit for any subventions from the State Government the Board shall carry on its operations so as not to incur a loss. Under section 64 the State Govern ment may advance loans to the Boards and under section 65 the Board itself has the power to borrow. Under Section 68, the State Govt. may advance loan to the Fund. But the interest on loan will have to be paid to the Government by the Board. The interest would also include the interest.

The respondent wife filed an application under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for grant of maintenance by the appellant on the ground that her husband was impotent and unable to discharge his marital obligations. The parties were married according to Sunni Muslim rites. After the marriage the respondent started living with her in July 1978. On November 17, 1978 the appellant sent a registered notice to the respondent informing him that he had no physical disability with respect to her. The respondent filed an applica tion before the Magistrate for awarding maintenance against the appellant. The Magistrate passed an order directing the appellant to pay maintenance to the appellant from the date of application till the date she was actually incapable of carrying on marital obligations, and also awarded maintenance to her husband. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court held that the appellant having been found to be impotency, the respondent could not have been unable to continue with the marital obligations; and that the wife had failed to prove that her consent to live with her husband had not been proved. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (i) the High Courts had erred in ignoring the legal effect of the second proviso to sub section (3) of section 125, which required a clear instance of circumstances which may be treated as a just ground for refusal of the wife to live in the husband; and (ii) the maintenance awarded by the Magistrate was not just a civil case or a criminal case. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have erred in holding that the respondent having been impotently prevented from discharging his marital obligation, more so when the wife has a reasonable apprehension arising from the conduct of the husband that she is likely to be physically harmed due to persistent demands of dowry from her husband 's parents or relations, such an apprehension also would be a just cause for refusal to live at the husband '. [707C D] 1.2 The High Court was wrong in holding the appellant guilty of the charge under section 5(1)(d) of the Act and awarding maintenance to him. [700F G] 1:3. The expression "cruelty" is not defined in the Code. It has been used in the sense of neglect or refusal to maintain a wife, such as, to give a clear case for her refusal to reside with her, or to provide a cause of action against her husband, and the husband, 's conduct towards her, is treated as "a criminal case". [708F G; 700A] 1 :4. The concept of cruelty is the same whether it is a civil offence or a civil proceeding or not.

The appellant was the owner of a plot in the city of Bhavnagar. The respondent State issued a notification under the Gujarat Municipalities Act, 1961 for acquiring certain lands belonging to the appellant for construction of buildings on the said land. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notification by filing a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that: (1) the suit property was not vested in the Municipality and therefore the notification issued under section 80 C.P.C., was invalid; (2) the notification was bad as it conferred an authority or authorising the State Government to sell the land within the limits of the Municipalities of Bhav Nagar City and of the District Towns, which should normally have been done by the State Govt.; (3) the High court should have given a finding on title as Article 65 of the Constitution is applicable in this case since the suit was filed on 3rd March 1964 and that on the finding of the Trial Court in favour of the plaintiff on the question of title in respect of 'Parade Ground ', and in the absence of specific plea of adverse possession in the writ petition, the Trial court 's decree should have been confirmed. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: ( 1 ) The suit property is not vested with the Municipality under Resolution 37. But since a number of Municipalities made representation to the Government to reconsider the same, the Government reconsider the entire case and decided that the right to sell plots of land given under Resolution No. 37 dated 19th January 1948 by the state of Gujarat to all the municipalities of Old Bhavnagar States and the right of the State to give it on rent lease and to take the income therefrom shall be enjoyed by the Municipalities subject to the condi tions mentioned in the letter of the Government dated 10th August 1965. [231D E] (2 ) The High Court should have taken a finding that title itself should have passed to the Municipality without buildings. [232E] (3 ) The fact that the title itself was not with the defendant but also there could not be any legal possession with the plaintiff as the title to the land is not transferred by the Municipality. The other documents relied on by the learned counsel in support of his contention that the plaintiff had not proved title, are inconsistent with the plaintiffs case of absolute ownership in themselves. [230F] (4) The High court was right in holding that possession of the land was also not taken by the Municipali ty at any time. It is not open to the appel lant to rely on the principle that possession follows title. In this case not only there is evidence to show that physical possession was with the respondent but also that there could never be any right with the appellant as the possession of land is also not vested.

The appellant was a class III servant employed as a metal examiner in the Railway Carriage Workshops at Ajmer. He was charged under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code and section 5(1)(d) of Act II of 1947 for having accepted from one Nanak Singh a sum of Rs. 150 as illegal gratification as a motive for securing a job for one Kallu. The appellant contended that he was an officer in the service or pay of Government and was performing public duty and therefore was not an officer within the meaning of section 21(9) Of the Indian penal Code. Held, that the appellant was an "officer" within the definition of section 2 of the Prevention of Corruption Act II Of 1947 and as such was a public servant within the terms of section 1(9), Indian Penal code. The word "office" in section 21 (9) of the Act includes a person employed to exercise the power of Government or is an officer of the Government, and therefore, a public servants within the purview of section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, are not public servants under section 21 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The fact that the officer in question was appointed to some office for the performance of some judicial duty does not affect his powers as such. The words "public servant" in the definition in section 2 Of the Prevention Of Corruption Act, 1947, mean a person who is appointed to any office for a specified period and includes a Government servant. The mere fact that an officer was appointed under the Works Manager who was certainly a public officer does not by itself constitute a public duty.

The appellants were granted liquor vending licence for the year 1968 69 by the Excise and Taxation Department of the State of Punjab, Patiala Division. The licences were to be sold in execution of a decree of civil court within a period of two years from the date of the said purchase. The respondent filed a suit in the Court of Sub Judge, Patiala, challenging the validity of the aforesaid order on the ground that the property attached and notified for sale was not exempt from attachment under clause (ccc) of the proviso to sub section (1) of Section 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908. The Trial Court upheld both these contentions and dismissed the suit with costs. The appellants ' appeal before the District Judge, was dismissed by the Additional District Judge. The High Court allowed the second appeal holding that the portion of the building used for residence was exempt from attached and sale under clause(ccc). Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. Section 60 is no application to attachment and sale in any proceedings other than in execution. The opening words of sub section(1) are "the following property is liable to attachment" and sale "in execution of such a decree". The opening word of sub sec tion (1), however, does not in the said Act corresponding to cl. (cc.) of the Proviso to sub sec.(1) thereof. So far as the said section is concerned it contains a complete code providing for the modes and machinery for recovery of arrears of revenue. [847E F] 2. Section 59 of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1908 provides that the following property was liable to be attached and sold in the execution of the decree. "The opening words 'or other buildings attached to it ' refer to the attachment and the sale mentioned in sub section 1) of section 60, that is to attachment 'and sale in execution '. The words 'such attachment or sale ' in the aforesaid proviso refers to the attached and the property mentioned in subsection (1). [848F G] 3. Section 61(1), Cr. P.C., provides for the mode and machinery of recovery of arrear of revenue, which is applicable only to execution of decrees of civil courts. The attachment levied on, and the auction sale notified in respect of, the respondent 's half share in the property were not in execution proceedings of any decree of a civil court but were in pursuance of the order made by an officer authorised to adopt proceedings under the said act for recovery, of revenue due to the State. There is no provision in the Act which makes the provisions of section60 of the code applicable to attachment. [884G H; 845A] 4. Section 6(1)(c) provides that "the provisions of the attachment in a suit shall apply to any property specifically charged with the debt sought to be recovered". The words "such attachment" in the proviso refer to attachment, and sale mentioned therein. The expression "such arrest or sale" in section 60 means the formal expression of an adjudication which, so far as regards the Court expressing it conclusively determines the rights of the parties with regard to all or any of the matters in controversy in the ' suit and may be either preliminary of final.

The appellant, a displaced person from the Indian Drugs and Pharmaceutical Ltd., was assessed to estate duty under section 59(a) of the , on the basis that he had acquired for the first time the lands in question by virtue of a notification issued under the Land Acquisition Act. The Special Deputy Collector awarded a total compensation of Rs.20,000/ . On appeal, the Additional Collector enhanced the compensation to Rs.4,29,360/ . The High Court held that the appellant 's claim for compensation was not maintainable as he had no right to claim further compensation which was merely a hope or expectation and could not be elevated to the status of an assets or property and as such there was no question of any property having escaped assessment to duty. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the accountable person had only one right which is to receive compensation for the lands at their market value on the date of the relevant notifications; (ii) the notification under section 61 was issued during his lifetime and therefore it was merely the right to receive the compensation. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that there are no two separate rights one a right to receiving compensation and other a right of property which will have to be evaluated by the assessing authority as on the dates of the death. [329F] 2.1 The notification under s.59(a), which was done on the assumption that there had been escapement of assessment to estate duties, could not therefore be regarded as valid and unsustainable in law. [330G] 2:2 In the instant case, the High Court was right that there were no two different rights one for a claim to compensation and another for a right which arose out of an order passed by the Special Deputy Collec tor under s,59(b) of Act. [328B C] 3.1 It is well settled that when the original assessment was made it was the duty of the respondent, after scrutinising the account filed and examining the materials produced before him, to value the estate of the deceased properly under section 73 A of the Act and when he accepted the compensation fixed by the special Deputy Collector as the proper valuation he must be deemed to have adopted that evaluation as his own estimated value of the lands which he wanted to enhance by relying upon the valuation made by another authority namely, the City Civil Court. [326C D] 3:2. The very issuance of the notice under section 58(a). which was issued on a wrong assumption that the acquired lands still formed part of the estate and that having regard to the glaring enhanced compensation granted by the Civil Court for the land, the said lands had escaped assessment, it could not have been held that there was a mistake apparent from the record. [325D E] 3 :3. The respondent is really seeking to change his opinion about the valuation of the acquired land because some other authority, namely, Civil Court, has valued the same differently. It cannot be said that he has only one rights which is being prosecuted by the heirs of the original owner on the relevant date. [324E] 3(a)(i) The High Courts have attempted to distinguish the instant cases from those decided by this Court in the case of the right of possession acquired under the Andhra Pradesh Act, and the decision of this Court upholding the issuance of notice under s 59(b). [325F G] (b) In the present case, it cannot be held that a fresh and an independent right to purchase the lands had been created. The fact that the land had vested in the Government long prior to the death of the respondents did not show that the acquisition was for a public purpose or that there existed any question of such property having been escaped assessment.

The appellant, a member of the Cooperative Society, was elected as Director of the Bank on 18.8.1986. His election was not called in question by the Deputy Registrar, Cooperative Societies, Nagpur, on the ground that he had defaulted in payment of the loan before the notice under section 78(1) of the Maharashtra State Co operative Land Development Bank Act, 1960 was issued. The appellant 's appeal against that order was dismissed by the Divisional Joint Registrar of the Co operative Society, Nagpur on 15.2.1988 holding that section 73FF of the Act came into force on 12.5.1986 and the appellant could be treated as a defaulter under that section. The Assistant Registrar, Co operative Societies, Chandrapur, in exercise of his powers under section 77(1), issued notice to the appellant under section 80(1). The appellant challenged the aforesaid order before the Cooperative Court by way of a Writ Petition. The Cooperative Court dismissed the petition holding that the dues calculated on 31.1.1986 became recurring dues every following day and on 12th May, 1986 when section 73F came into effect the outstanding dues continued even on 18 8.86 when the appellant contested the election; and that the question of giving retrospective effect to the section did not arise because the appellant was a defaulter when he contested the Election. The High Court dismissed his Writ Petition holding that Section 73FF(2) did not operate automatically and that he ceased to be a defaulter on the date of notice and the provisions of section 78 (1) were not attracted; and further held that even assuming that the disqualification on account of default was common both for election and for continuation as a Director in the Committee, the special provision for setting aside an election must prevail over section 78 as there would be apparent conflict between the two and the maxim generalia specialibus non derogant general words do not derogate from special, would apply, and that even if the disqualification is common both, the Special provision for set aside an order of removal must prevail. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the Appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellant was in arrear in respect of instalments on the dates of his election and till 21.10.1986 i.e. both prior and subsequent to his election on 18th August 1986. [683F] 1.2 The day an instalment falls due on its due date failure to pay results in default and that default continues from day to day until it is repaid. Every day thereafter until payment results in making of default and, therefore, it could not be said that default could be on the due date only and thereafter no default but only liability. [684H; 683A] 1:3 The appellant can be said to have made default on the first day of his directorship and on every subsequent day till the instalment or instalments were paid. The submission, has therefore to be rejected. [682B C] 2.1 Sub section (2) of section 73 of the Bombay Cooperative Societies Act deals with disqualification for membership. Sub section 3 of section 74FF says that a member who has incurred any disqualification under sub section (1), shall cease to be member of a committee and his seat shall thereupon be deemed to be vacant.

The respondent was in the service of the State Government as Supply Inspector and he retired from service on September 1, 1977. After his retirement, he was served with a charge sheet on October 16, 1978 containing allegations of misconduct and negligence against him for the period he was in service. Enquiry into those charges was held and the respondent was afforded full opportunity to defend himself. On the conclusion of the enquiry, the State Govt. issued orders on December 4, 1982 reducing the amount of pension payable to the respondent by 50 per cent permanently under Rule 188 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules. The respondent challenged the validity of the Government 's order by means of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court. A Division Bench allowed the writ petition and quashed the order reducing the pension by 50% holding that the State government had no authority in law to take any disciplinary proceedings against the respondent as he had already retired from serv ice on September, 1,1977 and charges were served on him on October16, 1978 after about a year of his retirement. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: The State Government 'Speaking its order dated December 4 1982 reducing or withdrawing pension to the extent of Re. 1 per month as it was disproportionate to the charges proved against the Respondent. [35D] B.J. Shelet vs State of Gujarat & Ors., ; , followed. The High Court was right in holding that since the State Govern ment had power to reduce the amount, the reduction of pension by fifty per cent was disproportionate.

The appellant, a tenant of the respondent, filed an application under section 3(3) Of the Bengal Alluvion and Diluvion Act, 1947, for permission to sue his tenant in ejectment. The Commissioner granted the permission on the ground that the permission had been refused by him without notice to the respondent. The respondent thereupon moved the Commissioner under section 6 of the Act for a decree for damages. The appellant contended that the application was bad for non joinder of necessary parties, and that the Commissioner had no jurisdiction to consider whether the permission granted by the Commissioner was valid or not. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court held that the appellant 's suit was incompetent. In appeal to this Court it was contended that section 3 (4) Of Act 1 of 1947 did not expressly exclude the jurisdiction of the civil courts, and as such the bar created by the relevant provisions of the said Act excluding the jurisdiction conferred by section 3 of the Bengal Act 1 Of 1947 could not operate in cases where the plea raised before the civil court went to the root of the matter and would, if upheld, lead to the conclusion that the impugned order was a nullity. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that the special statute did not intend to confer wide jurisdiction on the Commissioner by section 7 F of the Calcutta Act 1of 1947. [560 C] (ii)The words "any person" occurring in section 3 Of the Act refer to persons who are not a District Magistrate, and in the context, the inference that the civil Courts ' jurisdiction is intended to be excluded appears to be inescapable. The fact that the legislature has used the word "person" in its widest sense does not mean that the plea against the validity of the order passed by the District Magistrate or the Commissioner or the State Government can never be raised in a civil court. [561 F G] (iii)The High Court had no doubt that under section 7 H, the Commissioner could deal not only with the legality but also with the correctness and propriety of the orders passed by him. The order passed in violation of the principles of natural justice was therefore a nullity and the High Courts were justified in introducing a limitation pertaining to questions of jurisdiction in determining the scope of the width of the revisional power conferred on the commissioner by section 2 Of the West Bengal Alluldars and Dilvorion Act 1, 1949.

The appellant, a member of the Punjab Public Service Commission, physically assaulted her and threatened her that she would be favoured in those examinations. The Chief Minister of Punjab wrote to the Attorney General of India that the evidence should be allowed to be led only on the question whether the incident was proved or not. The Attorney General stated before the Court that the matter had been referred to him for consideration by a Committee consisting of three members, namely, Shri A.K. Sen, Shri Gopal Krishan Saini and Shri Gopal Krishna, who were members of the State Public Service Com mission. The Committee considered the report and came to the conclusion that a case was made out for obtaining a report from this Court on the questions of alleged misbehaviour or incapacity of one of the members of Punjab Public Services Commission. The matter was referred to the President of India under Article 317(1) of the Constitution. The President, however, did not agree with the report. The appellant filed an application before the High Court for quashing the reference on the ground that the President should have obtained the opinion of a fact finding body for his prima facie satisfaction that a criminal case had been made out against him and that he was guilty of misconduct and that the allegations made against him were proved at all. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the report of the Commission would automatically decide the fate of a prosecution or of a civil suit for damages. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the reference under Article 318(1), is not subject to the condition precedent laid down in article 317(2); (2) the report made by the President under Article 316(3) is not binding upon the President; and (3) the complaint should have been filed within three years of the date of the reference. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power of the President to make a reference to this court under article 317 (1), in regard to the allegations of misbehaviour is not specifically incorporated in the nature of condition precedent. It will have to be read in the latter order in order to enable this Court to pass proper orders in the interest of justice. [646C D] 2. The purpose of Article 317 (I) is to ensure that the person concerned is guilty of misbehaviour and if he is called upon to meet the allegation, he should not be removed from his office on that ground. [643D E] 3. The word "person" in article 318(3), which is not expressly incorporated in clause (a) of Article 145, means a person who has not filed an affidavit in this Court and indeed, section 146(3). [644E F] 4. The expression "the Chairman or any other member of a Public Service" in clause(c) of article 317 is not specific to the facts of the case but the allegations cannot be adjudicated upon on a consideration of the affidavits only. [641A B] 5. Article 317 provides that an inquiry has to be held by this Court in accordance with the procedure prescribed under that behalf under that Article. The procedure which this Court will have, is plainly not to be found in it, especially when the Court is called complaint against a person on the basis of allegations made in the petition. [651C D; F] 6. The Court has the power to summon witnesses and record their evidence. It is not necessary that the Court should record such evidence as it considers necessary or convenient. [661D] 7. The argument that the word "Person" in Article 317 is specifically incorporated by the Constitution with the limited powers of determining whether the facts found by some other body establish misconduct in one case and that this Court has no power to appoint any responsible delegate for doing so, cannot be accepted. [678E F; 671A] 8. The question whether a person is guilty or not is left open to be decided on consideration of all the relevant evidence.

The appellants, who were the deity installed in the temple, claimed to be the members of a family deity. The suit was decreed by the trial court and the High Court on appeal affirmed the decree. In this appeal it was contended that the temple was a public endowment within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Orissa Hindu Religious Endowment Act, 1939 (Act 4 of 1939), which provides for the establishment of a public temple and a trust and the endowment was held to be of a private nature and therefore the deity was not a public one. The High Court rejected this contention. In appeal to this Court it was urged that the endowment being a public trust, fell within the four corners of the Act and the respondent was fully entitled to pass orders for its management. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The temple is a public institution which has been established for the worship of a community idol in which the public are not interested. It is a private one. [833 B] (2) The question whether a religious endowment is of a purely private character or of a religious nature must depend on the facts and circumstances of each case. [ 834 C D] (3) The essential distinction between a private and a public purpose is that whereas in the former the beneficiaries are specified individuals, in the latter they are the general public or class of persons. In the latter it is not the primary object of the founder to create a family idol. [853 E F] (4) The mere fact that members of the public were allowed to worship by itself would not make an endowment a public or a private endowment. [851 C D, 832 A B] Mahant Ram Saroop Dasji vs S.P. Das, ; , referred to. (5) The High Courts have not properly construed some of the important features contained in the documents and the evidence and have given a clear indication of the fact that the dedication was of a charitable nature. [852 E F; 833 A] (6) The existence of a temple is not necessarily a condition precedent to the establishment or its user. It may be a circumstance where the evidence shows that there is provision for a scheme to be framed by associating the members with the public at large, but the mere fact of worship would not determine the nature of the endowment.

The appellant Bank was working as a contractor to the military and other authorities. The contract provided that all powers hereby granted were and shall be irrevocable as long as any claims of the attorneys against the bills for supplies under the contracts were made or to be made hereafter. The appellant bank then executed an irrevocable power of attorney in favour of the appellant on July 13, 1946. On July 19, 1948, the power of Attorney was revoked by the appellant and the appellant filed objections to the execution proceedings. The objections were dismissed by the trial court but on appeal the High Court allowed the appeal holding that there was no transfer of the decree or of the claim of the Attorneys against him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Bank that the power to finance the borrower and a power of agreement to receive payment of loans was not an equitable assignment of the funds by way of security and as such the power could not be transferred under section 130 of the Transfer of Property Act. HELD: The power of the agent coupled with endorsement on the bill dated July 19. 1948 was a clear engagement by Malhotra to pay the appellant Bank out of the monies receivable under the bill and amounted to an equitable assignmen of the fund by way off security. [777 D] Palmer vs Carey, , referred to. In the instant case the power conferred upon the agent to receive all monies due or to become due to Malhotra in respect of pending or future contracts with the government authorities.

The respondent was the manager of a Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s. Gillanders Arbuthnot & Co. Ltd., and had a Provident Fund scheme for its employees. The Income tax Officer assessed this amount as the assessee 's income from other sources. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that the receipt in question being profits in lieu of salary was assessable under section 15 and the same having not been assessed as his salary, the same had to be taxed under section 56. In appeal by the respondent, the Tribunal referred the following question for the opinion of the High Court: "Whether on the facts and circumstances of the case and having regard to the provisions of section 17(3) (ii) of the Income tax Act, 1961, the amount Rs. 27,948/ representing the interest on the amount of his own contribution to an unrecognised provident fund was assessable as a business income under section 14 of the Act?" The High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee and against the Revenue. In this appeal by certificate it was contended for the appellant that the receipts in question were profits in the nature of salary and not income from house property; that the amount was exempt from payment of tax in view of section 1.16(ii) (iii). HELD: The receipt of Rs.27,948 by the assessee in the relevant accounting year cannot be considered as salary though undoubtedly that is an income. Section 17(1)(iv) provides that income of every kind which is not to be excluded from the total income under the Act shall be chargeable to income tax under the head "income from other source" if it is not chargeable to incometax under any of the heads specified in section 1,4 items 'A ' to 'E '. In defining the expression "Profits in lieu Of salary", the legislature excluded from its scope the receipt of an interest on any investment and the amount received by the asses see from house pro perty; profits and gains of business or profession or capital gains. It has to be considered a "income" from other income" and brought to tax under section 12(1) (iv).
