The petitioners, who were buffaloes and female adults of a village, challenged the validity of the Bihar Act on the ground that it infringed their fundamental rights under article 19 (1) (g) and was, therefore, void. The Act provided for the regulation of slaughter of all animals belonging to the species of bovine cattle and the imposition of such restrictions on the exercise of the right conferred by article 19(i)(g). Held, that the impugned Acts were valid in so far as they prohibited the slaughter of the buffaloes and the provisions of the Act prohibiting the slaughter Of the buffaloes, breeding bulls and working bullocks (male or female) did not contravene article 19. The Bihar Act was constitutionally valid in respect of the same matter. The provisions of section 3(1)(a) and (b) of the impugned Act were not ultra vires the State Legislature as they infringed their right to carry on their occupation, trade or business guaranteed by article 301 of the Constitution. The impugned Acts did not infringe the fundamental rights of the petitioners under article 14 Of the Constitution and were therefore void. It was not possible to apply the doctrine of severability and uphold the ban on the slaughter even though it was imposed in a manner which would prevent the slaughter, of the animals. The State of Bombay vs R. M. D. Chamarbaugwala, [1957] S.C.R. 930, relied on. The Madhya Pradesh Act, as it stood at the relevant time, did not place any total ban on slaughter of buffaloes and was therefore void under article 13 Of the Con stitution. The entire provision banning the slaughter could not be struck down on the grounds that it imposed a total ban in respect Of the slaughter animals of all ages and calves of cows and cals of buffaloes. The petitioners were not entitled to any relief under article 32 of the Constitu tion as they had been deprived of their fundamental right under article 31(1) of their Constitution.

The respondent joined the service of the Company as a typist on a salary of Rs. 30 per month in July 1936. He was later promoted to the post of Deputy Manager and by an order dated January 31, 1956 he was informed that his services would be terminated as from December 5, 1955. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the said orders on the ground that the Standing Orders did not apply to him as he had no right to move the High Court for appropriate orders under article 32 of the Constitu tion and that the Industrial Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the applications. Held, that the respondent was not an employee within the meaning of the Standing Order No. 18 and his case must be governed by Standing Orders No. 2(a) and (b). The Standing Orders in question were not repugnant to the Standing order No. 1 and therefore could not prevail over the Standing orders No. 3 and 30 of 1946. The Standing Order no doubt provided that every workman, permanent or temporary, shall have a ticket or card, and an apprentice shall have an apprentice card; but this was not the essential characteristic of an employee as defined for the Standing Rules. The relevant Standing Orders were not objected to as being defective or incomplete by workmen and they had been approved by the appropriate authority and they must be construed with reference to their subject or context. Held further, that in view of the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the Standing Counsel for the respondent could not have contended that the standing orders applied to him. The definition clause " workman" in Standing Order NO. 2 (a) was employed in the office, Mains Department, eta., of the company either at Nagpur or at Nagpur and that of a workman the necessary declaration by the Company which would entitle him to a ticket under Standing Order 18 was not necessary.

The appellant company was an undertaking owned, controlled and managed by a Government Company. The workmen of the respondent company claimed bonus at the minimum rate prescribed under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965. The claim was resisted by the company on the ground that all profit was earned in the year 1964 65 and that the workmen were not entitled to any bonus. The Tribunal held that Alloy Steel Project was a separate establishment in respect of which separate balance sheets and profit and loss accounts were maintained for each separate undertaking and separate profit and Loss accounts were prepared only for the purpose of complying with the requirements of the companies Act, but that the proviso to section 3 Of the Act would not apply in such a case. The company appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD: (i) The Tribunal was wrong in holding that simply because Alloy steel Project is owned, it has to be treated as a separate Establishment and available surplus is calculated separately for each unit. [633 A] (ii) The proviso to sub section (2) of section 16 only comes in the way it bonus is paid in any year to the employees of all the units on the basis of consolidated profits of all such units. That has never been done in the case of the Hindustan Steel Ltd., and therefore, the Alloy ' Project should have been treated as separate establishment newly set up in the years in which the goods produced or manufactured are sold for the first time and, in the alternative, upto the year when the new establishment results in profit, whichever is earlier. [625 B C] (iii) The expression "establishment" in section 3 of the Act means a place established by an existing establishment. It cannot be said that the word "establishment " is intended to indicate something different from a company as defined in the . In the present case, there was no evidence that in any particular year after Alloy II was treated as an establishment newly setting up for purposes of section 3(1) the exemption claimed would be fully justified. [533 C D] (iv) The contention that the Alloys Project is a separate unit is not correct because the word 'establishment ' is used to indicate some kind of establishment, and therefore an establishment cannot be treated differently from a factory as defined by section 3. [643 E F] (v) The fact that the appellant company had a number of undertakings, undertakings or branches of the establishment of a company, would not make any difference because there was very clear evidence that though the Company, Hindustan Steel Limited, had a large number of Undertakings, separate accounts were kept for each distinct accounting year. [641 A B] (vi) The appellant company could not be equated with any one of these units. It is well settled that in the matter of taxation a separate department is created by the existing establishments of the company and the exemption under section 16(1). would be available to it. [651 C D, F G] (vii) The question whether the Ally Steel Project is an establishment or not has to depend on the nature of the work done by the employees in a particular industry. It may be that the establishment is not in the same industry for purposes other than those of its own. But it would be wrong to say that there was a unity of opinion between the two units undertakings or their separate accounts.

The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 was enacted by Parliament to control the pollution of rivers and streams which has assumed considerable importance and urgency in recent years. The Act provides for the establishment of a Central Board by the Central Government and State Governments to provide funds to the Central Boards for effective discharge of water pollution. Section 3 of the Act provides that no person shall, except as expressly provided in this Act, carry on any specified industry within the meaning of the expression "to undertake or undertake to be discharged into the water coarses without adequate treatment". The Cess Act is a fiscal enactment and is levied on persons carrying on the industries specified in the Schedule. The cess is payable by every person carrying on any particular industry and every local authority and is calculated on the basis of water consumed by such person or local authorities as the case may be for any of the purposes specified in column 1 of Schedule II to the Cess Act, at such rate not exceeding the rates specified in that column. The Cess is levied from the date of commencement of the cess. The petitioners in these appeals are sugar factories and sugar factories which have been manufacturing sugar on the specified dates. They also claim exemption from payment of cess under the Cess act. The Punjab & Haryana High Court held that sugar manufacturing industry would come within Entry 15 of Schedule I to the Act and that sugar factory would come under Entry 15 as "processing vegetable products industry". On appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellants that sugar factories would fall under Entry No. 15 of schedule I to The Cess act and that the cess and collection of cess provided under the cess Act is on water consumed in a kitchen garden or shop and are used for the table. It was further submitted that sugar industry would fall within Entry No, 15 of the Schedule I as processing of animal feed is an activity which falls within Entry 5 of Schedule 1 to the cess act. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The levy and collection are not in any way concerned with the manufacture of sugar. [530D] 2.1 The Cess was a fiscal statute. In the context in which the word 'vegetable ' is used in Entry 15 'vege Sabha industry. The process of subjecting ' goods to a particu larity for a long period of time as in cold storage amounts to processing of goods. [525F] 2:2. It is not possible to conclude sugar cane as vegetable. The word 'processing ' has been used in the context of trade and commerce. The term 'veg etable ' has, therefore, to be understood in common parlance and it must be given its popular sense meaning thereby all that belongs to the world of plants would come. [500F G] 2 :3. It cannot be said that sugar cane is not a vegetable although it may be an agricultural product.

The respondent, an Advocate, filed an application before the Rent Controller seeking eviction of the appellant from the premises in question on the ground that he required the premises for the purpose of carrying on his profession as an advocate. The application was contested by the appellant who contended that the practice of the profession of an advocate was not business within the meaning of Section 10(3) (a)(iii) and, therefore, the respondent could not seek the eviction of his tenant on the grounds that he requires the premises bona fide for the purposes of carrying out his profession. The Rent Controller held that the respondent bona fide required the suit premises for carrying on the profession as a advocate and that the tenancy was not such as could be split up. The Appellate Authority, however, dismissed the appeal. In revision, the High Court affirmed the order of the Rent Control Tribunal. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: 1. The expression business occurring in Section 10 (3)(a)(i) is used in a wide sense so as to include the practice or the profession which not confined to any classes of tenants nor is the right to evict under the Act limited to any class of landlords. There is no reason why a landlord who is a member of the legal or medical professions and who requires the same for carrying out the profession should be wholly debarred from obtaining possession of the premises. It is impossible to discover any reason for so making a discrimination against the liberal professions. But that would be the result if the expression 'business ' is given a narrow meaning which the appellant wants us to give to that expression. [14 C E] 2. The word business occurring under section 10(1) (c) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960 means everything that occupies the time attention and labour of men for the pur pose of livorce or profit. In a broad sense it is confined to commercial activity. It does not throw any light on the manner in which the term should be understood generally. [15 D E] 3.

The respondent was a creditor of M/s. India Supplies, and the appellant filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of Rs. 4,11,367.92P on the ground that it had advanced a sum of Rs 4,00,000 to the appellant and that the respondent had no concern with the business of the appellant. The trial court decreed the suit in favour of the respondent but the High Court dismissed the suit. In appeal by certificate to this Court, HELD: (1) The money was deposited with the appellant under an agreement that the same would be paid on demand. The transaction was between the appellant, the respondent and Lakshmi Ratan Cotton Mills. All figured in the transaction. A much larger loan of Rs., 4,000 would not have sufficed the needs of the appellants who were then unable to pay the dues of Lakshmi Ratan cotton Mills. Some of the partners of the firm were common. It would be more consistent to hold that by allowing India Supplies a deposit of Rs, 4,0,000 was relieved of the situation of repaying the money immediately. It is precisely because of the then inability of India Supplies to repay the money soon. It was precisely because the respondent demanded the money by a letter dated 27th April 1953 (exhibit 7) totally denied the claim. The respondent set out all the facts of deposit of the money with advancing loan. The non production of the account coupled with the appellants staying away from the witness box indicates the inherent infirmities in the appellant 's case. [578 D E] Nawab Major Sir Mohammad Akbar Khan vs Attar Singh & Ors., ; , referred to. (2) When the respondent asked the appellant to deposit money by the letter dated 29th September, 1942 (ex exhibit 7), the appellant in their reply stated that the account books were prepared for the purpose of showing the transaction, namely whether it was a case of deposit or loan. [580 E F] (3) The High Court was correct in decreeing the suit and dismissing the suit on the grounds that there was no unqualified demand for the whole sum before the limitation could star in case of demand for return of the amount deposited.

The petitioner was detained by an order of the Additional Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Home Affairs, dated February 28, 1986 under section 3(1) of the , with a view to preventing him from dealing in smuggled goods otherwise than by engaging in transporting or concealing or keeping smuggled goods. The petitioner challenged his detention on various grounds including that he was already in custody at the time of the order of detention and was therefore entitled to be freed from the detention. Dismissing the writ petition, HELD: 1.1 The fact that the detenu is in jail is not taken away by the order chooses to file a habeas corpus petition under Article 32 of the Constitution. [849F] 1.2 In the instant case, the detaining authority was aware of the fact that he had been called upon to attend office by the authorities concerned and that he would be informed accordingly. It would not take away the jurisdiction of the detaining au thority in making an order for detention. What is necessary in a case of that type is to satisfy the court when detention is challenged on that ground that the detaining author ity was aware that the petitioner was already involved in smuggling goods otherwise he would thereby be prevented from acting in a manner prejudicial to the security of the State. [850E G] 1:3 In the present case, there is no force in the contention that the order was not in existence. Once the summons is not in terms of the circumstances emerging in the pleadings, it cannot be said that there was prejudice to the detenu on account of the authority 's withholding the summons. [851B C] 1 :4 The fact of the detenu being in custody when the order is made, yet he was satisfied that his preventive detention was necessary. In the facts and circumstances of the present ease, there was sufficient material to show that the detain ing authority was unaware of the facts that the peti tioner was already under trial and yet he had not been detained. [852C D] 2.1 There is no substance in the argument that the detention order could only be justified against a person in detention if the detaining autho rity was satisfied of the existence of the particular case, and that it would not detract from the order being passed for preventive detention. [853E F] 2:2 In view of the specific material to support the contention of the petitioner that he is already in detention, the detention of the peti tions is illegal and the provisions of section 61 of the Code of Criminal Procedure will be applicable. That section provides that every summons issued by a Court under this Code shall be in writing.

The petitioners were working as casual labourers in the Posts and Telegraphs Department. They were not being paid wages far less than the minimum pay payable under the regular cadres of the posts and to direct the Union of India to regularise them regularly in its service and consequently they have been denied the benefits of the scheme. The petitioners contended that since the petitioners belong to the category of casual labour, the wages paid to them are very low and far less. They relied on the decision of this Court in Dhirendra Chamoli and Another vs State of U.P., ; , which held that the benefit amounts to exploitation of labour. The respondents contested the writ petitions contending that since they belonged to the categories of unskilled/skilled skilled casual labourers, they are not entitled to the same privileges which the regular employees were enjoying. The Court allowed the writ petition and directed the Union to pay them wages to the petitioners. The Union of the petitioners contended before this Court that since their case is covered by the decision in Dhirendra Chmoli & Another vs state of U P., this Court may be relied upon by the petitioners to show that in the instant case they have not been regularly recruited but many of them have been working continuously for more than a year in the Department and some of them had been engaged as casual labour for nearly ten years. Allowing the writ Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The classification of employees into unskilled/semi skilled/swounders is arbitrary and violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. It is also opposed to the spirit of Article 7 of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, 1966 which states that "the State shall, in particular, strive to minimise the inequalities in income, and endeavour to eliminate inequalities in status, facilities and opportunities not only amongst individuals but also amongst groups of people residing in different areas or engaged in different vacations". The further classification of casual labourers into three categories namely (i) those who have not completed 720 days of service; (ii) those working continuously beyond the prescribed strength of the cadre workers; and (iii) those, who have completed more than 1200 days of serv ice. [606C D] 2.1 It is a socialist republic that it implies the existence of certain important obligations which the State has to discharge. The right to work, the right to free choice of employment, the Right to just and favourable conditions of work, and the right of every one without discrimination of any kind to equal pay for equal work, are some of the rights which have to be ensured by appropriate legislative and executive measures. It was true that all these rights cannot be extended simultaneously. But they do indicate the socialist goal.

The assessee, a partner of an assessee firm, was assessed to tax on the income of his wife. The Income Tax Officer included the sum of Rs. 59,026 in the total income of the assessee and assessed it accordingly. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the notice under section 34(1) of the Act was invalid as it was issued after the assessee had filed a voluntary return on January 5, 1950, and that the assessment was valid in law. The Tribunal however rejected the contention of the appellant that since he had submitted a return under section 22(3), his failure to file a return within the time allowed by the notice did not amount to an "undertaking" within the meaning of cl. (c) of sub s.(1) and therefore, the best judgment assessment was bad. The High Court held that it was a voluntary returns showing a non taxable income and that it could not be treated as a return filed under section 24(3). In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The notice under s.23(2) of Act was only necessary if at the end of the assessment year no return had been made by the assesee, and the Income Tax officer could have avoided the result by issuing a notice under that section. [1194 A B] (ii)The notice under S.24(1), whether filed within the prescribed time or not, was valid. The words "has been issued" in cl. 2 of section 28, as it stood prior to its amendment in 1953, meant that the return must be submitted by the assesses before March 31, 1950. [118 C D] (iii)The word "has" in the context means "has a return in answer to a notice u/s 22(2). If a return of income below the taxable limit is a good return in answering a notice unders.22(1)(a), it would show an assessable income. [122 E F] (iv)The words "is required to make a return" in section 24, whether filed before or after March 31. 1950, are not words at all in the Act. The word " has been used in the sense of "has still a good". Therefore, it is futile for a person who has no such income need not make a declaration under section 23(2), and to bring the matter within the purview of cl.(c) Of sub s (1) Of section 28. [123 E F; 124 A B]. Harakchand Makanji & Co. vs Commissioner of Income tax, , referred to.

The first petitioner, a registered Central Trade Union, filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the circular dated 23.8.1982 (Annexure A) issued by the Joint Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Economic Affairs (Banking Division), New Delhi. The second petitioner, an employee of the first respondent Bank, was appointed as a member of the staff union of the nationalised banks. He was also a member in the Nationalised Banks. He challenged the circular on the ground that it violated the provisions of the Act and the Scheme insofar as it cuts at the root of the representative form of selection for appointment to the Board of Directors as contemplated by the statute. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the object of the circular is to neutralise and dis criminate the interests of the various categories of persons mentioned in the Act. Allowing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1.1 The object of section 9 of the is to give the Board a truly representative character so as to reflect the genuine interests of its various persons manning or dealing with the bank as an industry and a commercial enterprise. [857C] 1.2 The object is to provide for appointment of a person from out of the panel of three names furnished by the representative Union of workmen or Association of non workmen, as the case may be, would not be a perfect representation in keeping with the principle of election. That may or may not be so, and there is always room for improvements; but the petitioners have no complaint on that score. If the Central Government were to provide by a scheme to improve on the machinery for the conduct of an appropriate election, it is incumbent upon it, until any such amend ment is made, to work the present Scheme in such a way as to give maximum scope for the concerned employees to exer cise their choice in the selection of their representatives. That means, it would be perfectly in order for the Central Govern ment to continue the practice followed by it prior to the circular in question or to hold election of the repre sentatives of the concerned employee and, if necessary, to amend the Scheme suitably for that purpose. [862E G] 1:3 The transfer cases are accordingly disposed of.

The respondent was imposed penalties under section 271(1)(c) read with section 274(2) of the Income tax Act, 1961. The Appellate Tribunal declined to grant such a prayer and held that it had no power to stay proceedings relating to recovery of penalty or tax due from an assessee. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) The power to pass an order under section 255(1) of Income tax is not likely to be exercised in a routine way or as a matter of course in view when an appeal is pending before the Appellate Tribunal. It could well be said that when section 254 confers appellate jurisdiction it impliedly grants the power of doing all such acts, or employing such means, as are essentially necessary to its execution and that the statutory power carries with it the duty in proper cases to make such orders for staying proceedings as will prevent the appeal if successful from being rendered nugatory. A certain apprehension may legitimately arise in the minds of the authorities administering the Act that if the Appellate Tribunals proceed to stay recovery of taxes or penalties payable by or imposed on the assessees as a matters of course the revenue will be put to great loss because of the inordinate delay in the disposal of appeals by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. [68D E] (ii) The Appellate 'Tribunal must be held to have the power to grant stay as incidental or ancillary to its appellate jurisdiction. This is particularly so when section 220(6) deals expressly with a situation when an Appeal is pending.

The respondent was a constable in the U. P. Police Force and on his return to the service of the police station, he was charged under section 7 of the Police Act with remissness in the discharge of his duty and unfitness for the same inasmuch as while posted as a Station Officer he had been guilty of dishonesty, corruption and misbehaviour in that he had on nine occasions, particulars of which were given in the charge sheet. The trial was conducted by the Superintendent of Police and the respondent was found guilty of mis conduct. He was charged with remisness in discharge of duty and partly for misconduct and was therefore liable to be dismissed from service. On appeal, the Deputy Inspector General of Police cancelled the respondent 's dismissal order on the ground that he was not a habitual bribetaker but was due to his illness. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court of Allahabad for quashing the order of dismissal and for a writ of certiorari quashing the said order. The High Court held that the respondent had committed an offence under section 5(1) (d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and therefore sub para. (1) of para. 486 of the Rules made by the Inspector General amounted to a mere irregularity in the matter of the departmental trial and quashed the order. On the question whether the High court was competent to quash the order under article 227 of the constitution. Held, that the High Courts were right in holding that the departmental enquiry was only a further step in respect of the misconduct of the respondent in regard whereof he had no jurisdiction to proceed with a departmental trial without complying with the provisions of sub para (1). The State of U.P. vs Babu Ram Upadhya, ; , followed.

The appellant was appointed to the post of a Professor in the Medical Department of Health. He was promoted as Assistant Surgeon in July, 1978 and on being selected by the Departmental Promotion Committee he was promoted to supertime grade II. The promotion of respondents 4 to 24 was challenged by the appellant before the High Court by way of a Writ Petition. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the promotions were in contravention of rule 8 of 1966 Rules. It also held that the promotion of respondent 4 to 25 was in contravention thereof and therefore, invalid. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellant being conscious of this position tried to circumvent it by saying that he would be benefited even if his contention were to prevail. It is implicit in this arrangement that the person to be appointed to such a post would be one who is eligible to be promoted and not some one who was on top of the general seniority list in Specialists ' grade or general duty officers ' grade from which promotion is to be made. [53E] 1.2 The appellant was promoted by way off the promotion in the absence of any allegation that he had put in 8 years of service in the category of specialists ' post. He could not therefore be discriminated against because he was conscious of the position that when a post from amongst unspecified Specialists was converted into a specified post, it can only be filled by promotion and not otherwise. [54F] 1:3 The appellant having been promoted to the supertime scale in excess of what is prescribed for the Specialists, his contention that he should be considered eligible for promotion to super time grade II because he had not put in eight years of serv ice in those grades cannot be accepted. It was not correct to say that whenever unspecified specialists were promoted to Supertime grade 11 from departmental candidates could be promoted to that post and the post so vacated by him can be filled in either by promotion or by direct recruitment as the situation warrants according to the rule and as determined by the quota rule. But it was very much intended that a Specialists should become eligible for promo tion after he rendered 10 years of Service in that category which came into existence on September 9, 1966.

The object of the Act was to provide for the abolition of surplus area and to make the twin objects successful and so far as land owned by an heir is concerned, he was given a right to retain the surplus area for the resettlement of tenants ejected or to be ejected under cl. (i) sub section (1) of section 9 of the Punjab Security Of Land Tenures Rules, 1953. The Act provided that such decrees and orders of courts were to be ignored in computing the surplus areas. Section 19B provides that where a person acquires any land by inheritance or bequest or gift which, with the lands already held by him exceeds in the aggregate the permissible area, then he shall within the period prescribed, furnish to the Collector a return indicating the permissible areas he desires to retain. The appellant who owned some bighas and 9 biswas of land, acting through his mother, filed a suit for possession and permanent injunction restraining the respondent from interfering with the surplus lands. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in appeal reversed that decision holding that section 19B did not affect the petitioner 's rights. The appellants were the sons of one B and his brother. The estate was impartible in favour of B, who died issueless on December 3, 1950. The appellants claimed that the property in suit originally belonged to B and the family of B was entitled to succeed to the estate devised in their favour by the rule of primogeniture and Pratapshah. The claim was contested by the respondents on the ground that the father Thakur was a Hindu and as such he was entitled only to the properties mentioned in the schedule annexed to the plaint, and that the adoption of B in 1951 was not genuine and the adoption was valid. The trial court held that the appellants were entitled to receive compensation in respect of Malguzari lands and the decision of the Compensation Officer did not operate as res judicata. On appeal by the appellants the High Court confirmed the decree passed by the Trial Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The rule of lineal primogenogeniture furnishes a ground of preference. It is enacted with a view to put an end to disputes with regard to the claims to proprietary rights which by virtue of the notification issued under section 3 of the Act are extinguished. It was not intended by an Order under section 14 to determine complicated questions of title by the adjudication of a revenue officer in a summary inquiry without even a right of appeal and to make his adjudication conclusive unless a suit be filed within two months from the date of the order. That is also clear from the terms of section 35(7) of Act 1 of 1951 which provides that the payment of compensation under this Act to the creditors of a proprietor or to the proprietor in accordance with the prescribed manner shall be a full discharge of the State Government from all liability to pay compensation for the divesting of proprietary rights, but shall not prejudice any rights in respect Of the said rights to which any other person may be entitled by due process of law to enforce against the person to whom compensation has been paid as aforesaid. [337 B C] (ii) The High Court was in error in not reducing the amount of mesne profits awarded under section 15 of Act I of 1951. Section 14 is intended to determine only the proprietary rights in the land, qua the State. It does not invest the Compensation officer with jurisdiction to determine competing claims of persons claiming proprietary rights to the property vesting in the Government by the operation of section 3. [340 G H] (iii) The order of the compensation Officer under section 1(1) of the , is in the form of a memorandum addressed to the Deputy Commissioner, Chanda, and it states that "Government are pleased to recognise the estate as such in favour by virtue Of the powers conferred on them by section 3". [340 B] (iv) The provisions of section 14 of Act II of 1951 do not invest Government with jurisdiction under section 30(7). Section 14 of the is intended only to determine the proprietary right in the property, qua State. When a holder of the Zamindari is removed from office he is bound to hand over the Zamindari to the next heir in the order of succession if the Zamindar removed had died and the heir will get the right. [341 B C; 341 E] (v) The word "vest" in section 14 means actual physical possession of the property which may be taken under the general Hindu law, but it does not mean actual physical posses sion of the land or the transfer of the interest in the estate to the holder of a right. The expression "vestes" is used in section 3 to include all persons who are loyal or do not manage the property or do any act contrary to the rules of Hindu Law and the custom of the family.

The appellants filed a suit for recovery of possession of the premises on the ground that they were in arrears of rent from 1 September, 1964 and also on the grounds that the respondent landlord had failed to pay rent. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the appellants were in default as they did not comply with the provisions of section 12(3) (a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that the provisions contained in section 12 (3))(a) and (b) of Act 19 of 1947 are applicable to the suit; that the suit was governed by the provisions in section 11(4) (c) of Bombay Rents. Hotel and lodging House Rates (Control) Act,1947; that there was no dispute as to rent within one month of the service of notice under section 12 of the Act; that in any event the period of one month had expired on 1st December, 1964; that a notice terminating the tenancy was issued by the appellants on 18th April, 1963 and therefore there was a dispute as regards standard rent or permitted increases. HELD: (i) The High Court has not agreed with the view of the Gujarat High Court in Ambalal 's case. [637 B] Dattu Subha Subha vs Gajanan Vithoba Bobhate & Anr., ; and Chunilal Shivlal vs Chimanlal Nagindas, ; , referred to. (ii) The provisions in Section 11(3)(a), (b), (c), (d) and Explanation I of section 11 of the Rent Act deal with orders which may be passed by the Court during the pendency of the application disputing the rent. Provisions in section II(4), however, deal with applications for fixation of standard rent.

The respondent company was a subsidiary of the Aluminium Ltd. The Aluminium Ltd., a company incorporated in Canada, held a controlling interest in it as contemplated by section 2(21) of the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940, and its share capital was reduced to Rs. 10 per cent. In exercise of the power given to it by article 105 of the articles of association of the respondent company, the Aluminium Company appointed three permanent directors on the board of directors of the Respondent company. The appellant company paid the controlling interest to the Aluminium company at the rate of 1/2 per cent per annum and thereafter the shares held by the Aluminium Limited were allotted to the respondent. The respondent company filed a petition in the High Court under section 21 Of the Excess profits Tax Act for the assessment year 1949 to income tax for five chargeable accounting periods ending on December 31, 1941, and December 31 , 1942, and claimed that it should be regarded as a subsidiary. The Income tax Officer held that the directors of respondent company had a controlling interests in it and therefore the directors had a control over its affairs at general meetings and as such could control the affairs of the company and that in computing the standard profits the statutory percentage should be taken at 10 per annum, but not at 8 per cent on the company 's shares. The Appellate Tribunal held that in view of the powers conferred by section 21 of the Act read with section 66(1) of Indian Income tax Act, 1922, it was not open to the appellant to hold that the Directors had a majority of shares which on the contrary were registered in the name of the aluminium Ltd., and therefore could control its affairs. The High Court also held that though the directors did not themselves hold the majority of the shares they could control their affairs at the general meetings, as such they could not be said to have "a controlling interest" in the respondent Company. Held, that the decision of the High court was correct and must be affirmed. The decisions of the Bombay High Court in British American Tobacco Co. Ltd. vs Commissioners of Inland Revenue, , and Commissioner of Income tax vs Bipin Silk Mills Ltd., ; , applied.

The respondent was working as an Accountant in the Electricity Department of the former State of Hyderabad. On 1st October, 1957 he was allotted to the new State of Mysore with effect from 1st November 1956. The post which he held came to be equated with that of I Division Clerk in the former state of Mysore. On 30th December 1966, some persons junior to him were promoted as Assistant Accounts Officers on their having passed Part I and II of the S.A.S. examination while promotion was denied to them as they had not passed the examination. The respondent made several representations one such representation being on 24th December, 1970, but the same was rejected by the Board on 21st November, 1972. On 21st December, 1972, the respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court which allowed the writ petition and directed the appellant to consider his case of promotion as an Accounts Superin tendent as on 30th Decem ber, 1966. The Division Bench held that the writ was not thrown out on the ground of inordinate delay and laches on the part of the respondent and also on the grounds that in view of the later Resolution dated 5th January, 1970 it was no longer open to the respondent to rely on the Resolution dated 19th May, 1969. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the High Courts decision in the case of Karnataka Electrici ty Board vs The Karnataka Electricity Board, ; , did not affect the earlier decision and that in any event the plea of the respon dent that the allottees were exempted from passing the Departmental Examination before qualifying for promotion was not justified. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High Court rightly held that in the circumstances of the case the relief to the respond ent should not be denied on the basis of delay and belated approach. [511B] 1.2 In any event, the plea regarding the allottees and is not made applicable to them. It is not possible to infer from the Resolution that the allot ment was exempted from pass ing the Departmental Examinations before qualifying the examination and the language test. The resolution was passed by the respondent in pursuance of certain proceedings of the Government referred to in the Resolution itself. Paragraph 2 of the Resolution clearly states that unless in the Recruitment Rules relating to the service concerned Depart mental Examination had been incorporated and prescribed and unless it is clearly specified for what purpose the tests are prescribed viz., whether for increments or promotions, the passing of Departmental tests cannot be legally insist ed upon for grant of increments or for according promotion to higher posts. The three Government orders make it clear that the relaxation of the rule relating to passing of the Departmental examina tion was not relaxed by amending the Regulations. [512C E] 2.1 In any case, the contention of the re spondent that the allotment in question was exempted under the Rules cannot be accepted.

The petitioner 's son, who was a resident of the State of Orissa, was taken into custody and kept in the police custody. The petitioner 'son was arrested on January 1, 1987 by respondent No.6, a Superintendent of Police, who had been taken into police custody on February 2, 1987. On the basis of a complaint lodged by his son, the District Judge, Sunder Nagar, under Section theft and detained him for about 22 years. The State Government in Orissa, after considering the report of the District Magistrate, reduced the compensation to Rs.1,50,000. The High Court dismissed the petition filed by the petitioner under Article 32 of the Constitution. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) the liability of the respondent for the safety of his son was not limited to a sum of Rs. 1,50 lakhs; (ii) the State Government had acted in breach of fundamental rights to life guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitu tion and (iii) the compensation awarded by the High Court to the petitioner for violation of fundamental right to life under Article 22(2) of the Consti tution was not correct. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The State 's plea of sovereign immunity for tortious acts of its servants is confined to the sphere of liability in tort, which is distinct from the State 'Small death '. [608C] 1.2 In the instant case, on the finding reached, it was a clear case for award of compensation to the peti tioner for deprivation of his fundamental right under Article 31 of the Con stitution. The payment of compensation in such cases is not to be understood as it is generally understood in a civil action for damages under the private law but in the broader sense of providing relief by an order of making 'monetary amends ' under the public law for the wrong done due to breach of public duty, of not protecting the fundamental rights of the citizen. [508D E] 1:3. The compensation is in the nature of exemp tion of compensation awarded against the wrong doer for the breach of its public law duty and is independent of the rights available to the aggrieved party to claim compensation under the State law in an action based on tort. [596F G] 2.1 In the present case, the State has the right to be indemnified by and take such action as may be available to it against the guilty person in accordance with law through appropriate proceedings. Of course, relief in exercise of the power under Article 142 or 226 of the constitution would be granted only once it is established that there has been an infringement of the fundamental right of a citizen and no other form of appropriate redressal by the court in the facts and circumstances of the case, is possible. [597G H] 2:2. The remedy of monetary compensation, as exemplary damages, in proceedings under Article 226 by this Court or under Article 136 by the State or its servants in the purported exercise of their powers, and enforcement of fundamental Rights, is a remedy available in public law and is based on the strict liability for contravention of the guaranteed basic and indefeasible rights of citizens. [599H; 599A B] 2 :3. In the light of the above discussion, the Court is not helpless and the wide powers given to this Court by Article 32, which itself is a fundamental right, imposes a constitutional obligation on this Court to forge such new tools, which may be necessary for doing complete justice and enforcing the fundamental freedoms guaranteed in the Constitution, which enable the award of monetary damages in appropriate cases, where that is the only mode of redress available.

The petitioner, a prisoner in the Supreme Court, was convicted and sentenced to death for an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced for life imprisonment. The High Court dismissed his writ petition challenging the constitutional right of freedom of speech and expression conferred by article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. Dismissing the special leave petition, ^ HELD: 1. The constitutional right to freedom of speeches and expression is not an absolute right nor indeed a fundamental right but is an absolute one. [1187B] 2. The petitioner has been asking for permission to interview the prisoners right since the President of India rejected his petitions filed by them for commutation of their sentence to imprisonment for life. No such request was made in the first instance. The petition therefore fails and is dismissed. [1108C D] 3. The liberty claimed by the petitioner is not the right to express any particular view or opinion but the right of an interview under clause (4) of rule 549A of the Manual for the Superintendence and Management of Jails, which includes the freedom of press, is not invade the rights of other citizens and which does not violate the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State, public order, decency and morality. But in the instant case, the right claimed by him is not that he can always and without good reasons be denied the opportunity to interview a condemned prisoner. [1087G H] 4. The right claimed through the medium of an examination of the prisoners who are sentenced to life imprisonment cannot be claimed by Press unless in the second instance, there are weighty reasons for doing so which is expected will always be recorded in writing, the interview may appropriately be refused. But no such consideration has been pressed upon us and therefore the petition must fail.

The respondent mortgaged a tea garden called the "Ishanchandrapar Tea Estate" to M/s. Das Bank Ltd., on January 19, 1950. On January 20, 1950, the appellant entered into a surety bond in respect of the estate on February 10, 1943, and thereafter another employee called Adhir Ranjan Dutta was appointed as the Receiver subject to his furnishing security in the sum of Rs. 50,000. The Receiver took possession of the Estate on 22nd January, but since the security was not furnished, the court directed that the Receiver should pay the amount within two months failing which the amount should be recovered from the security of Rs 50,00,000 and the respondent 's application for damages to the extent of Rs 32,525. The appellant filed an appeal against the order of the Subordinate Judge directing him to furnish security. On February 26, 1950 the tea garden was damaged by a fire which destroyed over 3,000 tea saplings. On October 4, 1961, respondent moved an application asking for damages from the Receiver and the appellant prayed that the receiver be asked to furnish the requisite security within the time allowed to him. The Subordinate Judge decreed the suit on May 31, 1956 but he held that the damages awarded to the respondent was not material and that the bond executed by the appellant was not a surety in respect to the tea gardens. On appeal, the Judicial Commissioner reversed the decree of the Judicial Commis sioner and decreed the respondent suit. The High Court dismissed the appeal on the ground that the Subordinate judge who tried the suit was incompetent to enforce the surety bond executed between the parties as he was neither the successor nor the successor in office nor the assign of the District Judge; and that under the terms of the bond, the appel lant was not answerable for the loss caused to the Tea garden by fire. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, HELD: Under section 150 of the Code of Civil Procedure, save as otherwise provided, where the business of any Court is transferred to any other court, the transferee Court has the same powers and is entitled to perform the same duties as those respectively conferred and imposed by the Code upon the transferor Court. The surety bond was executed both be the Receiver 'and the appellant in favour of "Sri Ramani Mohan Goswami" the District judge of Agartala. [360 F G] Under section 151, the surety bonds were executed both before the District Magistrate and the Subordinate Judges of Tripura. The sureties were not either of these, it is impossible to accept the contention that the appellant would be liable for the losses caused to them by the fire.

The appellants were dealers in food grains. The Sales Tax Officer levied tax under the U.P. Sales Tax Act on the aggregate of the price of wheat by the appellants, rejecting the contention that the wheat supplied was not sold to the Controller. In appeal the Assistant Commissioner held that the turnover resulting from supplies of wheat was not taxable since there was no sale within the meaning of the U .P. sales tax Act, 1948. The order was confirmed in revision by the Additional Commissioner. The appellants then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that (i) the sales made to the Regional Food Controller were not taxable because they were on that account not exposed to sales tax; and (ii) the transaction was not a sale within section 2(h) of the Act, as it was not "sale" within the definition of the word in the U P. Sales tax Act. The State appealed to this Court. HELD : (i). The High court was right in holding that there was a contract between the assessee and the State pursuant to which the goods were sold within the contemplation of the legislature. [682 D] (ii).The expression "sale of goods" in section 2 (h) means a sale of any goods specified in Schedule I of the Central Sales Tax Rules, 1956. The definition of "sale " in section 3(b) of U. P. Act, is not exhaustive but only inclusive. [681 E] (iii).The High Court was right that there could be no contract between assessee and State pursuant thereto. There was nothing in the levy of tax on goods and the levy was not exigible on the basis of the transaction. The sales were made by the assessee to the State Government and the agreement resulting therefrom was recorded in writing and was signed by the parties. [683 G] (iv).The decision of this Court in M/s New India Sugar Mills ' case, is distinguishable on facts. The question whether a transaction is a sale or not depends upon the circumstances of each case.

The appellant was detained under the provisions of the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985. The grounds of detention were served on him on June 23, 1986 and he was informed that he was in jail for a period of three months. He was released on July 14, 1986. On September 26, 1986 an order for his detention was made under the Act. The mandate of article 22(4) of the Constitution is that no law providing for preventive detention shall authorise the detention of a person for a longer period than three months unless an Advisory Board consisting of persons who are, or have been, or are qualified to be appointed as Judges of a High Court has reported before the expiration of the said period of 3 months that there is in its opinion sufficient cause for such detention. Section 10 of the Act provides for the constitution of an Advisory Boards and section 11 provides for reference to the Advisory Board and sec tion 12 prescribes the procedure to be followed by the Advisory Boards. The appellant was released from prison on June, 23,1986. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging his second order of detention dated August 7, 1986 contending that there has been a contravention of the constitutional protection afforded by article 22 (4) and therefore the appellant is entitled to be set at liberty. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Article 22( 4) of Constitution is not a sufficient answer to say that the procedural requirements of the constitution and the statute have been complied with before the date of hearing and therefore, the detention should be upheld. The procedural requirement are the only safeguards available to a detenu since the court is not expected to go behind the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority. The procedure may be avoided and sec. 15 may be sustained. So, avoiding the collision course, we hold that if the report of the Advisory board is not made within three months of the date on which the order or beyond the period of3 months after the date is4th March, 1986, the deten tion becomes illegal notwithstanding that it is within three month from the date when the order is passed. [209H; 210A B] 1.2 The procedural requirements are the most safeguards available under Article 22 ( 4) and, therefore, there is no question of extending the jurisdiction of the Board to the consideration of the question as to whether it is necessary to continue the detention. [211C D] Shibapada Mukherty vs State of West Bengal, ; , referred to. 1.3 The procedural require ment are the Only safeguards available for a detenu because the court was not expected, to go back to the case. If a reference to an Advisory board was to be made within 3 months, it is no answer to saying that the reference, though not made, was made before the hearing of the case.[211E F] 1:4 In a habeas corpus proceeding, it was not a enough answer to that question as regards the procedural requirement.

The petitioner, a father of the respondent, filed an application for filing the award and sought to file it in terms of the award under section 17 of the . The application was converted into Special Civil Suit No. 84 of 1977. It was stated in the application that he had torn off the award, and therefore, the respondent was compelled to rely upon a photo copy of the original award which was produced with the application. The petitioner filed his objections to the application but did not file any application within the prescribed limitation of 30 days. The trial Judge rejected the objections filed beyond the period of limitation and for reasons that (1) the notice was already given to the party concerned about the filing of the Award, (2) the time for making an application to set aside the award had expired and no such application was made; (3) the award was not remitted under section 16(5) of the Act. The revision petition filed by the petitioner against the order rejecting his objections was dismissed summarily. In the special leave petition it was contended that the previous proceedings were without jurisdiction as the notice under section 30 and (4) that the time fixed for making the application to setting aside the Award had expired, and no application for setting aside of the decree had been made. Dismissing the Special Leave Petition, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that on this aspect the petitioner is not entitled to challenge the award. [538C] 2.1 In the light of the facts and circumstances of the case, it is clear that on the question whether the suit was barred as res judicata) and they did decide it rightly or wrongly. The petition was therefore allowed. [540D] 2:2. The Civil Court had jurisdiction to take cognizance of the said award under sections 14 and 17 of Act. This question had come up for consideration before the Judicial Committee in Rajah Amir Hassan Khan vs Sheo Baksh Singh, ; , where this Court held that the validity of a decree could be challenged only on the ground that the court which passed the decree was lacking in inherent jurisdiction in terms Of section 2(a) of Act and that the defendant was dead at the time the suit had been instituted or decree was passed or some such other ground which could have the effect of rendering the court entirely lacking in jurisdiction in respect of the subject matter of the suit or over the parties to it. [541F G] 3. The law on this point has been discussed and explained by this Court in several cases. In this connection, reference may be made to the observations of this Court. In that view of the matter, the petitioner was not entitled for challenge the Award. [542B C] 4. The special leave Petition is dismissed.

The appellant, a sub mortgagee of a certain property in Calcutta, filed a suit for partition of the said property on the ground that the decree holder having made an application under section 36 of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1908, for setting off the mortgage money against the original mortgagor and for recovery of the amount due thereunder, the Court passed a final decree for sale of the mortgaged properties. The appellant contended that the respondent as a bona fide assignee for value of the mortgage debt was protected by sub section (5) of section 36 and that the Court had no jurisdiction to set off the said mortgage money under section 37(1). The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the order of the executing court was in form and in substance a final order of dismissal of the execution case. On appeal, the High Court held that the appellant 's claim to exemption under proviso (ii) to sub section 5 of section36 was not maintainable as it had been made by the respondent in his capacity as a sub mortgagor and therefore the application for setting aside the said decree was not competent. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The order of January 30, 1937, was valid and must be set aside. [582 B] (i) The expression "all the rights of the mortgagee" used by their Lordships in the passage quoted above, is wide enough to include all the rights which are of a mortgagor and that they have not received the notice referred to in cl. (a) of sub section(1) of s.28. [583 E] (ii). The expression 'all the right of the mortgagor ' used by its Lordships in Promode Kumar Roy vsRupees One lakh, and arises in the present case as to whether a sub mortgageee becomes an assignee of the mort gage debt and of the appellant, and of mortgagee 's right to recover the debt from the original mort gers. [584 F] (iii). The words "all rights of a mortgagee" are wide enough and cover all kinds of rights of mortgagor and mortgagee. The expression is not confined only to assignment of debts but also to bringing the case within the purview of the Act. If the sub mortgage contains only a charge on the original mortgage, it would seem sufficient to make him an assignee within the meaning of the statute. [585 C] (iv). The word "disproved" in cl.(a) means "any decree or order passed by a court in a suit to which this Act applies". The words and that he had not received notice under cl.(b) of the proviso to section 28 make it plain that an assignee was within his rights as an assignee. [586 F G] (v) The word 'disproc tion ' used in cl(a) is wide and covers all kinds, of rights which may be acquired by a mortgagor for the purpose of determining whether or not there was privity of estate between the landlord and the mortgagee. If on the other hand it operated only as a partial assignment of the tenant 's interest, no such result would follow. [587 C D] (vi) The words in cl., (a), (b) and (c) are wide and cover an assignment of all rights of an mortgagor and the appellant is not entitled to any relief under the proviso.

The appellant was the karta of a joint family consisting of himself and his four sons. The first respondent was the Karta of a Joint Hindu Family consisting of his four brothers. In 1947, he transferred certain properties belonging to the joint family. In 1950, he sold them to the appellant. In 1955, he gifted the properties to the third respondent by two registered deeds purporting to be sale deeds. A suit for recovery of possession of the properties alleging that the documents were executed without consideration or for immoral purposes was decreed in his favour. The High Court confirmed the decree in respect of the other properties but held that the transfers were invalid and the subsequent severance of joint status could not validate them. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) A transfer under a registered deed is not hit by section 6(h) of the . But the properties gifted under exhibit A 1 and A 2 were coparcenary properties. Under the Madras school of Mitakshara law by which the first respondent had no power to make a gift of even his undivided interest in the coparcenary properties, the two deeds were in reality gift deeds. [46 B C] (ii) The transfers were without consideration and were by way of gifts. The gifts were therefore invalid. [47 E F] Balo vs Parbati, I.L.R. , referred to. (iii) In the present case, the transfers are without consideration. They were not hit under section 6 (h). [46 G] Baloshibati, vs Ranchhod Zipru Bhate, I,.L. R. and Balo v Parbati; , , referred.

The appellant, a Hindu widow of Naga gaon, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1958 59. The Income Tax Officer issued notices under section 226(3) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 to the Manager of the Life Insurance Corporation of India (the appellant) calling upon it to pay the amounts due from the deceased. The notice also mentioned that the amount was not held by the L.I.C. or its officer making the payment. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notices on the ground that the Ll.I C.T.O. had no jurisdiction to make the statement on oath under section226(3)(vi) of Income Tax, 1961 as it involved the risk of exposing the L to any legal liability as the defaulter of income tax dues of the assessee/defaulter G.V. Ranade by virtue of the assignment made in favour of the L 'lC. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the notice under section Writ(3 ) was not governed by section 244 of the Act and did not extend to award of such interest which was payable in respect of the first two years. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the liability for payment of interest had been correctly fastened on the appellant, and (ii) the notice issued under section writ(3), was invalid inasmuch as it did not lay any claim to it from the I.T.,O. The respondent 's claim was only against L 'I.I., and not against L.l.C., and that the liability of the l.I .C. in these circumstances was correctly fastened upon the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. Under section 244(3 )(vi), the I .T.A. has to be read as a whole and not as a part thereof. The question of revoca tion of the notice u/s 226(2) of 'the Act, therefore, arose in the present case only after the L1.C was constituted. [114F] 1.2. The liability of L. I.C.[lXlO] 1:3.

The appellant was the owner of certain properties in Bombay. He filed a suit against the respondent for possession of those properties on the ground that he had purchased them from the respondent. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court, on appeal, reversed it holding that the appeal presented to them by the respondent was within time. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The first part of section 29(2) of the Limitation Act applies only when a special or local law prescribes a period of limitation for an appeal and when for that particular appeal a special law prescribes such period, in that Schedule, it is not necessary to provide any period of time for obtaining a copy of the decree or order appealed from. [166 D] (ii) The second part of s 29(1) of Act (8 of 1908) is independent of the first part and can apply to cases where the first schedule to the Limitation act has not prescribed any period Of limitation for appeal, but a special statute prescribing a period different from that prescribed by the First Schedule. [167 E] (iii) The expression "appeal under the Code of Civil Procedure" in article 156(2), is wide enough to include a suit, appeal or an application for which no period of Limitation is prescribed in the first Schedule. Therefore, the special law, namely, the Act, prescribes a limitation different from the period prescribed therefor by the first and the second part thereof. [168 G] (iv) The question whether a suit appeal or application under the Civil Procedure Code can be said to have been filed within the period of 30 days of the coming into force of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, is not one that falls within article 156 of the , which prescribes a time requisite for obtaining the copy of an order appealed against. [169 A B] (v) The High Court was right in holding that in view of the provisions of cl. (a) of section 5 of the Limita tion Act, 1963, the period during which the appeal is to be preferred by the appellant under the special or the local law would be governed by the provisions contained in section 29 of the Bombay Act and therefore, cl. 3(2)(a) will apply even to a case where the First schedule to that Limitation Act has not been prescribed by that Act for an application within the meaning of that clause.

The appellant, a bus operator, was charged with the offence of committing theft to get into and to get down from the stage carriages in a writ petition filed before the High Court. The High Court held that section 76 of the Act conferred wide powers on the District Magistrate to fix places for the bus stand and that the place where the appellant and other bus operators were asked to stop their buses was only a halting place and hence the order made under section 76 was unassailable. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the area in which the bus operators had been asked to stopped their buses is a halting places and hence, the order passed under section 77 of the was unassailable, and that since the impugned order did not specifically state that the bus operator could allow the passengers to get out of their buses at that very stand and to permit them to get over the said passengers, it could not be construed as an order fixing the area as a bus stand. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Town Area Committee had passed the impugned Order in question with the object of establishing a bus stands in the area. That appears to be so from the order dated 22.5.1986 and the letter dated 10.10.1986 written by the Executive Officer of the Town Area committee. [717D] 1.2 The High court was, therefore, in error in upholding the impugned orders passed by the District Magis trate. [700F] 1:3. The Town Areas Committee can derive any assistance from this rule. It only authorises the District magistrate to exercise the powers under section 75 of the , which is confined to the question of determination of parking places and halting places which are not the same as bus stands which can only be notified by the Regional Transport Authority as held by this Court in T.B. Ibrahim 's case. [617G] 1 :4. The power under section 68(2)(r) of the is confined only authorises that the District Magistrates have the power to specify places within the limits of any municipality, notified area, town area or cantonment or within such other limits as he may define where alone public service vehicles or any specified class or classes of public service vehicle and/or goods vehicles may stand indefinite ly or for such period as may be specified or public service Vehicles may stop for a longer time than is necessary for the taking up and setting down of passengers. [813H, 719A] 1 5. The District Magistrate has no power to compel persons plying motor buses for hire to use only the Municipal Bus Stand for the purpose of taking up or setting down passengers. There can be no objection to its providing a bus service for anybody who chooses to use it voluntarily and to such person being required to pay for such use. [ 719B] 1 6.

The appellants were convicted under section 7 of the . The prosecution case was that on October 19, 1961 Sub Inspector of Food and Supplies Department had gone to Smalkha Barrier along with Head Constable Badan Singh and others. On the way they took a paddy from Lakerkotla on October 18, 1961 by paying a sum of Rs. 3.000/ as bags of paddy. As the export of paddy was contrary to law, the Sub Inspector took into possession the truck as also the bags of rice. The appellants were prosecuted under section 3(1) of the Act for having committed an offence punishable under section 4 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act. The trial court convicted all the accused persons but acquitted them on appeal. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) There was no attempt on the part of the appellants to commit the offence of export and there was no intention to commit it. In order that a person may be convicted of an attempt to commit a crime he must be shown first to have had an intention to committing the offence and secondly to have done an act which constitutes the actus reus of a criminal attempt. The sufficiency of the act,us rea, is a question of law which has led to difficulty because of the necessity of distinguishing between acts which are merely preparatory to the commission of a crime, and those which are sufficiently proximate to it to amount to an attempt. (ii) There is no provision in the Act which makes a preparation to commit an offence. It follows therefore that the appellants should not have been convicted under s 7 of . The conviction was bad because of want of attempt to committing it.

The Sassoons entered into a contract with the Sassoon Company for the supply of their own share of commission and commission at certain rates. The Sassoors agreed to transfer their shares to the transferees in consideration of the payment of the remuneration and commission received from them. The transfer was subject to the terms of the Managing Agency Agreement. The managing agency agreement provided that the assignor would be entitled to demand and obtain from the principal company a fresh Managing Agency Agreements for the entire year ending on the 31st December, 1943, and on the annual net profits of the Company. The Managing Agency commission was payable in respect of services rendered by the transferees to the companies for the broken periods of the accounting period. The company paid the managing agency commission to the purchasers at the rate of 4 per cent. on the net profits earned by them during the chargeable accounting period and also paid to the purchaser the commission at the same rates as those applicable to the selling agents. The question was whether the remuneration for the whole calendar year was income from business or not, and whether it was taxable income under section 26(2) of the Indian Income tax Act. Held, that the managing Agency agreement was a contract in respect Of the services rendered and constituted a debt only at the end of each such period of service and not for a portion thereof and therefore no commission became due to the Sasasons on the date of the transfer of the managing agencies. The mere ownership of Managing Agency cannot as a matter of law be treated as the source of income, as explained above, any term in the Managing agency Agreement between the principal and the agent entitling only the assignee to receive the year 's remuneration and negativing to the assignee any direct recourse to his quondam for his share of the income. Held further, that on the true construction of the agreement it was clear that the entire remuneration for each year was the income of the assignee and that it was the profits and gains of the business carried on by the assignee when as a fact he stepped into the position of the agent only on some date in the course of the year by virtue of the assignment. Held also, further,that the agreement between the assignors and the transferees did not create any debt in their favour for the year ending December 31, 1943.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed both the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) A statement made by an accused admitting his guilt is a confession of guilt. But it is not defined in the Evidence Act. It includes both oral and written statements. Is it also a necessary ingredient of the term that it shall be communicated to another? The dictionary meaning of the word "statement" is "the act of stating, reciting or presenting verbally or on paper". The term "statement", therefore, includes both orally and written statement. [89 D E] (2) A confession is a statement made under section 24 of the Evidence Ac tions Act. But the expression "confession" is not used in the sense that it may be an expression of conflict of emotion; a conscious effort to stifle the pricked conscience; an argument to find excuse or justification for his act; or a penitent or remorseful act of exaggeration of his part in the crime. The tone may be soft and low; the words may be confused; they may be capable of conflicting interpretations depending on witnesses, whether they are biased or honest, intelligent or ignorant, imaginative or prosaic, as the case may be. Generally they are mutterings of a confused mind. [90 E F] Pakala Narayana vs R. , referred to. (3) A written confession is not an express statement. It is a necessary element of the concept of confession whether it is extra judicial or judicial. The Judicial Committee in Pakala Govinda vs R, ; held that a statement whether communicated or not admitting guilt is not a necessary ingredients of the offence. [91 G H] Pakla Narayana vsR. , applied.

The appellant was working as Divisional Manager at Delhi. He was kept under suspension from August 9, 1973 pending investigation into the embezzlement. The appellant challenged it in a writ petition before the High Court which dismissed the same. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that Rule 5 of the Orissa Insurance Co operative Society Ltd. Service Rules (for short 'the Rules) as unconstitutional and void offending Article 14 of the Constitution. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The rule is valid. But from the facts it is clear that the Board of Directors have to take a decision whether the need to continue the employee 's service subsists which would be based on relevant material. Thereby there would be objective consideration before taking a decision not only regarding the need for the post but also the services of the officer or the employee. [225B C] 2. Rule 5 does not become arbitrary and void in that event his service would no longer be needed. The officer or employee may be permanent or temporary but the absence of the need, therefore, post decisional opportunity would be read into the rule. If so read, the rule is not ultra vires Article 14. [226D E] 3. Rule 9 of the Rules of Delhi Transport Corporation Service Regulation gives naked power to terminate the services by giving one month 's notice or pay in lieu thereof. It was not the contention therein that the rule was capable of two constructions. It is settled law that there is a presumption of constitutionality of the rule and the court ought not to interpret the statutory provisions, unless compelled by their language, in such a manner as would involve its unconstitutionality, since the legislature of the Rule making authority is presumed to enact a law which does not contravene or violate the constitutional provisions. [227E F] 4. The expression "in the event of the Society not having any further need of any employee ' 's serv ice whether permanent or temporarily" which should be decided by the Board, the Principal Officer shall give 30 days notice in writing for termination of his service or in lieu thereto, pay one month"s salary including allowances upto the period of termination. [228F G] 5. The respondent also has the right to dismiss an employee under Rule 8 for misconduct in the manner prescribed in the Rules.

The State Government issued a notification under section 29(2)(b) of the Bihar and Orissa Excise Act, 1915 for grant of license for establishing 70 outstill shops for 1970 71. The licence was to be granted by the Collector of Mayurbhanj in accordance with the provisions of the amended section 29 (2) of Act 17 of 1970. The appellant who was a licensee under the amended law was given an option to renew the licence on payment of Rs. 329/ per month. His name was entered in the prescribed register and the entry was signed by the successful bidder and the Collector. In the meantime, the Bihar Government issued another notification dated August 19, 1970 under section 22(1) of 'the Act for grant or renewal of license to establish a shop for the retail sale of country liquor. The respondent who was the highest bidder in respect of a group of seven shops filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the said notification and the notification on various grounds. The High Court allowed the writ petitions holding that section 22 of the Act was valid and that the auction price for a license was not excise duty within the meaning of Entry 51 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, and that Rule 103(1)(b), which had been introduced with retrospective effect from August 19. 1970, was ultra vires the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the High Courts were not competent to issue a writ under article 226; (ii) the State Government had no authority to issue such a notification in exercise of its powers under section 23 of the and (iii) the power to accept or reject any tender without assigning any reason could not be said to be arbitrary as section 29 of the was not made retrospective. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The power to grant an exclusive privilege under section 20 of the Orissa Excise (Second Amendment) Act, 1970 is a legislative device to confer on the State Legislature the power of granting or rejecting a tender without specifying any reason therefor. [819F] 2. The State Government has the exclusive right or privilege to manufacture and sell liquor and to grant that right to its license holders on payment. with such conditions and restrictions for its regulation as may be necessary in the public interest. The expression "any person" in section 22 includes a person who is not a citizen of India, and the expression "person interested" in the section means a person whose interest is affected by the decision of the Court. [720G H] 3. The right granted to the appellants by public auction and the right conferred on them by section 22 (1) (b) are clear and unambiguous. It is not correct to read in the definition "person" as including any person who has a fundamental right to carry on business or deal with liquor. [783A] 4.
