The word "person " in section 2 of the Amending Act, 1971 has been used in a wide sense to include all persons interested in liquor. It includes all persons who have interest in the business of excise and it is not necessary that the State should be concerned and did not in fact issue any public notice for purposes of sub section (1). [783C D] 5. The words "any other person" occurring in section 29, List II, of the Constitution are wide enough to include a citizen who has no right to sell liquor. In order that a citizen may sell intoxicating liquors by retail, it must not be possible to hold any public auction for sale or to obtain an order from the Collector or the Excise Commissioner. The fact that the provisions relating to the manner of fixation and realisation of the consideration for grant are contained in section 5(1), which has been amended with retrospective operation, itself provides that no grantee of such privilege shall exercise it "unless or until he has received a license in that behalf from the collector or the excise Commissioner. [784E F] 6.

The appellant was charged with the murder of Narendra. The prosecution case was that on 25th January, 1967 he and his grandson (the deceased) were seen by PW 19, the maternal uncle of the deceased and the other two persons who were sitting in the house of the accused at the time of the occurrence. The evidence of PW 19 was that when the deceased went to the bungalow of the appellant, he saw that the dead body of Narendra was found on the bed room of his brother 's shop and that the whole house had been looted and that he had with them a boy who was of fair skin and wore khaki shorts and a white shirt. The trial court acquitted the accused but convicted him under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that there was no corroboration of the actual participation in the murder and that accused No. 3 could be guilty of theft but not of murder. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant had been rightly convicted under section 120B I. P.C., read with sections 302, 454 and 201 I.p.C.[623D] 2. The High Court was right in holding that there is sufficient corroboration of evidence of the alleged actual participation of accused No 3 in the crime. [624F] 3. In view of the fact that there were no eye witnesses to the murder, the conviction of the appellants under section 201 read with Section 34 I P. C. could not be sustained. The conviction of accused NO. 3 was therefore set aside and he is sentenced to death. [625H; 625A B] 4. In order to find corroboration in regard to the crime, it must connect or tend to connect the accused with the crime with the commission of the crime.[626B C] 5. The mere fact that the evidence of a witness was not believed would not lead to any inference of guilt of the offence with which the accused is charged. [ 625C D] 6. In the present case, the evidence on record clearly established that the murder was committed by the appellant and his companions. There were no motive for the crime charged against them. The circumstances proved against the appellants did not connect them with the offence. They were rightly convicted.

The appellant was the owner of a Hindu undivided family. He was not provided with a plot in the final scheme. In 1970, the Town Planning Officer awarded compensation to the appellant at the rate of Rs. 50 per sq. The total compensation awarded was Rs. 331/2/ . The total amount awarded was about Rs. 1,40,000. The appellant 's grievance was that the compensation awarded by the Town planning officer was inadequate and further that the apportionment of compensation between the lessor and lessee was not proper. He also challenged the propriety of reserving such a large area of land for the scheme. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appeal was incompetent as the Act did not provide an appeal against a decision of the Town plan Officer on matters dealt with by him in his order dated November 4, 1971. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Act specifies a principle of compensation and provides for a method of determining compensation; (ii) the object of the Act is to provide for the better regulation of development and improvement of land use and for the prevention of any abuse of an original plot in accordance with the provisions of section 69; (iii) the scheme of the town planning scheme is a whole scheme and the size and shape of every reconstituted plot shall be determined by the local authority. HELD: (i). The Act contains the necessary provisions for estimating compensation payable to an owner of land who has not been given a reconstituted plot. [94C] (ii). The object of section 32(1) is to give relief to an owners of land in lieu of loss of land. It is made clear in clause (xiii) that the damage is for injurious affection of some property other than the land acquired. The sense in which the expression 'injurious affection ' is used in section 23(1), is the generally accepted meaning of that expression and it is not applicable to a reconstituted plots. [95F] (iii). The principle for determining compensation is the same whether an owner or owner of the property is given a reconstitution or not; compensation is payable on the basis of the market value of the plot at the date of declaration of intention to make a scheme. [96G H] Shantilal vs State of Bombay, ; , referred to. (iv) The principle laid down in Shantilal 's case is that the property or right which is injuriously affected by the making of a town planning Scheme is a property or a right other than that acquired for the purposes of the scheme.[96H; 96A] (v) The expression "person interested" as defined in section 3 of the Land Acquisition Act means all persons claiming an interest in compensation to be made on account of the acquisition of land under that Act. It does not mean all persons claim an interest therein. [97B C] (vi). The expression 'person interested ' as defined by section 3 includes a person who is given notice of a decision to make the scheme, and the compensation to him is determined in accordance therewith without the improvements.

The appellant was the brother of one of the sons of the testator. He died in 1934 leaving two daughters and a son. The widow of the minor daughter filed a suit for partition of land according to her share. The appellant contended that the daughters were entitled to their lands taking into account the income from the properties devised to them after the death of the widow, that they were entitled only to the shares of the other daughter and that the sisters were entitled not to the daughters to make the selection. Held, that the question whether the daughters had a right to choose in such circumstances was one for decision by the Court. The words "he shall give to the female children " in section 89 of the Indian Succession Act, 1908, mean the same thing as those used in the case of the foster son, the meaning of which would be taken from the words "in respect of aani land of the joint family to which the testator was entitled". The words are not intended to cover only cases where the will is not so uncertain that it is capable of being construed as an artificial rule of construction. Narayanasami Gramani vs Hindle, (1860) 5 N.I.A. 984 and Narayanasaswami Gramani 's case, , referred to. The testator had clearly the right to select the land to be handed over to the two daughters. He was not entitled to selection under the will as soon as the children obtained majority. The intention of the appellant was clearly to select only the land devised out of the vattam and not a specific area of land of both nanja and Punja lands.

The appellant was the widow of a co sharer in law. The respondent 's brother died leaving behind his widow, respondent No. 1 and two sons. The appellant filed a suit for joint possession over the land in dispute on the ground that she was living with her sons at Lucknow and her husband 's cousins. The respondents contested the suit by filing written statement. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff 's name was wrongly entered in the revenue records, and that the defendants were in separate occupation of the land or plots in dispute and the plaintiff had absolutely no concern with them. On appeal, the District Judge allowed the appeal and held that on the admitted facts even after the abolition of Zamindari by the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, the respondent ' s name was recorded as co sharers with the defendants and continued to be so until 1359 Fasli as would appear from the extract of the khewat produced by the appellant. The District Judge further held that the name of the plaintiff was suddenly deleted after 1359 Fasli and there was no order of any authority or court to show the circumstances under which the plaintiff came into possession, and therefore, the suit was barred by section 49 of the Act. In second appeal, a Division Bench of the High Court reversed the decision of the District judge and held in favour of the appellant on the basis that there was nothing to show that any fraud was practised upon the consolidation authorities so as to make the order a nullity. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The mere non participation in the rent and profits of the landlord does not amount to an ouster so as lo give title by adverse possession to the other co shar er in possession. Indeed even if this fact be admitted, then the legal position would be that Mohd. Basir and Mohd. Rashid, being co sharists with the plaintiff in the k khata and had also sirdari tenants under them, how could the sirdar of the co sharner do not amount or extinguish title to the others. Indeed, even if these two facts remain that the legal principle would be, that Mohd., Basir & Mohd. days before the suit came to a clear finding of fact after consideration of the evidence that a clear fraud was committed during the consolidation operation either by the defendants or by somebody else as a result of which the rights of the plain tiffs were sought to be extinguished. [867F H] 2. The High Court erred in law in holding that there is no bar of suit to establish title of the parties.

The petitioner, a Deputy Prime Minister of India, was elected to the State Legislative Assembly. The Chief Minister of Haryana, who was one of the members of the Council of Ministers, filed an affidavit in support of the petition. In the affidavit it was stated that the oath administered to him as Deputy Prime Minis ter was not the oath in accordance with the prescrip tion of the Constitution; and that describing Shri Devi Lal as Deputy Chief Minister was descriptive only and for all purposes he was a Minister. The petitioner also asserted that he was still functioning as the Chief Minister. Dismissing the petition, HELD: 1.1 The oath register is by the incumbent signed as Prime Minister and all other ministers sign as Ministers. He further indi cates that describing him as the Deputy Prime Ministers is descriptive only. [219G] 1.2 In view of the clear statement made by the learned Attorney General that respondent No. 1 is just a Minister like other members of Council of Minis ters, he takes the same oath as the other ministers and there is no separate form even for the Prime Minister. Since the petitioner himself has been described as Deputy Speaker in the Council, he describes himself as the Prime Ministers. [319H; 319A] 1:3 The oath registers are by the incumbents signed as Chief Minister and they have not been signed by his submis sioned as Ministers.[321B C] 1 :4 In view Of the clear statements made by respondent No 1 that Respondent No.1 is just one a Minister, he cannot press it.

The appellant company was a factory and its workmen were not entitled to any holidays with pay as provided by the Factories Act. The dispute between the management of the Mills and the workmen related to the question whether the strike was illegal and unjustified. Held, that the action of the workers on the night of 1st November, 1948, fell within the definition of "strike" in section 2(q) of the Industrial Disputes Act and as such the strike did not amount to a strike. The provisions of the Factories (Amendment) Act, 1934, were similar to those contained in section 49 A of the Act and it was held that the strike could not be said to be illegal merely because the workmen had failed to turn up for work. Held further, that as the workers had been given notice of the strike on 3rd November, 1949, they would not have been entitled to annual holidays with wages under the Factories ' Act. Section 49 A(2) of that Act provided that no substantial question of law in respect of the construction of the section arose for consideration and was applicable only to a case where the interruption in service is brought about by an illegal strike. Held also, further, in view of the fact that the workers were not as a body prepared to resume work unless their demand was conceded. The workers had no right to deprive them of the holidays under the Act. There was no force in the contention that the stoppage of work on 1st 11, 1948 amounted to a lock out by the appellant and the strike had ceased to be an illegal strikes.

The appellant, actor, photographer, was charged with offences under section 292 I.P.C., for having been duly certified for public show by the Board of Censors. The prosecution alleged that the fascinating title was misleadingly foul and beguiled the guileless into degenerate into degeneration in degeneracy. The trial court, after examining some witnesses, took cognizance of the offence and issued notice to the accused. Thereafter, the producer, namely, the appellant, moved the High Court under section 482 Cr. P.C. on the ground that the criminal proceeding was an abuse of judicial process and engineered by ulterior considerations and that no prosecution could be legally sustained in the circumstances of the case. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the film had been certified by the Central Board of Film Censor, acting within their jurisdiction under the Act, thereby sanctioning public exhibition of the film. Allowing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 Section 79 I. P .C. makes an offence a non offence. When only when the offending act is actually justified by law or is bona fide believed by mistake of fact to be so justified, section 79 does not come down to public exhibition. [515B C] 1.2 The High Courts in their judgments have held that the prosecution was unsustainable because section 79 I .P.c. was exculpatory when read with section 5A of the Act and the certificate issued thereunder. [511D E] 2.1 In the instant case, the prosecution is unsustainable because Section 79 is exculpatory when it says that a certificate granted under it by expert authority can be stultified by a simple prosecution of a shower of prosecutions for an offence under section 293 I.p.C.; driving the producer to satisfy a 'lay ' magistrate that the certificate of the Board was justificatory. [616G H] 2:2 The film is a great instrument for public good if geared to social ends and can be a public curse if directed to anti social objectives. The freedom of expression, the right to be equally treated and the guarantee of fair hearing before heavy investments in films are destroyed belong to Indian citizens under the Constitution. But all freedom is a promise, not a menace and, therefore, is subject to socially necessary restraints permitted by the Constitution.[516B C; 516C D] 2 :3 The film has been certified as suitable for public exhibition and for section 292 1.4. [ 516D E].

The petitioner, a practising advocate of the Patna District, was ordered to be dismissed from service by an order dated January 12, 1973. The petitioner challenged the said order in a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed on July 13, 1973 holding that the Government Pleader had no right to seek or cling to briefs and counsel for the petitioner. In this appeal it was contended that his client is entitled to be heard as a representative of the Government pleader who has been appointed by the State Government as per administrative rules of the State. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Government Pleader is more than an advocate for a litigant. He holds a public office. It is not exception. Since the rules stand, he has a number of other duties to discharge. Besides, even if his only duty is the conduct of cases in which Government have been impleaded, still as explained more than once before the public are interested in the manner in which he discharges his duties. [766D E] 2. The Court cannot ignore the duties of the government Pleader and deny justice to those who count, which is a pity. [764F G] 3. The practice of a counsel is vital for any State if he handles his cases badly, tempts against which law offices are created by him. [765G H] 4. The High Court has not been justified in the summary despatch of the judgment to the writ petition whose main merit was dared. [661A B] 5. The court is clearly of opinion that a Pleader and, in a sense, every member of the legal profession has a higher dedication to the people. [763C D] 6. The State is expected to fight and win its cases and sheer patronage is misuse of power. One effective method of achieving this object is to act on the advice of the District Judge regarding the choice of Government pleader. When there are several thousand cases in the Patna courts and hundreds of cases before a plurality of tribunals, it is but right that Government should engage competent lawyers without hunting for political partisans regardless of capability. Public offices and Government Pleader are not concealed conspiracies with 'effete, aristocratic, protective coloration ' which at the same time enables one to make a considerable sum of money without sullying his hands with a "job" or "trade". [763G H; 767A B C] 7. The very object of the petition is to get read as Order 27 Rule 5B of the Bihar State Public Service Commission Act, 1973, which has been enacted by Parliament with the aid of Article 233 of the Constitution. [ 767D E; 767E F] 8.

The appellants held out of a total issue of 800 shares of the Bank of India Ltd. The Mills purchased 5,000 shares of Bank ofIndia Ltd., at an extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders of the bank held on May 6, 1948, a resolution was passed increasing the share capital of the company and for that purpose offering new shares to the existing shareholders in the proportion of one new share for every three shares held by them. The appellants agreed to the allotment of these shares and ultimately transferred them to a private company Jesinghbai Investment Co. Ltd., which was a public limited company. The shares were issued at a premium of Rs. 50, but the shares were allotted at a lesser rate than the original share for each new share. The respondent No. 1, who was the holder of 5,00,000 equity shares in the Mills, applied to the Bank to allot them to its nominees and the appellants agreed that the said shares would be distributed amongst the shareholders on payment of Rs 50 as capital and Rs.50 as premium per each share. On receiving the circular letter, the Directors of the Mills passed a resolution increasing the shares to Rs. 100 and thereby transferring the right of the appellants to the remaining 1,600 shares. The Board of Directors of respondent No 1 passed a Resolution on May 25, 1948 increasing the capital of Bank and for this purpose offering the new shares. On receipt of the circular, the directors of the mills passed the following resolution: "Resolved that the company having a holding of 5000 ordinary shares in its capital of Rs 100 each with a premium up to Rs 50, the right to the balance 1, 600 shares being the same as of the original shares for every 3 shares held. The Directors of Mills passed the said resolution on May 10, 1948 and enclosed therewith three forms for acceptance form B for renunciation and form C which may compendiously be called a form for allotment to nominees. On received the circular dated May 25. 1948 and the company 's letter dated May, 25,1948, the Director of the Company passed the resolution increasing its share capital to Rs 100 per share. In the meantime, the respondent No, 1, on receiving the Circular letter, issued a notification under section 34(1)(a) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, declaring it as a "dividend" within the meaning of section 2(6A) of that Act for the purpose of offering new share to nominees and directing the allotment to the nominees. The appellant contended that the High Court was not justified in holding that the distribution of the right by the respondent amounted to a distribution of dividend within the extended meaning of that expression in section 2 (6A), and that in nominating its shareholders to exercise the option to purchase the new issue of the appellant, Mills did not distribute any dividend. Held, that the power to apply for and obtain two shares of a public company was not one of the widest possible amplitude and even if the distribution was by way of distributive share of the profits or income of a company given to its shareholders, it could be exercised by nominating persons who were to take over the shares and that is what the Mills did. The resolution dated May 10 1948, increasing the number of shares to 100 only and the difference between the amount payable for acquiring the new share and the amount paid as premium for acquiring those shares under the right offered by the Bank was manifestly not distribution of capital but distribution in money; it was open to the Mills to renounce the offer.

The appellant was declared elected to the Legislative Assembly. The respondent filed an election petition under section 81 of the Representation of People Act, 1951 for setting aside the election of the appellant on the ground that the names of witnesses whom he desired to produce were already mentioned in the list of witnesses submitted by him and that the petitioner would keep the witnesses present. The learned Judge held that except the witnesses who were not named in the lists of witnesses, no other witness could be examined and that as soon as the evidence of the witnesses was recorded, the Court would proceed to record the evidence on behalf of the returned candidate; and accordingly he quashed the election petition. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (i) the expression "any person" in section 81(1)(a) of the Act must be given a clear legislative exposition in that behalf and that (ii) the Court should not have entertained an application to examine witnesses on the date fixed for recording his evidence, and (iii) the court should ascertain how far sub rule (3) would carve out an exception to the enabling provision contained in Rule 1 of Order XVI. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The scheme of Rules 1, 1A and 2 of Order XV of the Code clearly envisages filing of a list only in respect of witnesses who are mentioned in List II. [532C] 2.1 Sub rule (1) of Rule 1 and Rule 1A operate in two different areas and cater to two different situations. The analysis of the relevant provisions would clearly bring out the underlying scheme under order XVI Rules 1 and 1A, and Rule 22 of the High Court Rules would not derogate from such scheme.

The appellant, a Principal of an educational institution run by the respondent State, was appointed as Principal in May 1980. He was required to appear before the Manager of the College and take charge within 10 days of receipt of the order of appointment failing which he would be disqualified for being appointed as Head of Government aided secondary schools except minority institutions pending further orders. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court praying that the respondent should be directed to interfere with his work as Principal of the college and also to pay salary. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the appointment of the appellant was not valid because the order contained in the radiogram had suspended or withdrawn its power of appointment of teaching staff including Principal and therefore the Committee of Management of the institution had no power to set up a selection committee nor the selection committee had any power to make any appointment. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the date on which appellant was appointed was not fixed in the order dated April 7, 1981 but circulated to the District Inspector of Schools and that the State Government was contemplating taking away the power of management of non government aided schools and therefore, the Committee had no authority to make appointment. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of the High court is primarily based on the report of the District Management which was communicated to the Manager. There is no affidavit in opposition of the then Manager of Institution or any responsible person then in charge of the management denying the receipt of letter dated May 1, 1981. This letter shows that on April 8, 1981 the institution has received the order that the power is suspended for the time being. The District Inspector has no power under section 13(1) to make the appointment and withdraw or suspend the power conferred on the Committee. [975D E] 2. The resolution of the State Govt. dated April 8 1981 shows that the Selection Committee had not been constituted and had no powers to make appointments. It is only a formidable rival and wanted him to be out of way. The private management at the instance of Shri Jagannath appears to have subsequently backed out from the appointment. [ 975E F] 3. The State Government promulgated the U.P. Secondary Education Service Commission and Selection Board ordinance, 1981 which was replaced by the act bearing the identical name. The Act envisages setting up a Committee for selecting and recommending appointments of teachers including Principals. In order to avoid forestalling of governmental action by private managements, the power to appoint teachers including Principal is conferred on tho Director of Education to cause inspection of recognised institutions to be made from time to time and sub section (1) of section 16 provides that where the State Govern ment has reason to believe that any person has been appointed as head of an institution in contravention of the provisions of the Act, the State government may after affording an opportunity of being heard to such person, cancel such appointment and pass such consequential order as it deems necessary. [986F G] 4. The power to constitute a Committee is conferred by the regulations. The Regulations confer power on the committee to make recommendations for appointments. The regulation confers power on it to make modifications or rescind any regulation. Armed with this power the State Gov ernment has authority to sanction or not to sanction the regulation proposed by the Board.

The respondent Commercial Tax officer was not subjected to tax on the ground that the goods called "rayon cord fabric" were not the "end product". The petitioner challenged the order of assessment by a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the "tyre cord fabric", manufactured by it is woven by its purchasers "into a fabric in the same way as is being done by the first petitioner. This was not disputed before this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The taxing authorities have the power to decide the question whether the "semi fabric" is more correctly capable of being described as a fabric or as merely cord pretending to pass off as ar textile fabric. A sample of the tyre cord fabric was actually produced before this product in the process of manufacture of a fabric. It consisted of cords which could be said to constitute warps, running length wise and wefts, running breadth wise. But, neither of the two views can be rejected outright as untenable. [502 D E] (2) The High Courts were right in not interfering with the decisions of the taxing authorities at this stage. [500 G] (3) For some reason, entry 22AA is "textile fabric" and not for any kind of fabric. Therefore even if the tyre fabric may be the end product for the Delhi Cloth Mills, the crucial question is: Does this product constitute a fabric which is a textile? A textile fabric does not cover everything which could he made into a fabric; mere cord does not become a textile fabric just because it requires some skill to make it. The rather wide dictionary meanings of the term "fabric" do not appear to be correct. [ 500 G H] (4) For the same reason, the High Courts had no jurisdiction to interfere under Article 32 with the decision of the Commercial Tax Officer.

The appellant company was ordered to be dismissed from service on the ground that it had committed theft of electromagnetic clutch plates kept concealed in the tool box of his scooter. The management moved the High Court by way of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of dismissal and the Labour Court, Dhanbad passed an order directing the Management to transfer the case to the Labour court. The appellant company challenged the said order before this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was misled by the representation of the workman. [302E] 1.2 The principles of natural justice know ing that justice must not only be done but be seen to be done is the essence of fairness equally applicable to administrative authorities. [304G] 1:3. The doctrine of natural justi fication as applicable to judicial power is a rule to ensure the vast power in the modern state is not abused but properly exercised. [305H] 1 :4. The principles are fundamental in the consti tutional set up of this country. Every organ of the State under our Constitution is regulated and controlled by the rule of law. The concept of rule of Law would lose its efficacy if the instrumentalities of the state are not charged with the duty of discharging their functions in a fair and just manner. [306H; 307A] 1 5. The principle of natural Justice being presumptive, it should be followed by the authorities unless it is excluded by express words of statute or by necessary implication. [307B] 1 6. The requirement of acting judicially in essence is nothing but a requirement to act justly and fairly and not arbitrarily or capriciously. [308C] 7. The procedural standards which are implied by the duty to act fairly, must be strictly complied with. [309D] 2:1. In the instant case, the State has withdrawn the pending refe ration from the Labour Commissioner Dhanbad and transferred it to another Labour Court at the distant District of Patna on the representation made by the workman without getting it veri fied from the management. The State in fairness ought to have got it verified by giving an opportunity to the manage ment which is a party to the pending reference. Denial of that opportunity is a fatal flaw to the decision of the Government. [310E F] 2.2. In workman of Punjab & Ors. vs Labour Court Dhanbad, ; this Court held that the concept that justice should not only he done but he seen to have a fair play in action and that becomes mandatory. The rule of natural neces sary which are implicit in every decision making function, call it judicial, quasi judicial or administrative, is a statutory requirement. [311G H] 2 :3. In Workman of Bihar & Ors., vs State of Bihar, ; , this Court observed that the doctrine of natu rity must not be used to act arbitrarily and capriciously or capricically. The procedure which are expressly implied by duty to acts fairly and reasonably is taken to imply compliance with the principles of justice.

The appellant company was a registered trade union of its employees. The company was formed on October 7, 1955, and the hotel was closed on December 31, 1955. On January 13, 1956, the company filed a writ application in the High Court challenging the order of reference on the ground that the reference was incompetent as it did not specify the names of the workers as the workmen concerned were involved in the dispute. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the references were vague and that the union could not be made a party to the reference under the , (1) ; , and (2) that even if the workmen were specified as its workmen, they would be represented by such and such union in the matter. Held, that the dispute which was referred for adjudication was between the employer and its workmen and not between the workmen who were responsible for the dispute and it went to this length that the hotel decided to dismiss a large number of workmen on October, 7, 1956. The reference was therefore bad simply because it did specify how many of the workmen of thirty different categories working in the hotel were involved. State of Madras vs C. P. Sarathy ; , referred to. Held further, that there is no force in the contention that even though the dispute was about workmen who had been responsible for their dispute, the reference could be made only by a reference in this case. The fact remains that the disputes which were referred for arbitration were between the management of the hotel and its employees which were mentioned as its workman. The nature of the dispute is also specified in the terms of reference.

The appellant is a manufacturer of the tyres bushes and parts thereof. The Assistant Collector and the Collector of Customs (Judicial) overruled the contention of the appellant that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the Notification No. 281 Cus/76, dated 2 8 1976 issued under Heading No. 84.06. The Customs, Excise and Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal of the appel lant. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant: (i) that the imported goods were parts of internal combustion piston engines falling under Heading 84.07; (ii) that they were not entitled to claim any exemption under the Notification; and (iii) that even assuming that Heading No, 84.05 also contemplates parts of the engine, such parts must be all the parts of a engines or engines in question and not a few parts thereof, and that even if bushings are the same as bearings, still they would come within the purview of the notification, provided they are parts of such engines mentioned under Heading Nos. 8406.06; (iv) that on the facts of the case, there was no material or evidence to hold that the bushes, which have been imported by the appellant, were parts and not under Heading NO. 8407, and (v) that it must be proved that the parts in respect of which the exemption is claimed are parts, of the internal combustionpiston engine, as mentioned under heading No.84.06, will get the benefit thereof. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Notification grants exemption to the parts mentioned under headings No. 8.06 and 84.08. [225B] 1.2 The intention of the Government is clear enough to provide that the part of the engines, mentioned under Entry No. 83.06 will get exemption under Notification No, 8.05. [226C D] 1:3. The Notification provides that the articles specified in column (2) of the Table and falling under heading Nos.8406.63 are exempt from payment of a certain portion of the customs duty. Paragraph 2 of the table makes it clear that the Notification not only intends to grant exemption to internal combustion Piston Engines, but also to 'parts thereof '. [227D E] 1 :4. The intention is clear and manifest, it will be unreasonable to take a narrow view of the Notifications and not to extend its benefit to the partes of the Vaidial pistons referred to in Heading No 84.09.06.[228F G] 2.1 In the instant case, the Notification grants an exemption to parts of engines, as mention under Heading no. 8408.06 not only contemplates the engine or engines, but even the parts thereof; and, although the parts are not mentioned under the heading No., 84.04, they are distinct and separate. [228G H] 2:2. The notification does not contain or refer to the Parts of internal firearms. Non mention of internal fire pistn engines under Heading 8.07 is not a mere technical defect but it must also be a substantial one.

The right of management was divided between the two sons each taking six months ' share in the offerings made by their father and the offerings received by right of inheritence. The plaintiffs claimed that they were entitled to be in possession of the said right on the basis of a will executed by their mother, but the defendants denied the right of the plaintiffs to manage the said property or to take any right of share in it. The Trial Court decreed the suit and in appeal the High Court affirmed the decree of the trial court except some modification in regard to the period of 27 days from February 1, 1972. In the appeal by special leave, on behalf of the appellants/plaintiffs it was contended that the Courts below proceeded upon an erroneous assumption as if it was the duty of the defendants to prove by what hostile assertion of title and possession ouster has been established. It was further contended that even assuming that the said judgment and decree were binding on the plaintiffs themselves, they could have no independent right to claim. On behalf of respondents/plaintiffs, it was submitted that the suit was barred by limitation as the alleged rights had become barred by Limitation by ouster and as such the plaintiffs who were also claiming through the Fathima Bee had lost their right by ouster. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court committed a serious error in reversing the finding and in taking a wrong approach in holding ouster on the strength of judgment and decrees given in Suit No. 116 of 1909 and on the ground that Fathina Bee had not made a demand or asked for her share of the hundial collections at any point of time till her death in 1957. [526F] 1.2 The High Courts in reversing concurrent findings of fact have reversed the finding of the courts below with regard to ouster of Fathula Bee from the right or management of the Dargah and on that account they were pleading an ouster of the Fila Bee as well as the plaintiffs. It is well settled that where one co heir pleads adverse possession against another co heir then it is not enough to show that one out of them is in sole posses sion and enjoyment of the profits of the properties. The possession of one co heirs is considered in law, as possession of all the co heirs. [525B C] 1:3. In order to make out a case of ouster against Fathuma Bee or the plaintiffs, it must be shown that there was an ouster from open assertion of hostile title, coupled with exclusive possession and enjoyment by one of them to the knowledge of the other so as to construe ouster. Thus in order to making out a cause of ouster the plaintiffs have become barred under limitation by ouster, and the appellants and their counsel are totally mistaken in taking the ground of ouster. [500F G] P.K. Ramachandra Iyer & Ors. vs K.S.R.M.P. Rao & Anr., ; , referred to. 1:4. The High courts in reversing a finding of fact arrived at by the first Appellate Court had held that the courts had proceeded upon clearer flaws and had recorded findings that there Was no proof of ouster in the present case.

The respondent was a gangman in the employ of the Central Railway. He was allotted railway quarters and paid house rent allowance at rates specified in their memorandum No. E47 CPC/14 dated January 1, 1951. The first respondent put in his claim before the Authority for Rs. 290 on the ground that he had been allotted railway quarter of a suitable type and as he refused to occupy those quarters he was not entitled under the rules to any house rent Allowance. The Authority condoned the delay and held that the house rent allowances claimed by the respondent were admissible under the Rules. On appeal, the Appellate Authority allowed the claim holding that the House rent allowance was not admissible under section 2(vi) of the , as it was not a source of profit but only a charge for house accommodation. The High Court in reference held against the appellant. In appeal to this Court by special leave : HELD: (i) The rules which must be included in the terms of contract between the employer and the employee contemplate that an employee posted at one of the specified places would be entitled to house rent allow, but that as soon as he is offered Government quarters for his accommodation, he ceases to be so entitled. whether he actually occupies or does not occupy the quarters offered to him. [1349 F] (ii) The rule clearly provides that the allowance will not be admissible to those who occupy Government quarters or to those to whom such quarters have been offered but who have refused it. Once an employee of the description given above has been offered suitable house accommodation and he has refused it, he ceased to be entitled thereto whether he actual occupies or did not occupy tho quarters offered. [ 1349 G] (iii) The definition of "wages" in section 2 (vi) includes all remuneration capable of being expressed in terms of money, which would be so payable and any sum payable to such person by reason of the termination of his employment, but does not include a value of any house accommodation supplied by the employer to the employee.

The detenu was detained under section 3(1) of the . The grounds of detention were served on him alongwith the order of detention on February 16, 1980. On March 25, 1980, the detenu filed a writ petition in this Court challenging his detention mainly on two grounds: (i) that the order was signed by the detaining authority and not by the Minister; (ii) that he had not been supplied with the copies of the relevant documents; and (iii) that there was non application of mind on the part of the detaining author ity. Allowing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. The detenu 's representation dated March 24, 1980 made to the Central Government for revocation of the detention under section 11 of the COFEPOSA has been wrongly rejected by an unauthorised person. [350G] 2. The mere fact that the grounds of deten tion served on the detenu are elaborate does not absolve the detaining au thority from its constitutional responsibility to supply all the basic facts and materials relied upon in the grounds to the detenu. In the instant case, the detaining autho rised the State Government to supply the copies thereof to the detenus. The representation dated February 18, 1980 was never put up before the Minister. [351B C] 3. The order of detentiOn was in fact passed by the Secretary to the Government of Maharashtra, Home Department on March 12, 1980 and therefore, the same was not reasonably possible to say that the disclosure of the full texts of their statements would endanger their safety or harm public interest. [352C D] 4. The non supply of copies given by the detenu is a denial of the right to the detenue under article 22(5) of our Constitution. [353D] 5. The detaining authority without applying its mind to the nature of the documents, the copies supplied to the detention lasted from various angles. It was on receiving a direction from the Central Govern ment that the copies were supplied. On account of this chill indifference and arbitrary refusal, the detenus, who had applied for copies on February 18 1980, could get the same only on March 27, 1980 i.e., after more than one month. Thus there was unreasonable delay of more than a month in supplying the copies to the petitioners of the material that had been relied upon or referred to in the "grounds" of detention. There was thus an infraction of the constitutional imperative that in addition to the supply of the grounds, all the essential material relied upon and referred to therein must be supplied to detenu with reasonable expedition to enable him to make a full and effective representation at the earliest. Of course, what is "reasonable expedition" is a question of fact depending upon the circumstances of the particular case. [354E G] Khudiram Das vs The State of West Bengal & Ors., ; , referred to.

The Gujarat High Court held that the scheme of Chapter XXXI of the Code as disclosed by sections 258, 410 and 423 of the code was against the maintainability of a joint appeal by several accused persons. The question for determination in this appeal was whether several accused person jointly tried under section 419 of the Indian Penal Code and convicted by the trial court, the state can prefer one appeal against the acquittal of all of them. ^ Held, that the High Court was wrong in holding that a joint appeals by the State against several accused were jointly tried and acquitted by the Trial Court by a common order, but the High court in its order referred to sections 258 and 410 of the Criminal Procedure Code. The power to frame this rule is specifically conferred on the High Courts by section 554(2)(c) Cr. P.C. and r. 6 does not seem to be inconsistent with any provisions of the said Code. It is well settled that a Joint appeal by the state against several persons acquitted at a joint trial has also to be held not to be contrary to any provision of the Cr. The High Court in its Order referred to section 419(2) (c) and came to the conclusion that the Scheme of Chapter XXXV of the Bombay High Court Appellate Side Rules, 1960 was against tile maintainability of joint appeal. The word "dismainder" in section 419 means a hand maid and not a mistress of law intended to subserve and facilitate the cause of justice and not to govern or obstruct it.

The appellant, a firm carrying on business in India and in the former Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, was assessed under the 1918 Act to income tax. The income tax authorities accepted the fact of partition amongst the members of the family. But the Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal of the assessee holding that the foreign business of the appellant could not be deemed to have been charged under the provisions of the 1918 and 1922 Act because what was taxed was the remittances received from the profits of the foreign firm and not the foreign income. The High Court on reference held in favour of the Revenue. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The assessee was entitled to relief under section 25(3) of the 1922 Act with regard to the rental income from house properties owned by the foreign company which was discontinued in the year of account. [910 B] Commissioner of Income tax, Madras vs section V.R.M. Palaniappa Chettiar and Others, , followed. (2) The High court was in error in holding that foreign business was not charged under section 3 of the Act because the assessee received the entire profits of foreign business in British India and the entire profit were assessed to income Tax in the hands of the asses see under the 1922 act.

The respondent assessee entered into a contract with the Public Works Department of the Government of Gujarat on September 6, 1965 for manufacture and supply of kiln burnt bricks to the said department for construction of a capital project. The assessee made an application under section 52 of the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1959, to the Deputy Commissioner of Sales Tax for determining whether the supplies of bricks by the assessee were sales or works contract. The Deputy Commissioner held that the supplies were not sales or work contracts and therefore the transaction envisaged by the contract was a works contract and not a works con tract. The High Court on reference held that as the supply of bricks was transferred to the department as a chattel for consideration, it was not liable to sales tax. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The contract in this case is a contract of sale and not one for sale of work and labour. [165 E] Chandra Bhan Gosain vs State of orissa & Ors., ; , followed. (2) The transaction in the instant case was a contract for sale and the assessee could not sell the bricks to other parties without previous permission of the company. [166 G] Chandra Mohan Gosain 's case, ; distinguished. (3) The property in the bricks was entirely of the assessee. He had not only to manufacture that but also to stack them for facilitating delivery. The essence of the contract is that the delivery of the bricks after manufacture is completed. manner of execution of the work regarding moulding and drying and provision against subletting which shall constitute a breach of the Contract resulting in forfeiture of security deposit. All these features do not negate the concept of a contract as one for sales of goods manufactured. [167 G H] Chandra Gopal Gosain & Ors. vs State Of Uttar Pradesh, ; , distinguished.

The President of India promulgated the Emergency Commission Ordinance, 1976. The said Ordinance was replaced by an Act 30 of 1976 which received the assent of the President on March 31, 1976 and came into force on April 3, 1976 in exercise of the powers conferred by sub clause (a) of clause (2) of Article 352 of the Constitution of India. Clause (3) of the said Ordinance provided that if a grave emergency existed whereby the security of India was threatened, whether by war or external aggression or internal disturbance, he might be arrested and may be detained under any law for a period not exceeding one year at a time. The President of the India issued a proclamation on March 3, 1977 stating that the Proclamation of Emergency had been revoked by the President acting as the President of States. The petitioner who was an assessee under the Income tax Act, 1961, challenged the validity of the aforesaid Ordinance and the President 's Order dated March 31. 1977 in exercise whereof he was assessed to income tax and wealth tax for the assessment year 1976 77. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the proclamation of Emergency by the Governor on March 23, 1971 had ceased to be in force at the expiration of two months from the date on which each of them was issued as the resolutions passed by the Houses of Parliament approving each of the Proclamation had not been published in the official Gazette. The Union of India appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The proclamation of emergency dated March 3. 1971 is valid and must be upheld. [445G] 2. The two Proclamations of Emergency were kept in force by virtue of the resolutions of Parliament until they were duly revoked by resolutions of both Houses of parliament. The newspapers, radio and television are also the other modern means which give publicity to all Acts and resolutions of the Parliament and the Legislatures of States.[445H] 3. The production of the Lok Sabha Debates and of the Rajya Sabha debate containing the proceedings of the two Houses of the Legislature relating to the period between the time when the resolutions were moved in each of these two Houses and the time which the resolutions in the Houses were duly adopted amounts to proof of the same. [444A] 4.

The appellant filed an application in the District Court for a declaration that the said premises were private property and for an order setting aside the decision of the authorities. The High Court held that the property was a public temple within the meaning of Madras Act 19 of 1951, and that the appellant had no market value and therefore was incapable of valuation. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the question whether the property in dispute was a private or a public trust could have no market Value and therefore the High Court ought to have valued the property accordingly. The suit was filed by the appellant in the form of an application under section 84(2) of Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1927. Under that Act only a fixed court fee was payable. That being so, the appellant did not have to pay court fees as it would in the case of an ordinary suit on a valuation made by him therefor. The question whether a property is a private one or a Public temple could have been raised before the High Courts and the High courts. The appellant had claimed that the properties were private properties and for the time being they belonged to the family of the said family. The respondents in their written statement contended that the suit was not a private suit on the valuation made under section 80, C.P.C. but was subsequently converted into a suit by an order of the High court. Held, further, that as the appellant 's case was that the subject matter of dispute in the suit, whether it was a Public Temple or public temple, could have any market value, and the property belonged to and was an alienable private property, it was incapable for valuation.

The appellant, a workman in the respondent 's establishment, was awarded a gratuity of Rs. 400 per mensem to its workmen. The Industrial Tribunal granted the first claim and directed that the clerical staff should be paid as compensation. In appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The workers of the appellant 's concern were entitled to receive wages in lieu of the tiffin arrangements at present made by the appellant. (ii) The Tribunal was wrong in holding that the appellant was under an obligation to provide some cash allowance for tiffins to its employees. Under the relevant provisions of the Factories Act a canteen had been started by the appel lant, but there is no obligation on the part of the employer to make any provision for the tifi al staff by way of giving them a cash allowance. (iii) The appellant ' s claim that the practice started by it of re employing retired persons should be stopped. The Tribunal had granted the relief to the workmen and directed the clerical Staff to be paid As. /8/ per day and the subordinate staff as also the subordinate Staff on all working days in lieu thereof. [572 D E] Chandi Charan Banerjee vs The State of West Bengal, ; , referred to. (iv) The fact that the wage structure which prevailed in the comparable concerns was not based solely on humanitarian considerations cannot be ignored. When a dispute is raised on this point it is necessary for the Tribunal to consider whether the appellant is under an obliga tion to make provision for its employees by way offi cer, and if the Tribunal took the view that the appellan ts were under an independent obligation to pay any cash allowance to its employee, it does not see how it can interfere with it on the ground that the impugned decision is erroneous in law.

The respondent who was a subscriber to the State Bank Provident Fund filed a suit for recovery of money due under a Provident Fund Account. The Union of India claimed immunity from attachment of the two cheques on the ground that they represented provident fund money which by section 3 of the , was immune from attachment. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court confirmed the order. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The money in the hands of the Reserve Bank of India had ceased to be provident fund property within the meaning of section 60(1)(k) of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 read with section 3 Of the , as the appellant was a trustee for the subscriber to it at the foot of the Provident Fund account in sterling if the country in which it is to be paid, the rupee is not legal tender. Browne had given intimation before he retired of his intention to receive the provident fund amount due to him at the time when he became entitled the money. The Bank was therefore in respect of the provident Fund money in its hands and was exempt from attachment under section 60 (1) (k). [32 D F] (ii)The Union of india had no interest in maintaining an application for removal of attachment. But the Union of lndia was a Trustee for the subscribers of the money and was not the agent of Browne to receive it on his behalf.

The appellant was employed in the respondent company as a pump operator in 1963. He was promoted as clerk in 1967 and collection of wages from his union activities was also done by him in 1967. The management terminated his services with immediate effect on the ground that he had been victimised for misconduct. The respondent filed an application before the Labour Court under section 33A of the , claiming that the termination of his service was illegal and unjustified and that the management should be reinstated without backwages. The Labour Court held that the appellant was not guilty of any misconduct and dismissed the application holding that the order of termination was legal and immune from challenge. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The respondent 's services were terminated in 1968. The termination was illegal because the employee who wilfully or anti socially had merely a good word for his employees. The power of the court to go behind the language of the order is preserved by this Court. [497E] (ii) The management could not have conducted the enquiry without a valid charge sheet and without giving an opportunity to the workman concerned. When the latter stated that the employee was not aware of the existence of the union, he was suspecting since 1968 that the said decision was bad and was liable to be set aside. [498F] (iii) The Labour court had misled itself on the law land. It was manifest therefore that the impugned action was not bona fide. [500G] (iv) The termination of service was not mala fide. The employer who believes or suspects that his employee, particularly one holding a position of confidence, has betrayed that confidence, can, if the conditions and terms of the employment permit, terminate his employment and discharge him without any stigma attaching to the discharge. It must rest on some tangible basis and the power has to be exercised by the employer objectively, in good faith, which means honestly with due care and prudence.

The petitioner, a doctor, was appointed as an Assistant Surgeon in the District Hospital at Jaipur. He was admitted to bail by the State Government on 24.4.1988. On 22.4 .88 he was admitted in the hospital where he was examined and found fit for performing his duties. The doctors were not allowed to take serious care of the patients. The petitioner filed a writ petition before this Court praying for directions to the respondents to initiate appropriate action against those responsible for the tragedy. This Court by its order dated 26.9.88 directed that the State should make an interim arrangement for the treatment of eye camp and in case the doctors were allowed to go back immediately after the operations, it was directed that they would be given a further sum of Rs. 12,500. The respondents filed counter affidavit stating that the guidelines issued by the Government on 9.2.1988 had been updated and revised. The Court also observed that the recommendations made by the sub committee were satisfactory and revised guidelines could be obtained from the Government. On behalf of the State it was contended that the petitioner should have conducted a thorough investigation into the incident, and if so, whether such a mistake was negligent or not. Allowing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The Revised norms issued by Union of India on 9th2.88 arrived at after a careful study of all aspects of the problem are quite comprehensive. However, it is not said so in so many words, the drift of the explanation is that the ailments occurred despite all precaution. [249D] 2.1 The guidelines dated 9.02.1988 with the suggested modifications, can be held to be satisfactory. [250E] 2.[2.2) The Revised guidelines issued on 9 2.88 are not in conformity with the directions issued by this Court. It is only a very low degree of care and competence judged in the light of the particular circumstances of each case is what the law re quires: [250G H] 3.1 In the instant case, the guidelines dated September 8, 1988 were duly followed and revised from time to time. The guidelines for conduct of eye camps earlier issued have been updated. The guideline has now been implemented after a thorough study of the various aspects of problem. [251F G] 3.(i) The guidelines are accorded to the policy of medical treatment in the Government hospitals, hospitals and other authorities laying down certain norms and guidelines for the conduct of 'eye camps '. [252H; 252A B] (ii) The new guidelines issued have now been reiterated after a detailed study of various aspects. However the limited scope of the proceedings no appeal could be made to the doctrine of State action. [253B C] 3(iii) The revised guidelines dated 8th February, 1988 are not consistent with the principles laid down by this court in Dr. B.R. Ambedkar 's case. [254C D] 4.(i). The Revised guideline dated 9 21988 is not in consonance with the practice followed by the Central Government on the part of the Indian Medical Council. [255D] (iv) The State would be willing to render help to the victims within the constraints of its resources. If that be so, the question of the li ability of the manufacturer for what is called 'product liability ' and the further question whether in such cases of mass use, a pre test for safety and purity of the article was necessary and whether failure to do so would be action able. [256E F] (v) The Medical Trust should take up this issue and process the claims of the victims for such other bene fits under any of the existing schemes providing for aid to the aged, the disabled, and the destitute, sub ject to the condi tion that the victims otherwise satisfy the conditions of those schemes.

The petitioner in this writ petition challenged the action taken by the respondent State Government under the Assam Panchayatbhasha Prachar Samiti (taking over of Management and Control) Act, 1984 on the ground that the management and administration of the Samiti were being run by elected bodies namely, the Manipur Hindi Prachar Sabha and Karyapalika Sabha. The petitioner contended that the provisions of the Act had been violated inasmuch as the State Government had not appointed the President or the Executive Committee as required under section 3 of the said Act. The respondent State contended that since the State Govern ment had no right to take over the management temporarily it could have provided for the restoration of the elected body in due course. It was further contended that even if the provisions were not attracted, the provisions could be invoked only to restore the elected bodies with the membership either chosen by the founders or regulated by rules made by the State Legislature and that the impugned Act had no legal validity as it was passed after the passing of the Assam Non Executive Committee (Amendment) Act. It is further contended on behalf of the petitioner that the procedure stated in the said section of the Constitution was not followed, and that since there was mismanagement, delay in examinations and results, it was because of that that the State had no point of time, even thought of restor ing the body to which the petitioner belonged. It has also been contended that by the operation of this Act those who have nothing to do with the Samiti or its ideals and who were not even the members of the Council have been nominated as the members.

The appellants were the sons of one Ram Gopal, a resident of Asansol in Bengal. The respondents brought a suit for a declaration that a deed of gift executed by her was void and inoperative under section 123 of the Transfer of Property Act. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court on appeal reversed the decree holding that the gift was not made at the time of the marriage or on the occasion of the Hindu Law, as it stood prior to its amendment in 1956. Held, that the question whether a particular gift is reasonable or not will have to be judged according to the state of the family at the date of the gift and the extent of the property immoveable property the indebtedness of the appellants and the fact that one of the sons has become indebted cannot take away the power of the father to make such a gift. The Hindu Law does not recognise any particular gift as a gift but only a gift of immovable property acquired by a female Hindu at a partition or by gift from her husband to her son in law. A Hindu widow gives her daughter in marriage and at the same time gives her a daughter in law a right to enjoy a reasonable portion of the estate of her husband. The test is whether there is an express or implied prohibition of a gift, but it must be shown that the donor has made a gift before he can acquire any such property. In the present case the gift in question was not by way of a valid gift and was binding on the reversioners. Kudutamma vs Narasimha Charyulu (I.L.R. , referred to.

The appellant was declared elected to the Punjab Legislative Assembly. The polling took place on May 31, 1980 and the counting was done on June 1, 1980. The margin of votes between the votes secured by Tej Singh (appellant) and Avtar Singh (Appellant) was only 123. In the election petition filed in the High Court, the appellant challenged the validity of the posters on the ground that they were published by a Congress party and that the payment was made to him by Darshan Singh and Mukhtiar Singh. The High Court dismissed the election petitions. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The allegations of corrupt practices indulged in by Tej singh have been clearly proved. The posters said to have been printed and circulated are Annexures P 1 and P 2 which appear at page 42 of the second paper book and it may be necessary to extract certain portions thereof "Keeping in view the present conditions in the country it is imperative to defeat the dictatorial Congress in these elections. Therefore, the irresistible inference and inescapable conclusion that can be arrived at is that Tej Singh had actually paid for the posters which were printed at his instance and Rup Lal was not collected with the printing of the poster. [419G H; 418A B] 1.2 The appellant has proved beyond reasonable doubt that Tej singh had indulged in corrupt practices particularly when the printing was clearly admitted by him, as indicated above. It is also clear to us that in view of the very narrow margin of vote (123) between Tej Singh and Avtar Kaur, a strong presumption and possibility that the votes polled in favour of Rup Lal would have gone to the appellant (Avail Singh) and, therefore, the result of the election would have been materially altered.

The appellant, a Forest Minister in the Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal, was defeated in the legislative assembly election held in 1982. The respondent No. 1, who was the Chief Minister of the State, filed an application for contempt against the appellant alleging that he had committed contempt of court and that after having failed to threaten and demoralise the appellant through indirect means, the respondent, the Superintendent of Police pressurised and threatened the appellant with direc tions to withdraw the writ petition. The Single Judge of the High Court dismissed the application holding that there were circumstances to indicate that it was not a fit case in which the court should exercise its jurisdiction under the Act. In appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 When no punishment is imposed by the High court, it is difficult to say that the High Courts have exercised their jurisdiction or power as conferred on it by Article 215 of the Constitution. It does not mean that when the High, Court erroneously acquits a contemnor guilty of criminal contempt, the petitioner who is interested in maintaining the dignity of the court will not be without any remedy. Even though no appeal is maintainable under section 19(1) of the Act, the appellant in such a case can move this Court under Article 136 of the Constitu tion. Therefore, the contention that there would be no remedy against the erroneous or perverse decision of the respondent No 1 in not exercising its jurisdiction to punish for contempt, cannot be accepted. [893C D] 1.2 The High Court exercises its jurisdiction or powers as conferred upon it by article 215 of tho Constitution when it imposes a punishment for contempt.

The appellant was the owner of two inam lands in Poona district. He had leased out his tenancy rights to one Girdhari for Rs. 7,999. The lease provided that in default of payment of rent he would have no right over the land. The tenant paid a premium of Rs. 999 for the lease and also agreed to pay the agreed rent in monthly instalments. The rent note provided that the lessee was liable to pay interest at 6% per annum on the amount of the annual instalment from the date of payment. The appellant filed a suit for possession on the ground that the lease had determined by forfeiture for non payment of the rent and that the tenant had no right to claim any compensation for nonpayment of rent. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in appeal reversed the decree holding that the notice was not necessary as the lease was executed prior to the coming into force of the . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the statutory provisions of section 111(g) of the Transfer of Property Act, which provided for the determination of a lease by forfeiture were mandatory and did not require the notice in writing to complete a forfeiture; (ii) the words "in accordance with law" in sub section (g) as it stood before the amendment of 1929 showed that the intention of the legislature was to give relief against forfeiture only where the statutory provision expressly provided for forfeiture and that no such provision was made in the Act which required the notice to complete the forfeiture.

The appellant, a contractor, was charged with having committed an offence under the Mines Act. The Inquiry Officer held that the enquiry was not in accordance with the Standing Order No. 17 and therefore the dismissal order was invalid. He further held that though before him the Management had by leading evidence proved their misconduct, the management served charge sheets on them in which four common charges were levelled against all of them. In addition to three charges, the appellant was also charged with indulging in unauthorised quarry workers. The Labour Court dismissed the respondents ' petition under section 33A of the Act holding that the inquiry was vitiated because no second opportunity was given to the respondents and that there was violation of principles of natural justice. The High Court confirmed the award of the Arbitrator by dismissing both the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Labour Court had misconstrued Standing Order 17 and that no second notice was required to be given to show cause against proposed punishment before the issuance of the dismissal orders as required by Standing Order NO. 17; (ii) assuming that the Enquiry Officer had power to interfere with the punishment in the instant case having regard to the gravity of misconduct, and the previous record of the worker, it would be difficult to attribute any intention to the framers thereof to provide for a second opportunity being given to a workman to offer his explanation; (iii) assuming the enquiry as vitiated for the reason mentioned by the Arbitrator even then the Labour had no jurisdiction to enter into merits of the case or interfere with punishment of dismissal inflicted upon Rama Shankar and Burma Pradhan, and (iv) assuming without affording an opportunity to showcause against the proposed punishment, having been given to him, the termination of his services was bad as he had not been afforded a second opportu nity. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have rightly held that Standing OrderNo. 17 deals with two different stages concerning disciplinary proceedings against a delinquent, first holding of a departmental inquiry into the charges where principles of Natural Justice must be implied and second the infliction of graver punishment before awarding which opportunity to showing cause against the proposal is provided for; but the plain reading of the Standing order read as a whole does not warrant any such assumption and, therefore, it does not call for any requirement of the ordinary law of the land or of industrial law. [368E F] 1.2 The word 'second opportunity ' to be construed in the last part of the standing order means that a second notice is given to an employee which suggests that the same is to be called for prior to the recording of finding that the delinquent is guilty of misconduct: it is the alleged misconduct that is to he explained by him and not the proposed penalty. [369F G] Hamdard Dawakhana vs Badri Das & Ors., ; , referred to. 1.3 The word `second ' in the Standing Orders means `an opportunity to offer any explanation '. In other words, different stages in domestic inquiry were never in the contemplation of the framers of the S.O.

The appellant 's father purchased the land in question from the respondent State. The lease deed purported to be a lease deed executed by the respondent No. 1 in favour of incompetent persons. The High Court held that the benefit of section 7D would apply only to persons whose occupa tion of the private forests or unsurveyed lands had a lawful origin and not to persons m unlawful occupation based on trespass or forcible and unlawful entry. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, HELD: 1.1 Section 7D of the Kerala Land Reforms Act 1963 is applicable to the facts of this case. The said section provides that certain persons occupying land for not less than ten years to be deemed tenants notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any law, or in any contract, custom or usage or in the any judgment, decree or order of court, any person who on 11th day of April 1957 was in occupation of such land for a period of not less then ten years preceding the commencement of Kerala Land Reform (Amendment) Act, 1969 shall be deemed to be tenant if he or his predecessor in interest was continuously in occupation thereof for not more than two years within a period Of twelve years immediately preceding the 11th April, 1967. [114F H] 1.2 The expression "in lawful possession" occurring in section 7B must be construed as meaning "in unlawful occupation". In the present case the finding of fact entered by the High Court is that the appellant had come into possession of the lands by trespass. His plea before the Courts below was that he was himself the owner of the area having acquired title to it by adverse possession. He did not actually transferred possession of land to the landlord before the commencement oF the Kerala Act. [115G H] 2.1 The expression 'in occupation ' occurring in Section 7 D must be interpreted as meaning 'in lawful occupation '. In the instant case the findings entered by High Court are that the appel lant had come in possession of his lands by encroachment. His contention before the courts below was not accepted by the Courts.

The appellant was found in possession of certain contraband goods. The police officers searched the room and recovered a portion of the box containing tobacco from his possession. He was also seized from the custody of the appellant together with the Godrej lock keys produced by him. Thereafter, the seized articles were made over to the Inspector of Central Excise who remanded them for further investigation. On the ground that the goods were liable to confiscation under section 111(d) of the , the appellant had committed offences punishable under section 135(a) and (b) of . The appellant contended that the presumption contained in section 123 of the Act corresponding to section 128(A) of that Act was not applicable as the goods in respect of which the appellant was prosecuted were not seized under the Act. HELD: The appellant had not produced evidence to show that the gold found, in the circumstances stated above, had been imported without payment of duty. [541 G] (1) Section 123(1) of , only lay down a procedural rule and they could be applied when the case came up for trial before the Presidency Magistrate who actually decided it on 15 7 1969. Indeed, the complaint itself was filed on 30 10 1968. It is immaterial that the appellant 's conduct including his untruthful denial of their possession, indicated consciousness of their smuggled character or means rea. [542 G H] (2) The appellant 'S had not been found in conscious possession of any of the bodies but knew something about the incriminating nature of their contents. Otherwise, why should he at first have refused to produce the key he had ? In any case there was some evidence to enable the courts to come to the conclusion that the articles must have been known to the appellant to be smuggled even if he was not a party to a fraudulent evasion of duty; and the fact that the person with whom the goods came from or when the goods are imported or that duty, if leviable was not P d on them. [543 G H, 543 A] (3) The High Court was in error in holding that the prosecution had failed to prove that the accused had knowledge of the smuggled character of their goods and that he was dealing with them knowing them to be smuggling goods.

The appellants were the Presidents of a registered society. The members of the said society were not entitled to any share in the profits made on the sale of yarn of Gwalior cloth and other things. The Association was formed for carrying on its business which had for its object the acquisition of gain by the individual members thereof and also for the benefit of their families. The appellants filed a suit against the Association claiming that they were entitled to a share in an account of profits made by them as a company under section 4 of the Rewa State Companies Act, 1935, and that the suit was not maintainable. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court on appeal held that the other members of a association were not liable to participate in the profit making profits made from the sale. Held, that the appellants had not asked for a return or refund of their subscriptions; they had asked for an adjustment of accounts in enforcement of an illegal contract of partnership. The suit was therefore maintainable under section 5 of the Vindhya State Companies (Amendment) Act, 1951, and the appeal must be dismissed. The provisions of section 4(2) of the Act were not applicable to the case as the appellants did not ask for a refund of subscriptions on the ground that they had no right to an account in respect of the partnership transactions. The suits were therefore maintainable. Held further, that under section 2(1)(a) of Madhya Pradesh Co operative Societies Act, 1936, the object of the Association was not to create any association but to give a party a protection of which he may avail himself or not as he pleases.

The respondents were charged with offences under sections 447, 429 and 379 IPC read with section 39 of the Wild Life Protection Act, 1972. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence and issued process to the accused. The respondents moved the High Court under section 482 Cr. P.C., 1973 for quashing the proceedings against them on the ground that they were not named in the complaint as they had no knowledge of the offences alleged. The High Court quashed the proceedings holding that the Magistrate had jurisdiction to take cognizance of an offence under sec. 9(1) read with Section 50(l) of the Act, and ordered issue of process to them.
