In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the complaint did not spell out the ingrediants of the alleged offences; that the offence envisaged by section 9(2) read along with sec. 50(1), Cr.P.C. in its ingredients and content, is the same or substantially the same as Sec. 429 IPC and that after due investigation and police had filed a final report that no offence was made out and that initiation of any fresh proceedings against respondents would be impermissible. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The cognizance of offences under secs. 9 (1) and 5(2), read with sec tion 50(I) of 'the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1973, is much wider than the one under section 42 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [467B] 1.2 In order that the prohibition is attracted the same act must constitute an offence of a different nature. If there two distinct and separate offences with different ingredients under two different enactments, a double punishment is not barred. [468F] 1:3. The proviso to section 56 has also a familiar ring and is a facet of the fundamental and salutory principles that permeate penalies and reflected in analogous provisions of sec. 300 of the Cr. Procedure Code, 1973 and constitutionally guaranteed under article 20(2). Provision as to offences punishable under two or more enactments is much narrower than Sec. 430 IPC and it is not a facet or preju dence of salutory provisions. [466D E] 1 :4. The expression "any act or omission which constitutes any offence under this Act" in sec. 56, means any act or omissions which constitute an offi cial offence under another law and therefore, the offences are the same i.e. they should be identical. If the two offences are distinct and different offences with separate ingredients under both different enactments a double sentence is not prohibited. [470E F] 1 5. The ingredients of an act or an omission can amount to and constitute an offences under the IPC and at the same time constitute an an offence u/s 9(i) read Section 50 (1). [470F G] 1 6. The offence envisaged in sec tion 9(I), read along Sec. 50 (l) is the offence of substantially the same offence. [471G H] 7. The offences under section 9, I.P .C., read with Sec.50(l), I. P .C. and Sec. 5(1)(a) of Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 are distinct offences.

The petitioner, a member of the Muslim community, was convicted for non bailable offences under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced to death on his brother 's appeal. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to life imprisonment. In the special leave petition it was contended that the petitioner 's brother had been treated alike by the State of Gujarat and the jailed defendant lost his job because of the denial of bail; that he and his assets were in a very large number of defendants interviewed could be recommended for release without sureties, and that the jailised defendant loses his job and is not available to defend himself. Dismissing the special Leave Petition, ^ HELD: 1. The petitioner ' s brother in law was not entitled to get bail on his own bond. [343G] 2. The State of Maharashtra has a long history of equal justice under article 6 of the Constitution. It is a well settled principle that the victims of an offence when bail is refused are not bound to attend at the appointed place. They cannot be compelled to participate in the trial if during trial when the presence to instruct lawyers is more necessary, an accused must buy release only with sureties while at the appellate level, suretyship is expendable, there is unreasonable restriction on personal liberty with discrimination writ on the provisions. [344H; 345A B] 3. The constitutional obligation of bail covers both release on one 's own bond and the candle stick maker shall be added the bonded labour and pavement dweller. To add insult to injury, the magistrate has demanded sureties from his own district. He may not know any one there and might have come in a batch or to seek a job or in a morcha. What law prescribes the geographical discrimination implicit in asking for sureties from the court district? [344C D] 4. The hornet 's nest of Part 111 need not be provoked it read ' lockers ' to mean that it popularly docs, and lexically and in American Jurisprudence is stated to Mean, viz., a generic expression used to describe judicial release from custodia. To addition insult to injuries, the Magistrate has demanded bail on the petitioner on his self bond without sureties. [345E F] 5. The court of appeal may release a convict on his personal bond without surety. Surely it cannot be that an under trial is worse of than a convict or that the power of the court to release increases when the guilt is established. It does not mean that an uneduced section of Part III need not he provoked. [346G H] 6. The judicialist frontiers of the Central Provinces and Berar are governed by the law, not the money tag. If the indigents are not to be betrayed by the Law including bail law re writing of many processual laws is in urgent desideratum; and the judiciary will do well to remember that the geo legal frontiers of Centralodes cannot be disfigured by cartographic dissection in the name of language of province. [347B C] 7. The jornet, 's Nestle 's case, referred to.

The assessee, a registered firm, had at different places in India branches one of which was an industrial undertaking conducted in the name of Eldee Velvet and Silk Mills called for the sake of brevity. In the assessment year 1951 52 the assessee claimed under section 15C of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 exemption from tax in respect of six% of its capital employed in 'Eldee ' as a newly established undertaking and sought to include in the computation of capital invested for the purpose of section 15 C. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the assessee had not been computed and included in the assessment of the assessee. But the Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the assessee 's claim. but the Tribunal modified the assessment by directing the Tribunal to state the case and refer it to the High Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The finding of the Tribunal that the income from 'Castle ' had not be computed and not included in its assessment was not conclusive. [429 A B] (1) The Tribunal erred in holding that the finding of fact was one of fact as it was based on the inference arising from non inclusion by the Income tax officer in the assess ment in question of the income of 'Cantle ' and that "the factor taken into consideration by the Appellate Tribunal in coming to its conclusion, was a relevant factor. [ 430 C D] (2) The finding that the constitution and ownership of the two businesses were the same, could not be regarded as a finding not giving rise to a question liable to be referred to the Court. Non inclusion of the Income of 'castle in the income, of 'Erdt ' in the present case, was merely an industrial dispute between the assessee and its employees.

The Minister in charge of Irrigation Department was impleaded as a party in the writ petition filed by him. The Minister concerned filed an affidavit stating that he had dealt with the matter directly and by passed the Secretary of the Department. The High Court allowed the petition on the ground that the Minister was not a necessary party to file the affidavit. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Minister in Charge of Irrigation department is directed to decide in the light of the allegations made in the petition as to whether he should or should not file an affidavit. [97 D] (ii) The High court was in error in directing that the minister be impleaded as party. [96 E F] (iii) The direction for impleading of the Minister as a necessary respondent was given by the High Court with a view to apprise the Minister of the allegation made in his petition and thus to afford him an opportunity of controverting those allegations, if he so deemed proper. Taking the totality of facts and circumstances of the case, the High court should not interfere with the order of the High Courts adding the Minister to the writ petitioner 's petition. [98 F G] (iv) The Secretary of Department is directed not to file an affidavits. [99 A B] (v) The order passed by the Court in the present case was set aside and the Minister concerned was directed to file his affidavit. The Secretary should also file his personal affidavit. If he so required, the Minister should file his own affidavit.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. The respondent filed an application under section 259 of the Cantonment Act for recovery of arrears of rent on the ground that the amount was due as arrears of land revenue and not as arrears within the meaning of section 259. The Magistrate held that he had no jurisdiction to recover the arrears of the rent due under a lease. On appeal, the Sessions Judge set aside the order of the Magistrate but the High Court in revision set aside that order holding that the expression "recoverable by a Board" in section 259 meant only a sum which was recoverable by the Board and not a sum payable by the respondent to the Board. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that (i) the words "recoversable by the board" in the definition of "recognition" refer to something of that kind which is recoverable under section 258 as otherwise the amendment would be meaningless; and (ii) the expression 'recoverables by a board ' or the Military Estate Officer under this Act or the rules made thereunder should not be given a restricted meaning. HELD : The words " recoversable under the Act" in s.259 of the Act refer to anything done by the committee committee or the Board, and they are not intended to include money due under an ordinary contract between the Cantonment Authority and others. [346 C] (i)(a) The word 'rent ' is used in section 258(1) in its widest sense and includes all payments made for services rendered by a committee under this section. Therefore, where rent of land or building under the management of the Board falls to be recovered, resort could be had either to a suit or to summary proceeding as provided in the section. [347 B] (b) The words 'recovers ' and 'recovered by the Act ' are not used in any other sense but are intended to be included in that expression in section 264. Therefore where the liability to pay money arises against a person by reason of something done by him as Committee or the military Estate Officer in exercise of a power or the performance of duty under the statute, that liability can be enforced by the authority concerned either by instituting the suit or by making an application to a Magistrate.

The appellant was appointed as a Section Salesman in the respondent company on 12th July, 1973. The services of the appellant were controlled by the head office through its territory office situated at Delhi. Section salesman neither sells nor collects any money from the wholesaler or retail dealer to sell the products of the Company and to collect the amount of sale. The section salesmen and local salesmen were employed by the company in order to canvass and promote the sales of the company. From perusal of the records produced before the Labour Court it was found that the appellant was employed for canvassing and pushing and promoting the sales. On these facts, the Tribunal held that the appel lant was not a "workman" within the meaning of the Industrial Disputes Act. The High Court also held that there was no violation of the provisions of the Act. In appeal to this Court it is contended on behalf of the appell lant that the finding of the Tribu nal on the nature of the work is a finding on a question of fact and it is not applicable to him and in view of the fact that a long period of over 16 years had passed, it would be unjust to leave the appellant without any remedy at this stage. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The finding of fact arrived at by the Labour court on the question whether the appellant is a " workman" is not sustainable. [474F] 2.1 A person cannot be termed as a workman is also the ratio of the decision of this Court in Burmah Shell Oil Storage and Distribution Company vs Burmah shell Management and Staff; , ; D.S. Nagraj vs Labour Officer, Kamal and others, 1973 F.J.R. (42) P. 440, referred to. 2.2 The finding that the workman is employed for manual, skilled, unskilled and/or clerical nature and that the provisions Of the Industrial Dispute Act was not applicable is not a case of the employer being a workman. [473G H] Burmahuri Shell Oil storage and Distribution Co. vs Burmahu Shell Management and staff; , , referred to and distinguished.

The respondent Company, a company registered under the M.P. Land Revenue Code, 1959, was granted lease of land for a period of one year in Samvat 1999. The lease was extended for a further period of ten years in Samwat 2007. When proceedings were initiated on 16.7.1952 to eject the Company, the Company filed Suit No. 14 of 1960 for declaration of title and perpetual injunction. The Additional Collector passed an order dated 1.10.1977 holding that the land was held by the Company under lease from the Government after it had been acquired by the Government for a public purpose of the State. The Company preferred an appeal before the Collector, who set aside the order of the Additional Collector and dismissed the Company 's appeal. The High Court in Second Appeal reversed the decision of the trial court and held that the Company was not a 'pakka ' tenant within the meaning of section 181 of the M .P. land Revenue Code 1959. In the appeal to this Court, on behalf of the Company it was contended that the company was not an occupancy tenant under section 185 of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, Samvat 2007, as it had not become an ordinary tenant earlier in Madhya Bharat under Act 66 of 1950. Allowing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The finding of the High Court to the contrary was totally unjustified and opposed to law. [179F] 2.1 A 'Government lessee ' is defined under the Madhya Pravat 2007 Act as "a person holding land from the State Government under section 181", Section 181 of Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. It is to be noticed that prior to the withdrawal of the appeal from this Court against the order dated January 10, 1977, fresh terms were agreed upon between the Company and the Government to enable the Com mission to remain in possession of the land as a lessee. The company was thus a person holding the land from State Government. This is so whether or not the Company is deemed to be holding over under the old lease or holding, upon termination of that lease under and in terms of the fresh conditions agreed upon. [180G H; 181A] 2:2 A ' Govern lessee ' as defined under Madhya Pradesh Act 66of 1950 as "an ordinary tenant" means a tenant who has been or whose predecessor in interest had been lawfully recorded in respect of his holding as a `Ryot Pattedar ', `Mamuli Maurusi ' and `Pukhta Maurushi ' when this Act comes into force or who may in future be duly recognised as such by a competent authority. Explanation 1 to section 181 provides that no order for ejectment of a Government lessee under this sub section shall be passed without giving him an opportunity of being heard in his defence.

The Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1960 was enacted by the State Legislature to provide for the acquisition of any land in an estate under section 45 of the principal Act. The object of the Act was to ensure agrarian reform and the lands held by the petitioners were "estates" within the meaning of article 31 A of the Constitution. By virtue of section 45, the interests of persons to whom the surplus lands relate and of all land holders mediately or immediately under whom the excess lands were being held are vested in the Government free from all encumbrances. The Act was not repealed by a notification issued under section 1(3) of the Principal Act which provided for payment of compensation at a rate which is less than the market value of the land falling within the ceiling limit as originally fixed under the Act and the guarantee of the second proviso to article 31A of the Constitu tion. The petitioners challenged the validity of the provisions of the impugned Act on the ground that it was inconsistent with or takes away or abridges any of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III of the constitution, and that the Act did not fall within the protection of article 19(1)(f) of that Constitution. Held: (i) The right to compensation which is not less than tho market value under any law providing for the acquisi tion by the state of any estate in an Estate in the personal cultivation of a person is guaranteed by the second Proviso only where the land is within the Ceiling limit applicable to him under any laws for the time being in force. The expression "law in force" must be interpreted as meaning "a law in operation in a constitutional sense". (ii) The power to repeal or amend the Act incorporated in the Ninth Schedule was not a law in force when the Act came into force and therefore the State could not claim protection of Article 31 B. The right of compensation which was not less then the market price under any statute providing for acquisition by the Government of any 'estate in an estates in the Personal cultivation of the holder, was guaranteed by this second proviso only where land is outside the ceiling area applicable to he holder under anylaw for the lime being in existence. (iii) The expression 'law in the force ' occurring in article 31 B(1) includes a law which is deemed to be law in the operation of the law providing that it shall not be lawful for the State to acquire any portion of such land as is within tho ceiling limit applicable under any other law providing, for the property acquired and either fixes the amount of compensation or specifies the principles on which, and the manner in which, the compensation is to be determined and given. (iv) The contention that provisions of Act 13 of 1965 which by a Notification could have been but were not brought into force must still be deemed to have been law in existence when the State Government came into existence was rejected.

The widow of her husband, who had inherited the property from his widow, was in possession of it by adverse possession against the widow. The widow obtained a decree for possession of the properties belonging to the last male owner during her lifetime and the widow having lost whatever interest she had in her husband 's estate, the deed of surrender executed by her did not become infructuous or inoperative thereby. The question was whether the widow could claim possession of those properties from the widow on the basis of the deed dated May 18, 1941, which was a registered one. Held, that the widow was entitled to recover possession of these properties from her husband and the order of the High Court was correct. Section 14(1) of the Hindu Law of surrender by a Hindu widow does not recognise any transfer of property made by a widow in excess of her powers but by reason of the opinion expressed by all the Smriti writers that the Hindu widow should live a life of moderation and cannot have any power of gift, sale or mortgage except for religious or spiritual purposes. The provisions of section 14(2) do not justify the inference that in case of alienation by a female the limited interest of a Hindu dying intestate has been lost by her death and the reversioner has no such interest as she can convey to others. Section 15(1)(a) does not contemplate any surrender of property by a husband against his widow but only when he has made an alienation without any legal necessity, or in the case of a stranger acquiring title by adverse Possession against her. The effect of the surrender is to destroy the widow 's rights in the property in the same way as if she suffered physical or civil death.

The appellant company was incorporated in the erstwhile princely State of Uttar Pradesh. The respondent No. 1, who was the Chairman and Managing Director of the Cotton Mills Company Ltd., filed a petition under sections 397 and 398 of the for winding up of the Mill on the ground that the appellant had committed oppression and mismanagement in its factory by reason of the appointment of a Receiver in respect of the shares held by it in the Polytex Company. The appellant contended that the extraordinary general meeting of the Swadeshi Cotton Mills Ltd., was not validly called since the Cotton mills company had ceased to enjoy the privileges of a member of the Polycess Company by reason only of the appoint ment of a receiver in respect thereof and that the shares were not liable to be taken into consideration for determining the required qualification to issue the notice under section 169 of the Act. The Collector appointed Receiver in favour of the appellant company. The order was confirmed by the Collector who held that the appointment was without jurisdiction. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the order of the Collector appointing a Receiver was not passed in accordance with the provisions of section 169 and that if those shares were omitted from consideration then the shares had to be deemed to have been allotted to the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the extraordinary General meeting had not been validly called as since the cotton Mills Company had ceased lo enjoy the benefits of a members of the polycess company by reason or the appointment Of a Receiver under section 153 of the Land Revenue Act read with section 5 of the U.P. Government Electrical Undertakings (Dueling of Undertakings) Act, 1951; and (ii) the requisition of a fresh public notice was not in accordance to the provisions contained in section 169(2) of the land Revenue Act as an attachment of the share under section 149 of the I.P .C. was not made by the order dated April 13, 1978. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power of the Company and its directors to deal with the property comprised in the appointment (both property subject to a floating charge and property subject only to a fixed charge) except under certain circumstances and conditions is not of much use to them. [887D] 2.1 The order of attachment cannot, therefore, have the effect of depriving the holder of the beneficial interest of his title to the shares.

The petitioners, who were owners of the suit land, filed a suit for declaration that they were owners in possession of the same. The Gram Panchayat, had also pleaded that the land was shamlat deh and it had been vested in it. The trial court framed an issue relating to its jurisdiction and tried it as a preliminary issue. It held that since the question involved in the suit was simply one of title to the suit property and it was not necessary to decide whether the suit lands were shamlat or not, and whether the land had validly vested in the Panchayat or not being shamlat ter, it had jurisdiction to try it. In appeal by the Panchayat, the High Court held that the issues involved in a suit were not triable by a civil court by virtue of section 11 read with section 13 of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961 and accordingly dismissed the revision petition. Dismissing the Special Leave Petition, ^ HELD: 1. The petitioners had failed to establish that the suit Land was shamat deh or not and whether it belonged to the Panchayat. [834C] 2. Section 11 of the Act provides that any person claiming right, title or interest in any land vested or deemed to have been vested under the Act, or claims that any land has not so vested in a Panchayat may submit to the Collector, within such time as may be prescribed, a statement of his claim in writing and signed and verified in the prescribed manner and that the Collector shall have jurisdiction to decide such claim in such manner as may he prescribed. Any person or a Panchayat aggrieved by an order of the Collector is entitled to prefer an appeal to the Commissioner. Under section 12 of the Haryana Village Common Land (Regulation), (Amendment) Act 1976, the right of the person claiming rights, title and interest in shamlat land was not shamlat lanted but the plaintiff had questioned the correctness of entries in the revenue records which showed that the Panchayat was entitled to the Suit land. The plaintiffs cannot by drawing their plaint cleverly by not claiming a declaration that the lands in question were not shamat ties deh or that they had no right or title in it, and that they could not by way of appeal or revision or in any original suit, application or execution proceedings. [884D E] Bhagu and Ors., vs Ram Sarup and Ors. ; , referred to.

The respondent Board, a public limited company, had been granted licence to establish a new industrial unit for the supply of electricity to its consumers. The Board was also granted a licence for the period from 1st April, 1985 to 31st March, 1985. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Electricity Supply (Supply) Regulations, 1981 and the order of the State Government dated 5th May, 1986. The High Court held that the Board had power to demand additional security but the Board was not entitled to adjust its tariffs against the bills. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant Board that the Electricity Board was in the position of a trustee in respect of this money since the money is deposited by the consumers in trust with the Board to secure the Board against default in payment of interest and that the conditions on which it is supplied being statutory, the provisions under the conditions of supply would be attracted and the Board could not charge penal interest at 2% per month for non payment of bills within the stipulated period. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Electricity Supply Act, 1948 clearly indicates that the board may supply electricity to any person upon such terms and conditions as laid down in the regulations. It also requires to be noted that the supply is in the nature of a security deposit representing the moneys of the Board. [273F] 2.1 The Board has been conferred statutory power under section 49(1) of the Act to determine the conditions for supply of electric energy and to give effect to any money payable by it to the Board on credit being made against the consumer. The condition of supply requiring a consumption security deposit has a direct bearing on the operations of the board which are to be conducted in such a manner as to ensure a surplus. [272G H] 2:2 In the case of daily supply of electrical energy there is a consequential liability to pay for each day 's consumption of electricity. Therefore, it is not necessary that the consumer should pay interest on the security deposit. The conditions of Supply are to secure payment of consumption charges. [274A B] 3.1 It is well settled that if there is an upward revision in the rate of tariff there must be an upward revisions in the consumption security deposits since it has direct bearing to the level of supply in consumption of Electricity. The revising authority has to ensure that the intentions of Parliament shall not be defeated a law is enacted which operates somewhat harshly on a small section of the public, taken in conjunction with the position that without a law in that form and with that amplitude smuggling might not be possible of being effectively checked, the question arises whether the law could be held to be violative of the freedom guaranteed by article 19(1)(f) & (g). [273D E] 3:2. The nature of consumption deposit is to secure prompt payment and is intended for appropriation. [275E F] 3 :3. In the instant case, the respondent Board has fixed the period of security deposit equal to the amount of energy consumed for a period of two months. It is not in dispute that the appellant has been given a right to adjust the tariffs for the purpose of the respondent Electricity Board 's finance. The appellant Board has clearly stipulated that no interest shall be payable on the securities furnished to the respondent credit to the Electricity Committee. [278F G] 4. The security amount should bear the same interest as admissible on fixed deposits of Scheduled Banks for a term of years and this would depend upon the monetary stability of the consumers. [279G H; 280A B, F] 5.

The petitioners in these petitions were working as officers in the Telecommunication Research Centre in the Telenganga Research Centre. They were promoted to the posts of S&TOs Grade I in the Telephone Department on the basis of Special Pay Rules, 1962. The Class I posts in the Telegraph Department were filled by direct recruitment through the Union Public Service Commission and the Recruitment Rules were framed by the President under Article 309 of the Constitution of India. During the period between 1956 and 1962, there was consensus on the question of granting special pay to the direct recruits as in the case of transferred officers as can be seen from the letter written by the Association on behalf of the Department of Posts and also by transfer of Group A posts. The petitioners were recruited in four batches in 1965, 1967 and 1973. They filed writ petitions challenging the said rules. During 21st and 22nd October, 1962, they were recruited by direct recruit through the UPSC after a rigorous competition examination followed by an interview held in May 1979 with Shri J.A. Dave Secretary, Communications, Government of India, there being consensus on these questions, the Central Administrative Tribunal dismissed them. In these petitions, it was contended that the petitioners were not competent to claim Special Pay as they had been appointed to the Telegraph Engineering Research Centre for a limited purpose and therefore could not be considered by the Central Adminis trative Tribunal. Dismissing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The direct recruits (to which category the petitioners belonged) in the telephone Research Centre are entitled to the Special Pay at the same rates at which it is paid to the transferred officers working in that centre with effect from the date from which the transferred officer have been drawing the Special pay. [1013C D] 2.1 The Central Administrative Tribu nal has virtually admitted that all relevant things such as qualifi cations, functions, duties and responsibilities are the same as between direct recruits and transferred officials and that the transferred officials had to be paid extra amount by way of Special pay in addition to their scale of pay which is the same. [10lB C] 2:2 The Indian Telecommunication Service Officers who are working in the telecommuni cation Research Centre were being given Special Pay of Rs. 300, Rs. 200 and Rs. 150 per month in addition tO their scale in the grades of Deputy Director, Assistant Director and Scientific and Technical Officers Grade I respectively with effect on the date of transfer of officers commenced to draw the SpecialPay upto date and to continue to pay it in future also as long as the transferred Officers continue to get it.

The appellant, a munshi in the Bidhishi factor at Bhandara, was appointed as an employee of the respondent company. He filed an application before the Labour Court under section 33(1) of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946, praying for reinstatement and payment of all back wages. The Labour Court held that the charge sheet served on the respondent was not proper and that the finding of the enquiry officer was perverse. On appeal by the State Government, the High Court confirmed the order of the Labour court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the third respondent had failed to comply with the provisions of section 42(1), because he did not make an application under section 82, and (ii) the finding was perverse as the order was based on no evidence and was vitiated by a manifest error of law. HELD : (i). The scheme of Chapter VIII is that in regard to any "change" in an matter there must be compliance with the provi sions of that chapter. In other words, effort must first be made by the employer intending to effect any change in respect of matters covered by section 42 (1) or an employee desiring a change in the industrial matter specified in Schedule III except item (5), thereof and matters arising out of such change; and if no application is made under section 83, the Court can only exercise such jurisdiction as the statute confers on it. If there are certain pre conditions to the exercise of its jurisdiction, it must refuse to entertain any such application unless such pre conditions are first complied with. [738 C D] (ii). The Scheme of ChapterVIII seems to be that disputes should be settled as far as possible and primarily through conciliation and agreement, it does not stand to reason that an employee should be able to side step all this by a direct reference to the Labour. Court. A Labour Court is a creature of the statute and it can only exercised such jurisdiction which if there are some pre conditions, to the exercises of its juris diction, it cannot refuse to entertained any such applications unless such Pre conditions arefirst complied with.[738 E F] (iii). The Statement of Objects and Reasons appended to the Schedule to the Act shows that the underlying dea was to enlarge the powers of the labour court. [ 738 C D].

The appellants filed an application under section 12 of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947 before the Munsif, Ranchi for eviction on the ground that they were the successors in interest of the lessor company. The respondents contested the said application contending that the appellants were the heirs and successors ininterest of the landlord company and that the tenancy was governed by section 12(3) of the Act. The Munsif allowed the application holding that the respondents were the successor in interest and the legal representatives of the deceased tenant, and that they had formed a partnership, as a result of which a new month to month tenancy was created, and the respondents could not be liable to eviction. The appellants filed revision before the Patna High Court, but the same was dismissed by the Judicial Commissioner. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the application under Section 12 was not maintainable as the respondents had not sought an extension of the term of tenancy; and (ii) the respondents, by their notice dated 16th July 1971, did not seek an extension for filing a suit under section 11 of the said Act. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The question does not affect the substantive right of the parties as the controversy was concluded by the first appellate court in favour of the appellant. What was left was only procedural in nature and inconsistent with its decision to treat the proceedings as a suit. [975C] 2.1 A similar approach was adopted in several cases decided by some High Courts and this Court in another case, held that the scope in which the proceeding under section II and an application for eviction are addressed to several authorities for decision of different issues, one of them being Control ler as defined in Section 2(b) of Act, and another 'Court as the court of general jurisdiction under the Code of Civil Procedure, as defined under section 2(bb). So far as the determination and redetermination of fair rent or issuing appro priate directions relating to amenities in the premises and several other matters are concerned, the power is vested in the Controller. But as regards the question of dealing with the eviction of tenants under section11 and extension of period of lease under section12, the civil court is the proper forum. [ 975D E] 2:2. The scope of the proceeding arising out of the appel lant 's application before the Munsiff should be treated as a plaint and the order passed by the Munsif as a decree therein. A further question may arise as to the effect of the Judicial Commis sion, Ranchi declining to pass a formal decree of eviction and directing the appellants to make an application tinder section 12 (3) for that purpose. [978B C] 2 :3. The High Court was right in holding otherwise. [979E F] 2(a).

The appellant, a registered society, filed a suit for declaration of his immovable property through its then Secretary. The trial court allowed the suit to be withdrawn and the suit was dismissed. In appeal, the High Court held that the application under section 15 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not maintainable. Allowing the appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) A court has inherent power to correct its own proceedings when it is satisfied that in passing a particular order it was misled by one of the parties. The principle was correctly discussed in Sadho Saran Rai and Others vs Anant Rai and Ors., AIR 1923 Patna 483. [238A] (2) In Vilakathala Raman vs Vayalil dilutegowda Yogangowda Yogagowda & Anr., I.L.R. 34 Bombay 408, the defendant applied to the court to set aside a compromise decree on the ground that he did not give his consent. The High Court was right in holding that the only remedy of the appellant is to file a fresh suit. [239C D] (3) In the instant case, the trial court had vacated its previous order regarding satisfaction of decree on ground that the same was obtained by the judgment debtor 's fraud on the court. The lower appellate court was clearly wrong in dismissing the appellant 's application as not maintainable, and the High court should have exercised its revisional power on the basis that the trial Court had failed to exercise a jurisdiction vested in it by law. [240D E] Sadho Sharan Rai and others vs Anant Raj and Others, AIR 1923 Pat 483; Vilkatha Raman vsVayalil Kochu, 27 Madras Law Jour nal Reports 172; Vlakathara Raman vs Vasanarayanappa, AIR 1924 Patna 483; Basangowda Hanmantgowda Patil and Others v Churchigirigowda Yoganagowda & Another, I. L.R . 34 Bombay 407, referred to.

The appellant was convicted under section 7 read with section 4 of the Ordinance read with s.109 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 1,800 in default to suffer six months ' rigorous imprisonment. The prosecution case against him was that on June 27, 1940, he was charged along with two others for offences under sections 7 and 8 of the ordinance read with sections 109 and 109 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. On July 11, 1953, the appellant was tried by the Additional Chief Presidency Magistrate, Bombay, and convicted and sentenced by the Sessions Judge, Bombay. The High Court on appeal held that the Ordinance was not in operation at the date when the offence was committed and that therefore the prosecution was not maintainable. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) as soon as the declaration of emergency under section 72 of the Act was made the original position was restored, the period specified in section 3 of the said Act for the original six months period and that accordingly on the expiration of that period the offence had to be deemed to have been in operation. HELD : (i)(a) The Ordinance in question having been promulgated during the period between June 27 and April 1, 1946, was perpetual in duration and continued in force until it was repealed. It was not a law to continue in force after April 1. 1946, when the Act came into force. [645 B] (b) The words " for the space of not more than six months from its promulgation" in section 72 were omitted from section 72 by section 26A and the Ordinance in effect continued in operation until it is repealed. The effect of such omission was that Ordinances promulgated under that sub section during the periods specified in s.3 of the , were subject to no time limit as regards their existence and validity unless imposed by the Ordinances themselves, or other amending or repealing legislation, whether by Ordinance or otherwise. [643 C] (c) The provisions of section 72 as they stood before the amendment of 1949 did not apply to the State of Jammu and Kashmir as the Ordinance had been promulgated in exercise of the emergency powers vested in him under section 73 of the 9th Sch. of the Government of India Act, 1935, and the effect of the omission of the words "for the space" in the sub section was that Ordinance No. III of 1946 was not applicable to the area which was committed by the appellant and the appellant could not be convicted for the period of the space specified in the section.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., and sentenced to death by the Additional Sessions Judge, on appeal, by the High Court of Punjab. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that: (1) the death sentence imposed upon them was not justified or legal; (2) the High court erred in confirming the death penalty on the ground that death sentence was unmerited; and (3) the sentence of death passed against each of them by the Sessions Judge is also illegal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The judgment under appeal is a hint of the judicial interpretation of section 354(3) Cr. P.C. and must be set aside. [1073G] 2.1 Section 302 I. P .C., gives a choice while section 354 (3), Cr.P C. merely requires 'special reasons ' to the indicated for imposing the death punishment. The question whether the death sentences should be awarded or not must, in the absence of any specific indication in that behalf 'special reason ' would relate both to the crime as such but to the criminal. [ 1073H; 1074A] 2:2. In the instant case, the High Courts were justified in confirming death sentence passed under section 368(1) and the sentence was confirmed by this Court. [1014B] 3. The judicial interpretation at the sentencing stage has been a functional failure because of the casual way the punishment factors are dealt with, as if the nature of crime was the sole determinant of the punishment. It is not within the province of the court while dealing with an appeal confined to sentence under article 136 to curtail the scope of death sentence. [1004C] Rajendra Prasad vs State of Bihar, ; , followed. The Court in its majority judgment has laid down that the ratio decidendi of Rajendra Prasad 's case is the material element in the decision for it determines finally their rights and liabilities in relation to the subject matter of the action. [1000D E] 3:1. The legislative wisdom made in Rajendra Prasad case is essentially a legislative, not a judicial function. It has been entrusted with a duty to record reasons and pass such orders as are necessary or desirable to do so. But the question whether death sentence should be passed or not need not depend upon the facts and circumstances of each particular case and the law applicable. [1001E] 3 :2. The legal position is essentially that the Court will have no sympathy for these trigger happy gentlemen and the sentences imposed on them are well merited. [1:3. The sentence of life imprisonment awarded to the two appellants was neither 'erroneous in principle ' nor 'arbitrary or excessive ', nor 'indicative of an improper exercise of discretion '. Nor does it suffer from any sympathy for those triggerful observations made by this court under article 141 of the Constitution. [1104C D] Rajendra Prashad vs State, ; and Rajendra Prasad & Ors. vs State Of Bihar, , referred to.

The appellant was a direct recruit and was promoted as Income tax Inspector in 1942. He was promoted to the post of Income tax Officer in 1945. His case was that he had worked to the entire satisfaction of his immediate superior officers and higher authorities and had earned a number of certificates highly appreciative of his work. He also claimed that there had been an enquiry in 1949 by the Deputy Director of Investigation who held the enquiry and by the punishing authority. The appellant 's defence was that a fresh enquiry into the same charges was not permissible under the Departmental Rules and was, therefore, barred by rules of natural justice. The departmental authorities rejected his application for a certificate of fitness which was granted by the Commissioner of Income Tax U.P., Lucknow on the ground that he did not have an enquiry into allegations involving corruption and violation of service rules. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant in limine. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: (1) The question whether the appellant was given a reasonable opportunity to lead evidence and to be heard or not is largely a question of fact. It is only when an opportunity denied is of such a nature that the denial contravenes a mandatory provision of law or a rule of natural Justice that it could vitiate the whole departmental trial. [583 F] (2) The appellant was discharged by the disciplinary authority after he had been found guilty and his integrity and sense of justice was not challenged. [584 C D] (3) In any case, the High Court refused to grant certificate of the fitness of the case for appeal to the Supreme Court under article 136 of the Constitution.

The appellants were the last purchasers of manganese ore from mines and minerals. The sales of manga nate ore to the Mines and Minerals Trading Corporation in short called the M.M.T.C. were complete within the State of Andhra Pradesh. The appellants contended that their contracts were inter alia, integrated into direct contracts with their foreign buyer and that they were not the last purchaser within the state, and therefore, the M .M. T.C., was liable to pay tax. The Sales Tax Authorities rejected the contention and held that there existed a bond between the contracts of sale entered into by the appellants with the M/s. M. M & T. C.C.; that the contract of sale occasioned the export and that the contracts were integrally connected with the contract entered into in the course of export, and that therefore, there should be examination of five other contracts. The High Court held that the transactions were inter se between the appellants and the Mm.T., and that there was no privity of contract between the manganese merchants and the foreign buyers from the S.T C.P.C, and the transfer of the goods to the Mimbs was not a sale in the nature of export within the meaning of section 5 of the . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that there were six contracts and it had been the case of the appel lants that the sales were inter interstate sales, that the transaction was integrally linked and connected and the sales effected were held to be sales in the way they were inter state sales; that the Mn. T.,C.P., was the exporter of goods and there was a privity of agreement between the M and the other foreign buyers; that there could not be two imports, and as such, there would be export receipt which he transmits to the buyer and the buyer exchanges this for the proper bill of lading. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The contracts between the appellant and the respondent are inter se, and, therefore, they should be examined by the High Court. [445B] 2.1 The contract between M.T .C. and the appellant is that the merchants were required to bring the goods on board the ship. The M.Ms. T,C. P.W.B., the S & Co., are the only authorities allowed to export out of India. These corporations enter into direct contract with their other foreign buyer. [444D] 2:2 There cannot be two last purchasers in the sale of same goods within the same State. Similarly there cannot be both imports and exports. The transactions between the merchants and M.P, are inter state transactions in the discharge of export. The taking of the good from the merchants ' place to the ship is completely separate from the transit pursuant to the export sale (See Serajuddin vs State of Orissa, ; and Seraju vs State Brothers Ltd., [1975] Supp. S.C R. 169; referred to. 2:3 In the instant case, the contracts between M/S. T & C. P., and the S,T. C., were different contracts and they had been in the present case, both as sales effected by the appellant to the mines and the export of goods out of the territory of India, and there could be two rival parties in the State. These Corporations enter into directly contracts with the foreign buyer, and hence, the transactions entered into directly or through several intermediaries not only did the mill give and its immediate buyer take actual delivery but eo instanti each middleman gave and takes actual delivery. This process of delivery of possession goes all along the chain at the same moment when delivery is made to the steamer. [ 445E F] 2 :4 The contracts entered into between the two companies are different contracts, and it is the S and M only agreed to sell the goods at the rate free on board.

The appellant was employed with the respondent company as Salesman at its Delhi Sales Depot on a salary of Rs. 520 per month from 8th December, 1973. His service was abruptly terminated by letter dated 12th October, 1974. The respondent moved an application before the Labour Court for reinstatement and compensation. The Labour Court held that the termination of the service was in accordance with the standing orders justifying the removal of the employee on unsuccessful probation during the initial or extended period of probation; that the appellant had been a salesman appointed on probation for six months and on the expiry of the probationary period, his service was terminated by notice dated 12.10.1974. The appellant filed an appeal before the Industrial Court which dismissed the same holding that the respondent was not shown to have been placed on probation in the initial appointment letter but in view of the subsequent orders there was a period of the probation prescribed for the appellant and therefore the termination was neither illegal nor improper or unjustified. The High Court, however, held that having regard to the fact that the mandatory pre condition for a valid retrenchment had not been satisfied, the appellant would be entitled to reinstatement with back wages or as contended by him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the mandatory requirement of section 25F for a period ' six months ' notice was not satisfied and (ii) the termination in the instant case was neither in accordance, with the Standing Orders nor in accordance within the meaning of section 2(oo) read with section 25 FF of the Industrial Disputes Act. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The requirement of Section 25F is that the workman should be in continuous service for one year and he will satisfy the eligibility qualification enacted in section 25G. [530D] 1.2 In order to invoke the fiction enacted in sub section 2 (a) it is necessary to determine first the relevant date i.e., the date of termination of service which is complained of as retrenchment. After that date is ascertained, move backward to a period for 12 months just preceding the date with reference to which calculation is to be made, has actually worked under that employer for not less than 240 days. Sub section (2) specifically comprehends a situation where a workman is not in continuous services within the mean ing of sub section (1) for a specified period and, therefore, he is deemed to be in continuously service for a further period of one year if he satisfies the conditions in clause (a). [531E F] 1:3. The requirement under section 25B(2) that the workmen should be continuous in service for not more than one year under that proviso is the core question. It comprehends, a situation when a workman was not in uninterrupted service within the defined period of his employment and he continues to be In continuous service within that meaning for a certain period. [32F G] 1 :4. The termination of services of the appellants does not fall within any of the excepted categories mentioned in section 2.(oo) (1). The requirement is that during the period of 12 calendar months, the workman has rendered service for 240 days within a period Of 12 calendar month and, consequently, his services are terminated for a continuous period of 9 months. [33G H] 1 5.

The appellant was appointed an Inspector of Consolidation by order dated October 5, 1953. He was served with a charge sheet on the ground that he had received Rs. 150/ as illegal gratification from one Darbara Singh and had demanded Rs. 30/ as bribe from one Ude Singh. The appellant submitted his explanation to the charge sheet but the enquiry officer held that the appellant had received the amount of Rs. 300 as illegal money from one N. The Settlement Officer recommended that the services of the appellant be terminated forthwith and in lieu thereof he was asked to show cause why disciplinary action should not be taken against him if the allegations in the charge sheets were proved. The Deputy Commissioner, however, ordered that the service of the respondent be terminated without giving any reason. The order was confirmed by the Government on appeal. The High Court held that it was not necessary for the appellant to give an opportunity to showcause against the order of dismissal and dismissed the petition. Held, that the enquiry against the respondent was for ascertaining whether he was fit to be confirmed. The enquiry was made with the object of ascertaining whether the appellant who was a temporary employee should be continued in service or should be discharged at any time during the period of probation. The fact of the holding of an enquiry is not decisive of the question. A temporary servant may appropriately be regarded as one by way of punishment and he may be entitled to the protection or article 311 (2) of the Constitution. State of Orissa vs Gopi Kishore Prasad, ; , referred to.

The appellant State Government issued a notification dated November 15, 1968 for selections to be made to posts of Professors in the colleges. The Commission was consulted by the Commission and it was brought to its notice that the Commission had considered the cases of the appellants as senior and more qualified persons and recommended their names to the State Government for appointment. It also recommended that it would be open to the appellant to make a fresh selection of Professors. The State Government, however, did not agree with the recommendation. In appeal by certificate, HELD : (i) The Commission had been consulted in regard to the principles to be followed in making appointments to civil services and posts and in making promotions and transfers from one service to another and on the suitability of candidates for such appointments, promotions or transfers. [875 B] (ii) The State Govt. at first framed rules on November 15 1968 for selection to be held to posts in the Colleges. By notification dated June 2, 1969 those rules were replaced by the rules made by the Governor specifically for the appointment of Professors and the second requirement of clause (b) of sub section (2) of section 133 was also complied with. [873 G H] (iii) The selection made by it was invalid for that reason. The selection was not therefore, consultation with the Commission in regard tO the principles set out in the rules. [874 B C] (iv) The High Court erred in taking a contrary view. [878 E F] (v) The Government had to consider the suitability and suitability of the candidates for promotion as Professors on the basis of the recommendations made by them. It was not provided by section 133 that all the members of the Commission should have interviewed all or any of the candi dates, or that it was not permissible for the Commission to entrust the selection to a committee consisting of only one of its members so long as the Commission reserved to itself the right to approve or disapprove the committee 's report and actually discharged that constitutional responsibility. No argument to the contrary had been urged in this Court.

The petitioner, who was the editor of a newspaper, had filed a petition under article 32 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the Speaker 's direction to the Press Commission for the publication of its proceedings. The Speaker issued a notice to show cause why action should not be taken against him for breach of privilege under article 19(1)(a) of the Constitu tion and also for an order that he should not take part in the proceedings of the House or any committee thereof. The petitioner challenged the validity on the ground, inter alia, that the privilege conferred on the Speaker by section 49 of the Act was subject to the provisions of article 19 (2), that the right to publish a true and faithful report of the debates or proceedings that would be taken in the Legislative Assembly of Bihar at the commencement of the constitution of India, that it had all the powers, privileges and immunities enjoyed by the House of Commons at the time of the passing of the said Constitution, that even if the privilege was not expressly made subject to such fundamental rights as were guaranteed by article 19, the petitioner could not be denied a privilege in view of article 194(3) and that the provisions Of article 13(2) and article 194 (3) were not applicable to him. Held, that on a proper construction of article 105(3), the powers privileges and immunity conferred by the said Article must be read subject to those of the fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution and the right guaranteed under article 194 was not confined to any fundamental rights. The expression "the privileges and privileges" in article 19 of the Consti tution means that the privileges, immunities and immunities of a House of Legislature of a State and of members and committees thereof must be such as may from time to time be defined by the legislature by law and that until so defined they shall be those of Parliament. The fundamental right conferred on a Minister of State by article 194 is not subject to any limitation or restriction imposed under clause (2) of article 13, but is subject to reasonable restrictions in the interest of the general public. The privileges and dignities of a member of the Legislature of the United Kingdom have been guaranteed by articles 19(5), 20(3)(a), 21 and 22 of the Covenant of Association of the Government of India dated August 18, 1948, which provided that "the House of the People shall be the supreme authority in respect of all matters with respect to which it is a State. " The fundamental rights conferred on Parliament by article 13 (1) are not absolute and unqualified. Article 194(2), as it was originally enacted, did not make any distinction between the privileges and the immunities enjoyed under the Constitution of India and those enjoyed by members and the committees and committees of a Legislature of that country. The provisions of articles 19 and 20(1) were intended to be in conformity with article 13 and therefore, if such a law had been made, it would have been void to the extent of the contravention of that Article. The Constitution was not intended to make any difference between the fundamental right guaranteed by clause (3), and the fundamental freedom conferred on members and Committees of Parliament under cl. (2). The privileges, privileges, dignities and immunities could be no longer subject to article 19 and were not saved by article 31(2). Article 194 (1)(b) gave freedom of speech and expression to a citizen, while article 194 provided for the right of free speech and assembly to make representation in respect thereof. Article 19(6) was not made subject only to the fundamental freedoms guaranteed under cl.(2), but also to the freedom of association and the members and committee of a legislature of a state. The freedom of expression conferred on certain persons by cls. (1), (3)(b), 21, 22 and 23 of article 195(1), could not therefore be said to infringe that right. Article 20(4) was intended to protect the freedom guaranteed by cl.

The appellant College was established in 1856. The college was affiliated to the State of Orissa. The Government of Orissa took over the management of the College on and from March 9, 1971. The services of the teaching staff of the college were terminated by the Govern ment in exercise of its power under section 5(1) of the Orissa Education Act, 1972. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of termination. The High Court held that the requirement of eight years ' teaching experience as mentioned in the Government Circular was not eight years experience in Class II, Orissa Education Service (O.E.S.). The High court allowed the writ petitions and held that since the appellant had all the requisite qualifications for appointment as Reader and they were all holding the posts of Reader before the take over and five of them were even confirmed Readers, the Government was not entitled to be considered by the Public Service Commission for appointment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Courts erred in directing the State Government to take into account as experience the service of the respondents while they were in the private college since according to them the necessary qualification is eight years, experience in class II, and teaching experience of a specified duration but com pletely no ground was taken in the petition on the basis of these Rules. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have erred in ordering the State Govern ment to take the view that the respondents were not entitled for appointment to the post of Reader as Readers. [778C] 1.2 In the instant case, the Respondents did not satisfy the test of educational qualifications as well as experience of teach ing in a recognised private college. They had to join the new service under the Government, for the first time, and so could be, in that sense fresh entrants. But to say that the teaching experience was completely effaced to the extent that they will not be even eligible, on the plea of absence of teaching experience in Government service, for consideration for appointment, is a seriously grim issue. [781E F] 1:3 The High courts were right in allowing the appellants claim in the writ applications. [780G H] 2.1 All the Respond ents are eligible to be referred to.

The appellants applied for temporary permits under section 68 F(1 C) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939. The U.P. State Road Transport Corporation (Corporation for short) also made an application for grant of three temporary permits for plying their vehicles on routes. The State Transport Authority granted three temporary permit to the appellants. The appellants applied to the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and writ petition was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that since the scheme had been published in view of the provision contained in section 68F(1 A) consequent upon the scheme being published by the Corporation under section 69 C, the Corporation alone could the exclusion of others, is entitled to apply for temporary permit and if such application is made by the corporation and granted no one else was entitled to obtain a temporary permit. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The correct approach would be that keeping in view the strength of the vehicles fixed by the competent authority, the authority should first examine the application for number of temporary permits made by tho Corporation. If the Corporation has made application for temporary applications covering all the vacancies the matter ends there. But if the Corporation does not apply for all the permits but only for some, the inescapable conclusion is that for the remaining strength the Corporation had made no application for the temporary permits and section 68 G(1 D) would be squarely attracted. [985C E] 2. The true scope of the scheme namely, the effect of the service is for the benefit of the travelling public should never be overlooked for a moment. Reverting to the facts of this case if the approach of the High Court was accepted it would lead to a startling result. If there were four vacancies for temporary routes and the Corporation was able to provide only one vehicle and therefore applied for only one permit, according to the state Transport Authority as well as the High court no temporary permit can be granted to any one else. [986F G] 3. The authority under the Act must not ever lose sight of the fact that the primary consideration must be the service available to the travelling Public.

The appellant was the son of a Hindu father. He executed a registered mortgage deed in respect of certain property in favour of his maternal grandfather, the predecessor in interest of the respondents. The mortgage deed provided that the property in suit was ancestral property and he was entitled to challenge its alienation by his father. The trial court held that the transaction was ancestral as it was not ancestral property but was a gift of immovable property and decreed the suit. On appeal the High Court set aside the decree holding that the appellant was not born at the time when the mortgage deed was executed and that the respondents had no right to challenge it. Held, that the question whether a Hindu widow has acquired by birth an interest in her property or not was a mixed question of law and fact and the High court was in error in reversing the decision of the first Full Bench on the point of law. The doctrine of stare decisis is thus stated in Halsbury 's Laws of England (4th Edn.) Vol. 2, p. 879, as follows: "The rule of stareoppel is not so imperative or inflexible as to preclude a departure therefrom in any case but its application must be determined in each case by the discretion of the court and previous decisions should not be followed to the extent that error may be perpetuated and grievous wrong may result. The principle of stare finality is in applicable and should present no obstacle in holding that earlier cases of the Full Bench of the Punjab High Court were not correctly decided. Attar Singh vs Thakar Singh, (1937) L.R. 35 I.A. 110, relied on.

The appellants were tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Birbhum for offences under sections 449 and 307/34 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on the night of the 14th November, 1950 when Haji Ebrar Ali was sleeping on his hut, these appellants entered Ebr Ali 's house with the common intention of killing him and some of them held him down. Fortunately, the injury inflicted on Ebri Ali did not prove fatal. The Sessions Judge accepted that verdict and convicted them all under sections 448 and 307 read with section 34 of the Code. On appeal by the appellants the High Court acquitted them but convicted them under section 302/34 I.P.C. and sentenced them to rigorous imprisonment for four years under section 307/149. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that there could be no conviction under section 449 unless murder had actually been committed and that a charge under section307 read with s 34 of Indian Penal code is not sustainable in law. HELD : The fact that the murder was not actually committed will not affect the applicability of section 449 of the I. P.C., [982 B] Section 449 of I.p.C runs thus: "Whoever does any act with such intention or knowledge and under such circumstances that if he by that act caused death, he would be guilty of murder shall be punished with imprisonment for life". The word "in order to" has been used in the two succeeding sections, namely, 450, 451 and again in section 454 and section 457 of the Penal Code, which makes punishable the commission of an offence of house trespass if it is done "in the order to the committing of any offence punishable with imprisonment. [983 E G] In the present case when it was found that the four appellants attacked Haji E brar Ali in furtherance of the common object of all of them to kill him and others held him on the basis of one used the dagger on him, each of the four is in law considered to have done the entire act of holding Ebris Ali down and applying the dagger. If Matiullah by himself had held Ebirs Ali down, and struck him with the dagger, with the intention of causing his death and the injury had actually resulted in his death, then he would have been guilty of offence under section 448 read with Section 34 of I P. C.

The appellant was the daughter of one Harnam Singh who died in 1947 leaving behind his widow Musammat and a daughter Musamm Devi. The respondent contested the suit on the ground that the suit for declaration of title to the properties was maintainable as all the lands in suit were not ancestral, and that there was no custom whereunder collaterals of the last male holder excluded the daughter from succession to the self acquired property of her father. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed the decree holding that the appellant had discharged the initial onus that was on him by producing in evidence the Riwaj i am of Gurdaspur district prepared by Mr. Kennaway in 1913 and 1893, and the statement made by him in the Rwsid case showed that he had discharged this initial burden to rebut the presumption arising on these Riws. The High Court also held that the evidence as to the succession to property of Harnam Singh was reliable and trustworthy and could not displace the initial presumption of the general custom recorded in Rattigan 's book so as to shift the onus to the daughter who is the res pondent. Held, that the statement in the appellant 's favour must be accepted and the appeal must fail. The evidence on record showed that the collaterals were not excluded from succession by the collateral. The custom as recorded in the Rattigans was consistent with the general agricultural custom of the province. The statements in a Riwaji am of the Gurdaspur District prepared by the latter in 1913, did not prevail and could be regarded as reliable or trustworthy document. The statement in a riwaj is not a reliable or truthful document and cannot displace the basic custom of a district in which collaterals excluded the collateral from succession. The appellant had failed to discharge the onus that had been cast on him to displace the general customs recorded in paragraph 23 of Rattigyan 's Digest of Customary Law.

The respondent, who was the Managing Agent of several companies and had on occasions acted as an agent of several Companies registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, entered into a power of attorney in respect of certain properties which fell under two categories, namely, (1) property which fell within two categories being immovable property, and (2) other investments. The respondent filed a suit for partition against the appellant on the ground that the power of Attorney was not properly stamped. The trial court held that the instrument contained distinct matters and that the proper duty payable on the instrument was Rs. 10 under article 48(d)(1) of Schedule 1 A of the Stamp Act, 1899, as amended by section 13 Of the Indian Stamp Act. On appeal the High Court set aside the decree holding that the instruments were not properly chargeable with the aggregate amount of duty payable in respect thereof and that they were not chargeable with a duty of one rupee. Held, that the words "distinct matters" occurring in section 5 of the Indian stamp Act, 1908, are wide enough to include allmatters which form part of the same description as those relating to immovable property. The question whether a power is of attorney or a combination of several of them depends on the terms of the instrument and the nature and extent of the authority conferred thereby. The words "contrary to law" in section 4 Of the Act are not defined in the Indian Penal Code, but they have been used in a sense different from those which are used in the same sense as if different persons join in executing a power in respect Of matters which are unrelated. In the present case the instrument did not contain distinct matters but consisted of one matter only and that matter was the execution of a general power of agreement by the donor in favour of the donees constituting the donee. The document in question cannot be split up into separate instruments each comprising or relating to a distinct matter in so far as the different capacities of the donor are concerned.

The assessee firm was a company in the erstwhile State of Saurashtra. The profits of business by the two appellants were assessed to income tax for the year 1949 50 under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. In assessing the profits of the business by two of the appellants companies for the years 1949 50 and 1949 50 the Income tax Officer had to proceed in accordance with the provisions of the Ordinance. For the purpose of calculating depreciation allowance under section 10(5)(b) of the Act the written down value was to be computed by deducting not only the depreciation allowed in the assessment year 1950 51 but also the depreciation admissible in the relevant accounting year. The assessee firm contended that no deduction should have been made on the strength of the words "any law relating to tax on profits of, business" in paragraph 2 and the expression "any laws relating to taxation on profits" in the said paragraph was not intended to cover such a case. Held, that the word "law relating to income" in para 2 of the Removal of Difficulties Order must be given its ordinary meaning and it is only when a difficulty arises in giving effect to the provisions contained in the Indian Incometax Act that the provision of the Order can come into operation in a particular case. The words "of a Part B State" were used to qualify the phrase "anylaw relatingto tax on ' profits of ' business". The word " law relating" in this paragraph was intended and it meant that the Income Tax Officer should be satisfied that in certain cases difficulties have actually arisen in giving affect to the provision.

The appellant was a contractor of the respondent State. He had been awarded a contract for construction of a Main Station Building by the Karnataka Power Corporation Ltd., an instrumentality of the State. The agreement contained three clauses, namely, (a) Audited Balance Sheet/Taxes and (b) Latest income tax clearance Certificate. The appellant was not satisfied with these conditions and hence filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the award of contract. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the prequalifying requirements for supply of tender forms were only the three conditions set out in para I of the agreement, and that all the documents referred to in para V were not supplied along with the request for application of tender form. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the contract pertained to the construction of the Main Station building of a Company which had been established under the Karnataka State Electricity Corporation Act, 1957; (ii) the terms and conditions set forth in para IV were only for information and not for inspection; (iii) the supply of documents called for was also of some significance; (iv) the appellant 's tender had been rejected by the Tender Committee on the ground that it did not comply with the pre scribed condition of eligibility to submit a tender form; and (v) the performance of the three prequali fied conditions set up in para II was not mandatory. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The requirement of para V is a note appended to the "annual output of the works of the above nature" and that it is only a note on the tendering system that the appellant should satisfy the three requirements set out therein. [239D] 1.2 In the instant case, the appellant had no doubt also urged that the clauses in para VI were not complied with in as much as they related to the three essential conditions set apart in Para V. The tender of M.C.C., was rejected by a Committee constituted under the Act and the application other than the mini mum qualifying requirement should be prerogative of K.P.C.[239E] 1:3. The clause requiring the completion of the capabilities of the tenderers as well as their eligibility and simply because they had not complied the pre quali fication, was not a mere directory one. [240G H] 1 :4. The requirement in para 11 was mandatory for submitting the tender forms. It was not known on what grounds that application was rejected nor was it shown on what ground that application had been refused or that the party came to Court with any such grievance. The question whether the course adopted by the K. P.C, has caused any real prejudice to the appellant and other parties who had already supplied all the materials in time and sought no extension at all? It is true that the relaxations of the time schedule in the case of one party does affect even such a person in the sense that he would otherwise have had one competitor less. But, it is not known whether this party came within the mischief of the clause. [241H; 242A B] 1 5. The fact that a document was belatedly entertained from one of the applicants will cause substantial prejudice to another party who wanted, likewise an extension of time for filing a similar certificate or document but was declined the benefit. It may perhaps be said to cause prejudice also to a party which can show that it had refrained from applying for the tender documents only because it thought it would not be able to produce the document by the time stipulated but would have applied had it known that the rule was likely to be relaxed. But it is hardly known on how many days after the expiry of the period referred to above, the KP. C.C./D.T., in this case, had received due and full consideration.

The appellant was the owner of a house in Lahore. He had been put in possession of it on 10th October, 1947, and the Custodian General passed an order confirming the exchange of land and consequent transfer to her of the property in Pakistan. The appellant challenged the validity of the order confirming it by a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order under appeal was one passed by virtue of section 27 of the Central Act XXXI of 1950 which provides that "anything done or any action taken in exercise of any power conferred by or under the Ordinance shall be deemed to have been done or taken in the exercise of the powers conferred by this Ordinance as if this Act were in force on the day on which such thing was done or action was taken". The order passed by the Custodian under section 5A of the East Punjab Evacuees ' (Administration of Property) Act, 1947 was therefore a quasi judicial order and could not be challenged in an appeal under article 136 of the Constitution. [1137 B C] (ii)The contention that the Custodian had no jurisdiction to revise the original orders of the Custodian or the Custodian was without substance because under section 40(4) of the Act the Custodian could exercise revisional powers "for the purpose of satisfying himself as to the legality or propriety of any order of the custodian". The power conferred on him by section 27 is not confined only to matters of jurisdiction or illegality as is contended, but also extends to matters relating to matters covered by it. [1102 B C; 1137 F G] (iii)The Custodian General had himself in his order under section 27, before he passed an Order confirming the original order of confirmation, stated that "the orders were confirmed by the Additional Custodian and that the confirmation was subject to revision".
