The Custodian General did not have power to revise his own orders. [111 F G; 112 A] (iv)The order under Appeal was one made by virtue Of section 27(4)(q) of East Punjab Act XIV of 1947 which specifically provided that a pending action was to be deemed as an action commenced under the new Ordinance as it stood before the amendment in 1948. The effect of this provision is that if the CustodianGeneral had passed an appeal provided he must be taken to have exercised his discretion properly in not giving any notice to the allottees and a proper consideration of the policy and directives for the purposes of this case would be necessary. [112 G H] (v)The power conferred upon the Custodian by section 6(4), which was intended to operate only with respect to matters enumerated in the negative list, is subject to the revisional powers of the High Courts under article 226 of the Constitu tion. The jurisdiction conferred on the Custodian 's Court under section 28(3) of Act XXXI Of 1950 is not restricted only to such matters as are specified in cl. (c) and (d) but also includes the power to pass any order which may be passed by him in a pending proceeding.

The appellant, a locality in Bombay, was a locality where the respondents were working as workmen and had been employed by the appellant in tiny, but had not completed their service. The dispute referred to the Tribunal was whether the demand for bonus made by the respondent company was justified on the ground that it was a mere small scale bonus or one which was a term of the employment itself. The Tribunal held that the claim for bonus was barred by res judicata and that the award of the Industrial Tribunal was binding on the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The dispute in question was not one relating to a business employing less than 20 workmen and all but four of them were admittedly such small undertakings with the result that the death knock out of the employers 's right to bonus resulted in the termination of their services. [603 D E] (ii) The Tribunal had no jurisdiction to try the dispute referred by the State Government. It was not open to the appellant to raise a fresh industrial dispute on the short ground that what was pleaded was profit based on custom and service condition not one based on profit. Viewed from this angle, the claim of bonus based on profits and the question whether it was available for a particular industry in the present case was a matter of mere pleading and not a mere technical or technical plea. [503 G H] (iii) The reference to the Industrial Court was bad because the dispute was one relating purely to a profit bonus, it could be raised by the workmen only if they were entitled to claim bonus under the or such other Act. But the question of profit may arise only when the Bonus Act deals wholly and solely with profit bonus. [600 C D] (iv) The Industrial Tribunal had jurisdiction to entertain the dispute on merits. It did not go beyond the award in question. The fact that the bonus was paid on the occasion of special festival does not detract from its claim for customary bonus. The settlement between the parties clearly stated that the subject matter of the statute is 'the question of payment of bonus ' based on the profit to employees employed in establishments '. [599 F] (v) The award of Industrial Tribunal relating to the claim, which had not been put an end to, was unsustainable on the facts and circumstances of the case. [500 G] (vi) The settlement clearly stated the terms of reference and the surrounding circumstances. It is clear that the terms were not intended by the parties to be binding on them. [401 A B] (vii) The bonus Act speaks and speaks as a whole Code, on the sole subject of profit based bonus but is silent on, and cannot therefore annihilate by implication, other distinct and different kinds of bonus such as the one oriented on custom. The concept of bonus does not necessarily imply that it must be paid at a uniform rate throughout to justify an inference that the payment at such and such a rate had become customary and traditional in the particular concern.

The appellants were appointed directly by the Haryana Superior Judicial Service as Additional District and Sessions Judges in the State of Punjab. They were promoted to the Higher Judicial Services in accordance with the provisions of the Punjab Superior Judicial Services (Second Amendment) Rules, 1976. The High Court of Punjab and Haryana accepted their claim that they should be deemed to have been confirmed in the service for a period of two years as provided by the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the ratio of 2:1 between the promotees and direct recruits had to be maintained at all stages, that the length of continuous officiation in a post is the true test of seniority and that with reference to the dates of confirmation, the length must be determined by the length Of continuous service on a post in the Service irrespective of the date of confirmation. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellants are entitled to the benefit of the rule of rotation at the time of confirmation of the members of the Superior Judicial service who were appointed to that service by promotion and by direct recruitment. [1050C] 2.1 The High Courts were not justified in applying the rule as of rotation. [ 1051E] 1.2 In Haryana, the seniority of the Judicial Officers is to be determined with reference tO the dates on which their confirmation was due to the Rules. [1154F] 2:3 The High court was not justified under Rule 12 of the High Court Rules in applying that rule of the rotation at tho time of the confirmation of members of service, who were promoted or appointed to the Superior judicial Service prior to December 31, 1976 on the basis of the respective dates of their confirmation allotted to them in compliance with the direction given by this Court in Haryana State.

The respondent No. 1, a local cadre holder of Warangal, was appointed as Junior Assistant to the post of Senior Assistant in the Commercial Taxes Department of the Commercial Tax Division of the appellant State on November 20, 1982. The respondent No 2, G. Satya Rao, filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order dated April 1, 1982 and the Tribunal allowed the said petition holding that the zonal seniority was the criteria for recruitment, seniority, promotion etc., of the State Government and different provisions of the Andhra Pradesh Public Employment (Organisa tion of Local Cadres and Regulation of Direct Recruitment) Order 1975 were issued by the President under proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution. The appellant State filed a Civil Appeal No. 3203 of 1989 against the said order of the Tribunal which was dismissed by this Court on April 1.1990. Thereafter, the respondent No 3, G Satya Rao filed a Writ Petition before the Andhra High Court for quashing the order of his appointment and directing the State to promote the appellant as Commercial Taxes Officer. The High Court allowed the Writ Petition holding that G.O.Ms. No. 1648 dated November 20 1982 was issued under Article 371 D of the Constitu tion and the said G.0.Ms No. 728 dated November 1, 1975 was a special provision in respect of the state of Andhra Pradesh empower ing the President to organise any local cadre within the zone for the Commercial taxes of, and class or classes of civil posts under the State into different local cadres. The State Government preferred an appeal against this order before the Supreme Court. On the question whether G.S.R. No, 1648 was issued in exercise of powers under proviso (1) to Article 371D of the Consti tution. Allowing the Appeal, HELD: 1.1 The power to organise class or class of posts of civil service of and class of civil post under the state into different Local cadres should be exercised by the State Govern ment in accordance with para 3(1) before the expiry of twelve months from October 20, 1975. Obviously realising this reality and the need to organise local cadres, subsequent thereto the amendment was made and was published in G. O. Ms. No,. 1648, dated November lO, 1975 seeking to achieve. The words "or constituted otherwise" occurring in paragraph 2(e) read with paragraph 3(7) give ample power to the State Govt. to organise a zone within a zone. [575F H] 1.2 The expression "constituted otherwise" is of wide import and includes all other matters which may be included in the Schedule to the Constitution except in accordance therewith. It is only relatable to the power given by the Presi dent to the state Government to organise Local cadres in respect any class or categories of posts in any department when more than one cadre in respect thereof is allotted in each department. [574G H] 2.1 In exercise of the power under proviso 1(1), it is for the President notwithstanding the expiry Of the period of twelve month prescribed in sub paragraph (1 ) of para graph 3, by an order require the State Gov ernment whenever he considers it expedient so to do to have the power to bifurcate or reorganise a zone or cadres therein.

The appellant was the owner of a plot in execution of a decree passed by the trial court. The respondents filed a suit against the appellant for possession of the said plots on the ground that the decree which had been passed in the mortgage suit was binding on the appellant and that he was not entitled to recover khas possession from the defendants. The trial court held that the appellant was subrogated to the position of the Bank, that the Bank was bound by the decree and that the respondent No. 1 was fully represented in the mortgaged suit and that it was not necessary for the auction sale of the mortgaged property to make an end to the mortgage. On appeal the High Court confirmed the decree holding that the lease in question had been binding on both the parties, and that as long as nothing took place which impaired the value or impeded the operation of the mortgage, the mortgagor was well within his powers under section 66 of the Transfer of Property Act and that so long as anything taken place which affected the property in the usual course of management, the lease granted by him could be rightly deemed operative against the mortgagee. Held, that a mortgagor who had no interest in the property demised to him could not enforce a right of redemption against the mortgagor. The mere fact that a lessee acquires an interest in a mortgaged property which is sufficient to enable him to redeem the mortgage does not affect the mortgagor 's rights under the mortgage and the mortgagor has no power to alienate the mortgaged properties. The true position has been stated in the following terms by section 66: "Where a lease of immovable property or from month to month in the case of agricultural land or from months to month, in the ease of agricultural lands or from monthly payment of a certain amount is known as permissive waste, i.e., for omission to repair or to prevent natural deterioration, he is not liable for destructive waste is acts which are destructive or permanently injurious to the mortgaged Property if the security was insufficient or would be rendered insufficient by such acts."

The petitioner filed an arbitration suit in the Calcutta High Court under sections 5, 12 and 33 of the for the appointment of an arbitrator. The respondent filed an application under section 5 of the Arbitration Act for referring the matter to arbitration. The petitioner filed the arbitration suits in the High Court. The Single Judge of the High court held that the claim was hopelessly barred by limitation as the petitioner had sent the bills on July 12, 1979 and payment was not made. The Division Bench dismissed the appeals preferred by the respondent. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) since the petitioner was said to have made the claim for the first time in July 1979, he did not move his little finger to approach the Engineer and later filed a suit for damages; (ii) since there was no proof in that behalf, the petitioner could not be proceeded with by the Engineer; and (iii) Section 5 of 'the Act barred the jurisdiction of the Court where arbitration proceedings were pending. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Court has the power to enlarge the time so agreed. It is a well settled rule that in mercantile reference of the kind in question it is an implied term of the contract that the arbitrator must decide the dispute according to the existing law of contract and that every defence which would have been open in a court of law can be equally proponed for the arbitrator 's decision unless the parties have agreed which is not suggested here. [368C D] 1.2 The Court further held that it was clear from the language of sections 5 and 12 (2) (b) that the Court had power to extend the time for arbitration. [369E F] 2.1 In the mercantile reference, the principles of equity must be applied just as they would now be applied in a Court of law.

The appellants, who were the estate of a Zamindar, applied to the State Government under section 14 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act for passing final decree on the mortgage suit. The Estate mortgaged was an Estate within the meaning of that Act and the mortgagor 's interest in the estate was extinguished by the notification issued under section 3(1) of the Act. The appellants contended that the objection as regards executability of the decree pleaded by the judgment debtors was barred by the principles of res judicata and that the bar of section 4(d) of Bihar Land Reform Act, 1950 did not operate as res judicata in view of the provisions of the Abolition Act. Held: (i) Under the circumstances of this case it is not open to the appellants to proceed with the execution. Their only remedy is to get compensation under the Act and not to have the protection of section 3 (d). The consequence of vesting of an estate is set out in section 4. Section 4(a) provides that no suit shall lie in any Civil Court for the recovery of any money due from such proprietor (proprietor whose estate has vested in the State) or tenure holder the payment of which is secured by a mortgage of, or is a charge on such estate or tenure and all suits and proceedings for the realisation of any such money which may be pending on the date of vesting shall be dropped. The effect of the vesting of the Estates and the deemed settlement of raiyats rights in respect of certain classes of lands in cluded in the Estates took place simultaneously, in law the two must be treated as different transactions; first there was a vesting of estates in the Government absolutely and free from all encumbrances. Then followed the deemed settlements by the State of raiyat 's rights on the quondum proprietors. Therefore, in view Of section 4 (d) it is clear that all Estates notified under section3 vest in the state free of all encumbrances and the right to hold them as a raiyat under the State having been extinguished by virtue of the notification under section 4, the right of raiyats to hold the properties of the debtor was that provided in Ch. IV of the Orissa Land Reforms Rules, 1950. The provisions contained in section 16 in regard to the scaling down of debts due by proprietors and tenure holders clearly indicate that another object which the Act wanted to achieve was to give some redress to the debtors whose estates have been taken away from them by the notifications issued under s.3.

The respondents in the appeals were allocated to the I.P.S. or Central Services Group 'A ' and they were allowed to sit at the next Civil Service Examination, provided they were within the permissible age limit, without having to resign from the service to which they had been allocated. The respondents challenged the validity of the second proviso to Rule 4 of C.S .E. Rules, 1989 on the ground that a candidate who was permitted to abstain from probationary training in order to appear at the first Civil Service examination and who accepted the allocation to a service subsequently and is appointed to the service "shall not be eligible to appear again in the Civil Services Examination unless he first resigns from the Service" and that such reasons are arbitrary, unfair and unjust. The High Court dismissed their writ petitions. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The second proviso is not unconstitutional as it does not go beyond the intent of the main rule putting any unjustifiable embargo on the number of attempts at the examination to the examination. [79F] 1.2 In all, there are 46 Group 'B ' Central Services listed in the C. S.E. (Main) Rules, which only for 16 Group 'C ' services, recruitment is made through the Civil Service Examinations conducted by UPSC annually and it is only in respect of candidates who on the basis of the results of the previous CSE had been allotted to the Indian Police or Central Service Group ' A ' that is why this restriction has been imposed. [80G H] 1:3 The proviso to rule 4 of the CS.E Rules does not travel beyond the intendment of the scheme putting any unreasonable embargo on a candidate from appearing in the next CSE, even though he has been approved for appointment to the IPS or Central services Group 'D '. [81A B] 1 :4 A candidate who has been allocated to a Service under the I .P. S., or to a Central Services, Group 'E ' will be eligible for appearing again in Civil Services Exami nation unless he is first resigning from the serv ice and in other words it declares a candidate, who is otherwise eligible in terms of Regulation 4 as ineligible unless he has first resigned from the services. [82B C] 1 5 The proviso is also not unconstitutional because it makes a discrimination against candidates appointed to IPS or to have been otherwise eligible for appear again at the Civil services Examination. [83C D] 1 6 The proviso cannot be said to be discriminatory against the candidates appointed under Rule 17 of the Central Civil Services (Prelimi nary) Rules. [84E] 1 7 The proviso has no application because the services under Group ' C ' are different services and, therefore, the condition of service of a particular service cannot be compared with other service especially when the services are not at par and more so when the other service, namely, Group `B ' service is less in rank and merit to that of Group 'F ' Service. [85G H; 86A] 2.1 In all these cases, there is no discrimination between the direct recruits and the promotees appointed to Indian Police Service Group A or I. P.S., or Central Serv ices, Group A service, and as such it is violative of Article 14. [86H; 87B] 2:2 The proviso must be read in a manner so as to give an unfair advantage to any one who accepts allocation to the Service and is not discriminatory. [87D E] 3.1 It is well settled that the proviso to sub rule (4) of Rule 4 does not deal with the suitability of candidates appointed through the same open competition to the remaining members of the service, to which he is allo cated if he is unable to take training with his own Batch.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1)(i) of the . The grounds of detention were that he filed a petition requesting the Advisory Board to permit one Mr. Sundararajan, a retired Assistant Collector of Central Excise to assist him as a friend. The Board rejected the request and the counter affidavit filed by the appellant in this Court was also rejected. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the detention order was not vitiated because the detenu had requested the Board to allow him to represent the case of the detenu. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Advisory Board has no justification to refuse assistance of a person as a lawyer. [790B] 2.1 The Board had no justification for refusing assistance of the Deputy Collector of Customs and a Superintendent of Central excise. [789D] 2:2. The word 'friend ' used in the judgments of this Court is more in this sense than meaning 'a person known well to another and regarded with liking, affection and loyalty. ' A person not being a friend in the normal sense could be picked up for rendering assistance within the frame of the law as settled by this Court. The detaining authority or the Government has to examine whether what prejudice has been caused to the appellant on account of such denial. [788E F] 2 :3. In view of the position of law and the facts of the case, the refusal by the Advisory Boards to permit the appellant to be assisted by a retired assistant Collector of central Excise unjust and should the same had been refused. [ 791H; 792A B] 2 .4. The rule in A. K. Roy etc. vs Union of India & Anr., ; applied.

The appellants were the owners of certain premises in Calcutta. The requisition orders provided that the goods requisitioned and acquired were subject to pucca delivery orders and in view of the usage that pucca delivery order was only issued against payment, were passed from hand to hand by endorsement and were sold and dealt with in the market as absolutely representing the goods to which they related. The appellants filed a suit challenging the validity of the requisition on the grounds (1) that the requisition orders did not apply to them as they had been served on the managing agents of the mills as required by r. 75 A(2) of the Rules framed under the Defence of India Act, 1939, and (2) that as the goods were in the possession of the appellants they could not be served with the notices of acquisition. Held, that the orders of requisition and notices of acquisi tion were valid and binding on the appellants. The words "the service of the notice" in r. 77 of the Defence Of India Rules, 1939 did not mean that the service of a notice must be effected by actual service. The word "service" in the context of section 18 of the Act means service of notice on the owner of the property requisitioned and does not include service of any kind whatsoever. In the present case the requisition order was served on a corporation which had been constituted under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, and the appellants were not personally responsible to the company for the service. Held further, that in view Of section 18 Of the Defenceof India Rules the orders were valid. The provisions of r. 78A(2), of the rules framed under it, did not require that the notice must have been served upon the owner thereof and that this was sufficient compliance with the manner of service.

The assessee company was a Private Limited Company. The assessment year concerned is 1963 64. The assessee company claimed deduction of the amount paid as depreciated in income tax (in its books for the year ending March 31, 1956) on the ground that it was a reserve and should be included in its capital for the purposes of the Act. The Income Tax Officer disallowed the claim holding that the said sum was a provision made towards a liability which had attached on account of issuance of a notice under section 23A of the Income Tax Act, 1922. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that no action can be taken against the assessee under Section 23A. The Tribunal referred to the High Court for decision. In reference it was contended that since no order levying additional tax under Section 3(2) was made on or before the date relevant to the assessment year 1963 64, the said amount cannot be treated as a provision and not a reserve. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions made against anticipated losses and contingencies are charges against profits and, therefore, to be taken into account against gross receipts in the P. & L. accounts and the balance sheet. On the other hand reserves are appropriations of profits, the assets by which they are repre sented being retained to form part of the capital employed in the business. Provisions are usually shown in the balance sheets by way of deductions from the assets in respect of which they were made whereas general reserves and reserve funds are shown as part of proprietor 's interest. [113B C] 2. The High Court was right in holding it to be a provision, and not an reserve. [114D] Metal Box Company of India Limited vs Their Workmen, ; Vazir Sultan Tobacco Co. Ltd. etc. vs Commissioner of Income Tax, Andhra Pradesh etc., , referred to.

The petitioners, who were direct recruits to the Indian Railway Service of Engineers (Class 1) were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the year 1965. They challenged the validity of the seniority list dated December 17, 1965 on the ground that officers appointed to temporary posts on the cadre of Engineers and that their seniority had to be reckoned on the basis of their length of continuous service though they conceded that in any given year the candidates appointed as Engineers on the principle of inter se seniority were placed above those appointed on the same basis. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the classification of temporary Assistant Engineers separately from the Indian Railways Service was neither discriminatory nor violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution, for the reason that it had nexus to the object sought to be achieved by the impugned rules. In the appeals to this Court on behalf of the petitioners it was contended that (i) the principle laid down in Katyani Dayal 's case was not permissible by means of successive writ petitions; and (ii) the principles of constructive res judicata would bar the re agitation of the issues decided in Kattyani Dayal vs Union of India, [1990] Supp. SCC 519 at 691, and that the principle was reasonable and this is a pattern which has been noticed and approved in many a Service. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The distinction between the two services was well marked in Kathayani Dayal & Ors. vs Secretary Home (Police) Department, Government of Bihar & Ors., [1988] Supp SCC 519 and Katyni Dayal 'S case, referred to. 2.1 In the instant case, the distinction and the classification between the petitioners and those appointed as Executive Engineers across also in a representative capacity across which stand arrayed the Union of lndia and the Railway Board as respondents, is not permissible under the equality clause in the Constitution. [1025C D] Katyini Dayal ' case specifically said that relief of equality was being denied to the then petitioners because of the history, origin, and structure of the Services. No opinion was expressed however as to the validity or otherwise of the given weightage of half the length of service subject to a maximum of five years, since the rules had gone a long way so as to shed the views expressed in Katyanani Dayal case. [ 1026D E] Kattyni Dayal & ors. vs Union Of India & Ors, ; , referred to 2.2 In the present case, there is no compelling reasons to deviate from the principles enunciated in Kathyani Dayals case. The cases aforementioned relied upon by learned counsel for the petitioners do not remove this hurdle, however broadly may Article 14 and16 be viewed and expanded. It is thus unnecessary to elaborate those cases and discover their ratio. [1126F G] Kathayi Dayal ' s case specifically stated that relief for equality was never asked for. The State is prohibited to create separate channels of service and create discrimination by making one as an isolated one, and not providing for promotional avenues reasonably, falls to the ground in view of the bar of re agitation erected by Direct Recruit 's cases (supra). [1026G H] Kathyan Dayal & others vs Secretary, Home ( Police) Department Government ofBihar & Ors ; , followed.

The appellant was convicted and sentenced to death under section 302, Indian Penal Code. His appeal to the High Court failed. The State appealed to this Court by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Ordinance of 1949 which was promulgated in 1948 was discriminatory and void as it contravened article 14 Of the Constitution; (ii) the Act was discriminatory inasmuch as it imposed a punishment not only for offences committed by persons who were to be tried under the Special Court but also for offences which had a rack to be committed on a special class by themselves and to provide that such offences shall be tried as expeditiously as possible in accordance with a special procedure devised for the purpose; (iii) section 11 of the Ordinance was discriminatory in that it conferred a right on the State Government to direct any class of cases or offences to be transferred by Special Courts, and (iv) the provisions of article 14 were not violated. Held:(i) The Act in so far as it authorised the State Govern ment to direct classes of offences or cases to be triable by the Special court was void under article 13 Of the Consti tution. (ii)(a) The Ordinance of 1948 which was passed in 1948, was a law relating to "offences" within the meaning of section 11 and was not discriminatory in character as it conferred on the Government power to direct such classes or offences or classes of cases to he tried by the special court. (b) The provisions of the Act were not discriminatory and did not contravene article 14 of the Constitution. (c) The classification implied in this part of the sub section had no reference to, and was therefore invalid. (d) The object of the ordinance was to provide for public safety, maintenance of public order and preservation of peace and tranquillity in the State of Saurashtra. (e) The provision in the Ordinance that "the State Government shall try such offences or class of offences as the Government of the United State of Gujrania may by general or special order in writing direct" was not unconstitutional because it contravened articles 14 Of, the Constitution inasmuch as the Act had been passed with a view to secure public safety. (f) The notification issued under section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act which authorised the state Government to make a classifi cation of "offenses", "classes of offences" or "classions of cases" was bad as it offended article 14. (g) The notifications were discriminatory and violative of article 13 of the Constitu tion.

The appellants were convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 396 I.P.C. and sentenced to death on the ground that they had committed theft of timber belonging to the village school managed by one Ram Prasad who was a Pradhan of the village and his wife and brother in law. The High Court dismissed their appeals against conviction and sentences. In appeal to this Court it was contended that having regard to the size of the eastern kotha of the house of the deceased it is not probable that the appellants armed with various weapons could have been present in that kothas at the time of occurrence, and that the evidence of P.W. 2 who had seen the incident was corroborated by the evidence given by P.Ws. 1, 7 and 8 to the extent that they were injured witnesses to the occurrence. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The prosecution has proved the case against the appellants beyond reasonable doubt and the conviction of the appellants for the offence under section 302 I. P.C., is not sustainable. [575F] (2) There is no reason whatsoever for rejecting the evidence on record altogether. It is not possible to agree with the Sessions judge that no reliance could be placed on the evidence in question. The evidence of the doctor who had been believed by not only the learned Sessions Judge but also by the learned Judges of the High Court was not convincing. [574G] (3) There was no reason for rejecting a evidence of a witness who had deposed to the fact that his evidence was corroborated from other prosecution witnesses to any extent. The opinion of P,W.2 that the assailants entered the house and assaulted her husband fatally and that some of them caused injuries to her and committed dacoity by looting properties worth about Rs. 2,700/ from her house is not convincing because it is admitted by P W. 7 who was an eye witness to the incident. [576H; 576A B] (4) The evidence regarding the presence of the appellant in the house at the scene of occurrence is corroborated by P 's evidence that he entered the room and assaulted his husband fatly and that there was sufficient light at the place where the dead body of the daughter was found lying.

The appellant State Road Transport Corporation created under a State Act, entitled the Transport Authority to run an industrial establishment. The respondent terminated the employment of some of its employees during the initial period of probation and of some others during the extended period on the ground of unsatisfactory service. Thereupon an industrial dispute was raised by the appellant State Government which referred the dispute to the Labour Court for adjudication under section 10 of the . The Labour Court held that section 25F of the Act did not apply to the case of the respondent and dismissed the reference. The employer filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Labour court. A Division Bench of the High COurt upheld the decision of the single Judge. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that (i) the services of the employees were terminated on the grounds of unsuitability and therefore the termination was bad; (ii) the discharge was invalid; and (iii) the Labour Appellate Tribunal had wrongly held that the discharge amounted to retrenchment as defined in section 2(oo) of the and those orders were bad for noncompliance with section 25 F. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression 'termination of service for any reason whatsoever ' now covers every kind of termination of service except those not expressly included in section 25G or not expressly provided for by other provisions of the Payment of Wages Act such as sections 25FF and 25FFF. [790B] 2. (i). The expression "termination of services" is not retrenchment within the meaning of the word 'termination '. It is not necessary to dilate on the point nor to refer to the earlier decisions of this Court in Hariprasad Shivshanker Shukla vs A. N. Sundara Money, ; and State Bank of India vs N. Sukharam, ; , referred to. (ii). The requirement of section 25FF of the has not been complied with in these cases. [789D] 3. (a) The expression `termination of ' in section2(oo), and the words "the termination by the employer of a service of a probationer" in section 10, have no wider meaning than the ordinary accepted connotation of the term. It means the discharge of surplus labour or staff by the employers for any reasons whatsoever.

The assessee South Eastern Railway disposed of unclaimed and unconnected goods for money consideration. On 1 April 1952 the assessee applied to the Commercial Tax Officer for cancellation of registration as a "dealer" under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. The Commercial Tax officer rejected the application on the ground that the disposal of unclaimed or unconnected goods was a regular feature of the assessee 's activities and that therefore the assessee fell within the scope of the Act. The assessee preferred an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who dismissed the same. The Tribunal held that the sale effected by the assessee were sales under the Act and that the assessee was a " dealer" within the meaning of section 2(c) of the Bengal Taxation (Sales tax) Act 1941, and therefore liable to assessment under that Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the goods sold were unclaimed goods and that when such good came into possession of the asses see it acquired rights over the said goods under section 56 of the Railways Act enabling it tO sell the goods. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The activity of so disposing of the goods was adjunctive to the principal activity of the carriage of goods by the Railway. It is an activity which may be regarded as necessarily incidental or ancillary to its business as carrier of the good. It seems to South Eastern railway was a 'dealer ' for the purposes of the Calcutta Finance ( Sales Tax)Act, 1941 and therefore the sale took place. The goods were unclaimed and unrelated goods lying with it. [781E F] 2. In the instant case, the assessee Eastern Railway dis puted on 1 April, 1952, the assessment of the sales tax department in respect of the four quarters ending March 1959 and paid sales tax pursu ant to the assessments made by the Sales Tax Department. However, in assessment proceedings for the four quarter ending March, 1959, the assesseee applied for cancellation on the basis that the disposed of dead goods for valuable consideration was a irregular or unauthorised goods. The case of the assesses was that unclaimed or uncon stitutional goods came into his possession and not as a result of any activity of purchase or of manufacture for sale. It was contended that no tax was payable under the West Bengal Finance Act, 1942. [782B C] 3. In view of the fact that the sales effected by assessee were trans ferred to the assessee of unclaimed & unconnected goods, the order of the Tribunal was set aside and the questions referred to the High Court were answered in favour of the Revenue and against the assessee.

The appellant was a Director of the Indian Insurance Company. He had been appointed as Managing Director on March 1, 1949 and was later promoted as Chairman of the Union Agencies. In 1953 he made an application to the Union agencies for the purchase of certain securities from the brokers without mentioning that the securities had not been actually received or that the cheques in payment of the purchase price were issued to him. The appellant contended that the purchase and sale transactions were genuine and that the money was being paid to the Bank by way of credit facilities, that the transactions were fictitious and that they were not authorised to purchase or sell securities on behalf of the Insurance Company unless they were authorised by the Chairman. Held, that in view of the fact that the appellant had made a false statement about the source of the money he was guilty of cheating and that he had no knowledge of the transaction. The transactions were voluntary and were entered into with the brokers for the purpose of obtaining loans from the Bank. The conduct of the appellant showed that he used to visit the various places of business in Bombay, Calcutta, etc., and that it was not possible to know what was required to be done by one earring one person as a Director or Manager of the Bank and that most of the transactions had been entered into without his knowledge. The fact that he did not know about the transactions was immaterial because he had nothing to do with the movement of the securities held by him. It is only when he knew that the transaction was in reality a mere ruse to show that he misappropriated the amount which had been either spent on the purchase or on the acquisition of the shares which were not in existence, or realised by the sale of securities and which was shown to be utilised in fictitious purchase of securities, that it would appear from his conduct that he knew about the transaction and had knowledge of it. The mere fact that a Director 's communication to him of the day of the transfer of moneys to the bank was not made as part of his duty to do so, would not make him guilty of any offence under section 409 I.P.C. Nor could he be said to have knowledge of such an act.

The appellants were holding permanent posts in the ministerial service of the Secretariat Service of the State of Gujarat. The State Government sanctioned certain rules called the Allocated Government Servants (Absorption, Seniority, Pay and Allowances) Rules, 1957. These rules provided that the officers who immediately before November 1, 1956 were serving in connection with the affairs of a State and were allotted to serve in connection therewith shall be deemed to have been allotted to service in connection With the affairs. of another State. The appellants were not absorbed in the secretariats of the Part B State of Saurashtra and Kutch. By virtue of section 115 of the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1956, they were allotted certain posts to serve as clerks in the Secretariat Services. The respondents who were holding a permanent post in the Ministerial Service of Gujarat and Kutch filed a petition before the High Court for an order directing the State Government to treat their appointment as servants of the ministerial staff in theariat service on the ground that they were regularly appointed in the posts shown against their names in column 4 of the statement. The High Court held that since the impugned order purported to amalgamate the former Saurashtra and Gujarat States personnel with the Gujarat Secretariat Service contrary to the terms of r. 138 of the Recruitment Rules, the orders of transfer to the Secretariat which was not made in the process of integration could not operate as absorption under the All India Services (Auto cation) Act, 1960. The appeal filed by the State was dismissed by this Court. HELD : The High court was right in holding that the order violated r.138 of the Rules framed by the Government of Bombay in 1957. [521 B] N. Raghavendra Rao vs Deputy Commissioner South Kanara, Mangalore, ; , followed.

The petitioners who were dealers in cotton and oil seeds, were assessed to purchase ginned and unginned cotton for manufacturing yarn and selling the same to other dealers. The petitioners challenged the validity of the Punjab General Sales Tax (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967 on the ground that they had failed to pay tax on the sale or purchase of declared goods within a State. The High Court dismissed their petitions holding that the provisions of the Haryana General Sales tax (Amendment & Validation) Amendment Act were not in conflict with articles 301 and 304 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the effect of the Amending Act was to levy tax on sale or purchases of declared Goods within a state, and that the amendment was retrospective but no machinery was provided for making the assessment at more than one stage. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The Punjab General sales Tax (Amend ment & Validation), Act,1967 is not in operation since it has been made retrospective but with effect from the date of the notification. [553 B] (2) The object of the Act is to levy a tax on declared goods and not to include such transactions in their return saves them from liability to pay the tax till they are the dealer liable to pay it. It is only when a person has purchased cotton and sells it after the period mentioned in cl. (a) that he is liable to be assessed to tax. [554 E] (3) The Act has been amended in the year 1956 by the Punjab Legislature which was later on amended in 1967. The effect of this amendment is that the maximum has been provided without indication of the circumstances under which the tax is to be levied. It cannot be said that a person who is not liable for payment of tax at all, at any time, the collection of a tax from him with a possible contingency, of refund at a later stage will not make the original levy valid. [555 E F] (4) The contention that there was discrimination between imported goods and local goods cannot be accepted. The Act is a piece of legislation intended to protect the interests of the general public. It has been enacted to provide for the better regulation of trade, commerce and intercourse throughout the country. It does not provide for any machinery for collecting tax at one stage or the other. [557 F G] (5) The levy of tax on goods is a valid levy at more then three stages. It can be imposed only in respect of goods which are actually delivered for the purpose of consumption in the State and not where the goods are exempt from taxation altogether.

The appellants, who were the representatives of three original plaintiffs, instituted a suit against the respondent for recovery of certain amount due from them on the ground that they had been agriculturists and hence entitled to the benefits of the Agriculturists Relief Act. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed the decree holding that the mortgage debt was one and indivisible and exceptions to this rule were admitted in special circumstances where the integrity of the mortgage has been disrupted at the instance of the mortgagee himself; and that the question whether a purchaser could get the benefit of the debt scaled down under the Agriculturists ' Relief Act, could not be decided by the lower courts. Held, that the view taken by the High Courts was correct. The fact that in a mortgage decree when the loan has been advanced to more than one person, if one of the debtors happens to be an agriculturist while others are not, the agriculturist debtor would certainly be entitled to have his debts scaled under the provisions of the Act in spite of the provision of general law which prevents a mortgagor from denying the liability of the interest which he owns in the mortgaged property to satisfy the entire mortgage debt. The Punjab Relief Act is a special statute which aims at giving relief not to debtors in general but only to a specified class of debtors, viz., those who are agriculturists as defined in the Act. It is enough if it is clear from the provisions that the legislature intended to give relief not merely to a certain class of creditors, namely, those who were agriculturists as contemplated by the Act, but also to a specific class of debtor, viz. those who have been agriculturists as specified under the general law and the Act does not deprive him of the fruits of his own purchase under the Act; it is enough to say that he is entitled to get the benefits conferred by the statute even though he is not an agriculturist himself, being entitled to a benefit of a decree which has been scaled over under the special circumstances. The judgment debtors are the mortgagors themselves and according to the plain provisions of section 8 of the Madras Agriculturists Relief act they were agriculturists and therefore entitled to claim the benefit thereof.

The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for recovery of rent and eviction. The respondents contended that they were tenants and had no right to be on the premises. The trial Court decreed the suit but the High Court in appeal reversed the decree holding that the City Civil Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. Held, that the suit was not one between a landlord and a tenant because the defendants of the suit did not admit that the plaintiffs were the tenants of the premises within the meaning of section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. The City Civil court had no power to entertain it and try the suit as it was barred by section 29A of the Act. The suit filed in the City civil Court was one relating to possession of premises to which the provisions of Part 11 of the City of Bombay Rents. Hotel and lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1944, applied and the appellants were ordered to be evicted. The High Court correctly decided that the suits filed by the plaintiffs could not be determined by the City 's Court. The provisions of section 41 of the Presidency Small Causes Courts Act, 1887, apply only to suits between a landlords and tenants in which that relationship is admitted but also a suit in which it is claimed that the relationship of landlord and tenant within the mean ing of the Rent Act subsists between the parties. The Bombay Rents Hotel and Hotels (Control), Act, 1946, was enacted by the Legislature clearly intended that no finality should be attached to the decision of a court trying a suit under section 28 on a question of title de hors the Act and any one who was a landlord or tenant as defined in the Act would have to conform to the provisions Of the Act, and all claims to such a status would have been to be determined under the Act as they would be claims arising out of it.

The appellant was appointed managing director of a private company in the year 1955. He was appointed as the managing director on July 7, 1955. In his place an agreement was made between him and the company on July 14, 1955, whereby he agreed to appoint the appellant as the Managing Director. The appellant challenged the legality of this appointment by a petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court. It was contended that the appointment of the appellant was void because (i) the appointment was not made by the will of the company and (ii) the appellant had not been legally appointed as director. Held, that the word "assign" in section 312 of the new Act means "appoint". The word "appoint" does not mean "appointment". The appointment is not an assignment of his office by him for the old Act. It is intended to be an assignment which is made altogether void and would not become valid even if approved by a special resolution of the Company. The word 'assign ' in section 255 of the Act means the appointment by the company itself, but it does not include "appointment" as such. In view of the fact that the power to appoint an alternate director may be conferred by the articles, the word 'appointment ' would also include appointment. The words "appointing a person as". in section 252 of the old act are used in the main part of section 86B of the , and they indicate that there should be no perpetual management. It does not necessarily mean merely to make an assignment but to appoint someone else.

The appellants are the partners of a partnership firm. The respondent filed an eviction petition against the appellants and one other partnership firm, under section 10(2)(ii)(a) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 on the ground that they were unlawful sub tenants. The Trial Court held that the appellants had unlawfully and without the consent of the respondent sublet the shop let out to the said M/s Adeshwar Glass Mart and were liable to be evicted for contravening section 10 (2)(i)(a). The Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal, but the High Court in second appeal reversed the finding of eviction. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. It is not open to the appellants to raise this contention at this stage at all. [420D] Chhotelal Pyarelal, the partnership firm and others vs Shikharchand, In that case an eviction order was passed against the appellant on the grounds of sub letting under section I(2) (ii)(b). The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction against the tenant and one another partner of the partnership. The appellants were also joined as respondents in the eviction petition on the plea that they had unlawfully sub tenants, and that the said shop was liable to he evicted for unlawful subletting under the provisions of section 10. [421E F] Chh Clubal Pyare Lal vs Shikher, ; , relied upon. Chhotelals Pyarelal the partnership Firm and others v Shikhar Chand, In this case no such objection has been raised at all till the stage of Special Leave and it is surely not open for the appellants now to raise such an objection at this belated stage and thereby delay matters for a number of years. [ 420F G] Chh Mahalal Pyare lal, the partner of a firm and another vs Shikhachand, in that case also, relied upon by Mr. Nayar, was not a case which would have been fatal to eviction petition. Had this contention been raised in the Trial Court or even in the first appeal, it would have be open to him to amend the eviction petitions and join the partners as re spondents. [416G H] Chhotalal Pyareilal, the firm and other partnership firms were carried on business in the said premises even for some time during which the appellants firm had ceased to carry on the business there. Moreover, although a notice was given by the respondent to the appellant and M/S Adeshwar glass Mart to produce their income tax returns, assessment orders as well as account books and ledgers for the relevant period, these were not produced. It was surely open to them to amend their eviction petition and join them as re quired under section10(2). [417A B] ChhMeotelal Beharilal,the partnership firm & others vs Shri Shikharlal, In the instant case no objection has now been raised by the appellants that the main tain name of M/ s Adeshwar Chettiar was carry ing on business at the said prem ises even for certain time during the pendency of the appeal. [414B C] Chh landlady Pyarelal vs Shikharichand, ; and Chhotelala Pyarelal 's case, relied on.

The Andhra Pradesh Act was passed by the State Legislature in exercise of its power under Entry 54 of List I of Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The validity of the Act was challenged on the ground that it was beyond the legislative competence of the Andhra Pradesh Legislature. It was contended for the landholders that the Andhra Act was ultra vires and void as being outside the legislative competency of the State legislature. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms Act is not within the legislative power of the Parliament to provide for imposition of ceiling on vacant land situate within these urban agglomerations. It is only in respect of land situated within the urban agglomeration that the Central Act would apply if and when the area in question is notified to be an urban agglompanied by the eventual imposition of a ceiling on immovable property of every other description, the Parliament enacted the Central legislation with a view to imposing ceiling on such vacant land. [1156E F] (2) The definition of 'family unit ' in section 2(n)(A)(ii) of the Central Acquisition Act, 1951 is materially in the same terms as the definition of "family unit" in Andhra Pradesh Acts. The definition is substantially in the similar terms as that of the definition in Andhra Acts. [1105G H] (3) The expression 'vacant land ' in the Andhra Acts is not defined in the State Act but in the Central Acts of the States of Andhra Pradesh and Andhra Pradesh. [1056H; 1157A B] (4) The term "land" is used in two different senses, namely, (a) a building site or a part thereof which is capable of being used for purposes of agriculture, (b) a house site or any other structure or structure which may be prescribed by the Rules and (c) a residential building. [1257B C] (5) The word "land", in section 3(f) of that Act, means land held by a person in excess of the ceiling area, but does not include raising of grass, dairy farming, poultry farming, breeding live stock and cultivation or the growing of such plants as may be Prescribed by the rules. [1357C D] (6) The definitions of "vacant" and "vacants" in section 1(f)(A) are materially different from those of the two Acts. In order to fall within the exclusion, the land must be entered in the revenue or land record before the appointed day as for the purpose of agriculture and must also not have been specified in the master plan for a purpose other than agriculture. [1457E F; G H] Union of India vs V. P. Gupta & Ors., ; , referred to. (7) The Act is a piece of colourable legislation and it is not possible to sustain the contention that the whole of the levy was ultravires. It has been held by this Court in Union of lndia vs Vardhaman Rao, [1963] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 946 that the definition is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution and that the Act cannot be said to be outside the competence of Parliament. [1109B C; 1158D E] (8) The State Legislature was not competent to enact the impugned Act in so far as land situate in the other States of the state of Andhra pradesh is concerned. [111E F]. (9) The entire State of Andhra Pra desh Act is ultra vires, and void.

The appellant company was ordered to be reinstated with effect from August 24, 1953. The workmen raised an industrial dispute which was referred to the Labour Court under section 33 Of the , for adjudication. The Tribunal held that all the workmen who turned up on or before October 2, 1953, were entitled to be taken back into employment without condition and of the two men who came later, but failed to produce evidence satisfactory to the company of their absence as required by the Standing Orders. Held, that the Industrial Tribunal had no jurisdiction to interfere with the decision of the Company 's workmen on the ground that they did not join or perform duty if they reported for duty after October 2. 1953, and that the order of suspension was therefore illegal. The first two questions which arose for determination were whether the discharge and dismissal of the workmen amounted to punishment and whether the second one was justified by the provisions of section 33 of the , as it did not involve any substantial question of law. Held further, that when the words used in the notices served on the workmen showed that they were not harmful to the running of the factory, the work of the company will be paralysed if the company is forced to give leave to all of them for a " more or less indefinite period". The second question was whether the workmen were entitled under Standing Orders to be paid any wages and other reliefs. Held also that the second question did not arise out of the facts of the case. The second point raised by the workmen was fully considered by the Tribunal, which found that the company had decided to terminate the services of the workman on the grounds of his prejudicial and subversive activities and therefore dismissed him.

The University of Rajas than invited applications for the post of Professor in Botany. The Selection Committee constituted under section 5 of the Rajasthan University Teachers and Offi cers (Selection for Appointment) Act, 1974 recommended the names of Dr. G.S. Nathawat for the said post. The name of Dr, Urea Kant was mentioned in the reserve list by the Selection Committee. The Syndicate of the University approved the list and appointed Dr. Natik as Professor in the department of Bot any. The appellant Dr. Urea Kurnool was already selected and kept in the reserved list for appointment on the post. On a writ petition filed by him, the High Court held that the constitution of the Selection Commit tee was valid but as regards the appointment of Dr Nati kurnool, it was held that once a person selected by the selection committee had joined, that post was filled and some vacancy was caused thereafter a fresh Selection Committee should have been constituted. In appeal to this Court, it Was contended on behalf of the appellant that the reserve List was exhausted as soon as the person recommended in the main list joined the post, and that even out of the petitioners who had filed the writ petition, Dr. Uma Kant also was appointed as Professor. Allowing the appeals, HELD: 1.1 The High Court committed a clear error in restricting the scope of the reserve lists only against the post for which the selection was made and which according to the High court could only be available to the incumbent in the Reserve List if the person selected in the preliminary list did not join such post. Such interpretation is not borne out from any of the provisions of Section 3(1), Section 5 or sub section (4) of Section 6 of the Act of 1974. [420C D] 1.2 The High court was wrong in taking the view that a regular vacancy of Professor having arisen on the retirement of Dr Botall, and such Selection Committee had approved and recommended the name of the appel lant Dr. S.U. Bhardwaj in the reserves list finding him suitable for appointment.

The petitioners challenged the validity of sections 9, 10 and 11 of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954 on the ground that they were violative of their fundamental rights under articles 14, 19(1)(f) and 31 of the Constitution. The petitioners contended that the provisions of section 9 were ultra vires the Constitution as they had been made without giving any opportunity to the local authority to make representations against them. Held: (i) Section 11 of Bombay Town planning Act, 1955, is not violative of article 14 of the Constitu tion. It only provides for a reasonable restriction on the right of owners of land to erect or proceed with any building or remove, pull down, alter, make additions to or any substantial repair to any building, and section 12 empowers the local authori ty to acquire any land designated in the development plan for a purpose specified in cls. (b) and (e) of section 7 and if such land does not vest in the local Authority, the State Government shall not include the said purpose in the scheme. The power to acquire land designated under the Act is discretionary and it can be exercised only by a Municipal Corporation or any other authority established by law in India. The provisions of sections 4 to 16 are unreasonable restrictions on the rights of a land owner to deal with his land as he pleased, it is enough to say that in view of the immensity of the task of the local authorities to find funds for the acquisition of lands for public purposes, a period of ten years was not too long. The preparation of the tentative plan or the final development plan was not something which was left to the pleasure or discretion of the authority. In the present case the preparation of a development plan is an immense task and the authorities proceeded with it in a manner to which no exception can be taken. The scheme is a simple one as to whether the commencement certificate should be granted or not.

The appellant State of Gujarat filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the award of the Tribunal, which was dismissed. The appellant contended that the award merely fixed or demarcates the boundary between the State of Kutch and the Rann of Kutch as shown in the pre partition maps, which needs to be demarcated on the ground. The State of Bombay filed a separate counter affidavit stating that the boundaries of the State were not correctly ascertained. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the dispute related to the boundary of the Ronda and not to exercise rights to move freely throughout the territory of India under article 19(1)(d) of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The award did not purport to nor did it operate as giving rise to an obligation to cede Indian territory. [151 F] (ii) The dispute related only to the location of the boundary line and the operative part of the Award declared the alignment of the boundaries as erroneous. [152 G] (iii) The reference to the High Courts was not intended to be a mere matter of law, but was intended to cover all the territorial disputes as well as the question whether there was an intention to constitute a part of India or to confer jurisdiction on the executive which extended to matters with respect to which Parliament had power to make laws. [153 A B] (iv) The contention that the Award merely fixed the boundary and demarcats the boundary, was not correct. It did not give rise to any question as to whether there existed a territorial dispute as there was a well established boundary running through the boundaries. [154 C D] (v) The High Courts of Gujarat and Delhi had rightly held that the reference made by the Government of India to the Bombay State merged with the Dominion of India.

The mortgagor executed a mortgage deed in favour of one Mahendra Nath Chakravarty and executed on August 27, 1922 an endorsement dated April 1, 1937, relating to payment of the principal and interest. The mortgagor 's right to redeem the mortgaged property was extinguished by reason of the sale of the mortgagee 's interest in Mauza Bahaldih. The mortgagee applied for a decree for enforcement of the mortgage but the suit was dismissed on July 12, 1946. On August 16, 1934, an application was made by the mortgagor praying that the mortgage might be redeemed and the mortgagee should be directed to pay the amount due under the mortgage money. The trial Court rejected the defence raised by the plaintiff and held that the suit in respect of the first mortgage was not barred by limitation. The High Court on appeal took the view that as the plaintiff had in her plaint not relied upon any other part payment of principal or interest to extend the period of limitation for the suit, she could still maintain the suit relying on the dispossession of the mortgagor from Mauza Bahaboodih and the sale made by him in favour the later mortgage had become due on April 14, 1925. In appeal to this Court it was contended that: (1) The mortgagee ' interest in the mortgaged properties was not extinguished because the mortgage "was partly simple and partly usufructuary" and even though the mortgagor 'S had lost his interest in all the properties mortgaged by him, he could still be maintained under section 68 of the Transfer of Property Act; (2) The suit to enforce payment of money charged upon immoveable property may be filed within twelve years from the date on which the money sued for becomes due and the period during which the payment was made would not extend the time of limitation. HELD: (i) The right conferred by section 68 is again not a right to enforce the mortgage, but a right of sue for the mortgage amount on the personal covenant or to claim compensation when the mortgagee is deprived of his security. [644 D] (ii) The mortgagor had parted with his interest during the period April 14 and 19 5, 1947, in satisfaction of the debt due from the mortgagor. The period of twelve years commencing from April 14 was not a period of one year but three months after the mortgage deed. The right to sue where the mortgagee was deprived of the mortgaged security or where he was not secured in his possession of the property or where possession was not delivered to him as agreed, the claim maintainable by the mortgagee. [643 D] In the present case the mortgagor had lost interest inall his properties and the suit filed on July12, 1946, regarded as one to enforce that claim to recover the mortgage moneys under section 69 of the Indian Registration Act. The suit was therefore barred by the law of limitation and the right conferred on the mortgagee by section 69 was again not an right to enforcing the mortgage. [641 H] (iii) The period for filing a suit or extension of time prescribed by the Limitation Act for filing the suit is three years from April 1 and the date of expiry of twelve months commencing from the dates of such extension under article 132 of the Limitation act. In the instant case, the mortgagor was entitled to sue for execution of the decree. [651 B] (iv) The High court was right in holding that the mortgagor could not enforce the claim to enforce a mortgage by enforcing payment of moneys at the time when money sued had become payable.

The appellants employ as many as 7000 workmen in those factories. In order to provide transport facilities to their employees, the appellants provided transport facilities for their employees to come to the factories from their respective villages. The appellants provided Transport facilities to the employees from their depots. The company had also provided transport facility to their employee. The Company was prepared to grant free transport facilities. The appellant company was directed by the Commissioner of Pune Division to grant transport facilities in the State of Maharashtra to its employees. The said directions were not implemented by the company. The High Court dismissed the appeals filed by the appellants. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that even if a nominal charge is realised from the employees that would not make the transport a public service vehicle carrying passenger; so as to attract the provisions of section 3 which is the charging section of the Act, the said amenities should not be extended to the other employees and that the transport facilities provided to the employee by the appellant were not to be exempted under section 3. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The transport service in the present case was registered as private service vehicle falls squarely within the ambit of the definition of "stage carriage" given in section 2(7) of the Bombay Motor Vehicles Act, 1939, passengers must be carried for hire or reward at separate fares paid by or for individual passengers either for the whole journey or for stages of the journey. Rule 2(i) of Bombay Motor Vehicle Rules, 1940 framed under the Bombay Act is a statute which authorises the levy of passenger tax on certain classes of public service vehicles. [361 E F] 2. The word "public" has got a well known connotation and means a carriage to which any member of the public can have free access on payment of the usual charges. It cannot by any process of reasoning or stretch of imagination be deemed to include employees of a private company who are given facilities not as members of the Public but as holding a special status, namely, the employees of that company. [362 G H] 3. The words "public service vehicle" have got a very wide connotation and mean a carriage by road. It is true that the term 'public service vehicles ' has not been defined either by the Act or by the Rules but that however does not create any difficulty because having regard to the Preamble of the . it is of the opinion that the tax can be levied only on passengers who are carried by a stage carriage which is of tho nature of a public services vehicle. The term "public servants" has been defined in section 3(7), but that is to say, as defined in s 2(8) of Act, passengers shall be carried by road in stage carriages. [360 F G] 4. The definition of 'stage service ' has no doubt, because having regards to the preamble of the , it is not possible to construe the word "Public" with reference to the Act as meaning a motor vehicle which cannot be termed as public service Vehicles falling within the purview of the provisions Of the Bombay . [361 H] 5. The Bombay Motor vehicles (Taxation on Passengers) Act, 1958 clearly indicates that the Tax would be leviable only if the passengers are carried on a public serv ice vehicle. It does not by any processes of reasoning, or stretch the imagination be considered to include persons of a Private company who were given facilities, not as Members of thepublic but as held in the case of the present appellants.

The appellant, a cinema house owner, was granted a licence for a period of six years under the M.P. Cinemas (Regulation) Rules, 1952. The District Magistrate issued a no objection certificate to the third respondent, who filed an appeal against the refusal of the renewal of his licence by the appellate authority. The appellate authority allowed the appeal and set aside the order granting the licence for quasi permanent cinema licence. The High Court in a writ petition filed by the third Respondent held that the District Magistrate was not influenced by any extraneous consideration that a cinema licence had been granted to the fourth respondent, and that it being a matter left to the subjective satisfaction of the State Government, the State Govt. on being satisfied that there was no impediment to grant of such a licence, was perfectly justified in granting the same and therefore it set aside that order. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that (i) the appellants who had objected to the grant of a noobjection certificate to them, were not acting bona fide in vindication of their own rights but were a fence or a cloak for the owners of Paras Cinema, the holders of permanent cinema licences in the locality and the appellants thus being prose cuted by the District Magis trate were bound to have the matter decided by him; (ii) the licensing authority was influenced by an extraneous consideration, namely, re opening of Para cinema with a permanent cinema license while rejecting the application of third respondent for renewal of licence by order dated 29th June 1977. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The right to object is at the initial stage when a noti fication is applied for by the intending applicant for such a certificate. But there is nothing in the Act or Rules which requires the licensing authori ty to invite objections before grant of licence. [899C] 2.1 Rule 3 envisages construction of a cinema houses and as a first step, selection of a site where the cinema house is to be located is necessary. Selection of the site and its clearance by the licensing Authority by the issuance of a notification under rule 3(2) is an important step to be taken in the direction of finally constructing a cinema theatre and obtaining a licence from the licensing authorities. [800G H] 2:2 The right of object to public interest is at tho initial stage, when a No objection certificate is applied by the proposed applicant for a cinema, but there is no provision for inviting objections when the application is for a permanent or quasi permanent Cinema licence or a touring cinema licence, and there is also no provision in the Rules which required advertisement of such an application inviting objections. [900D] 2 :3 The right is at present available to the appellant only if he satisfies all the conditions laid down by Rule 3(1). [801E] 2 .4 In the instant case, the application for a licence was made on the ground that there were mosque, a "madarsa" and a temple in the vicinity of the place where the Cinema house is being constructed. The appellant had not raised any objection to the renewal application. When the appeal against this order was pending before the State Govern ment, the appellant filed a writ Petition challenging the validity of the said order on the grounds that there is a mosque, and a Temple in the proximity of the premises where cinema house was to be constructed, but he was influenced only by an income tax licence while rejecting his application for renewal. The petition was dismissed by the High Court.

The respondent entered into a contract with the appellant for the supply of float iron lying in the mining area and gave them the right to win and remove the iron ore. The appellant filed a suit against the respondent claiming a declaration that he was entitled to remain in possession of the mining lease. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) The plaint in the present case was not an acceptance and the service of a copy of the plaint along with the writ of summons was a communication of the acceptance. Under section 2(6), the contract to take shares was concluded on September 2, 1957 and that in breach of the contract the respondent failed to apply for and obtain the necessary consent of the Central Government. The plea that the appellant had not agreed to purchase the mining leases was not accepted by the trial court as it was an offer only. [584 F G] (ii) The pleadings and issues raised the question whether a con tract was made on September, 2, could not be considered or decided in this case. The plaint was not a suit for specific performance of the contracts. Before the present suit for Specific performance of a contract was instituted, the offer had been withdrawn. [585 F G]. Bloxam vs Ayerst (I.L.R. 1822 approved. Bloxham vs Akerst (A.I.R , referred to. (iii) The plea of the appellant that he had not accepted the offer was not raised in this Court. The pleadings, and issues raise the question as to whether a contract is made on Sept. 2,1957. If the plaintiffs desired to set up a new case that the contract was concluded in November 1957 they should have amended their pleadings accordingly. [586 A B]. Bliton vs Aierst (L.J.

The appellants were office bearers of a company. A complaint was filed against them under section 7 of the Essential Supplies (Temporary Powers) Act, 1946, alleging that they had failed to pay to the sellers the price of sugarcane purchased by them within the time prescribed. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence and issued process. The appellants contended that the investigation which was being carried on against them was in accordance with law and therefore the complaint could not have been filed under section 3 of the Act. Held, that the complaint did not disclose a cognizable offence and the police could not take up the investigation of that complaint. Section 3(1) provides that unless there is an agreement in writing to the contrary between the parties the purchaser shall pay to seller the price fixed by the Government. The section does not say anything more on this question. It only says that unless the Central Government is of opinion, that it is necessary or expedient so to do for maintaining or increasing the supply of essential commodities and trade and commerce therein, it may provide for regulating or prohibiting the sale of food crops generally or of specified food crops. The Bihar Act was a pre Constitution Act and it could have continued to be in force only till it was altered, repealed o.r amended by a competent legislature or other competent authority. Ch. Tika Ramji and Ors. vs The State of U.P., ; , referred to. Held further that the power conferred on the Government under section 6 of the , cannot be challenged as invalid. Section 2(a) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act defines essential commodity. Sub section (3) of that section provides for controlling the price at which any essential commodity may be bought or sold. The Central Government was well within its powers in issuing the Sugarcane Control Order, 1955 in the manner it did because all this was in exercise of the concurrent power of legislation under Entry 33 of List III.

The Government of Karnataka decided to adopt a policy to encourage rapid industrialisation. An Order No. CI 58 FM 69 dated 30th June, 1969 was issued which recited that the Government had on 30th November 1966 issued directions indicating incentives that would be given to entrepreneurs starting new industries in Mysore State. The Government of Mysore issued another order which stated that the reasons for making the said order of 12th January, 1977 were that the scheme of concessions adopted by the Government earlier had given room for many types of misuse and the earlier orders had not prescribed any ceiling limits or restrictions on the quantum of refund of sales tax or concession to be granted. The said order dated 12th 1st August, 1975 was issued under which the Governor of Mysore was pleased to sanction the following incentives and concessions to entrepreneurs for starting new industrial units in Mysore. "The Government, namely, the Government of India, decided to introduce a policy of encourage rapid Industrialisation and that the said scheme should be implemented with effect from 12th December, 1966". The procedure prescribed for obtaining the concession given under the orders referred to earlier was that the concession of refund would be allowed on all sales tax paid by a new industry on raw materials purchased by it for the first five years from the date the industry goes into production. The State Government issued another Order dated 12.1.1977 providing that the concessions of refund should be allowed only in all sales Tax paid by the new industry. The order dated December 30, 1966 was challenged before the High Court by the appellants who contended that the doctrine of Promissory Estoppel was not applicable in the present case because it was found by the State Government that the benefits granted under the said Order had given to the entrepreneurs starting a industrial unit in the Mysore State and issued directions. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions.
