In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellants it was contended that (i) the doctrine was not applied in the instant case because the concession granted under an order dated 30.6.1969 had given rooms for many type of misuse but such a recital by itself cannot establish that the facilities were in fact misused; and (ii) the concession was granted to entrepreneurs only on the basis of a certificate issued earlier. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The doctrine of promissory Estoppel is not applicable to the instant cases because it is found by this Court that the State has no authority to provide for the grant of refund. [950E] 2.1 In order to test the validity of an order passed by the High Courts under Article 226 of the Constitution, one has to see the substance of the concession conferred under the Order and not merely certain words used out of context. Although the benefit regarding sales tax granted to the new industries is by way of refund, of sales Tax pay able in the State for the second time, the mere fact that the order of 30th July 1969 did not specify the power under which it was issued will make no difference because such a power is clearly there in Section 8A and where the source of power underwhich it is issued is not stated in an order but can be found on examination of the relevant Act, the exercise of the power must be attributed to that source. [951F G] 2:2 The mere fact of the fact that an order of thirty six June 1969 did no specify the powers under which was issued would make no distinction because such power is specifically mentioned in an Order but can he found on the examination of relevant Act. [953B C] Union of India vs M/s Indo Afghan Agencies Ltd., ; , referred to.

The appellants were charged with offences under Sections 147, 148 and 323 read with Section 149 I.P.C. for causing the death of one Madda Laksha mandas of village Ramaraogudem on November 1, 1980 near the Tobacco garden of A 1. The Trial Court acquitted all the charges. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of A 4 to A 6 under Sections 148 and 302 read with 149 I .P. C. and acquit them of all the offences. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellants being only three in number, there was no question of their forming an unlawful assembly within the meaning of Section 141 I. P.C., if the evidence disclosed commission of an offence in furtherance of the common intention of them all. [8B] 1.2 In so far as the presence and partic ipation of the accused in the attack on the deceased is concerned, it is not the prosecution case that apart from the seven accused persons there were some other unidentified persons who were involved in the crime. The High Court clearly fell into error in confirming the conviction of A 2 under Sections 302 readwith Section 34 I.p.C.[8D] 1:3. The appellants acted in fur ther, the appellants acted, in further, while found guilty for the offences punishable under Sections 149 and 302 I.PC. [9E F] 1 4. The prosecution case from the very beginning was that A 1 to A 7, the named persons formed the Unlawful assembly. A 4, A 5 and A 6 were armed with spears, A 2, A 4 and A 3 chopped of the fingers of left hand of the deceased with the knife blows. There were injuries all over the body. The number and nature of injuries, however, did not indicate that the accused persons had some other unlawful assembly.

The assessee was the owner of a house situated in Ernakulam, which he had purchased in 1958 for the price of Rs. 16,500. On 25th December 1965, the assessee sold the house to his daughter in law and five children. The assessment of the assessee for the assessment year 1966 67 was completed on the basis of the house being sold by him at the same price at which it was purchased and no capital gains accrued or arose to him as a result of the transfer. On 4th April 1968, the Income tax officer issued a notice under section 148 of the Act seeking to reopen the assessment of assessee for its assessment year 1967 67 and requiring the assessee to submit a return of income within 30 days of the service of the notice. The assessee submitted a return on 25th March 1965 stating that there was no under statement of consideration in respect of the transferred house and it was not possible to say that the transfer was effected by the assessee with the object of avoidance or reduction of his liability under section 45. On 2nd April 1968 the Income Tax officer issued notice under Section 148 of Act seeking reopen the assess ment of the respondent for the year 1966 68 and requiring him to submit fresh return of the income within thirty days of service of notice. 48 The assessee filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the reopening of assessment on the ground that the fair market value of the property as on the date of transfer exceeded the full value of consideration declared by the respondent in respect thereof and taking the view that this sub section did not require as a condition precedent for attracting the applicability of Section 52(2) of the Income ' tax Act, 1961. The High Court dismissed the petition.

The appellant was charged with the offence of committing an offence under section 16(1)(a) (i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, for selling adulterated food. The prosecution case was that the appellant had gone to "a shop to make purchases", without giving either the name of the shop or approximate date or time of his visit. Under cross examination he said that he did not know whether it was a foodgrain shop. He also stated that he had seen the complainant pick up a jar, open it and look at its contents. The appellant was convicted under section 7(1) (a)(i) and section 16 (1) of that Act. On appeal by special leave: HELD : The prosecution has to prove beyond reasonable doubt that what was kept by a seller was "food" at all, this must be resolved in favour of the complainant. It is not necessary for the prosecution to prove affirmatively that what Was stored or sold was "for human consumption". The charge was that it was part of the prosecution case that the Til seeds with which we are concerned were meant for human consumption. This necessarily meant that it had been supported by what the appellant bad written on the cash memo when he sold these Til seeds to the Food Inspector. [329 G H] Bhagwan Das vs Delhi Administration, ; , applied. The fact that the signatures of Tambe were absent on all those documents on which they would have been present if section 10(7) of Act had been strictly complied with does not affect the case of the appellant.

The appellant was dismissed from service by the Collector on 13.1.1966. He filed a suit for declaration that the order of dismissal was inoperative and he continued to be in service. The trial Judge held that the dismissal was valid and that the appellant continued to remain in service, and that he had continued to serve till the decision of the State Government on his appeal. On appeal by the respondent, the Divisional Commissioner confirmed the finding of the trial Court that it had no effective steps for the purpose of section 326(2) of the . The High Court dismissed the second appeal preferred by the appellant. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the suit was barred by limitation as the order dated 13. 1.1966 was not passed within a period of three years from that date and that in any event, the appeal filed by the Divisional Commis sioner was time barred. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) The cause of action shall be taken to arise not from the date of the original adverse order but on the date when the order is passed or representation was made. [52E] (2) The expression 'or the remedies which are available to him under the relevant service rules as to redressal of grievances ' in section 21 of the is wide enough to include all those who have been given liberty to file a suit under the appropriate service rules, as to redress of grievances. [53F G] (3) The word 'or ' has not been defined in the Act. It is well settled that if it had been passed before the Constitution came into force on January 26, 1950, the petitioner would have had no remedy in the Courts. But he has not done so. He has thus a vested right to file an application under article 226 of the Constitution. [54H; 55A] (4) The order of the Divisional Commi sioners is final and conclusive. It does not operate as res judicata between the parties. [55D] (5) In the instant case, the cause of actions shall be deemed to arise when the remedies available to the public servant under the rele vant service rules are disposed of. The question for consideration is whether it should be disposal of one appeal or the entire hierarchy of reliefs as may have been provided.

The appellant filed a suit for partition against his father and several alienees from him. The trial court rejected the claim of the plaintiff and dismissed his suit. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decision of the trial court and held that the trial Court was not bound to allow the respondent 's application for execution of the decree in respect of the said properties. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the High Courts had taken a contrary view and therefore the High court should have interfered with the decision in revision; and (ii) the words "judgment, decree or final order appealed from" in the relevant clause of Explanation 1 to section 2(1)(c) of the Indian , were not intended to cover an appeal against a part only of the original decree. HELD : The High Courts in construing the clause have taken a different view and have taken the same view which is consistent with the provisions of explanation 1 to Explanation 1. [465 F] (i). The words "decree" and "decree", in Explanation 1, are not defined in the Act. They are used in the sense of an adjudication or award. It is well settled that a judgment pronounced by the trial judge on the merits does not mean the whole of the decision but the whole judgment must be read as a whole in relation to the decision. [466 B C] (ii). The word "decree " means not a part of the final order but the entire decree. It means the final expression of an order which conclusively determines the rights of parties with regard to all or any of the matters in controversy in suit, and it is also true that a party aggrieved by a decree may appeal only against a portion of it and is not bound by it. But it does not follow generally that the word "judgment" in Explanation I must mean the final adjudication of the suit. [467 C D] (iii). The expression "decree ' means not merely a part but also a whole of it. It has been used in Order XX, Rule 1, Civil Procedure Code, for the purpose of determining whether an order passed by the High or Court is a decree of affirmance and this is not affected either by the extent of the variation made or by the fact that the variation is made in favour of the intending appellant and not against him.

The provisions of section 115, Code of Civil Procedure, read with the Bombay High Court (Amendment) Act, 1972, are in pari materia with the original section 115. The High Court has exclusive jurisdiction under section 115 to entertain a revision petition against an order of the District Court under section 25, Provincial Small Cause Courts Act disposing of a revision application. Section 25, which is a special provision, is a self sufficient code so far as the present enquiry is concerned. Under the originals, before the amendment of section 5, the High Court alone shall be competent to make an order under this section. The proviso thereto declares that in respect of all cases arising out of original suits or other proceedings of any valuation decided by the District Judge, the decision of the district court shall be final. The language of the first proviso is clear and unambiguous. It does not require that the matter should be referred to the District judge for determination as to whether the legislature intended a further revision petition to the High court. [39 C D] In the present case, the trial court had jurisdiction under Section 115 in cases arising from original suits of the value of Rs. 20,000/ and above, and the revisional jurisdiction was concurrently shared between the High Courts. The appellate court had no power under section 5 to exercise revisional jurisdiction in respect off a revisional order under section 50, Provincial small Cause Courts act.

The respondent State Government issued a notification under section 52(1) of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959 for acquisition of certain lands belonging to the appellants. The appellants challenged the said notification before the High Court by way of a writ petition. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the notice issued under section 51(2) of Act was duly served on the respondents and they had no right to take any steps to take possession of the land acquired. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the petition filed by the respondents purporting to be under article 226 of the Constitution in the Calcutta High Court and the rule nisi thereon were not maintainable as the writ petitions were not properly constituted. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order dated March 13 , 1984 issued by the State Government under section 49(1), of the Act became effective the moment it was published in the official Gazette as thereupon the notified land became vested in the State Govern ment free from all encumbrances. It was not necessary for the respondents to plead the service of notice on them by the Special Officer, Town Planning Department , Jaipur under section 50(2). [606C D] 2. The entire cause of action culminating in the acquisition of the lands under section 54(1 ) arose within the State of Rajasthan i.e. within the territorial jurisdiction of the High Courts at the time. [607D] 3. The respondents had been shifting their stand before the Special officer. The notification dated February 8, 1984 issued under Section 52(2), became effective only on August 13 ,1984 within the geographical limits of the State. The Notification dated February8 , 1984 was not applicable to the instant case because the Government were primarily thinking of making the land available for construction of residential houses before making provisions for construction for construction. [065E F] 4. The expression 'cause of action ' is tersely defined in Mulla 's Code of Civil Procedure: "the cause of a action" means every fact which, if traversed it would be necessary for plaintiff ties to prove in order to support his right to a judgment of the Court". [608F G] 5. The word 'cause ' is a bundle of facts which taken with the law applicable to them gives the plaintiff a right to relief against the defendant. The mere service of the notice under section52(2 ) of the , on the respond ent at their registered office at 18 B , Brabourne Road, Calcutta i. e., within the area of the state of West Bengal could not give rise to a cause of ' action within that territory unless the service was an integral part of the cause of the action. [076G H] 6. The whole cause of actions culminating in acquisition of land under section 55(1 )(2) arose within tho State of Rajas than within the jurisdiction of Rajasthan High Court at the Jaipur Bench. [086A B] 7. The fact that service of notices under section 53(2 ), on the respondent at their Registered office at18 B , brabourna Road, Delhi i.

The respondent filed a suit for eviction of the appellant tenant from the premises in dispute on the ground that the appellant was inducted as a tenant of the premises by a co operative society and therefore, the building was not covered by the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the building in question was exempt from the operation of the new Rent Act on two grounds: (1) that the premises were not ten years old on the date of the suit and therefore the new rent Act had no application to the building; and (2) that since the building had been constructed substantially out of funds obtained from sources mentioned in the proviso to s.2(2), the building could not be deemed to have been completed on the dates of assessment of house tax and water tax. The Additional District Judge affirmed the findings of the trial court on all other points except the finding that the tenant was not ten year old on date of suit, but during the pendency of the litigation it completed ten years. In appeal by special leave, the appellant contended: (i) that in view of sub s.(2) of s.20 of the Act, a sum of Rs. 1000 per month could be deducted from his rent; and that since he had failed to prove that the spent Rs. 1500 was repairs of the building, the suit was not maintainable. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that by seeking the benefit of s.(20) of the Small Causes Act, the new Act will be applicable to a building during the period of ten years from the date on which its construction is completed. [334C] 2.1 In the instant case, admittedly a sum Of Rs. 1,000 was paid by the appellant to the landlord through a crossed cheque dated 16th March, 1978. But when the plaintiff was in the witness box payment by cheque was not specifically put to him and it has not been established as to for which period the payment by cheques was made. The defence of the defendant that he had not paid the amount of Rs 1500 was not accepted. [340D E] 2:2.2 In a suit filed under section 14(1) for eviction on the grounds mentioned in cl.(a) to sub s (2), viz., arrears of rent, if at the first hearing of the Suit the tenant in default pays all arrears of land revenue and damages for use and occupation of the buildings due from him, such damages for used and occupation being calculated at the same rate as rent together with interest thereon at the rate of nine per cent per annum and the landlord 's cost of the suits in respect thereof after deducting there from any amount already deposited by the tenant under sub section (1), the court may, in lieu of passing a decree for eviction, pass an order relieving the tenant against his liability for eviction. [341E G] 2 :3.

The appellant filed a petition under sections 17 and 20 of the Indian , for a decree in terms of the award. The respondents contended that there was a valid agreement of reference to arbitration and that the agreement was not one relating to execution of works as that had been completed and the dispute related only to payment of bills, contracts and other instrument. Held, that the appellant was entitled to the decree. The agreement dated February 6, 1948, was executed by a person who was authorised to do so by the Governor General acting through his Secretary to execute the agreement for reference to Arbitration. It was not a certified copy of the order passed in the suit filed in the court. The Government had been authorised under section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935, to execute an agreement dated January 2, 1948. The Secretary was not authorised by the Government to execute it. The appellant could not be said to have been authorised by notification in the Official Gazette to execute a contract. The order of the Secretary was executed on February 6. 1948 and the copy of it was sent to the Government would appear to have had been insufficiently stamped. The copy of an instrument cannot be validated under section 176(3). The law is no doubt well settled that the copy could not he validated if it did not fall within Entry 12 in which case he would not be competent to execute. The fact that the Secretary undoubtedly intended that Y. K. Lall, the Executive Engineer had been authorized to do the work was a sufficient reason for the High Court to hold that the award passed in proceedings founded thereon is a nullity and that no decree could be passed thereon.

The appellant was working as Executive Engineer in Public Works Department. On various dates in the year 1979, he placed orders for purchase of sign boards and import lincences. The requisite sign boards were purchased in pursuance of the orders. In 1980 some complaints were received against him pertaining to the purchase of the sign boards. Vigilance enquiry was instituted against him under sub sections (1) and (2) of section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. In the meantime, the respondent retired from service on October 31, 1982. The First Information Report was lodged on August 27, 1985 in respect of the purchase and import of sign Boards in 1979. The respondent filed a Criminal Miscellaneous Petition before the High Court for quashing the First Information Reports on the ground that the same having been lodged about three years after his retirement and about six years after the event of purchase of signs and import, he was liable to be quashed. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the said FIR was not lodged within four years of his retirement or the event took place more than four years before his retirement; that the State had no power under section 5(2) to initiate judicial proceedings for prosecution of a government servant on the expiry of four years from the date of cause of action or event mentioned therein. The appellant filed an appeal in this Court against the High Courts order and the High court allowed the same holding that it was not necessary to decide afresh the petition under section 482 Cr. P.C. as the case had been lodged more than six years before the institution of the criminal proceedings; and that the High COurt committed error in taking the view that the Criminal Appeal No. 422 of 1988 filed by the respondent was barred by limitation. The State appealed to this Court. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have been clearly in error in holding that section 5 (2 ) of the Act has not been designed to confer a right on government servant even if he is guilty of grave misconduct or negligence which constitutes an offence punishable either under the Penal Code or under the Prevention or Prevention of corruption Act, or an analogous law.

The respondent company was a public limited company under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The shares of the company were held by directors including Ramayamma and Kamakashamma, his daughter, who had two sons. The preference shareholders were entitled to vote at the meeting of the Company each shareholder being entitled to exercise one vote for each share. In the course of assessment proceedings the Income tax Officer found that for three years ending March 31, 1948, March 31 and March 31 1949, the company had declared each year a total dividend of Rs. 38,750/ . The respondent company took over the business conducted by Nageswara Rao Panthulu, a limited company. In September 1936, the respondent company sold its ordinary shares to the appellant company. The respondent challenged the competence of the income tax officer to pass an order under section 23 A of the Income Tax Act, 1922, on the ground that the provisions of section 23A were not applicable to the said provision as it stood at the material time. The High Court held that the respondent was one in which public were substantially interested and there fore the Income 'tax Officer had no jurisdiction to pass the order under s 23 A. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The distinction between the controlling group and the public is not along the line which distinguishes directors from the remaining members of the 16 company. If a director does not belong to the controlling Group, he will be regarded as a member of the public for the purposes of the third proviso and the Explanation to section 23(A) even though such director was directly entrusted with the management of the affairs of the respondent. The Explanation has no operation. Whether inview of the 3 proviso the company may be regarded in which the public are substantially interested, is a question to which no attention was paid by the Tribunal. [17 B C] (ii) The Explanation to sub section (1) of section23A is in reality a clause which defines what a company, in which, the public were directly interested, as meaning not twenty five per cent of the voting power, but power exercisable in respect of shares other than shares entitled to a fixed rate of dividend. [18 C D] (iii) The explanation has no application because no presumption on the facts found could arise thereunder. The Revenue authorities have not made any investigation on the question whether there existed any controlling interest in a group of persons. so as to bring the case within the third Proviso. The explanation had no operation and the finding that there existed no controlling interest was not binding on the respondent, [18 E F] (iv) The Tribunal has not made an investigation on this question whether the shares carrying not less than twenty five percent of the assessable income of the appellant Company were vested in persons other than the controlling groups. For the purpose of ascertaining the voting powers, voting rights attached to all the shares must be taken into account. No investigation had been made by the Income. tax Officer whether there was any group of Persons controlling the working of the assessee company. It is true that the preference shareholders are entitled to votes at each shareholder 's meeting and the Articles of Association of the Compa ny of the Respondent Company made no distinction between those controlling group 'and the public was not along line which distinguish directors from those remaining members.

The appellants were convicted under sections 7 and 9 of the Essential Supplies Act, 1947 on two counts, namely, (1) that the bales remained in the physical possession of the first appellant at all material times and were not physically delivered to the second appellant; (2) that they had been authorised to take delivery of the goods and the price thereof. The first appellant contended that the delivery was not by the quota holder but by a person who was in such a relation with the first appel lant, and therefore, no longer had title to them, and (3) that as there was physical delivery to Dwarkadas Khetan, the delivery order was illegal. Held, that the goods left the Mills premises, the property in them had passed and when Dharsi Moolji refused to receive them they were handed over to the appellants. The delivery order made by the first appellants was not a mere device for the delivery of goods but was one intended to be used as custody rather than possession. The fact that the appellants had delivered the bales to the first respondent could not make the delivery illegal, because, the goods remained in their possession and were in the possession of a person to whom delivery was made. Dwarkadasi vs Ram Gopal, (1923) L.R. 46 I.A. 129, referred to. The law books divide its concept into two broad categories, (i) physical possession or possession in fact and (ii) legal possession which need not coincide with possession in the facts of the case. Dwarakas Khetan could, in the circumstances given above, be described without any straining of language as the person to whose goods were actually delivered.

The appellant was a Professor in a Government College. He was charged with having committed an offence under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code and section 5(2) read with section 5 (1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The Special Judge who tried both the accused found them guilty of the offence with which they were charged. On appeal by the State, the High Court held that the last part of the Ninth clause was not applicable to the case and accordingly acquitted the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) since the first part of a Ninth clause had been omitted from the Ninth Clause as it stood before its amendment in 1964, the second part could not be applied to the present case; and (ii) since there was abuse by a Government servant of his position as a public servant, he was liable under section 5 of the Corruption Act. HELD : (i). The appellant was guilty of an offence punishable under section5(1)(a) of Prevention of ' Corruption Act because he was a lecturer in a government College and was not a public Servant when he was appointed for that purpose. [337 B] (ii).The second part of Ninth clause which provided that the expression "every person" shall be deemed to have been a public servants, whether appointed by Government or not, includes a person in the service or pay of the Government or remunerated by fees or commission for the performance of any public duty. The word "other wise" refers to means other than corrupt or illegal means and does not form two clauses. If the meaning to be given to the word "otherwise" is, as earlier stated, the words "by corrupt or legal means" or "by otherwise" form a single clause and do not form one of them. [320 D] (iii).The use of the word 'other wise ' in the Ninth Schedule shows that the connection with Government was necessary either in respect of the payment of remuneration or in respect Of the performance by any of the public services. The use of this word is not conclusive and must be read as a whole. [322 E] (iv).The expression "public servant" in section 5 means a person who is appointed an examiner, and who receives remuneration by fees. It does not include a person employed by a government servant to whom the duties are assigned. The definition of public servant ' includes a public officer. The words "otherwise" refer to means all the Government servants as defined in section 161. If that be so the abuse of position as public servant that is referred to is the abuse by corrupt or illegally means or by otherwise". [322 H 322 A] (v)The use "by the Government" in the definition of a public office, does not mean that the means are corrupt or illegality or illegal. The expression "otherary" refers only to acts done by a public authority as a person engaged in any work which is remunerated or commission and for those in the regular service of any other person. [323 B C] (vi)The word "employee" used in section 6(1) (d)(i) means a government employee who has been employed by the Government to gain for himself or for any other public servant any valuable thing or pecuniary advantage. The term "other similarly" refers not only to corrupt or unlawful means but also to corrupt and illegal means. [324 E] In the present ease, the appellant was appointed as an Examiner of University which was a non gazetted post under the Government of India. He had been given a charge of office in remuneration paid by the University. The appointment was made on the recommendation of the Public Service Commission. The appellant 's name did not find place in the list of members of the Institute which was the subject matter of the election to the Legislative Assembly.

The petitioners, who were casual labour engaged on terms of casual labour for periods varying between 10 and 16 years in the construction Department of the Signal Unit in Northern Railway, challenged their claim before the Central Administrative Tribunal contending that they had put in more than 360 days of service. The Tribunal allowed their writ petitions holding that the respondents were not entitled to all the privileges like House Rent Allowance, City Compensatory Allowance, Casual Leave, increment etc., and directed regularisation of services and declaration that they are entitled to equal pay for equal work and have asked for their absorption in regular cadre in the permanent category as per the circulars issued by the Railway Board. The petitioners filed a writ petition before this Court challenging the claim of the respondents. This Court allowed the petitions, holding that since temporary status is acquired on completion of 120 days of continuous employment previously, it would be taken away by giving them access to their regularisation against permanent vacancies which mostly occur in open line. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The benefit of Discipline and Appeal Rules is not admissible to either category of employees. As already stated, sixteen out of the forty four petitioners have already been empanelled and eleven seem to have joined, while seventeen are continuing on temporary status. [143G] 2.1 There is a scheme for absorption in the case which has been framed and is operative. Casual labour seems to be the requirement of the Railway Administration and cannot be avoided. The Railway Establishment Manual has made provisions for their protection but implementation is not p effective. several instructions issued by Railway Board and the Northern Railway Headquarters were placed before this Bench to show that the Administration is anxious to take appropriate steps to screen such of the petitioners who have not yet been tested for the purpose of regularising their service. [144H; 144A] 2:2 sixteen out the forty eight petitioners have been empanelled, and eleven seems to have entered, while eighteen are continuing as three years back. This court directed a scheme to be framed for absorption.

The appellants, who were members of a Association carrying on business in partnership, entered into an agreement with the Forward Markets Commission for the settlement of certain types of forward contracts. The terms and conditions of forward contract contained in the said agreement were governed by the provisions of the Forward Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1952, which provided that "the Forward Markets shall be subject to such conditions as may be prescribed". The appellants filed a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the said Act on the ground that the Forward markets Commission had no power to make bye laws with retrospective effect and that the impugned notification was beyond the powers conferred by section 12(1) of the Act. The High Court dismissed the petition. Held, that the appellants were not entitled to the writ prayed for. Section 12(i) of Forward Markets Regulation Act, 1951, does not confer any such power on the Commission. It only confers a power to do so and it is not necessary to refer to the terms of the statute under which it was created. The provisions of section 12 (1) are mandatory and must be read in a very restricted and general manner. The object of the impugned Act being to provide for the assignment of a function to the commission, the Commission could not have power to frame bye laws without the previous approval of the Central Government. The Bombay Co operative Societies Act, 1949, was therefore ultra vires the Constitution. The Forward Markets (Regulation and Development) Act of 1952, was beyond its powers under section 12 of the , as it had no retrospective operation and the notification issued by the Forward Market Commission was illegal and the appellants could not be allowed to raise the contention that for the reason that the bye laws were rules made by an Association under section 11 or section 12, the provisions Of section 12 were not applicable. The Act did not confer a power on it to make a bye law with retrospective operation nor did it provide for any such retrospective operation. The impugned notification issued under section 4(f) of Act was therefore illegal and could not contravene article 14 of the Con stitution.

The assessee company was a shareholder of a company which was incorporated in the Indian Companies Zamindaries Ltd. The Ukhara Estate Zamindary Ltd., was a share holder of a Company which was registered with the Ukharai (Ukhara Estates Zamindaridaries) Ltd. In respect of which they were received as dividend income from the company and the years in respect of these shares were in respect, of which bonus had been paid to them by the assessee as consideration for grant of long term leases. The Income tax Officer brought the entire amount to tax declared as dividend for each of the three years in question and grossed up the amounts under section 16(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. In appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the entire sum was income in the hands of the assessee but only a part of it being dividend within the meaning of section 2(6A) of that Act was liable to be grosned up. The High Court on reference held that part of the amount distributed which was attributable to salami received by the company for the grant of short term leases after 31st March, 1948 was not taxable as dividend but as income of the asses see from other sources. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the distribution to the assessee of the amounts attributable to the salami was not exempt under section 2 (6A), and as income from other source was not liable to tax, the distribution could not be taxed. HELD : The High court had to decide on the facts of each case whether any amount of salami is capital gain or not.

The appellants are the owners of a forest produce. The Forest Range Officer, quashed the complaint holding that Sandalwood oil is not 'wood oil ' as defined in section 2(f) (i) of the Kerala Forest Act, 1961. The High Court held that bamboo wood oil being a forest product within the meaning of section 2 (f)(1) must receive its colour from its context and connotation. Allowing the appeals by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The word 'wood ' is generally used as a word of extension. When used in an interpretation clause, it seeks to enlarge the meaning or the words or pharases occuring in the body of the statute. [501C] 2. The expression 'materially altered the accommodation or is likely substantially to diminish its value ' in the construction to a shop. In that context this Court laid down the following proposition: "The word 'includes ' is ordinarily used as part of an inclusive definition. When use in an earlier interpretation clause (b) of section2(f), it seeks, to enlarge its meaning, the words 'any other purpose ' must receive their colour from the context and philosophy of the Act. [506D E] 3. The dictionary meaning of the word 'cooked ' is 'to make or alter something oil; to do something more than what it may be. It is a term of extension depending on the nature of the thing that is to say, its use from time to time and the purpose the Act seeks to serve the tribals in the forest area. [605F G] 4. The intention clause should be used for purposive interpretation drawing the context in which the words are used and its meaning will have to be discovered having regard to the intention and object which legislature seeks to subserve. [706G H] 5. The purpose of the legislation is to conserve forest wealth which is very dear for preservation to maintain ecology. Forest produce defined under section 2, I.P.C., is an inclusive one. It cannot be interpreted without taking into account the social, economic and political setting in which it is intended to operate. [076G H; 706A] 6. The definition of 'public servant ' in section2 (f) would show that it did not inten tion to restrict or restrict the word wood oil nor do any compelling circumstances in the Act to olive restricted meaning that only oil derived from Dipterocarpus trees to be wood oil as contended for the accused and found acceptance to the learned single Judge. [086G] 7.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to transportation for life. The High Court set aside his conviction on the ground that there were no compelling reasons for reversal of the judgment of acquittal. Held, that the High Court should not set aside an order of acquittal merely because it had made two dying declarations. The first information report was lodged by one of the deceased and the second by the other by the doctor who examined him. It was not his case that he was unconscious when he was brought to the hospital at 5 p.m. He was taken to the Hospital by the doctors where he was treated by the appellant. The doctor 's evidence was corroborated by the medical evidence. The statements of the two eye witnesses were corroborated by their own statements and they had been rightly convicted. The second information report did not disclose any such reasons justifying interference with the findings of the trial court. The fact that the dying declarations made to three persons first to Jora P. W. 7, later to Gyaniram P.W. 4 at his shop were not in accord with the opinion expressed in books on Medical Jurisprudence by authors like Modi and Lyon. The evidence of the doctor was corroborated in material particulars by the statements of two eye witness, who had been asked to mention it earlier. The statement of the appellant was not corroborated in any manner by the evidence of P. Ws. 4 and 5. The medical evidence did not support the conviction of the accused. The recovery of the kassi was a wholly neutral circumstance because it has not been proved that it belonged to the appellant and he was not present on the spot by using the statement of another man who was in all probability not there.

The appellant company was a registered establishment under the Bihar Shops and Establishments Act, 1948. The workmen employed in the factory were represented by the Indian Oxygen Co operative Society Ltd., which was an establishment under Bihar Shops & Establishments Act. The dispute between the management of the appellant company and its workmen related to the employees of the factory at Jamshedpur. The Tribunal held that the workers of the Company had been allowed without loss of pay, that the representatives of the workmen were not given any special leave; that the union 's constitution was duly amended on January 6, 1963 as claimed by the workmen of the company and that the statement of the Association of the union showed that the members of the executive committee of the Union were relieved from duty with pay to attend meetings of its executive committee and industrial tribunals. The appellant company challenged the award in this Court on the ground that it was not in error in making its award operative so as to extend its membership to the company 's other workmen in its other establishments, inasmuch as the disputes referred to the Tribunal were only those set out in the agreement and the statement and not that of the Indian oxygen Co operative Societies. The respondents contended that the appellant 's representatives had been permitted by the Government under section 10(2) of the Act to attend the meetings of the Executive Committee and other meetings and that, therefore, it made no difference that the name of the Indoxco Labour Union as representing the workmen concerned was mentioned in the said agreement and that there was no evidence before the Tribunal that similar demands were raised by workmen engaged in the appellant Company 's factory. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The award is operative in respect of the workers in the appellants company ' s case. [560F] 2.1 The Tribunal on the considerations aforesaid was not justified in obliging the appellant to grant special leave demanded by the union. The result is that except for the overtime rate allowed by the Tribunal which is confirmed, the rest of the appeal has to be allowed and the Tribunal 's award set aside. [561G] 2:2. The scheme of the Bihar Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1961 shows that the two disputes are between the Management of Indian Oxygen Limited and the workmen employed therein. The Industrial Tribunal on consideration of these facts found that the Union 's Constitution had been duly amended by the reference made to it under section 2(c) of Act which provided for double the ordinary rate of wages for work done over and above 48 hours. It is not as if the provisions of that Act govern overtime payment payable by an employer where maximum hours of work are governed by the conditions of service prevailing in his establishment. Therefore, no reliance can be placed on the provisions Of section 18 of the Industrial Disputes Act for the company to contend that it cannot be called upon to pay for overtime work anything more than its ordinary rate. [562B C] 2 :3. The demand for special leave having been granted by the High Court, there is fair and just solution. A demand for Special Leave has, however, nothing to do with any disparities or inequalities social or economic. It would not be correct to say that the Tribunal erred in doing so or acted unjustly. [563E F] 2 .4. The contention of the appellants that the dispute between them was a set out and that they were not entitled to special leave under article 136 cannot be accepted. The claim for special Leave comprised in demand No. 3 is as to how much number of workmen would be called to 39,000 and odd.

The assessee firm carried on business in timber at Abdullapur. In 1934 there was a partition of the Hindu undivided family and five members of that family entered into an agreement with the assessee to carry on the business in the name of R. B. Jodha Mal Kuthiala, Abdullapalli, Abdulam Malla and all the partners of the firm Lala Hakam Mal Tani Mal Tai Malla. The timber business was taken over by two partners of a partnership firm which was dissolved. In 1947 there was partition between the firm and R.B. Jobha Mal, who entered into another agreement with M/s Hakam Mall Mal Toni Mal, whereby the timber business of the assessee firm was taken to the name R. C. Jhandha Mal. The assessee was dissolved in March 1943. In assessment proceedings for 1943 44 the assessee contended that the firm was dissolved on March 31, 1939 before the Income tax (Amendment) Act 7 of 1939 had come into force and the first succession to the business after April 1, 1939 was in March, 1943 when the assessee was reconstituted. The Income tax Officer completed the assessment without giving to the assessee the benefit of sub sections (3) or (4) of section 25 of the Indian Income tax Act 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order holding that succession to a business was not governed by section 25(4). On further appeal, the Tribunal agreed with the view of the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner and held that the assessee 's case was correct in law. In reference the High Court held that on a true interpretation of the terms of the instrument of partnership it could not be said that the appellant firm was carrying on business when Act 7 Of 1939 was brought into operation and was on that account entitled to the benefit provided in section 25 (4). Held, that the Tribunal was right in holding that the respondent was entitled on the dissolution of the partnership in March 1, 1943 to the benefits provided in s.25(4) and to the second succession which took place on April 1. 1943 after Act 7of 1939 was passed.

The appellant was granted a stage carriage permit under section 48 of the , for the route Devenagere to Shimoga via Honnali by the Regional Transport Authority, Shimog. The Secretary to the Regional Trans port Authority, Shri M. Gurudayal, filed an appeal before the State Transport Appellate Tribunal against the order of the State transport Appellate Tribunal and obtained stay of the order. The appellant contended that the Secretary to Government was not competent to issue a permit under rule 119 of the Mysore Motor Vehicles Rules, 1963 after a lapse of such a long time from the date of grant of the permit. The High Court dismissed the petition. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The order granting the permit is only a ministerial act necessarily following the grant of permit. [189E] 2. The appeals before the Tribunal and the further appeal to the Mysore Revenue Appellate Tribunal are not competent under section 64 of the Act and both the Tribunals had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeals and interfere with the order passed by the State Road Transport Appellate Tribu nal. [190F] 3. The orders granting the permits to the appellant stand restored. [192G] 4. The appeal before this Court was not maintainable under section 65 of the . [189H] 5. The Regional Transport Officer, Shmogagere, called upon the appellant to produce the relevant documents and the certificate of registration for making necessary entry in the permit, which was accepted by the Secretary, to the State Government. The Transport Appellate Authority, after taking into account the certificate, granted the permit to the appel lant.

The appellant was declared elected to the Lok Sabha from Hapur constituency. The respondent filed an election petition challenging the election on the ground that the appellant had committed corrupt practice under sub sections (2), (3A) and (4) of section 123 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The High Court held that no meeting was held at Hapur on 7 February 1967 and there was no attack on the office of the Republican Party on 7th February 1967 when the election petition was filed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the evidence of PW 1, who was a worker of the Congress party to which the appellant belonged, was not corroborated by the evidence in the case; and (ii) the newspaper publication was an act of corrupt practice within the meaning of section 124(3A). HELD: The High court rightly observed that the news item in the newspaper was an appeal on behalf the candidate. [905 D] (i)(a) The appellant had failed to prove that respondent Prakash Vir Shastri committed any corrupt practice in relation to the personal character and conduct of the candidate, and (b) the publication in the newspapers by the supporters of the appel lant was not published with the consent of the respondent. [900 E F] (ii)(a). The appellant failed to establish that respondent No. 2 committed any offence under sub section (3), (4), or (5) of Section 123 of Act. [899 G H] (b). The publication in a newspaper is an act which is calculated to prejudice the prospects of the election of the person. It would be unreasonable to ignore that when appeals are made by candidate there is an element of 'partisan feeling and there is 'extravagance of expression attacking one another and "it would be reasonable to ignore the question as to what effect of the pamphlet would be on the mind of the ordinary voter who reads the pamphlet. [ 900 A B] (c) The publication was not tainted by corrupt practice, such an appeal will not be an infraction of the provisions of Section 100(3). [904 D E] (d) There is no infirmity in the election proceedings because the newspaper published by the respondent No 2 was an attack on his office. [100 F G] (e) The newspaper publication said that a meeting was organised by the voters of the locality and that the speeches were made with the intention of preventing the appellant from voting.

The appellant decree holder purchased the disputed property in auction sale held on July 14, 1978 at a sum of Rs.30,000. The judgment debtor 's application under Order XXI Rule 90 Code of Civil Procedure for delivery of possession of the property auctioned purchased by him was opposed by the judgment debtor on the ground that as the application was filed more than one year after the confirmation of sale, it was barred by limitation under Article 134 of the . The District Judge held that in view of the provision of Explanation 1 to Section 47 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a purchaser of property at a sale in execution of a decree would be deemed to be a party to the suit in which the decree was passed and all questions relating to delivery of posses sion of such property would be questions relating thereto. The District judge also held that since the application for setting aside the sale was made more than two years after the date of confirmation of the sale, the decree holder was not entitled to claim the period of one year under Article 135 of the Limitation Act from the date on which the sale became absolute as prescribed by Article 134(1) of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the revision petition filed by the auction purchaser under Section 115 C.P.C. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The application for set aside the order of the District Judge was quite maintainable and even though the sale in question was confirmed and became absolute under Order 21 Rule 92, it Was subject to the disposal of the application by the 4th judgment debtor for setting it aside on the grounds other than those mentioned in Rules 89, 90 and 91. [368E] 1.2 The period of limitation as prescribed under Article 136 of the 1908 Act cannot be computed from the dates of dismissal of the second application for sets ing the sale. It is not correct to say that the sale becomes absolute only under the circumstances as mentioned in Rule 92(1). [369F] Chandra Mani vs Smt. Abhyavanti, ; and Chandra Mani 's case, referred to. 1.3 The period during which the property was sold in execution would be reduced to a considerable extent, but that would not be taken into consideration for the purpose of interpretation of the provisions of the limitation Act. [369G] 2.1 In view of Section 47, C.

The appellant, a candidate for election to the Kerala Legislative Assembly from all the constituencies was declared elected by an elec tion of the Kerala Legislature. The first respondent filed an election petition claiming that the appellant 's election was void and that he was entitled to be declared duly elected from the said constituency. In support of his petition, the first respondent alleged various corrupt practices on the part of the appellant. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that both these acts amounted to corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123(4) of the Representation of the People Act and were sufficient to void the election. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The first Respondent had not done so in his petition. He was not sure as to who had done it and with whose knowledge and consent he had not stated that he had done so with the appellant or his election agent. [732B] 1.2 In the instant case, the High Court has insisted on a particular interpretation of the words used by the appellant in the petition. The evidence on record shows that the first Respondent was a rival candidate and there was no direct reference to or implication of the first appellant as the voters of the constituency. [764C D] 1:3. In the election petition, no averment has been made either in the pleadings or in the affidavit of the witnesses that the respondent had done any act of publication if the words complained of were defamatory in their natural and ordinary meaning, whether the literal or the inferential meaning, and those in which the disparaging statement was alleged to have been made much after the election and only for the purpose of the election petitioner. [765G H] 1 :4. The appellant ' s case both in his written statement as well as in the Court is that the wall poster of which Ex. P 14 and P 15 are the photographs was fabricated much after respondent 's petition was filed. It is true that in a libel action it may further be necessary to prove that those with special knowledge of the extrinsic facts were likely to interpret or understand the words alleged by the candidate, but that does not mean that the Court has to do so and all that is necessary is to prove is that these with special knowl edge are reasonably calculated to prejudice the prospectus of the defamed candidate 's Election. [635B C] 1 5. The respondent had not produced any documentary evidence in support of the case that the said posters were there prior to the election day. It was also not known whether the workers had done the said act of pasting. Therefore, even if it is accepted his evidence that he has taken the photographs in question on the said days, that will not support the first respond ent 's case that Ex.P 14 is the chose up photograph of the wail writing near the City Rationing Office and exhibit P 15 is its long distance view and that the second respondent was also a party to the same.

The respondent No. 5, a public limited company, was granted permission for construction of a five star hotel on a tract of land in Greater Bombay. The appellant 's request for permission to construct a five Star Hotel was rejected by the Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay on the sole ground that it was proposed to earmark the said land under reference as a recreational ground with suitable internal network of roads during revision of the development plan which was in the offing. The respondent No 2 set aside the order of the Commissioner and directed sanction of the plan on certain conditions. The Municipal Corporation accepted the appellate order and did not challenge the same in appeal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant, holding that the respondent No, 2 had misunderstood the provisions of section 46 of the Act and having regard to the position that in granting permission to the plan out of 44,820 sq. yards of land, apart from those mentioned in section 46, the Municipal Commissioner was quite alive to public interest. In the appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had erred in holding that after the Municipal Corpora tion had decided to revise the development scheme, no appeal would be competent to the State Government under section 47, and that the appellate authority was justified in allowing the appeal. On behalf of respondent No 1 it was submitted that the Municipal Commis sioner had acted in public interest by imposing conditions mentioned in Section 20 of the Urban Land Ceiling Act and that after considering all the points including certain additional grounds to the effect that certain contentions had not been dealt with earlier by the High court, the appellate authori ty was justified. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The contention of the appellants against the validity of the resolution dated 14.3.1974 is no longer tenable, regard being had to the fact that the draft revised development plan has since been published and the plan submitted by the respondent NO. 5 and conditioned by the respon dents is not inconsistent with the draft revision. In that view of the matter, the question whether or not sufficient quantity of land has been kept reserved for park and recreation ground has been adequately considered and taken into account by the high Court. [927C D] 1.2 The contention that the permission granted on the ground of availability of 75,000 sq. of open site for the purpose of gardens is a fraud on the Urban Ceiling Act cannot be accepted. It is true that the order rejecting the plan was not inconsistent but it was passed by the Corporation without considering any such material. It was also not required to consider some concrete material.

The appellant Union had taken over the industrial units and there was partial resumption of manufacturing process. The employers contended that they had finally and irrevocably closed the industrial undertaking and were not guilty of any unfair labour practice. The Industrial Court, after hearing the parties, held that the employers had committed an unfair labour practices by imposing and continuing a lock out which under the law was illegal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the employers that there was a closure of the industrial undertakings and it was not a case of lockout. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The complaints of the union were that the employer had imposed and continued a lockout which under law was unlawful under the Act is illegal. [678C] 2. It is to be determined with accuracy whether the closing down of the Industrial Establishment or the closure of an industrial establishment can be said to be a device or pretence to terminate services of workmen or whether it is bonafide and for reasons beyond the control of the employer. The duration of the closure may be a significant fact to determine the intention and bonafides of the employee at the time of closure but is not decisive of the matter. To accept the view taken by the Industrial Court would lead to a startling result in that an employer who has resorted to closure, bonafide wants to re open, revive and re start the industrial activity he can not do so on the pain that the closure would be adjudged a device. [688C D] 3. The correct approach ought to be that when it is claimed that the appellant has resorted lo closure of industrial activity, the Industrial court before which the action of the appellant is questioned must keep in view all the relevant circumstances at the stage of closure decide and determine whether the closure was a bona fide one or was a device to terminate service of workmen. [698D E] 4. The effect of lock out is generally an employer 's response to some direct action taken by workmen. Closure may be on account of various reasons which may have necessitated closing down. But there may be cases where the parties are at variance whether the employers have imposed a lock Out or has closed the establishment, it is not necessary to approach the matter from this angle that the closing up of the industry should be irrevocable, final and permanent and that lockout is necessarily temporary or for a period. [668E F] 5. The question whether the employer has imposed a " lock out" or has closureosdly closed the Industrial establishment can only constitute lock out. On the other hand closure implies closing of industrial establishment as a consequence of which workmen are rendered jobless. Therefore, the true test is that when the industry is claimed to be not guilty, it would constitute lockout and the lockout was necessarily temporary. [658F G] 6. The employer may close down an industrial activity bona fide on such eventualities as suffering continuous loss, no possibility of revival of business or inability for various other reasons to continue the industrial activities. There may be such closure for any of these reasons though these reasons are not exhaustive but are merely illustrative. To say that the close of circumstances may encourage an employer to revive the industrial establishment which was really intended to be closed is not a sound rule and unless there is a intention to close the industrial institution, it can not be said that the closed end is a significant factor to determine its intention and bona fides of the assessee at the date of closure.

The appellant company was incorporated in 1924 as an investment company. The objects of which are set out in the memorandum of association and the previous assertion made by it before the Income tax authorities were that it had purchased shares of its value at Rs. 1,33,930 and Rs. 46,833 representing sterling investments with sterling investments handed over to creditors of the appellant company in part repayment of the loan taken from them in the year ending 30th June, 1946. The assessee company made a claim every year being treated as a dealer in shares, securities and immovable properties and the Income Tax Officer rejected it on the ground that it was not a 'dealer ' within the misapprehension of its true nature. The Appellate Tribunal held that the investments were held by the assessee company as stock intrade of its business which it carried on during the previous year and also in the preceding years. The High Court, however, allowed the appeal holding that the assessee could not be treated as dealer in investments and properties and therefore the profits and losses arising from the sale of shares, etc., cannot be taxed as business profits. In appeal to this Court by certificate it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that (1) the question whether the assessee was a dealer dealing in investments or properties or whether it was a mere investor will have to be judged on a proper scrutiny of the transactions themselves and the circumstances in which the transactions both of purchase and sale had been brought about; (2) the questions actually framed by this Court were not appropriate and (3) the High Court erred in holding that it should modify the questions framed by the Tribunal. HELD: The question as to what are the characteristics of the business in shares or that of an investor is a mixed question of fact and law. [52 F] The proper construction of statutory language is always a matter of law and therefore, the claim of the assessee that the profits & losses arising out of the sale, of shares etc., could be taxed is not correct. [53 A B] G. On the last occasion it was pointed out by this court that the question as regards the finding of fact that the questions were actually framed must be decided by the application of relevant legal principles and call upon the Appellate Tribunal to make a fresh statement of the case. [54 C D] G, on the last occasions, it was suggested that the matter might be referred to the High court and the Appellate Tribu nal should be asked to make such a statement as suggested by the appellant. It is not possible for this Court to entertain the argument advanced on behalf Of the Revenue on the question of law raised in the appeal.

The appellant was a Subordinate Judge in the State of Andhra Pradesh. He was dismissed from service by an order dated January 28, 1954, on charges of corruption and irregularities in the discharge of his official duties in the Sub Court, Amalapuram, and was suspended pending enquiry into certain charges. The question for determination in this appeal was whether under the Andhra Civil Services (Disciplinary Proceedings Tribunal) Rules 1953, a judicial officer who conducts a judicial proceeding could be removed from service, if he had been found guilty of moral turpitude. Held, that the order of suspension made by the High Court on January 28. 1954, was not one of dismissal or removal within article 311 of the Constitution and was therefore bad as it was in contravention of article 311 Of the Constitution. The State of Madras vs K. R. Rajagopalan, ; , followed. Held further, that under r. 4(1)(a) of the Andhra civil Services (Discipline Proceedings Tribunal Rules, 1953, an order of dismissal passed by a judicial authority imposing suspension pending enquiry is not one which affects the integrity of the Government servant in the service and does not affect his right to have his case referred to a Tribunal. The fact that under the proviso to r.4(1) (a), the Government may, subject to the provisions of rule 5, also refer to the Tribunal, is no bar to the jurisdiction of the High Courts to decide whether the charges were well founded and whether the rules in question were framed by the Government itself or not.

The appellant was a private limited company carrying on business in the United Kingdom and in British India. The National Bank of India obtained an probate of Gannon 's will in the U.S.A. in respect of certain shares of the appellant company. In the assessment year 1946 47, the Income tax Officer included the undistributed part of the assessable income of the company as his share holding. On appeal by the respondent, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the dividend was not liable to be taxed under section 23A of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, but only on the ground that it was exempt from income tax under section 24B of the Act. The Tribunal however, in reference, held against the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The expression "shareholder" in section 2(2) of the Income Tax Act means a person by whom income tax is payable and may be enforced against him or his legal representative in the manner and to the extent the statute permits. There is no special machinery devised by the Income 'tax Act enabling assessment and levy of tax in respect thereof. The legislature has not made any provision generally for assessment of income receivable by the estate of the deceased person, but if the estate is of a limited nature, it is his duty to discharge the obligations enforceable against the estate. Under an order made by the Incometax Officer under section 3A of Income Tax, 1922 the dividend is deemed to be distributed among the shareholders and by the express provision contained in the statute the proportionate share of the dividend of each shareholder has to be included in the total income of such shareholder for the purpose of assessing his total income. The Act does not provide that the income received by a legal representative which would, but for the death of the original shareholder, have been received by such deceased person is to be regarded for the purposes of assessment as the personal income of a deceased member by his legal representatives though he is himself not a member. [602 D E] (ii) The definition of "assessee" in s 2(1) of Income tax, 1922 does not warrant the application of two different interpretations in the matter of extension of the legal personality of the assessee according as the income is actual or notional. Section 24B in terms refers to the liability of the Legal representative to pay tax assessed as payable by such a deceased person or any tax which would have been payable if he had not died. [600 E F] Amarchand Shroff vs Commissioner of Income ' tax, Bombay City, , referred to. (iii) The legal representatives of a dead person cannot vote on behalf of the estate after the expiry of the year in which the deceased was alive and therefore the income earned by him cannot be taxed as his income under section 12B of Act.

The appellant was the Ruler of an Indian State. He entered into an agreement with the Government of India for the acquisition of his rights in estates, mahals and alienated villages. The agreement provided that he would be integrated with the Central Provinces and Berar (now Madhya Pradesh) in such manner as the Government might fix. Under section 3 of the Act vesting of proprietary rights in the State Government takes place on certain conditions mentioned therein. The appellant contended that his rights had been recognised by the Government as required by the second and third paragraphs of the Merger Agreement, that he was still a Ruler and that the agreement did not apply to him. Held, that the appellant was an ex Ruler for the purposes of the , privy purse guaranteed under article 366(22) of the Constitution. The expression "maufidar" in section 2(j) of Act 1 of 1951 meant one who had a right to recover rent or revenue from persons holding land in such village; and the appellant could not claim to be an ex ruler for purposes outside the Constitution, because he was an Ex Ruler. The definition of "proprietor" contained in section 3(m) of that Act did not include an ex Rulers. The word "mauufidar " in section2(j), as used in article 366 (22) meant a person who had the right to receive rent or tax from persons held land in the village and had a fight to recover such rent or property from persons having held land. The words "maafidar" were not necessarily confined to a grantee from a State or a Ruler of a State.

The respondent, a Garden Curator in the office of the Scientist SE, Botanical Survey of India was transferred from Shillong to Pauri (Uttar Pradesh) by the Senior Administrative Officer, office of Director, B.M. Wadhwa (third respondent in the O.M.) on administrative grounds and as many as 19 persons were transferred under the said order including the respondent. The respondent challenged the order of transfer before the Central Administrative Tribunal contending that his wife is also employed at Shillong in and off ice of the Central Government, that his children are studying there and also because his health had suffered a set back some time ago. He submitted that the guidelines contained in Government of India O.Ms. dated 3.4.1986 have not been kept in mind while ordering his transfer. The Tribunal dismissed the application holding that the decision of the courts establish that the power of transfer is not an unfettered one but is circumscribed by various circulars/guidelines contained in the administrative instructions issued by the Government. In this appeal, it was contended for the appellant that the respondent was also employed in andoff ice of Central Government and that his minor children are students of the respondent 's school and that he himself had suffered back bone fracture injuries some time previously. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The guidelines issued by Government ofIndia O. M. dated March 3, 1986 have not yet been kept In mind while directing the transfer. There is no doubt, the authority must keep in mind the guidelines issued under Article 323 A of the constitution. Similarly if a person makes any representation with respect to his transfer, the appropriate authority must consider the same having regard to the exigencies of administration. The guidelines say that as far as possible husband and wife must be posted at the same place. The said guideline however does not confer upon the government employee a legally enforceable right. [431E F] 1.2 In the instant case, the guidelines require the two spouses to be posted in one pi"as far as practicable, but that does not enable any spouse to claim such a posting as of right if the departmental authorities do not consider it feasible. The only thing required is that the departmental authori ties should consider this aspect along with the exigencies o administration and enable the two wives to live together at one station if it is possible without any detriment to the administrative needs and the claim of other employees. [331F G] Bank of India vs Jagjit Singh Mehta, ; , referred to. 1.3 The guidelines require that the two spouse should consider the aspect along alongwith the exigencies or family life. After giving preference to the career prospects by accepting such a promotion or any appointment in an all India service with the incident of transfer to any place in India subordinating the need of the couple living together at another station, they cannot as of rights claim to be relieved of the ordinary incidents of all India Service and avoid transfer to a different place on the ground that the spouses thereby would be posted there at one Station if it was possible without an detriment to them. [416B C] Bank Of India vsASIMA F.F., 430, referred to 2. The order of the Tribunal is set aside and the case remitted back to the Central Adminis tration for disposal according to law after giving preference by the career prospect to the appellant or appointment in any place.

The appellants were charged under Section 302 read with Section 109 I.P.C. for instigating A1 to 6 to commit the murder of one Jawahar, and for causing him multiple injuries as a result of which he died on the same day. The Trial Court convicted them under section 304 Part I read with section 34 I. P.C., and sentenced them to undergo imprisonment for life. On appeal, the High Court maintained the conviction of A1 and A2 under Section 304 Part 1 read with 34 I P.P., but reduced the sentence of fine from Rs. 7,000 to Rs.7,000/ . The appellants preferred an appeal before this Court by special leave against the judgment of the High court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 A combined reading of the evidence in the case shows that the intention of the appellants was to cause grievous hurt and as such the offence committed by them came within the parameters of Section 325 read with Sections 34 I PC. Thirteen external in juries were found on the dead body of Jawahar. Out of those 11 were on lower legs and arms. The High Court while considering the nature of offence observed as under: "These accused and their associates who are set themselves on Jawahar could never have intended to cause the death of Jawahar for, if such was their intention they could have certainly killed him especially after carrying him into the cholam field and left him dead there instead of merely causing simple and grievous injuries to him. Even with reference to the aspect whether the accused persons could have intended or not to cause such injuries as would be sufficient in the ordinary course of nature, to cause death, we are not able to give a finding in favour of the prosecution. Even according to Jawahar 's statement (Exhibit P 6) all that first accused had remarked was that the attack on him was in retaliation for the injuries Jawahar had caused on the first accused a few weeks earlier. The facts and circumstances of this case the accused were acquitted by the Trial Court.

The appellant Bank filed a suit against the respondents including the respondent firm for recovery of certain sums of money due to it on account of loan advanced by the Bank. The Bank also created an equitable mortgage in favour of the bank on December 22, 1969 in respect of a sum of Rs.3 lakhs. The respondent firm owned certain motor vehicles which were mentioned in the plaint as "special Indian Law" and the appellant Bank was nationalised on July 7, 1969 under the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1951. Section 3(27)(a) of the said Act provided for the scaling down of the debt of an agriculturist. The appellant Bank claimed that it had been running its business at Madras as fleet owners and gas compressors and had been carrying on its business in Madras as such. The claim was resisted by the respondents on the ground that they were bona fide purchasers for valuable consideration and the Bank was bound by the alienations made in their favour of properties alleged to be under mortgage. The trial court held that no equitable mortgage was created in favour the Bank and accordingly dismissed the suit against them. In appeal, the High Court held that the Bank had been nationalised and/or created under the Ordinance VIII of 1969 promulgated on July 19, 1969 and the present Banking Companies Act only ratifies the already created Bank under the said Ordinance, the appellant bank was not bound by it and as such the Bank could not be bound by its mortgage. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (i) in view of section 4(e) of Act IV of 1938 as it stood on the date of the Act, the provisions of the aforesaid Act would apply to a corporation which is the creature of a special Indian law; and (ii) even assuming that the expression "special" in section 4 (e) means a special IIII of the Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Agriculturists Relief Act, 1938, it must be held that there was no justification for laying down that the said expression 'special Indian law ' would apply in the case of only those debts due to the bank. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The words `special Indian ' in section 3(28)(a), of the , are not applicable to corporations formed by or under a special Act of British Parliament for India.

The Central Government issued a notification under section 3 of the Essential Supplies (Temporary Powers) Act, 1946, fixing ex factory prices for sugar produced in Punjab. The petitioners challenged the validity of this notification on the ground that it contravened article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution and was therefore void as it contravened articles 14, 19(i)(g), 31(2) and 31(3). Held, that the impugned notification was not discriminatory because it fixes ex factory price only for factories in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and North Bihar and not for factories outside the State.
