The object of the Act is to provide for control of production, supply and distribution of trade and commerce in essential commodities in the interests of general public, so that the prices at which any essential commodity may be bought or sold are not lower than those fixed by the impugned Notification. The power conferred on the Central Government by section 3(1) and section 3 (2)(c) of Act is control at any time during the pendency of a proceeding under the Act if it is necessary or expedient so to do for maintaining or increasing supplies of any essential commodities, and in the circumstances of this case it cannot be said that there was discrimination between different regions or between producers and middlemen in view of what is called "uncontrolled" power. The fact that factories are being compelled to sell at below the cost of production does not affect the validity or otherwise of the impugned notifications. The prices fixed by them are above the cost price.

The Government of West Bengal by a notification dated September 15, 1956, transferred the dispute from the file of the Second Industrial Tribunal to that of the Fifth Industrial Tribunal. The Government made an award on August 26, 1957, and it was duly notified in the Calcutta Gazette on September 26,1957. On September 26 the Company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the said award on the ground that the award dated June 21, 1951, was not terminated in accordance with the provisions of section 19(6) of the Act and therefore the reference was bad in law. The High Court held that the Tribunal went wrong in taking the rise in the cost of living index since it had no jurisdiction to transfer the dispute pending before it to another tribunal. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) In respect of matters covered by it, the agreement replaced the earlier award and therefore, the date of the agreement was the crucial one for ascertaining whether there was substantial change in the working class cost of live index in the year 1957. The Tribunal wrongly relied on the correspondence between the parties which showed that there was a change of circumstances which entitled the employees to claim an increase in their dearness allowance. (ii)The award of 1951 was not a termination of service under section 19 (6) and therefore could not be said to have been terminated in accord with law. (iii)The Tribunal wrongly held that there had been a rise in cost of the living index by dearness allowance could not, therefore, permit the workmen to raise the plea before it and allow them only 75 per cent. of the increase in the dearness allowance to which they would have otherwise been entitled on the basis of the rise In the cost.

The appellant was the owner of certain properties belonging to the propagation and promotion of the tenets of the Veera Saiva cult of Hinduism. The property was situated at U.P. in the district of Anantapur, which was a religious institution dedicated to the State of propagation. The said institution was established by the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, and it had been declared as such under section 63 of that Act. The appellant 's father died in 1952 and his widow, who was impleaded as legal representative, filed a suit challenging the scheme on the ground that the scheme was invalid because it contravened the provisions of article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the suit holding that the Scheme having been framed under the Act, the appellant could not be evicted by the authorities under the scheme. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The scheme was framed and the Executive Officer was appointed as early as 1939. If the Executive officer could not take over the actual administration of the Mutt and its properties it was partly because the appellant had continuously challenged the implementation of the scheme by legal proceedings and partly because he has otherwise obstructed the said implementation. But it is clear that when the scheme is framed and a challenge made by the appellant to its validity failed in courts of law, his property rights had been taken away. The fact that the order was not implemented does not make any difference to this legal position. [257 D F] (ii) The contention that since the scheme has not been fully implemented till 1952, it is open to the appellant challenging the validity of the Scheme on the grounds that it deprives him of his fundamental rights under article 19 (1)(g), must be rejected. [258 E] (iii) The order against which the petition was filed was not in accordance with law and was not warranted by the provisions Of section 103(d) of that section. The scheme as a whole, will be deemed to have been made under the latter Act and will be continued modifications in it can be effected by adopting the procedure prescribed by section 62(3). [258 G] (iv) The fact of the order being not implemented till the date of the application for the scheme did not make no difference to the legal position, because, when the Scheme was framed, and a attack made by him to its invalidity, it still be open to challenge on the basis that they contravened the Mataducture. [260 A] (v) The deprivation of the appellant ' property rights was brought about by invalid orders and it was in respect of such invalid orders that the Court held that the petitioner was entitled to seek the protection of article 31(2). Such a plea does not appear to have ever been raised and, in our opinion, cannot be validly raised for the simple reason that the further damental rights are not retrospective in their operation.

The appellant was appointed as Hindi Teacher in Bani gochha, M.E. School (Orrisa) for a period of 89 days or till a candidate selected by the State Selection Board was made available. He joined the school on July 12, 1982. The appointment was made by the District Inspector (Schools) on the recommendation of the managing committee of the school. He continued to serve the school with repeated spells of 89 day appointments and one day break in between the spells, till May 25, 1986. He was not paid the salary for the period of summer vacations during all these years. The appellant filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the Orissa High Court claiming regularisation as Hindi teacher with effect from July 12 1982. A Single Judge of the High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the appellant was not entitled to be regularised in terms of Section 3 of the Orissa Aided Educational Institutions (Appointment of Teachers Validation) Act, 1989. The State preferred an appeal by special leave before this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court erred in denying the benefit of the Validation Act to the appellant on the ground that his initial appointment for 89 days was conditioned by the stipulation that he would continue until replaced by a candidate from the select list. [995B] Rattan Lal vs State of Haryana, A.I.R. 1987 S.C. 478; Rattan Lal v State of Punjab, AJ.R 1987 S C. 478 and Rattan Lal V State of J & K, A J.T. 1989 (1) SC 478, referred to. 1.2 The High court erred in denied the benefit to the petitioner on the grounds that his initially appointment for89 days was conse quently conditioned by stipulation that the he would be continued until replaced. [996C D] Rattan Lai vs State Of Haryana, ; , distinguished. 1:3. The Validation Act covers the field upto December 31, 1984. The High Courts erred in deny the benefit on the plea that his continuance for 89 day was conditioned. Education is the dire need of the country. There are neither enough schools nor teachers to teach. Insecurity is writ large on the face of the teaching community because of nebulous and unsatisfactory conditions of service. [994C D, G] Rattanlal vs State, A,I.L.R., 1987 S .C. 477; Rattan Lai v State Of Punjab, ; ; Rattan Lalv. State of H.P., AJ.,T.

The appellant was elected to the Punjab Vidhan Sabha from a constituency in the General Election of 1967. The respondent, who was one of the members of the Panchayat Samiti, challenged the election on the ground that he was disqualified from being chosen as a member of the Assembly, because he was holding an office of profit under the State Government at the relevant time. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that : (i) the payment of allowance under rules 3 to 7 made by the appellant was in addition to the payment under r. 3 and payment of two sets of aLayances must necessarily result in profit to the payee; (ii) the amount of daily allowance was not salary, remuneration or honorarium; and (iii) the respondent represented the amount which he was expected to spend on an average every month for the purpose of properly discharging his official duties. HELD : The High court was right in holding that the allowances paid under rules were in addition 'to the payment prescribed by r.3. [427 G] (i)(a) Rule 3 only covers payment to compensate a Chairman for journeys performed by him for his official duty within the district in which the Panchayat is situated, while rules 4 to 7 govern cases where the journey is performed outside the district. The rule does not contemplate pecuniary gain. There was also no evidence from which an inference may be drawn that the amount received by a Chairman was in excess of the amount 'of expenditure which he would have to incur for the purposes of performing the journeys in order to discharge his official functions.

The appellant was the tenant of a shop in dispute. The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction against the appellant on the ground that the appellant had made constructions materially altering the accommodation without obtaining the consent of the landlord. The appellant 's defence was that the premises were sub stantial in nature which could be removed without causing any damage to it and that the construction was not material alteration. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the tin shed shown by letters ABCD did not constitute material alteration and that it further held that the respondent landlord had constructed a tin shed on the open land adjoining the accommodation and it could be remove without causing damage to the accommodation. On appeal, the Additional Civil Judge set aside the trial court 's order and dismissed the suit. The High Court in second appeal interfered with the findings of the first appellate court on the question whether tin shed and the partition wall were material alteration or not. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the two courts below had failed to consider the third condition, namely, whether the constructions constitute material alterations. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The nature of the constructions whether they are permanent or temporary, is a relevant consideration in determining the question of 'material alteration '. A permanent construction tends to make changes in the accommodation on a permanent basis while a temporary construction is on temporary basis which does not ordinarily affects the form or structure of the building, as it can easily be removed after causing any damages to the building. The question whether disputed constructions constitute materials alter ing material alteration is a mixed question of fact and law. [975C D] 2.1 In deciding this question the court must address itself to the nature, character, of the construction and the extent to which they make changes. [ 977D] 2:2. The material alterations contemplated by the two words show that the expression 'materially altered ' means "a substantial change in the character, form and the structure of a building, without destroying its identity". The essential element which needs consideration is as to whether the construction are sub stances which bring about substantial change. [978E] 2 :3. In deciding the question the Court must address himself to the facts of each case. [979F] 2I2.

The appellant company had filed a suit against the respondent for setting aside an ex parte decree for Rs. 28,479/ passed in favour of the respondent firm on 22 4 1975 against the appellant. The trial court held that summons in the suit was not duly served on the company and it came to know about the decree on 29 7 1975. The Trial Court held that the summons was not properly served on it and dismissed the application filed by the appellant under Order 9 Rule 13 C.P.C. The High Court allowed the revision petition of the appellant against the order of the trial court setting aside the ex parte judgment. Allowing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: 1. The respondent in its rejoinder filed in the Miscellaneous Petition before the High Court had stated that the summon was duly served as stated in the first part of clause (b) of Rule 2 of Order 29 of C. P.C., and that it is denied that service on the appellant company was due to its own negligence or any other principal Officer of the company because either he refuses to sign the summons or is not to be found by the serving person even after due diligence then he can leave the summons at the registered office of the Company and make a report to that effect. In the instant case nothing of the kind was done. It was not the case of the Respondent in its reply filed in Miscellaneous Petition that the service of the summons as effected in accordance with the first para of clause(b) was due service on respondent for the purpose of Order 9 rule 13 C P. C. [1032C D] 2. The order of 29 7 is correct and the appeal must be allowed. [ 1033D] 3. The appellant under the orders of the Court had furnished bank guarantee for the decretal amount. It has agreed to continue the same till disposal of the suit. [1131F] 4. No error of jurisdiction was committed by it. The judgment by the Trial Court setting aside that decree was correct.

The Magistrate recorded reasons for his being satisfied that a breach of the peace existed. The Magistrate called upon the parties to file their written statements and then after a full enquiry as provided by section 145(5) Cr. P.C., passed an order on 17th July, 1978 declaring the appellant to be in possession of the land in dispute. Against this order the respondents moved the High Court under section 482 Cr.P.C. for quashing the said order. The High Court found that as there was no clear finding by the Magistrate in the final order that there was an apprehension of breach of peace, therefore, the final orders were bad and quashed the order of the Magistrate. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the High court erred in holding that the final report of the police was vitiated in absence of a finding that breach of such peace existed at the time when the order was passed; (ii) mere absence of finding by a Magistrate in a final order in the circumstances as mentioned above cannot be such a manifest defect so as to attract the extraordinary jurisdiction of the High Courts under section 561 Cr. The respondents submitted that there were no clear findings by the magistrate in the preliminary order that the apprehension of the breach of a peace existed which was sufficient to give jurisdiction to the Magistrate to initiate proceedings; and (iii) mere non mention of finding of the first Magistrate in his final order did not amount to an error apparent on the face of the record. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order passed by the High Curt is legally erroneous and cannot be allowed to stand. [94C] 2. Under section 145 it is for the Magistrate, to be satisfied regarding the existence of a breach or peace and once he records his satisfaction in the main order, the High COurt in revision cannot go into the sufficiency or otherwise of the materials on the basis of which the satisfaction of the magistrate is based. [95F] 3. The contradictory stands taken by the parties clearly show that there Was no question of the dispute having ended so as lo bring to their logical end the final Order under sub section (6) of section 145. [96G] 4. If a Magistrate has recorded his satisfaction, in the order, he is thereafter expected to call upon the par ties concerned in such dispute to attend his court in person or by pleader and put in written statements of their respective claims as respects the fact of actual possession of subject of dispute. The enquiry under section 145 is limited to the question to who was in actual possession on the date of preliminary order irrespective of the rights of the parties. [97H; 98A] 5. If there is no such contingency arises, the proceedings have to be carried to their practical end resulting in the finality of the final decision under sub s.(6) and as such it was not necessary for the magistrate to repeat what he had said in the revisional order. [98B C] 6. The objection raised by the respondents that there is an omission on the part of the Magis trate to mention in his report that there has been apprehension of a threat of breach or disturbance from their side, cannot be accepted. [99C D] 7. If the Magistrate had given a finding on this aspect of the matter also but in the circum stances, it can be safely presumed that apprehension of such breach of law was not sufficient to vitiate the order passed under sub sec tion (5) of s.145. [92D E] 8. The question whether the prejudice was caused to any of the respondents who had the full opportunity to produce their evidence before the Court has to be decided on a purely technical ground when the aggrieved party had a clear remedy in the civil court. For these reasons therefore, there is nothing to show that any prejudice was resulted to any one of the particu lars.

The appellant, a public limited company carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of yarn, was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1941 42, 1942 43 and 1943 44. The question was whether the amounts received by the appellant were liable to tax under section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, as they had not been treated as profits made by it in those transactions, that is to say, sales effected by them outside British India, and that therefore, they purchased cotton only from the intermediaries and did not pay them the amounts as shown in their accounts. Held, that the question whether a particular transaction was a sale or not must be decided on the facts of each case and it is not necessary for the Tribunal to decide whether the transactions were benami or not. The decision of the Tribunal was final and binding on the parties. It was open to the High Court to review under section 11(1), if it found that the decision was erroneous in law, only on a reference being made to it under section 67(1). If it found the decision of an appellate tribunal is final, even though the court might not have taken into account any evidence or materials to support it or if it was perverse, it could be corrected by the High Courts. The case was remanded for a finding thereon and the Tribunal had decided in favour of the appellant. Commissioner of Income tax vs Ahmedbhai Umarbhai and Co., ; , referred to. Held further, that on the findings of the tribunal, the question as framed by the Tribunal did not arise either because the decision in the case was a mixed question of law and fact; nor was it open to attack under section 14(2)(c) on any of the grounds set out in the judgment of the High court.

The assessee, a manufacturer of blankets and other woollen cloth, was converted into a company and the mill suffered a loss. The Income tax Officer disallowed the claim on the ground that it was excessive and quite unreasonable looking to the salary paid to the General Manager who was given the charge of the conduct of business after his death. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that Rs. 5,000 as reasonable amount payable as commission to Shri J.P. Vaish was an amount laid out or expended wholly or exclusively for the purpose of the business of the assessee and was wrongly disallowed by the Income tax Appellate Tribunal. The High Court on reference held against the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended that in the circumstances of the case the entire amount of Rs. 75,465 paid to Shri Vaish was not really paid wholly for the purposes of carrying on business and therefore the sum of Rs 37,732 paid as commission could not be regarded as an amount lay out or spent wholly or partly for the purpo se of business of assessee. HELD: The question whether an amount claimed as expenditure was laid out Or expended wholly and exclusively for purpose of business, profession or vocation as required under section 10(2)(Xv) of the Income Tax Act has to be decided on the facts and in the light of the circumstances Of each particular case. But as observed by this Court in Swadeshi Cotton Mills Co. Ltd. vs C.I.T., U.P., ; , the final conclusion on the admissibility of an allowance is one of law. [529 G H] Swadesha Cotton Mills Company Ltd.v. C. I.T. Bombay, ; and Swadesh Cotton Mills Cooperative Ltd. v C.l.T, U. P., ; referred to.

The appellant was a workman employed in the Digha factory of which he was a member. On January 13, 1954, the management and the Union filed a written statement denying the charge and asking for an interim order restraining the union from entering into any agreement with the union. The company made an application praying that the agreement be terminated on the ground that it had not authorised the Fateh Singh to enter into any compromise in his case and prayed for an issue of an appropriate writ or direction quashing the said order. The High Court dismissed the application holding that the appellant was entitled to a writ under article 226 of the Constitution. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the dispute between the employer and the workmen was not an industrial dispute as defined in section 2(k) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 unless it is taken up by a Union of workmen or by a considerable number of workmen. The question whether when a dispute concerning an individual workman is taken upto the Conciliation Board under the Industrial Dispute Act, he is a party to the industrial dispute independently of the union which has espoused his cause was not raised either in the present case or in the application under articles 226 and 227 of the constitution. Central Provinces Transport Service Ltd. vs Raghunath Gopal Patwardhan ; , followed. The Union of India vs Raghunath Ram Patwardan, [1954] S.C.R. 956, referred to. Held, further that the reference was not barred by article 226 as it did not raise any industrial dispute in the absence of a specific provision in the Act or in articles 226 & 227 of Constitution.

The appellants were the tenants in respect of a portion of a house. The respondent No. 1 instituted a suit for ejectment and recovery of rent against the appellants on the ground that they had sub let the premises to defendant No. 2. The appellants contended that the suit was barred by limitation under r. 4 of 0. XXII, r. 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellants were competent to continue the appeal and that the Court could pass a decree in favour of the respondents. On appeal the High Court held that the entire appeal had abated as no application for bringing on record the legal representatives of the deceased respondent No 2 was made within the period prescribed by 0. XLI, r, 4 of the Civil Procedure Code. In appeal to this Court it was contended that : (1) the provisions of r. 2 of O. XXII were not applicable to the facts of the case as the nine appellants constituted a joint Hindu family and the surviving plaintiffs could continue the appeals; (2) if the provisions Of r. 33 of 0, XXII had not been correctly construed in this case, it would have been applicable to all the original plaintiffs and could have granted relief with respect to rights and interests of Kedar Nath as well; (3) if there was a conflict between the previsions of rs. 4 and those of r, 3 of O, XXII, the principle behind the provisions would be that any one of the plaintiffs or defendants in filing such an appeal should have filed the appeal as representing all the other non appealing plaintiffs or others; (4) if no application was made by any one or more of the defendants as he wanted the reversal or modification of the decree in his favour, the entire decree would be in accordance with what the appellant had been found to be entitled. HELD : (i) The High Court could not have heard the appeal of the surviving appellants when the appeal by kedar Nath had abated. [560 C] (ii) Rule 3 of 0 XXII was applicable only to appeals which were filed against the premises when the decree proceeds on a ground common to all of them. It does not apply to appeals from the premises where the decree appealed from is passed and it cannot be said that the decree of the High court could have been passed in appeal as an appeal filed by some of the appellants against the whole decree or defendants, if all the plaintiffs had a joint right to eject him or to have him as their tenant. [561 F G] (iii) The rule is under the sub heading 'judgment in appeal '. Rule 3 deals with a matter different from the matter dealt with by r. 9 of O XXII and no question of its provisions overriding those of rr. 9, 10 of O., XXII or vice versa arises. In fact such an exercise of power will lead to difficulties in adjustment of rights of the various parties. A case like the present is not a case of such a kind.

The appellant was the tenant of a building in Delhi. The respondent landlord filed a petition for eviction under section 1967(1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 on the ground that the premises were required by him bona fide for personal cultivation and that the forfeiture of tenancy caused by sub letting contrary to the terms of the deed of demise could not be justified. The appellant contended that the lease was created prior to the extension of the contractual tenancy to Delhi and therefore the requirement of notice in writing under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act could not apply to the lease. The Rent Controller held that no notice was necessary since the lease had expired by efflux of time limited thereby under section 111(g) of that Act to Delhi, and that there was a determination by forfeiture even without issuance of a notice. The appellate authority confirmed the order of eviction. In second appeal the High Court held that the tenancy stood terminated by forfeiture under section III (g) because no notice as required by section 106 had been given to the lessee in the present case. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the renewal of a lease under section 11 could not amount to a determination of the lease and that even if the lease stood terminated, the tenancy could be forfeited under section 112(g). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of the Act which are but a statutory recognition of the rules of justice, equity and good conscience have not been made applicable to leases executed prior to 1929 or even prior to that coming into force. [918C] 2.1 The requirement as to written notice in English law is in consonance with justice. If the purpose of the rule as to notice is to indicate the intention of the lessor to determine the lease, and to avail himself of the tenant 's breach of covenant it could, as effectively, be achieved by an oral intimation as by a written one without in any way disturbing the mind of the chancery judge. [936D] 2:2 The requirement of a statutory notice under section 108(g), which is in conformity with justice, must be read as a statutory form part of justice and not merely a statutory formality. [948F] 3.1 In the present ease, the appellant had all along staked his case on the application of the Rules of Justice to the Delhi High Court. The High Court was right in holding that the notice dated February 10, 1983 did not suffer from any infirmity. [949B C] 3:2. The requirement under section II(g)(g) is a statutory protection which does not require notice in terms of section 111 (g). It cannot be gainsaid that a notice as contemplated by section 11(g ) is one where the time is not limited and therefore section III(g); will not apply and is terminable on the part of the landlord only in the manner provided by section 112. [947E F] 3 :3. The requirements of a written notice under the section are not based upon any general rule of equity. It is not necessary that there should be a specific statutory provision, that even where a statute provides for a particular remedy, it may be available in law to the landlord if so chooses, but the latter would not by itself bring about an effective operation of the statute. [946F G] 4:4. The language of section III is clear and unambiguous and cannot be read into the provisions of section 11 (g), as it now stands. [945G H] 5:1. The provision in sub section (g)(a) of section II of the is in accord with justice and good faith. It has to be seen in every case whether the particular provision of the act has been breached and whether the lessor has, by some overt act, brought home to the tenant his election to eject on the strength of the said breach.

The Governor of Assam appointed a Commission to enquire into the allegations against the appellants, who were dismissed from service. The Commission submitted two orders in terms of article 311(2) of the Constitution and served on them. They were not satisfied with the requirements of sub clause (c) of cl. (2) Of article 311. The Governor passed an order under cl. 2 of article 31(2). The appellants challenged the validity of the order by a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order of dismissal from service was not passed in violation of article 14 of the Constitu tion as it stood before its amendment by the Constitution (Fifteenth Amendment) Act, 1963. [488 B] (ii) The satisfaction under cl.(c) is recorded in writing and after the punishing authority has accepted it. It is the principal clause of article 320(3)(c) which lays down when the Public Service Commission shall be consulted. Sub clause (d) of that Article does not confer any rights on a public servant so that the absence of consultation or any irregularity in consultation does not afford him a cause of action in a court of law, vide State of U.P. vs P. K. Hore, ; and Khem Chand vs The Union of India & Ors., [1969] Vol. VI Assam Law Reports 192; referred to. (iii) The words used in the Article before the amendment were interpreted by this Court in Khem Chand 's case as meaning that the Governor had to arrive at a decision on the question of inexpediency of holding the inquiry as required by the amended article 311 and that it was not necessary for him to record any satisfaction that it had been not expedient to give the Government servant an opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him.

The petitioners and the Shia community of Mohalla Doshipura, Varanasi, were members of a Muslim Waqf Board in U.P. State, which was established by the Sunni Central Waqfs Board Act, 1936. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said Act before the High Court on various grounds including the ground that the provisions of the Act had been violated and that the impugned Act was ultra vires the powers of the Board under section 144 Cr. P.C., 1908. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the petitioners were not entitled to challenge the impugned order passed by the City Magistrate, Varanasi on 24th November, 1979 in view of the decision of this Court in Haji Mohammad Ismail vs Munshi Barkat Ali and Ors. [1962] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 1. The said decision was rendered in a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution filed before it by the petitioners and their Shia Community of Mohalla Develi, Varanasi. The writ petition was dismissed by the High court on the ground of laches. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The impugned Act is a judicial order or quasi judicial order, the function thereunder being essential and integral to the maintenance of public order and functions on the subject in question as claimed by the parties. [1133C] 1.2 The High Courts have been given power under Article 226 to issue writs for enforcement of fundamental rights and apprehended danger to public tranquility under section 145 Cr.P C., 1973, which is a self contained code. It is well settled that the powers conferred on the District Magistrate, Chief Presidency Magistrates, Sub Divisional Magistrate or any other Executive Magistrate specially empowered by the State Government in that behalf cannot be regarded as having been exercised by "a District Magistrate" within the meaning of section 144 Criminal Procedure Code, 1973. [1103C D] 1:3. The power to issue a writ under article 32 is conferred on "District Magistrates, Chief Metropolitan Magistrates, sub Divisional Magistrates or any Executive Magistrate specifically empowered by State Government". Having regard to such implementation of the concept of separation of judicial functions from executive or administrative functions and allocation of the former to the Judicial Magistrates and the latter to the Executive Magistrates under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, it will be difficult to accept the contention that the order passed in the present case is a "judicial order" or quasi judicially order. [111D E] 1 :4. The fact remains that there was no adjudication or decision on merits as a result of the final order passed under section 5(1) Cr. It cannot be said that the High Courts had acted perversely in passing the impugned judgment or that they were wrong in holding that it was a judicial one. [112E F] 1 5. The contention that since the petitioners ' application for quashing the proceedings before the City Magistrates was not maintainable, the same being barred by res judicata or principle analogous to res judicata, cannot be accepted. [113G H] 6. The order passed on 24.11.1979 in the earlier litigation is a nullity and it is not open to the respondents 5 and 6 to challenge that order in any manner either by way of an appeal or revision under article 136 of the Constitu tion. [114A B] 7. The petition for special leave was filed in this Court after a lapse of nearly two years from the date of the judgment in the appeal. It was only in an extremely extraordinary situation when other measures were bound to fail, that a total prohibition or suspension of their rights may be resorted to as a last measure. [115E F; 116A B].

The assessee, a limited company, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1965 66 under the Income Tax Act, 1961. The assessee claimed set off of capital loss of Rs.3.10 lakhs sustained by it during the assessment years 1957 58 and 1960 61. The Income Tax Officer disallowed the claim on the footing that when in the assessment Year 1957 58 the loss was claimed it was excluded in the computa tion of income as capital loss and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that there was no genuine loss, and set off had been claimed by the assessee. In its appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the claim for set off was admissible under Section 24(3) of the 1922 Act, as far as relevant provided in Section 80 of the 1961 Act, and that the assessee was entitled to the benefit of set off only if there was genuine loss. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the benefit conferred under Section24 of 1922 Act continued to be given effect to under the 1961 act and notwithstanding the wordings of section 80 of that Act, the High Court had not merited any loss could be said to have been determined for the relevant assessment year 1957 58, which could be carried forward to subsequent years. [1164E F] 2.1 The benefit conferred by Section 24 of 1922 act continued to remain given effect and there is no merit in the appeal. [1106F G] 2:2. In the instant case, the assessee had made the claim and he took note of it. his failure to comply strictly with the requirement of sub section (3) Of section 24 should not be permitted to be taken advantage of by the Revenue nor should it be used to the prejudice of the assessee.[1164G H] 2 :3. The benefit under Section 25(1)(a) continued to he given effect from the assessment for the year 196566 and there was a failure to carry forward the capital loss as provided in section 24(2A).

The respondent was recruited as a Senior Scientific Officer on October 12, 1966 in the Defence Science Service. He was posted in the Directorate of Technical Development and Production (Prevention) (Amendment) Rules, 1979. The appellant who was working in DTD & P. became a member of DAQAS. When the trifurcation was made, the service rules governing the three units had a common Rule which was Rule 12 in DAQAs and DLS. In the year 1979, the Defence Research Service was reconstituted as Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) and Production(DN) and P. The respondent approached the Administrative Tribunal for reinstatement on the ground that he was entitled to remain in service upto the superannuation age of 60 years. The Tribunal held that the re spondent was not liable to be retired at the age of 58 years, but directed the appellant to reinstate him with all his emoluments from the date of his arbitrary retirement till the date o f his re instatement in service as if he had not been retired. In appeal by the Union of India, this Court held that since the respondent was entitled tO be deemed to have been increased to 60 years in view of the OM dated 24.12.85 read with the Office Memorandum dated 10.2.86, referred to above, it could not be said that he had ceased to be a member, and that his service conditions would have to run parallel and no discrim ination can be made between them by an unilateral action. Dismissing the appeal, this court, HELD: 1. The decision of the Tribunal is both proper and valid, and there is no substance in the present appeal. [22E] 2.1 In the instant case, the respondent had been recruited to the Defence science Service, and after the recruitment, he was posted according to the exigency of service in any of the said three units. His service conditions will have to be run parallel, and no nexus of such classification to the object sought to be achieved has been shown to us by the appellant. [23F] 2:2 The decision taken by the Tribunal was both proper as well as valid, but there is nothing in it which would show that any nexus of the classification to tho object sought lo be achieved had been shown.

The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Judge for publishing a pamphlet in the Official Gazette on June 15, 1967. The petition was filed on the 24th June, 1967 and the High Court dismissed it in limine. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the procedure adopted by the trial court was wrong in that the two witnesses who were examined as court witnesses had been cited earlier and the Judge had given no reasons for allowing them to be called as court witness. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court was not justified in setting aside the order of the trial Court under article 227 of the Constitution. [975 B] (2) Under section 21(1) of the Act, the Judge is given powers wider than those given by the Code of Civil Procedure under 0. 14, r. 1, C.P.C., to correct errors apparent on the face of the record or to correct any error apparent on a review of the judgment. The power of the court in this respect is of wide amplitude specially when investigation is being made into allegations about the commission of a corrupt practice. It may be that in the instant case, if the two persons had not been examined, the judge might well have decided the issue the other way. But the Act certainly gave him the power to do so and no exception can be taken to the course adopted by him although it must be recorded that his earlier order refusing to issue summons to them in the first instance when asked to do it on the 21st August was hardly justifiable. [ 975 D E] (3) The expression "any person" occurring in section 21 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 which does not contain a similar provision has been held by this Court to be wide enough to include even persons who are not parties to the suit and not called as a witness by a party to the litigation. [980 G H] (4) The word "court" in section 2(c) of that Act, which has been used in connection with the trial of a civil suit, means the verbatim reprint of the other. The first bears the date 8th June and the second bears the dates of the election.

The petitioner, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, and its registered office in Kanpur, was assessed to sales tax on sales effected between April 1, 1956 and July 31, 1956. The Sales Tax Officer levied a tax of one anna in the rupee on the sale proceeds of jute. In exercise of the power conferred by section 3 of the U. P. Sales Tax Act, 1948, the Governor of Uttar Pradesh issued a notification dated March 31,1956, purporting to levy a tax on the sales effected during the period April 1 1956 and August 31, 1957. The petitioner challenged the validity of this notification in a writ petition before the High Court. It was contended that (i) the Validation Act was ultra vires the powers of the State Legislature under Entry 54, List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution; (ii) the validation Act was not ultra vires as it was passed after section 3 A was in operation and the impugned notification was therefore invalid; (iii) the validating Act was beyond the competence of the legislature because it imposed a tax retrospectively and that the Validation act was not saved by article 31A of the Constitution. Held, that the validation of the impugned Act was valid as it had not been passed after the enactment of the Validation Acts. The Validation Act is intra vires and the validity thereof cannot be challenged on the ground that it contravened articles 14, 19(1)(f) and 31(2). The State of Madras vs Gannon Dunkerley & Co., ; , relied on. Held further, that a tax imposed by a Provincial Legislature on transactions which are not authorised by the entry, is not an indirect tax but a tax levied on the occasion of sale. The power to enact a law with reference to a topic entrusted to it, is plenary and unrestricted subject only to any limitation imposed by the Constitution, and in the exercise of such a power it will be competent for the legislature to impose a tax thereon treating it as a sale, and that it is not within the competence Of the Legislature to impose the tax on transactions. The State vs Sales Tax officer, ; , referred to.

The appellant, a student of 22nd year, was sentenced to imprisonment for 4 years R.I. and a fine of Rs. 2 lakhs. The High Court affirmed it in appeal. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended that the sentence imposed on him was too severe and he had no vicious antecedents except this fugitive, sex sanity, criminal companionship, versatile vices through bio mining techniques, and that the extreme penalty of death was not excessive. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The sentence of imprisonment is reduced to 2 years RI. [591B] Sunil Batra 's case ; , followed. In prison treatment must, therefore, be geared to psychic healing, release of stresses, restoration of self respect and cultural normalisation, apart from training to adapt oneself to the life outside. The functional failure of our pachydermic prison projects exacerbated by its tension and trauma on the one hand and the reverse ethos inside on the other, deserves judicial cognizance. [592C D] Sunil, Batra ' s case ; Sunil Batra vs Marwah & Ors., ; , referred to. 2.1 The extreme penalty is not excessive, but is more important. It may be marginally extenuatory to mention that modern Indian conditions are drifting into societal exemp tion on the barbaric front promoting proneness to pornos in life, what wit nenitis normally degenerated by human intervention of society and its values with an indelible stigma as convict stamped on him a potentially good person 'successfully ' processed into a hardened delinquent, thanks to the penal illiteracy of the Prison system. [593C D; 593D] 2.2 In prisonation must, however, be25 in the instant case, and not by a negative reduction in the prison term. What is more crucial is a set of positive prescriptions which will ensure his turning a new leaf. One major method in securing this goal is to keep alive the family tie of the person in prison so that he may not deteriorate into a non person. Within limits of the prison Act and Rules thereunder, the State Government or the Inspector General of Prisons will ensure that on paroleitality lives, release from young Appellant Reversing into a balanced person, given propitious social environs, curative and congenial work and techniques of internal stress release or of reformatory self expression. [594D E] Sunil Neogly extenuating the sentence, this Court has held that the special circumstances of this case constrain us to relent a little on principle because the restorative approach to sentencing has been jettisoned by the courts below. The task is not done by a positive reduction in prison term and what is more vital is a sets of positive prescription which will ensuring his turninga mental aurvation, punitive and congenerating work release or sentenceatory self declaration. [595C D, F G] Sunil Bosal vs Marwahastship, ; , relied on.

The respondent assessee, a limited company dealing in land, was awarded compensation for the acquired land. The Land Acquisition Officer awarded a sum of Rs.24,97,249 as compensation payable to the assessee. The assessee deposited the amount in its suspense account on the same date. During the assessment proceedings for the assessment year 1956 57, the relevant accounting period being the year ended March 31, 1956, the Income Tax Officer brought to tax a sum Of Rs.7,24,914 in the assessee 's business income. This represented the difference between the amount of compensation received by the assessee and the amount paid by the State Government on April 25, 1956 without furnishing security bond for refunding the amount. The Income Tax officer treated the sum as liable to income tax during that year on the basis that the income accrued to the assesse on the date of the award. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. In second appeal by the respondent assessee before the Income Tact Tribunal, two contentions were raised by it. Firstly, that the amount was not taxable in the assessment years 1956 57 and 1957 58, but was a trading receipt of the business carried on by the assesee on the dates of the awards, and secondly, that in any event the amount did not accrue to the appellant as its income during the relevant previous year ended 31st March, 1956 relevant to the assessment for the relevant assessment years. The High Court answered both the contentions in favour of the assessee, but held that the compensation received was not a receipt of revenue nature and that it could be said that the sum did not accrued to it as its source of income. In appeal by certificate, this Court, HELD: (1) The expression "arising or accruing" used in section 4(1)(b)(i), includes a right to receive profits and that there must be a debt owed by some body. [395 D] (2) The word "arising" in section 3 of the Act means "a liability to pay additional compensation or enhanced compensation as claimed by a party aggrieved". If there is an existing liability, the mere fact that the payment is postponed to the future would not detract that liability from becoming a debt but the liability to paid unliquidated damages or additional compensation which are inchoate or contingent would not create a debt. [397 E F] (3) The High court was right in holding otherwise. [398 G] Kedarnath Jute Mfg. Co. Ltd.

The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for eviction of the respondent on the ground that they were required bona fide by them to vacate the shop. The appellants objected to the execution of the decree and the executing court accepted their objection and dismissed the execution case. A miscellaneous appeal was also dismissed by the High Court. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that the compromise decree was void and inexecutable as being against the provisions of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The language of section 12(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961 is somewhat different from many similar State Statutes. Section 12(2) says that notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any other law or contract, no suit shall be filed in any Civil Court against a tenant for his eviction from any accommodation except on one or more of the grounds enumerated in section 12 (1). A perusal of the provision shows that the inhibition related to the filing of the suit only. No suit can be filed for eviction except on the one or two of the ground mentioned in section12(1). [882 D E] The language is somewhat differ from many other States. Section 13(2), which deals with eviction of tenants from residential accommodation, provides that notwithstanding any other reasonably suitable non residential accommodation of his own in his occupation in the city or town concerned, no decree for eviction against a landlord shall be passed except on either one or several of the three grounds enumerated therein mentioned in s 12(11). [888 D E; 883 A B] In the instant case, the ground for eviction from the accommodation let for non residential purposes mentioned in clause (f) of section12 is that the accommodation "is required bona bonafide by the landlord for the purpose of continuing or starting his business. and that the landord has no other reasonably alternative non residential premises of his self in his possession in the City or town. [883 E F] The ground for ejectment from the premises let for residential purposes was that the tenant 's need was bona fide. The High Court was right in holding that the provisions Of section 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot apply to eviction suits governed by the special statutes. [889 G H; 884 A B].

The assessee company was a limited company doing business as selling agents of a Textile Mill. For the assessment year 1955 56, the Income tax Officer included in its total income the amount paid for the shares purchased by it for the sake of acquiring the managing agency of the Elphinstone Mills Ltd., of Bombay. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that under the circumstances the Directors were justified in not declaring any dividend in respect of the profits that had accrued in the accounting years. In appeal, the Tribunal held that the loss incurred by the company was capital loss and that the directors were justified as they had a capital loss of Rs. 12 lakhs. The High Court on reference held that there could be no doubt that the Directors had suffered a capital losses of Rs 12 lakhs and that therefore cancelled the orders of the Income Tax Officer under section 23A(1). In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question whether the payment of a dividend or a larger dividend than that declared by a company would be unreasonable within the meaning of section 23 A of the Act does not assess any income to tax. He only does what the directors should have done putting himself in their place. [864 F] Commissioner of Income Tax, West Bengal vs Gangadliar Bannerjee and Co., , applied. (ii) The loss incurred being a capital one, it is not open for the Income. tax Officer to constitute himself as a super director. As observed by this Court in Commissioner of Incometax, WestBengal vs Gangadhar Beamblejee & Co., ; , the loss any reasonable body of Directors of a company will have done just what the Directors of the company did. [874 F G] Commissioner Of Income Tax vs Williamson Diamonds Ltd., and Commissioner of income tax, West Calcutta vs Gangadhali Bannerji and Co. (Pvt.) Ltd., , referred to.

The U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1954, was passed by the State Government under section 12(4) of the Act in respect of certain disputes between the appellant and the respondents. The dispute was referred to the arbitrator who gave his award on May 14, 1956. The appellant filed objections before the Civil Judge that the Civil judge was not justified under section 15 of the , in modifying the award merely because he disagreed with the finding. The Civil Judge overruled the objection and set aside the order of the Civil Court modifying the Award. On appeal by special leave, Held, that section 12 (6) of Act V of 1954, does not make any distinction between provisions like section 39 and section 15, and section 37 of the Indian , applies to arbitrations under the Consolidation of Holding Act. The effect of section 46 and section 47 is that all the provisions of the except sub section (1) of section 6, sections 7, 12, 36 and 37 apply to arbitrations. Section 37 of Act VI of 1954 does not made any distinction in respect to provisions like s.39 and section 48 of the . Further, the effect of s.46 read with sections 46 and 47 is inter alia to apply sections 15 and 39 of the to proceedings under the Act. Section 12(6) must be read with section 37 as it stands. The result of section 16 read with ss. 46 and47 of the is that the decision of the arbitrator under sub section(4), shall be final.

The petitioner, diploma holder in Engineering and holds the post of Executive Engineer in the respondent Corporation. Till 1974 he was a degree holder Junior Engineers. The promotion post of Superintending Engineer was available both for diploma holders and degree holders according to merit cum seniority. This was so according to the practice followed by the corporation without making any rules or regulation in that behalf. In 1974, the corporation made regulations by passing a resolution by passing the resolution and continued the same practice. The petitioner challenged the said regulation before the High Court contending that no classification could be made among the Executive Engineers on the basis of their educational qualification for the purpose of promotion to the post. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that if at all such a discrimination was permissible, it could be done only by a statutory rule or regulation framed under section 64 of the Maharashtra Industrial Development Act, 1961. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The law can made among other things, a valid classification can made amongst the members holding the same post on the ground that they belong to the same cadre of Executive Engineers and do the same work. [372F] 1.2 In the absence of rule or regulations, the authority can prescribe service conditions by executive instructions and this is what was done till the year 1988 and is also sought to be done since 1988 by the impugned resolution. The proposition that in the absence Of rules or regulations the authority could act by executive instruction finds direct support in Mysore State Road Transport Corporation vs Gopinath Gundachar char, ; and The Union of India & Ors. vs Dr. (Mrs.) S.B. Kholi; , , relied on. 1.3 In the instant case, the impugned regulation was not made under section 65 of the Act. It is now well settled that for the purposes of promotion a valid class can made between the members hold the same posts on the one hand and those drawn from different sources. The degree holders Junior Engineers had sought a relief that such a quota be kept. It was for the authorities if they so desire, taking into consideration the nature of work, the requisite qualification for making such a classification that quotas could be prescribed on the principle of educational qualification. [373B C] 1:4. In State of Mysore & Anr. vs Triloki Nath Khosa & Ors., ; , this Court held that in State of Karnataka & Anr., vs P. Narasing Rao, ; , it was held that classification on the strength of educational qualifications was permissible and did not violate Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. [375B C; 376C] 2.1 In the present case, since the petitioner had wanted such a class to be made, it cannot be said that if the classification was already made which was challenged before the Court. The impugned resolution was therefore no authority for the proposition that if direct recruits and promotees are integrated into one class they cannot be classified for purposed of promotion on a basis other than that in case before them the classified for purpose of promo tion to the higher post on a principle of merit and, is also seeking a higher scale than non matriculate Tracers thought their duties were identical. [374F G] 2:2 In view of the above, the petition stands dismissed.

The first petitioner, an advocate practising in the Supreme Court, was appointed as a Judge of the High Court. The appointment was challenged by the second respondent on the ground that he had been denied the opportunity to meet the charges and that the Chief Justice had acted mala fide in passing the order dated May 22, 1987. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that there were no selection of particular Judges to be appointed in the vacancies and that there was no violation of any principle or guidelines laid down by this Court in S.P. Gupta 's case. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) as the place and process of appointments had been expedited, the writ petitions should not have been entertained; (ii) the Chief Justices of the States and their respective counsel were not present when the matter was taken up for hearing; (iii) the High Courts should be directed to dispose of the applications on merits without any delay. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The Chief Justice of India is the head of the Indian Judiciary and he has a constitutional obligation to act in accordance with the Constitution. [448B] 2.1 There are no guidelines for the exercise of the power of judicial review by the Supreme Courts. It is well settled that the jurisdiction of this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution is not to be exercised lightly, but only to be confined to a mere formality and not to the form. [494C D] 2:2 The Chief justice of India, the Chief justice, the chief Justice of the State who consulted in the matter also came to be considered by the Chief Minister for the purpose of constituting a Bench of nine Judges of the Supreme court and this Court was directed to constitute a Bench presided over by the President of India. [50F G] 2 :3 The Chief Justices have been given an interim order, but they are not required to give any direction to the Chief Secretaries to obtain from all the addition al judges working in the High courts their consent to be present before the Chief Secretary. [51A B] 2 .4 In view of the fact that the Judges of this court have already been appointed as Judges of a High Court, the question whether the said Judge is entitled to hold an appointment should be confined only to suggesting appropriate names to the chief justice of the country and not for the transfer of judges.

The respondent was serving as a Sub Inspector in the Delhi Police. He was served with a charge sheet dated October 12, 1978 on May 15, 1978 for unauthorised absence from April 17, 1978 to May 16, 1980 and a second show cause notice dated September 30, 1979 was issued by the respondent calling upon him to furnish details of persons who traveled and the amounts received by him. The respondent filed an appeal against the said order before the Deputy Commissioner, Delhi. The appeal was dismissed on June 17, 1980. The Respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court which quashed the impugned order of punishment and directed that the respondent be paid all consequential benefits. The appellant preferred a Letters Patent Appeal against the aforesaid order of the Single Judge. The Division Bench allowed the Letters Patent appeal and set aside the order of dismissal and directed the appellant to pay all consequential reliefs. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The de facto doctrine can have no application to the case of a person who is not the holder of an office but is merely a bank employee for that matter an ex employee. [204C] 1.2 In the instant case, the respondent did not attribute any bias or mala fides to the Enquiry Officer nor did he com plain that he was in any manner prejudiced on account of the said enquiry conducted by the said Enquiry Officer and therefore the High court ought to have remitted the matter to the competent Disciplinary Authority to take a fresh decision based on the report of the Enquiry officer. [205E] 1:3 The respondent did nothing but attribute any biased or mala fide to the enquiry officer nor did it appear that he had made the claim of bias or malafide. He, therefore, was not entitled to have the order quashed. [206G] 1 :4. If one were to go by the charge le velled against the respondent and the reply thereto one may carry the impression that the respond ent had made his claim on the basis of the fake receipt; whether the respondent himself was duped or not would be a different matter. The fact, however, remains that the impugned ordi narily doctrine saves official acts done by an officer whose appointment is defective and with and it fails the entire edifice. It is a case more or less akin to a case tried by a court lacking in inherent jurisdiction.

The respondents were owners of a building in the main stream of Delhi. The appellant Corporation, by its order dated February 4, 1966, directed the respondents to submit their application for execution of work under section 336 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957. The Commissioner of the appellant Corporation by his letter dated April 30, 1966 informed the respondents that their application was rejected on the grounds "that the proposal was under acquisition and also affected in the road widening". The respondents thereupon filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Commissioner refusing to accord sanction. The High Court accepted the writ petition holding that the appellant had no power to refuse sanction for erection or development of any building or work on either side of the existing road, and that the plan submitted by the respondents did not contravene section 14 of the Development Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Corporation that (i) the Master Plan prepared under section 7 of the Act by the Authority was not in conformity with the Master plan; (ii) the land in question had been utilised for building operations and, therefore, the proposed construction would be hit by section 14. HELD: (i). The High court was right in issuing a writ of mandamus to the appellant to approve the plans submitted and that it was proposed to be used in a different manner. [171 E] (ii). The Master Plan is prepared under Section 7 by the authority on September 1, 1962 and it has also come into force as contemplated by section 11. Since the Master 's plan does not state that any part of the property belonging to the respondents will be covered by the proposed road, it cannot be stated that when the respondents are attempting to renovate the building they are using the land for building or other work in a zone otherwise than in conformity With the Master plans. [172 G H] (iii).

The appellant No. 1 was the Minister of Industries and the Additional District Magistrate, who had been asked by the police authorities to make a statement before him that he would be present at the time when the confession was made. The statements were recorded by the Additional Sessions Judge under section 164 Of the Code of Criminal Procedure and the same were produced before him by the prosecution. The appellant No 1 was examined as a witness in the case but his evidence was not recorded on the ground that he had not exactly remembered what transpired on that night in the bedroom of the appellant No, 1. The Additional District Magis trate who tried the case did not record any statement of the accused under section 161 Of the Criminal Procedure Code and therefore the statements were inadmissible in evidence. The High Court dismissed the appeal of the appellants No. 2 and convicted them under section 120 B I.P.C. and sentenced them to rigorous imprisonment for one year and a fine of Rs. 2,000 each. On appeal by special leave it was contended that the statement made by the appellant no doubt amounted to an admission of guilt but that the statements made by him to the two witnesses were inadmissible under section 162 Of the Cr. P.C., as they were not recorded in accordance with the provisions of section 164 of the Code and were therefore inadmissible in their evidence. Held, that the evidence of these witnesses being highly discrepant and contradictory it was unsafe to act upon them. The statement made to the three police officers by the two accused persons was admissible under section I34 Of the Indian Penal Code as they had not been recorded in terms of section 165 of the Criminal Proce dure Code. The fact that the appellant Nos. 1 and 2 were not examined in Court did not affect their veracity. The evidence of the witnesses being so inadmissible it could not be relied upon to base a conviction on them.

The respondent plaintiff was serving as a constable when an incident took place on 17.2.1971, which led to the prosecution of the appellant along with the Head Constable, and the Sub Inspector, Baldev Singh. The charge made against the plaintiff was that he physically assaulted and detained one Gurdial Singh. He was acquitted by the trial court but on appeal, the High Court set aside the order of dismissal and remitted the case for fresh disposal in accordance with law. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the bar of limitation would not apply; (ii) the suit was barred by limitation; and (iii) the finding of the Additional District Judge on the question of limitation was patently illegal inasmuch as the judgment assumes that no law of limitation is applicable to suits where an order is impugned as being void. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The question involved in the suit should not have been lightly brushed aside by the High court in limine. It would be open to the appellants to file an application for admitting additional evidence in regard to the further orders passed against Kahan Singh subsequent to the civil court 's decree in his favour and to argue before the High Courts that the case was distinguishable. [825F G] 2. The High Court should call for the records and decide the case finally at the motion stage itself as the case is an old one. In view of the fact that the question involved is a pure question of law, it should not be ignored on the ground that in the case of another member of the police force a mistake was committed. [826F G; 825A] 3. The point involved in this suit should be considered as a preliminary issue and the High has rightly rejected by the courts below.

The appellant, a private limited company carrying on business in tea garden tools and requisites and also acting as agents for selling tea. The respondent entered into certain transactions in jute. In the relevant previous year which ended on June 30, 1958, the assessee had contracted to purchase a quantity of Twill and 2500 bales of corn sacks from various parties after paying full price of the goods covered by the delivery orders and transferred those P.D.Os. to buyers after receiving the price fixed for the sale of those goods. The assessee had no godown for keeping the goods and had not handled them. The goods were in the godown of the mills and only the delivery order was issued to the mills. The amount realised on sale to M/s. Lachhmi Chand Rataria was not credited to the account books of the Mills. The Income tax Officer held that the transactions amounted to speculative transactions within the meaning of Explanation 2 to section 24(1) of the Act and the loss could be set off only against speculation profits, and as there were no speculation profits in that year he held that it was carried forward and set off against speculation profit in the future. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner on appeal confirmed the order of the Income tax officer. In reference the High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee. On appeal by special leave: Held: (i) The Explanation to section 2(1)(b)(i) of West Bengal Jute Goods Future ordinance, 1949, does not invalidate speculative transactions of sale wherein the goods were not physically delivered by the seller to the buyer but only laid down that if there was no actual delivery meaning to that expressing for purposes of income tax only. In considering the effect of the position that the property in the goods passed to the ultimate endorsee of the delivery Orders, it is not necessary that the transfer in question should be followed up by actual delivery of the commodity or the scrips has taken place; on the other hand a transaction which is not otherwise speculative in nature may yet be speculative according to explanation 2 if there is no actual deliverance of the commodities or the market. The Explanation does not render any such provision invalid merely because there is an actual delivery but also because the goods are not physically, delivered by a seller to a buyer, but only lay down that where the speculative transactions are of such a nature as to constitute a business, the business shall be deemed to be distinct and separate from any other business. The explanation does not vitiate speculative according as Explanation 2 says that where a speculative transaction is of such kind as to constitutes a transaction in which a contract for purchase and sale of any commodity is periodically or ultimately settled otherwise than by the actual delivery or transfer of the goodps, the stock of goods and gains, i any, in a similar business only. Explanation 1 says that when the speculative transaction are of a certain kind the transactions are not speculative transactions but are also intended to be speculative. The words "actual delivery in explanation 2 means real as opposed to notional delivery". For income tax purposes speculative transactions means what the definition of that expression in Explanation 2 does. Whether a transaction is speculative in the general sense or under the Contract Act is not relevant for the purpose of this explanation.

The first respondent was declared elected to the Punjab Legislative Assembly. The appellant filed an election petition challenging the validity of the election on the ground that he had committed a technical defect of an unsubstantial character which the Returning Officer should disregard under section 36(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The High Court held that the first respondent had not been " qualified under the Rules of the Election Commission" and set aside his election. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The word "subscribe" in the General Clauses Act means "to sign". The General Clauses act is necessary for the purpose of the Act. It must be construed in the sense set out above. Therefore, if a person who is unable to write his name his " signature " must be authenticated in " such manner as may be prescribed by the Rules. If he does not do so, he cannot be said to have been guilty of an act or omission in any one of the four nomination papers. [488 B C] (ii) The Returning Officer was bound to reject them under section 37(2)(d) of Act because there was a failure to comply with section 33 unless he could and should have had resort to section 36 (4). That sub section is as follows: "For the purposes of the . or these rules, a person shall be deemed to have signed an instrument or other paper if he has placed a mark on such instrument or document in the presence of the Returning officer or such other officer as may, by order, be specified. " [488 E F] (iii) The words " signing" and "subscribing" in section 36 are not defined but it is equally clear when the Act is read as "a writing containing a mark". Therefore, where the signature cannot be written it must be authorised in the manner prescribed by Rules. Whether this attaches exaggerated importance to the authorisation is not for the Court to decide.

The appellants were employees of the respondent company. During the pendency of the reference, the workmen raised a dispute relating to their retrenchment and the same was referred to the Industrial Tribunal under section 33(A) of the . The Company sent separate communications to the appellants and 10 others asking them to report for duty on or before September 18, 1972 failing which their absence would be construed as voluntary abandonment of service. On October 23, 1972, the respondent wrote a letter to the appellant stating that since by not reporting for duty they had confirmed its presumption that they were no longer interested to continue in service of the company and had totally abandoned the Company 's service, their names had been struck off from the muster rolls of the Company from that date. The appellants sent a cheque to each one of them for the amount due to him on account of gratuity, leave salary and one month 's salary. On September 26, 1972 the respondent sent a reply stating therein that it did not wish to revise its earlier decision under which their names were struck off the rolls. On July 5, 1973, the appellants wrote to the Company returning the cheques sent by the company with them on account o the leave salary gratuity etc. The Company replied that they had not abandoned their service and that they would report for work if no settlement was reached between them. On August 30, 1972 a letter was addressed to the respondent to the effect that they did not intend to abandon the service but had also returned the cheques. On June 20, 1973 the company sent a notice stating therein "that the strike ends in the company 's services" and that it does not wish either to continue the company in service or to have totally abandoned its service. The respondent replied on September 26. 1972 that they could report for duties only on September 20, 1972. On November 5, 1972 they wrote a reply to the company saying that they never intended to abandon their service but wanted to do so and that the company had neither voluntarily abandoned the service nor did they wish to do any work. The company sent another letter dated September 21, 1972 stating therein the fact that it was interested in the service of respondent and had neither withdrawn his services nor did it wish to make them absent from duty on the ground that they have abandoned their services. On December 26, 1973 a formal demand notice calling upon the appellants to report at or before Sept. 18,1972 failing which they would be deemed to have abandoned the company service. In reply the Company sent a letter dated October 2, 1972 to the Labour Commissioner complaining about the arbitrary termination of service of 25 workmen and emphasising that they should not abandon their services and that at any rate the termination of their services could only be in terms of the appellant 's standing orders and since the standing orders did not provide for treating the workmen as having abandoned service in case they were absent in connection with the notified strike, the company was manifestly illegal and invalid. The Labour Court dismissed the application under section 34 of the Act holding that the action of the appellants in removing the names of the appel lants from its rolls was illegal and arbitrary and that their services had been duly terminated by the Company. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the workmen that (1) the action was manifestly unlawful and invalid; (2) the appellants had not withdrawn their company 'Session 's Service, and (3) the termination was in contravention of section 33A of the , as no notice was served upon them. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The failure to perform the duties pertaining to the office must be with actual or imputed intention on the part of the officer to abandon and relinquish the office. [621D] 2.1 The failure of the workman to return to work by a notified date clearly implied abandonment of his employment.

The appellant mortgaged a house belonging to the trust. The mortgage was redeemed and the entire amount remaining unpaid was paid by the respondent. The trustees of the trust filed a suit for recovery of the amount on the ground that the mortgagee had agreed to abandon the execution proceeding and to abandon it. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in revision set aside the order holding that since the trustees had failed to comply with the requirements of r. 89 of 0. 21, r.89 of the Code of Civil Procedure, they were not entitled to commence fresh proceedings for sale of the property. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the transaction of mortgage did not satisfy the requirements under r.88 and (ii) the mortgagee having agreed to abandoned the execution proceed ings, the High court had no jurisdiction to set aside a sale held in execution of the decree. HELD:(i) The High Court was right in holding that the requirements were complied with. [459 C] (ii).The High Court 's view that the requirement of 0 21, Rule 89 was not fulfilled was correct. The High court was right when it found that the decision of the Full Bench of the High COurt was binding on the respondent and that the High 'Court had no power to refer a case to a Full Bench for determination of a question of law arising before him as a question affecting public religious or charitable purpose is involved in the trial of a case. [460 C] The appeal must accordingly be allowed. (iii).The decision of a Full bench of the Bombay High Court on a reference made on a Reference made on the reference "had no existence in law". The effect of a precedent of a court of coordinate authority is that the sale of immovable property in execution would not be valid unless it chooses of the Chief Justice. A Single Judge of a High Court before he enters upon his office takes an oath of office that he will bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution of India as by law established and that he would duly and faithfully and to the best of his ability, knowledge and judgment perform the duties of office without fear or favour, affection or illwill and that lie will uphold the Constitution and the laws.

The appellant joined the post of Telegraph Officer in 1935. He was compulsorily retired from service under Rule 2(2) of the Liberalised Pension Rules, 1950 on the ground that he had attained the age of 55 years and had not attained the prescribed age of 58 years. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of retirement. The learned single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that there was no in firmity in Rule 2 (2) as it did not provide anything to the contrary in the Rule, and as such there was neither any guidelines nor any guidelines for the exercise of power by the Government.
