In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Government had issued instruc tions dated July 11, 1955 and February 8, 1956 which lay down that the retirement under Rule 1 2(1) should be effected when such retirement is necessary in public interest. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The object of Rule 2 is to chop off the dead wood. Rule 2 of Pension Rules on the other hand provides no guide line and gives absolute discretion to the Government to retire a government servant at any time after he has completed 30 years of qualifying service though he has a right to continue till the age Of superannuation which is 58 years.[801D] The object is to bar the government servant from retiring in 'public interest ' after he had completed 30 year of qualifying serv ice. [800F] In the instant case, the memorandum dated November 30, 1962 was issued by the President of India and under Article 77(1), it was a compendious rule and was identical to Fundamental Rule 56(j). The words "weed out unsuit able employees" can only be read qua the power to retire under para 6 and not under Rule2(2). There is thus no force in the argument that para 620 of the Railway Pension Manual, which is identical to Rule 2. (800G H] Union of India & Ors. vs R. Narasimhan, ; , referred to.

The assessee firm was carrying on business of manufacture and sale of katechu under the two contracts entered into with a foreign company. The sales of kutechu were effected by M/s. Biharilal Balkishan at their shops in Kanpur. The Sales Tax Officer held that there could be no profit arising during the chargeable accounting period, but the assessee was entitled to set off in respect of the deficiency in the year 1940 41. As the assessee did not maintain any books of account for the relevant assessment years, the provisions of section 13 of the Income tax Act, 1922 were applicable. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee could not be said to have suffered any deficiency of profits during the period 28th October, 1940 to 31st March, 1944 and therefore, the standard profits as provided in the Act became the deficiency of the said two chargeable accounting periods which should have been allowed set off. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that although chargeable levy was an annual charge and generally for the purpose of the levy of the annual charge the profits of the year preceding the year of charge were taken into consideration if the manufacturing activity leading to the production of finished article which was subsequently sold contributed to the profits realised, according to the High Court. The High Court also held that it was not disputed before them that the business carried on in Nepal on or about 23rd November 1942 and that the sales took place in the Bombay State and that there were no sales during the relevant accounting period. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The assessee firm had been carrying on the same business from 28th January, 1943 to 31th March,1944. It was not a case of carrying on any manufacturing activity but it was carrying out the manufacturing activities and therefore could be carried forward but a necessary pre condition was that profit must be made in the accounting period to which the adventure in question relates. [608 D] (2) The concept of "accounting period" in the background of the 'chargeable accounting period ' can thus be invoked. The concept is the same as in the income tax one, and then makes appropriate adjustments. Therefore, the profits and losses of each year must be computed on yearly basis in terms of the definition of " accountsing period". [609 G] Haji Rahmat Ullah & Co. vs Commissioner of Income tax, U.P., ; , followed. (3) The question must be answered in the negative and in favour of the revenue. [613 B C] Haji Muhammad Ullah and Co. V. Commissioner of Inland Revenue, at 780, referred to.

The Kerala Public Service Commission invited applications for filling up 130 expected vacancies in the posts of Junior Engineers in the Public Works Department as per notification published in the Kerala Gazette dated 16th May, 1978. The qualifications specified for the posts were B.Sc. in Civil Engineering or Mechanical Engineering of the Kerala University or its equivalent as prescribed by the special rules of the State Government (General Branch). The applicants had to appear in the written test conducted by the KPSC and there after in an interview held by it. There was a common question paper which contained, in category I, questions in Civil engineering and in Category II, questions relating to Civil Engineering and in category III. In the case of any category for which the number of options is more than the appointment by transfer aud the junior persons will be admitted to the services as and when vacancies arise. The Kerala Public Services Commission, however, did not prepare a common list. On receiving information from the Government on the above lines, the Public Service Commis sioner reported that there were directions to the K PSC to prepare two separate rank lists one for Civil Engineering graduates and the other for Mechanical Engineering graduates. The KP SC candidates were called in the test conducted. Thereafter, the Kerala Public service Commission prepared a common rank list and also the procedure of the examination and a method of selection was challenged by the applicants who had qualified in Civil Engineers. The High Court allowed the Writ Petitions and directed the Government to prepare the two separate seniority lists. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the K.PSC has advised candidates according to the separate list for Civil Engineers and Mechanical Engineering graduate graduates; (ii) the Kerala State Public Service Commissioner having given effect to the directions given by the High Court, the Government and the Public Services Commis tions are not included in a common seniority list after the interview; and (iii) the appointments made by the Commission were not properly conducted or approved. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The K. P.SC. has advised candidate according to its own order or by the Division Bench of the High court. [747B] 1.2 In view of the difficulties faced by the Kerala Government and Government of Kerala it is necessary to clarify the position and give necessary directions. Clause 4 gave unconditional options to those in the K List of B. Sc. in civil Engineering or mechanical Engineering of Kerala University, or its equal equivalent as provided in rule 749 of the Rules of the Public Health Department (General branch). [748F G] 1:3 The K P.S.C. was not directed to prepare a Common list. common list was referred to in the earlier orders in this Court through certain misapprehensions. The judgment of the Single Judge and the Division Benches of the same High Court are subsequently recalled by this Court by its order dated 7th April, 1981.

The respondent plaintiff filed a suit for dissolution of partnership and accounts. During his life time the business was under the control of Abdul Samad, but on his death the defendants Nos. 1 and 2 were subsequently converted into a partnership firm by a regular deed. During their lifetime the business came to an end and the business of auctioneer known as "Russell Exchange" was under its control. During her life time, the business being under the management of Abdul samed, but after his death, the defendants nos. 1 & 2 have effectively taken charge of the business and excluded the plaintiff. A suggestion to re constitute and partnership made and repeated by the plaintiff has been ignored. In reply to the plaintiff 's letter seeking information that he had no interest in the firm, the defendant Nos.1 and 2 have actually taken charge on behalf of the firm. The plaintiff filed an application for amendment of the plaint which was allowed by the trial court. The defendants challenged the valuation given by the appellant as grossly undervalued and arbitrary. The High Court dismissed the appeal. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 When a plaintiff is required to place the valuation on his claim he must state a valuation which need only be approximately correct but qualified it by saying that "it must not be arbitrary or manifestly inadequate". It is true that in a suit of accounts the correct amount payable by one party to the other can be ascertained only when the accounts are examined and it is not possible to give an accurate valuation of the claim at the inception of the suit. The defendant cannot act arbitrarily in this matter. If a plaintiff chooses whimsically a ridiculous figure it is tantamount to not exercising his right in this regard. [512C D] 1.2 In a suit under challenge for accounts, the plaintiff is not obliged to state the exact amount which would result after taking all the accounts and he may, therefore, put a tentative valuation upon the suit, but he is not permitted to choose an unreasonable and arbitrary figure for that purpose. At page 392 of the judgment in Meenakshisundaram Chettiar vs Venkatachalam Chettiar, ; , this Court while considering the question as to whether the plaintiff can give an arbitrary valuation in the plaint, observed that when a plaintiff was required to placed the valuation of his claim, he must stated a valuation not be approximately incorrect but qualified. It is also true that the plaintiff cannot act unilaterally in this case. If the plaintiff chooses pickically a reverse figure it would be tantamount to non exercising his rights in this regards.

The respondents are manufacturers of industrial units in Madhya Pradesh. The State Government issued a Full Bench of the High Court in the case of G.S. Doe vs Union (M.P.) and others, ; The State of Madhya Pradesh was aggrieved by the judgment of the Full Bench on the ground that the exemption sought for was originally granted but subsequently revoked. However, the State Government withdrew its earlier decision in G. S. Dogee vs M/s. B.S., Doe, ; In the case the respondents challenged the validity of the Notification dated 1st September, 1983 issued under Section 23(1)(i) with a view to avoid liability to pay sales tax on the basis that the industries run by them were "traditional" industries which were not eligible for exemption. The High Court dismissed the writ petition and held that the notification did not apply to industries run in any of the districts of Madhya Bharat or any officer authorised by the State Govt. and as such it was immaterial what type of industry went in there and whether the industry proposed to be set up was a "tractive industry" one or not. The respondents filed appeals against the judgment before this Court. On behalf of the State it was contended that the State had no power to grant exemption under the notification and that the Director of Industries should have granted them a certificate to this effect. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts were right in holding that the Notification did not set out the conditions on which and the procedure in accordance with which the Director was to issue the eligibility certificate. [608C] 1.2 The notification does not set forth the conditions for exemption but only lays down that they will not be available to the industries listed in rule 14 particularly when rule 4 has incorporated the requirement of an eligibil ity certificate in accordance With the previous instructions for the said purpose. [509D E] 1:3 The High courts were right, in holding otherwise. Even if the retrospective promulgation of these rules provide no assistance in the interpretation of the notification, the same should be the position in regard to the exemption provision also. [625E F] 1 :4 In view of this interpretation, the 1987 amendment has the effect of rescinding the exemption granted by the 1981 notification in respect of the industries mentioned by it. Section 12 is clear that while a notification under it can be prospective or retrospective, only prospective operation can be given to a notification rescinding an exemption granted earlier.

The Delhi Judicial Service consists of the following categories: (1) direct recruits; (2) promotees appointed as Additional District and Sessions Judges after the promotees are so appointed, but before the promotees were so appointed; (3) promotees who are appointed as Addl. District & Sessions Judges on an ad hoc basis or for fortuitous reasons or by way of a stop gap arrangement; (4) promotees promoted to the Delhi Higher Judicial Service. The petitioners in their writ petitions challenged the validity of Rule 7 and 8 which provided that recruitment to the service shall be made by promotion from amongst members of the Delhi Judicial Services, who have completed not less than 10 years of service in the Delhi judicial Service. They contended that seniority between promotees and direct recruits must be determined according to the dates on which their appointments were made and that the first available vacancy would be filled by a direct recruit, and that seniority should be determined in accordance with the respective dates of their continuous officiation as Additional Distt. and Sessions Judge and that direct recruits who are not less then ten years of age in the service should be considered for promotion to the Service on the basis of the length of their actual officiating service as Addl District & Session Judges, and (2). The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that seniority cannot be determined either by direct recruitment or by promotion; that the quota rule does not use the negative language, as the proviso to Rule 7(b) provides that in case there were recruitment from Bar as well as by promotions, based on the quotas of vacancies reserved for both categories by Rule 7 provided that the First available vacancy will be filled up by a person who is appointed in consultation with the High Court; and that if the rule of "quota and rota" ceased to apply when appointments are made under Rules 16 and 17, the seniority of direct recruits vis a vis promotees shall be determined on the date of rotation vacancies between the direct recruits and promotees based on quotas of vacancy reserved for them. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The inter se seniority of members of Delhi Judicial service promoted to that Service shall be the same as in the case of promotees appointed to the Services under Rule 16(2) of the Rules. [395C] 1.2 In the instant case, the petitioners had made representations to the High Courts in 1977 and 1977. If appointments have to be made from two different sources, then the authorities should so plan that the recruits come from two distinct sources in time and officers from one source are not required to function substantively and effectively in the jobs which are intended to be performed by recruits of other source and face the prospect of being either pushed back or thrown out. [397F G] 1:3 The seniority list which is impugned in these cases has been prepared on the assumption that the rule was not adhered to and the fulfilment of the rule cannot be maintained. The mere fact that there are numerous decisions of this Court, dealing with rights and privileges of promotees vis avis direct recruits, does not make it possible for the High court to accept the position that there is any quota rule specially in view of the fact that working of the said rules over all these years indicate that the Rule was not followed.

The appellant was a partner in a trading venture conducted in the name of his father. The Income tax Officer assessed the Ambala Flour Mills to income tax for the assessment year 1950 51, and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer. In appeal by the respondent, the Appellate Tribunal reversed the orders of the Appellate Authority. On reference, the High Court held that the order was competent and could not be questioned in a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution. In the appeal to this Court, HELD : The expression 'any person ' in the setting in which it appears must be confined to a person intimately connected in the aforesaid sense with the assessments of the year under appeal. "In making a direction against Debi Parshad the Tribunal did not exercise his powers qua a stranger to the assessment proceeding. [392 D] Commissioner of Income tax, U.P. vs Kanpur Coal Syndicate and others, ; , followed. The expression "any person" in the set out in section 34(3) proviso 2 at p. 346 : "Any person" means any person who is liable to be assessed for the income of the said assessment years. A combined reading of section 30(1) and section 31(3), shows that cases where persons other than the appealing assessee might be affected by orders passed by the Appellate Commissioner, are not covered by the expression "person ' in its widest connotation may take in any person, whether connected or not with the assessee whose income for any year has escaped assessment but this construction cannot be accepted.

The appellant filed a suit for partition of his share and separate possession of certain sites in Madras High Court. The respondent filed an application under section 7(iv)(b) of the Madras City Civil Courts Act, 1908, praying that the court fee payable on the plaint should be calculated at the rate of Rs. 15,00,000. The appellant contended that the suit was barred by article 17 B of Schedule II of the Act and that the proper court fees to be paid on the memorandum of appeal had to be determined under section 8(iv) (b). Held, that the question whether a court fee is payable on a plaint filed on the Original Side of the High Court or on the petition for special leave under article 136 of the Constitution was essentially one of general importance and the court could not decide the correctness of the view taken by the learned Chamber Judge. The question about the levy of court fees in respect of suits falling under section7(iv), (b) and (c) of that Act depends upon the valuation that the plaintiff makes in respect Of his claim. In cases in which the plaintiff is given the option to value his claim, it is really difficult to value or definiteness. Where the plaintiff seeks to pay the fixed court fee as required by article 16(iv). The result is that it is the amount at which the defendant has valued the relief sought for the purpose of court fee that determines the value for jurisdiction in the suit and not vice versa. In the present case, the question about its proper valuation was a matter to be decided solely by reference to the Act.

The Delhi Development Act, 1957 was enacted to provide for the regulation of development of industries in the ratio of one sq. metre per person on each floor and for matters connected therewith. Section 3(1) provides that the Central Government may, by notification, declare that the provisions of the Act shall be deemed to have been substantially amended or applied to the safety of factories within the meaning of section 9. The appellant, a company registered under the Companies Act, was granted a lease in perpetuity from Government of the plot No. 148, Barakhamba Road, New Delhi. In May, 1985, the Central Govern ment issued a notification under section 3(2) of the Delhi Development Authority (DDA), seeking to erect a high rise building on plot No, 148, barakhambas Road, and paid Rs.63,40,918 as betterment charges. On 4.5.1982, the Government of India issued a further notification under Section 9(2). The appellant filed an application before the Delhi Rent Control Tribunal for permission to erect high rise buildings on plot Nos. 148 and 40, Barkhamba road, New No. 14, Bargakhambar Road, Delhi. The Tribunal allowed the application and granted permission to the appellant to construct a high tension building of an area of 1,62,000 square feet and pay Rs.64,40.18 as charges for construction of the said building. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court held that the authorities were not justified in granting the sanction to the plan. The High Court also held that there was no impediment to the sanction. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the permission granted to the respondent to erect the high tension buildings was not permissible and that at best, the high rise structures could be raised by the respondent; (ii) the clearance from the Chief Fire Officer envisaged by Bye law 16.4.8, was in addition to the requirements of bye laws 16. 4.8.1; (iii) the approval of the Chief fire officer was an additional condition and not a limitation on the power of the NDMC to satisfy itself that the building plans provide for adequate fire safety measures; (iv) the authorities had failed to take into account the relevant factors, and (v) the requirements in bye law 16(4) were not inflexible and wherever more liberal and better standards of fire precautions were incor porated in the designs, the bye laws did not prevent such better measures being adopted by the NDMC. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The approval by the Chief Executive of the Municipal Corporation envisaged by bye law 17.1 is an additional requirement and not the limitation on its power to satisfy it. [608C] 1.2 The clearance from Chief Fire officer envisaged by the Bye laws was an addition to a wall constructed in an interior open space, and the bye law recognised the importance of, and finality, to the decision of the chief fire Officer. [509D] 1:3. In view of the findings recorded on various contentions, the order dated 24.4, 1989 of the High court requires to be and is hereby set aside. However, it is directed that the appellant should commence the construction work according to the plans submitted by them, on the condi tions that they file a written undertaking before the NDMC that the construction would be at the risk of the Respond ents 1 & 2 and it would not progress beyond a height of 15 metres and in the event of an ultimate rejection of the plans, they would have no claim against the NDMC for any loss occasioned to respondent No. 1 and 2. [613H; 614A B] 1 :4. The clearance by the chief Fire Officer is an addition of certain minimum requirements of Bye law 17, 8.1, which requires the location and distribution of the refuge areas in each floor.

The joint family carried on business of a grocery shop. The members of the family were living and messing together and the income from the family business was to be divided equally among all the brothers. The parties entered into an agreement in respect of the motor garage and the parties agreed that the parties would have agreed to separate the business from April 1, 1946, but the parties did not agree. In 1947 the joint family entered into a compromise with the plaintiff and his father for the payment of one sixth share to him. The plaintiff was to pay the price of one fifth share to the defendant. On March 31, 1946 the plaintiff paid the price and the balance was to come to an end on March 31. 1946. The agreement was that the accounts of all the businesses should be taken up to March 31 and the accounts should be submitted to the date when the business started. The defendant did not want his brothers to interfere with his exclusive running of the liquor shop after March 31 1946, and the plaintiff filed a suit for partition against the defendant on the ground that the compromise was made in a hurry and that the agreement was void under section 90 of the Indian Trusts Act. The trial court found that the suit was not barred by res judicata as it was based on an unregistered partnership deed dated March 7, 1946. On appeal the High Court held that the cause of action in the two suits was different from the cause for action in one suit and the other in the other. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The plaintiff 's claim is barred by section 90(2)(3), of the Act. [106 E] (ii) The cause of actions in the subsequent suit was the desire of the plaintiff to separate from his brothers and to divide the joint property. That suit embraced the entire property without any reservation and was compromised, the plaintiff having abandoned his claim to account in respect thereof. His subsequent suit to enforce a part of the claim is founded on the same cause of Action which he deliberately relinquished. [107 G] (iii) The defendant 's conduct in going back upon that arrangement by filing a fresh suit in regard to the motor business only was nothing but honest. The plaint filed in the previous suit leaves no manner of doubt that the plaintiff had made out his intention to confine the taking of all accounts upto March 31,. 1946, when the joint Hindu family entered on March 7 and the defendant had abandoned his right to account after March 1,1946. [108 E F] (iv) The conduct of the parties in going to the extent of taking any account of the joint families including the motor transport business after the 31st March, 1946 and the respondent 's suit to recover the share of profits and assets of the said business from the defendant was not therefore barred by the principle of res judicata.

The appellant was employed as a factory in the factory. On the sea side of the sea water into salt, it was removed from the sea to the sea and the tank was found in order to prevent sea water flooding. The appellant was prosecuted for working the Wool Board for the work of converting sea water to sea water and for an offence under section 92 of the , for his working the wetland. The question was whether the salt works "installed" within the definition of the word "factory" in section 2 of the Act. Held, that the expression " premises " in the definition in section 3(1) of the Bombay (Act No. LXIII of 1948), includes a mine subject to the operation of the or a railway running shed. The word " factory" in the context of the definition is used in the sense of building and its adjuncts. The term "factory " in section 4(2) means any premises including precincts thereof, which are used for working, or for purposes of gain. The expression "premises " in that section includes a building as well as a part of land with buildings or buildings alone. The definition of " factory " in cl. (k) of section 2 is not restricted to buildings and the word 'factory ' has been defined in the Act to mean any premises in which certain type of work is carried on by way of trade or for purpose of gain, and includes a factory subject to such operations as are ordinarily carried on in the premises. The words " premises" in cl.(k) refer to buildings as well. The dictionary meaning of the term " factory", as given in the Oxford Dictionary, means "any premises in any place where any manufacturing process is carried out". The word 'premises ' has not been defined either in the Indian Act or in the Bombay Act LXIII. The context and the context show that the word includes a "factory". The definition in cl., (k), of section 3 of the Indian , is wide enough to include all buildings and premises used for work on any day of the preceding twelve months. The process of converting the sea waters into salt was carried on with the aid of power, and so it was not necessary that the water should be converted into salt. The use of the words "any building" in el. (m) of s 2 of Act LXV of 1948 showed that nothing would come within the expression ' premises ' unless it had a building and unless the factory Act definitely provided for the application of the provisions to it. The present case was not one where the salt work was carried out in the Salt Works, but was carried in the salt water which was used in connection with the manufacture of salt. It was not possible to say that the salt Works would come under the definition Of "factory", because, as the factory had been put into the condition of a finished article by the processes to which it had been subjected in the hereditament, the process would fall within the meaning of section 4 (2) of Act LIX of 1948.

The respondent was appointed as Instructor in the Department of Public Instructions. In 1949, he was promoted to the post of Instructor in Tailoring and he joined duty there on December 1, 1949. On June 11, 1956, he made a representation to the Government that his case be considered back to the parent department. The State Government by order dated February 19, 1964 ordered the absorption of the respondent in the department of Technical Education with effect from November 28, 1949, and to give him benefits of revisions of pay scales effected in 1957 and 1961. The respondent filed a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the order of his absorption on the ground that he had been invidiously discriminated against in the matter of absorption and appointment while his junior K. Narayanaswamy Chetty was absorbed in the Polytechnics Department subsequently. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the State Government had acted arbitrarily and in violation of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitu tion. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the absorption in the respondent 's department of technical Education was not made in pursuance of any principle of policy or statutory rule but was done as a matter of concession; (ii) the respondent had no legal right to be absorbed in his service of the Department and (iii) the State had acted illegally and arbitrarily in violation Of Articles 14 & 16 of ' the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of the High Court was not justified on the basis that he was not similarly situated as K.N. Chetty. [259E] 2. In the instant case, the acceptance of the State Public Service Commission by the respondent did not lead to any untoward results such as were apprehended in Rajalakshmiah Setty 's case. Indeed, it has not been shown that the absorption was due to any fault of the Respondent. It is not the appellant 's contention that this principle whereby the absorption had been related back to date on which a person initially came on deputation was ever departed from, excepting in the case of the respond ent. This being the case, there was no justification whatever to depart from this principle of law in the instant ease. [260F G] 3. The acceptance of respondent 'S ' N. Chetty and five others with effect form a date onwhich he initially came, could not by any reckoning be treated as a break in his serv ice, this period having been treated as leave. Nor did it amount to reduction in rank. In any case, this being the position, the High court was justified in granting the relief. [261F G; 262A] 4. The appellant 'S had not been able to show that the respondent was similarly situated because there was a break of his service with the Department. This is not a good deal of evidence to show the respondent who was similarly situate as K, N.

The petitioner, a foreign national and the Indian Council of Social Welfare, was recognised as an advocate under the . The petitioner filed a petition in this Court challenging the validity of the adoption of the petitioner. This petition was resisted by the petitioner on the ground that the child should be allowed to be adopted by foreign parents only through a recognised social or child welfare agency recognised or licensed by the Government of India or the Government, and that the procedure to be followed for such adoption should be in conformity with the principles laid down by this Court. The petitioner also contended that the Indian Medical Council had no authority or agency in the country to adopt a child in adoption and that it was not open to any and every agency or individual to process an application from a foreigner for taking a child, in adoption, unless such institution or agency was licensed as a social or a child welfare agent recognised or approved by the government of India. The respondent contended that since the Indian medical and child welfare agencies were not recognised by the foreign parents, they could not be permitted to take the child in adopt. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Indian Medical and Children Welfare Fund Act, 1956 has been enacted with a view to ensure that the adoption in accordance with law of that country can be made in the Country of adoption. [842C] 1.2 In order to enable a recognised family to take a child under its care, it would be necessary for the foreign parent to take into account who are the biological parents of the child, if the adoptive parents are handicapped or is in bad state of health needing urgent medical attention which is not possible for the social or the child welfare authority looking after the child to provide, the recognised social and child Welfare agency need not wait until social or children welfare agencies are recognised by it. [852E F] 1:3. The recognised social, or child Welfare Agency through which an application of a foreigner is made directly without the intervention of a social, educational or child security agency, has to be recognised as a " guardian" of the person of the minor child with whom he seeks to adopt. Every recognised social/ child welfare Agency must maintain a register in which the names and particulars of all children proposed to be given in inter country adoption through it must be entered and in regard to each such child, the recognized social or Child welfare agency must prepare a list of recognised social (and child welfare) agencies with their names, addresses and other particulars and send them to the appropriate department of the Government. [850E F; 843A B] 1 :4. The recognition of the foreigner for take a Children in adoption is made by an Indian parent or a foreign agency. It will ensure that it will be for the welfare of the children to be provided in the foreign country. [851C D] 2:1. In order that a recognised Social or child agency may have the child study report with them before they select the child for adoption and in case they do not have the children study report, the same should be supplied to them by recognised social Or child welfare organisation. [864D E] 2 :2. The recognized social/child welfare agencies will have to ensure regular attention to the needs of the foreign employers and their children. [874E] 3:1 The recognised Social/ Child Welfare Agency will, on receiving an application form, send two certified copies of the application to the social/arrearship report of such a child as study report and other relevant material in order to facilitate the adoption or the making by it of the applications for guardianship. [877G] 3 :2 The recognised labour agency will, after forwarding the application, hand over the application form to the Social or Child Welfare agency in India. [878A B; 845C] 3.3. In the event of disruption of the family of the foreigners before adoption, the court will have the power to appoint a guardian of the said child.

The appellant company, a registered firm, was assessed to pay 13.51% of the gross profits for the accounting year 1964 65 on the basis that the amount of available surplus was Rs. 2,48,65,450. The workmen were dissatisfied with this offer of bonus at 13.50% offered by the Company and demanded payment of bonus for the year 1965 66. The Tribunal accepted the evidence of the appellant and rejected the claim of the workmen. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) under sections 6 and 7 of the Act, the amount payable by the appellant to its workmen was 20% of their actual wages or wages; (ii) the Tribunal had not taken into account the available surplus as well as the available profits for calculating direct tax or alternatively rebate for bonus found short in considering the claim for bonus. HELD: (i). The Tribunal was justified in declining to add back this amount to gross profits. [110 D] (ii). The claim of Rs. 15,23,195. was made by the workmen before the Tribunal after making a calculation of direct tax without deducting bonus payable for the years 1965 66 and 1966 67 on the profit and loss account. The claim was therefore not justified. [111 F G] Management of Northern Railway Co operative Society vs Industrial Tribunal Rajasthan, ; , referred to. (iii). The dispute regarding the amount paid by the company to its employees for repairs and renewals was pending before the tribunal. It was not a case of any dispute having been raised by the Unions. [112 A B] (iv) The claim for deduction of bonus to be made under section 33(1) of the Income tax Act, 1961 was not justified as it had not been shown that the workmen on which the amount was paid were of commercial expense in order to facilitate carrying on of the business and it was an expenditure allowable under section 37(1). [112 G H] (v) The Tribunal 's award regarding set on cannot be accepted. The payment of compensation to induce the workmen to retire prematurely was an item of expenditure incurred by the respondent company on the ground of commercial expenses in order that it might be an item which could not be deducted from the gross profit.

The appellant was a Deputy Commercial Tax officer in the State and later as Joint Commercial Tax Officer in 1962, he was promoted as an Assistant Commercial Tax officers in 1954. He was posted as Member of the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal in the same cadre. On promotion as Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes he was posted at the Joint Commercial tax officer in 1957 and thereafter as Joint Assistant Commissioner of the Commercial Taxes on 7 S 1975. His service book shows that he had an excellent record of service. He had earned several encomiums, commendations and appreciations. The various promotions gained by him during the period from May to September, under the rule which enables the Government to retire a Government servant in the public interest after he has attained the age of SO years or after he had completed 25 years of qualifying service. One wonders whether the failure to note the result of the enquiry in the personal file led to the impugned order. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant will be reinstated in service and paid arrears of salary due to him under the rules. He is entitled to his costs. [771 D] 2. The Government is entitled only to take into consideration the entire history of the appellant including that part of it which was prior to his promotion, 80 read them all in conjunction and conclude that the time had arrived for the Government servant to quit Government service. But with nothing of the sort, it is indeed odd to retire the Government Servant a few months after promoting him to a Selection post. [761 D E] 3. The order of November 29, 1974 of the Government was quashed by the High Court and the effect of the order of the government was to grant absolution to the appellant from the repercussions of the note of the Deputy Commissioner, of Commercial Tax, made in 1969. If there was any ambiguity about the effect thereof, it was cleared by the circumstance that within a few month, on May 7, 1975 he was promotion as Joint Sales Tax officer. [760 E F] 4. The word "rejected" in the note meant that the enquiry was pending before the Vigilance and Anti Corruption Department in regard to allegations against the appellant apart from the 1969 entry. All that it could find was some stray mildly deprecating entries such as the one in 1964 which said: "He is sincere and hardworking". [756 G H] 5. The fact that the appellant had an experienced record of serv ice does not mean that he has outlived his utility as a Government Servant. If, therefore, past events may help to assess present conduct. But when there is nothing in the present conduct casting any doubt on the wisdom of the promotion, it cannot be said that the previous history casting any doubts on the propriety of the promo tion. [777 E F; 778 A] 6. The last history of a Government employee should be completely ignored once he is promoted. Sometimes past events might help to assessment present conduct and may help him to assess absent conduct or make him wonder whether the right hand knows what the left hand has done. If in the month of May a Government serv ice is found to possess 'such high merit and ability which naturally includes integrity, as to entitle him not merely to be promoted to a selection post but to be appointed to a very responsible and much desired post in that cadre, what could have happened between May and September to merit his being weeded out altogether from service in September under the Rule which enables Government to retirement on a Selection Post or selection grade.

The appellants were the owners of certain routes in the Kumool District of Andhra Pradesh. The State Transport Undertaking, which was a nationalised one, had been constituted under the . After the nationalisation of transport services in the State of Andhra, the routes covered by the said routes were taken over by the State Government and the routes in question were nationalised. The appellants challenged the validity of the schemes on the grounds that they violated article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as they were not the Corporation which was responsible for the defeat of their fundamental rights under articles 14 and 16 of the constitution. The High Court dismissed the petitions. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The scheme framed by the Corporation was valid and did not contravene article 14. [362 E] (ii) The schemes were vitiated by non compliance with section 68 C(1). The scheme was as a result of policy decision taken by the Chief Minister and the direction given to the Corporation that the routes should be taken up for nationalisation, but it was not done in conformity with the requirements of section 68 D. [363 G] (iii) The contention that the scheme was vitiated by mala fides cannot be accepted. The scheme is a part of the policy decision of the State and its action must be by a formal Government order in writing. It does not require the same authority to act as a statutory authority for the purpose of the article. [361 E] In the instant case, it was as much as the Chief Secretary who had been appointed under the Corporation 's orders had stated that he had no power to issue the permits. The fact that some of the variations between the maxima and the minima in the number of vehicles proposed to be operated on each route are such as adopting the test suggested by the learned Advocate General himself, to really contravene Rule 4. [364 E F] (iv) The policy decision was taken by a State Undertaking which had been formed under section 68C of the Act. The Government was not bound to give effect to it. The policy was to be taken either as a whole or in part. [365 G H] (v) The mere prescription of the maxim,a and minima, particularly for the reasons set out in the affidavit of the Assistant Secretary to the Transport Department, constituted a violation of section 69 E of the Motor Vehicles Act.

The appellant was a dealer under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. In respect of the accounting year ending 31st December 1954 in the return for the assessment year the assessee showed his taxable turnover at Rs. 218 9 0 and deposited the tax of Rs. 9 12 6 on the said amount in the treasury. The Commercial Tax Officer assessed the appellant under section 5(2)(a)(ii) of the Act to pay additional tax of RS. 1,33,730 6 6. The appellant contended that the assessment was not made under section5(2) (a)(i) of that Act and that the appellant had no exemption from taxation under the said sub clause. Held, that the substantive clause gives the exemption and the proviso qualifies the substantive cl. In order to claim exemption under the sub clause, it must be shown that the dealer had sold the specified goods to another for the purposes mentioned in the section. The proviso does not require that the person claiming the exemption shall furnish a declaration form in the manner prescribed by the Act. It is well settled that "the effect of an excepting or qualifying proviso, according to the ordinary rules of construction, is to except out of the preceding portion of the enactment, or to qualify something enacted therein which but for the proviso would be within it": "but not to include a declaration in the prescribed form". The expression "on demand" only fixes the point of time when the declaration forms are to be produced; otherwise the rule would be inconsistent with section 5 (2)(b) of Act.

The Bihar State Jail Manual, 1978 provides that a person who has been in jail for long periods of time and is still in jail, must be forthwith tried by the Magistrates. The State Government should provide them a lawyer at its own cost for the purpose of making an application for bail, provided no objection is raised to such lawyer on behalf of such under trial prisoners and if any application for such lawyer is made, the Magistrates should dispose of it in accordance with the broad outlines set out by this Court in its judgment dated 12th February 1979. The High Court of Patna has issued a circular on the subject regarding the maintenance of trials after trial prisoners were produced before the Magistrates or the Sessions Courts, as required by the proviso to section 167(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The circular also provides that the State Government shall provide them with a lawyer who is in jail during the period of remand for a period of over five years. The appellants filed writ petitions in this Court challenging the validity of the said circular on two grounds: (1) that the under trial prisoner whose name was not furnished to him, was not afforded an opportunity of being heard before the Magistrate could be examined by the Magistrate; and (2) that there has been inordinate delay in bringing the under trials to trial. The respondents contended that the appellants were entitled to bail because they had already been in prison for a long period of time, and that the High Court should have given them a lawyers at its disposal and that they should be allowed to continue to indulge in dilatory tactics. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The State shall produce all the trial prisoners before the Sessions Court within six months from today as on 31st December, 1978 and where such cases have been pending investigation for more than six months, the State of Bihar will furnish broadly the reasons why there has not been such delay in the investigative process. [541C D] 1.2 The High Courts should give a similar activist approach and issue to the State directions which may involve taking of positive action with a view to securing enforcement of fundamental rights to speedy trial. But in order to enable the Court to discharge this constitutional obligation it is necessary that the Court should be able to have the requisite information bearing on the problem. [542F G] 1:3 The High courts should give directions which might involve taking into account the problem and also explaining why it has not already been possible to dispose of such of those cases as have been disposed of by the High Courts in accordance With broad guidelines set out in our judgment dated December 12, 1979. [543G H] 1 :4. The Court in the last mentioned case asserted that it "has the duty of fashioning a decree that will require defendants to eliminate the conditions and practices at the trial run by the court after giving them full particulars as to the location of courts of magistrates and courts of sessions in the State". [543A] 1 5.

The appellant gave notice of termination of tenancy to the respondent under section 34(1) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. The notice was for one year as required by section 34 (1). The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for possession of the land under section 29(2) of that Act on December 31, 1951, and obtained possession of it. In the meantime an amendment was made to the Act by the insertion of sub section (2 A) to section 34 by the Amending Act No. XXXIII of 1952 which came into force on January 12, 1953. By this amendment certain further restrictions were placed on the right of the landlord to terminate the tenancy and to take possession of land leased to him. The respondent thereupon filed a petition under article 227 of the Constitution before the High Court of Bombay challenging the validity of the amendment on the ground that it was not applicable to notices given before the Amending act came into operation. The High Court allowed the application holding that the amendment did not affect any vested right of landlord and that the Amending Acts were in force when the Amendment Act came into effect. In appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The amendment made by the amending Act No, XXXIII of 1953 was prospective and could not affect the rights of the landlords till the tenancy actually stood terminated after the expiry of the notice. The amendment did take away vested right to obtain possession of a land. Therefore, the Amending legislation did not effect any vested rights of landlord until the tenancy commenced after the Amendment came into existence. (ii)The amendment was prospective in operation and could be taken away only by subsequent amendments. In this view it was clear that the legislature could not have intended that the benefit of the beneficent measure should not be extended to tenants in whose cases the tenancy had not yet terminated, though notices had been given, when the further restrictions on the landlord 's right to terminate tenancy were being put on the rights to terminate. (iii)The Amending Act did not take away any vested interest of the tenant till the date when the tenancy was terminated and he became entitled to possession that he was so entitled in law as it then stood.

The petitioners were the owners of a house in which they had never been declared an evacuee and their interest therein was vested in the Custodian under section 8 of the , and he took possession of them. The petitioners contended that they had been wrongly deprived of their rights by the action of the Custodian. Held, that the acts of the custodian in so far as they deprive the petitioners of their property could not be upheld. The acts of a person in so respect which he was entitled to have his property cannot be upheld unless he has first been given a notice under section 7 of the Act and has made time barred and which he need never have filed at all. The act of the evacuee in so much as it had been done by him was not a quasi judicial decision. Ebrahim Aboobaker vs Tek Chand Dolwani, ; , applied. The order of January 10, 1952, was without jurisdiction so far it affected the rights of the petitioners and was liable to be set aside. EBrahim Abichandaker vs Chet Chand Dholwani, A.I.R. (1954) S.C. 1029, referred to. The proceedings in the present case were not barred by article 31 of the Constitution. E brahim Abiveraker vsust Chand Dhenolwani ; , distinguished. The orders of January I, 1952 and January 1053 were without jurisdiction as they had not been passed within the time prescribed for it. EfbrahimAboobaker V. Tek Chand, A,I. R. (1956) S C. 829, followed.

The assessee company entered into an agreement with the agents on October 20, 1953 for the sale of yarn to them. The agents agreed to pay 6% interest on the advances to be made by the agents and further agreed to make payment of 2% interest thereon at 6% p.a. On December 15, 1953 the agents executed a deed of agency in favour of the agents. Clause 7 of the agreement provided that the agents would get 6% of their commission on the net profits of the business. The assessee company paid 2% commission on net sales and 50% commission to the agents 1/2% commission. On October 20 the assessee company filed an application before the Income tax Officer claiming deduction of Rs. 10,000/ being the amount paid by the selling agents to the selling agent as remuneration for services rendered. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner allowed the claim holding that the agreement amounted to a joint venture for distribution of profit, and therefore the amount was not liable to be included in the assessable income. On appeal the Tribunal held that the payment in question was a joint business for the distribution of profits, and that the amount could not be claimed by the assessee as a deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The High Court on reference answered the questions in favour o f the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant company: (1) that there being an express provision in the agreement dated October 20 1955 by which the agents agreed inter alia that the commission paid to the agent would be deducted from the remuneration payable to the commission; and (2) that the High Court had exceeded its jurisdiction in travelling beyond the agreed statement of the case framed by the Tribunal and had relied on certain materials which were not at all found by the tribunal in its order nor were those materials referred to in the statement of case. HELD: (i) The agreement clearly provided for the consent of the agent not only at the beginning of the manufacture of the yarn by the plant to be installed by the appellant but at every stage in the pro gramme of manufacture. On the loan advanced to the assessee and a percentage in the profits of business would be quite consistent with a remuneration in lieu of services lent and would certainly amount to an expenditure incurred by the asses see wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the assessee 's business which was conducted by the company. [200 C] (ii) The High court was right in holding that payments in question were not legally deductible under section I(2) (xv). [200 D] (iii) The view taken by the High court that the amounts in question are deductible under s 10(1)(vi) appears to be legally erroneous.

The assessee, a private limited company, was assessed for the assessment year 1959 60 (the relevant previous year being the year ended March 31, 1959) on a total income of Rs. 43,407/ . The Income Tax Officer held that the accumulated profits of the company amounted to Rs. 1,050 only and that amount alone could be considered as "dividend" under section 2(6A)(e) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. He also determined a sum of Rs, 25,107/ by way of dividend on the balance of Rs 18,950 in the profit & loss account. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed an appeal filed by the assessee. The Tribunal held that Rs. 11,000 were dividend under section2(6 A)(e), and that the amount alone was liable to be treated as "current profits" for the purpose of section 2 (6A) of Income Tax, 1922, and that it should be taken into account in determining the figure of accumulated profits. The High Court on reference held against the assessee and the Tribunal. In appeal by certificate, the appellant contended that the words "accumulated profits" occurring in section 2 of the Act must mean profits which had accumulated prior to the accounting year of which the income profits and gains were being assessed, while current profits would mean the profits which have accumulated prior before the accounting years of which income profits were being assessment. The Revenue contended that this question should not have been referred by the Appellate Tribunal to the High Court at the instance of the assessee because no reference application was made by the appellant. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "accusation" in section 6(2A) (e), cannot take in current profits. [950C] 2.1 The words "cotton profits" and "cold profits" have long held the field, and as the learned judges of the High Courts of Australia observed that the word "accu larly" must be given its ordinary meaning, it has been well known in judicial decisions that except for Tights in which a non applicant can ask for the reference of questions of law on the application made by him, there is no right to refer the question of law sought by him. [940F G] 2:2 In the present case, the question whether the provision of Rs 11,500 for tax and Rs. 6,900 for dividend could be taken in current profit making entirely against one party, although in the course of making the order relating to the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commission was not competent to refer it to the extent that it covers the grant of separate and distinct reliefs and the decision on one question does not affect the decision. [943F G; 944A B] 2 :3 The High Courts were not competent in reference to the second question on its merits. [942G H] 3:1. The question whether a provision of income can be taken to have been included within section 2, sub clause (e) or section 2A(e), is one of construction of the word 'accumulation ' and cannot be decided by reference to a judgment of the Appellate Court. [947B C] 3 :2. The fact that rule was not applied in the Twelfth Report of the Law Commission of India shows that the intention of the Legislature was to include current profits in section 1, 2 or 4A(a) (c). The statute expressly contemplates an application in that behalf by a party desiring a reference to it. [948C D] 3.3.

The appellant was the Mahant of a religious institution known as Rajgunj Asthal, and was in possession of certain plots of land. He had been in possession for over 200 years under an assertion of title without challenge. The respondents contended that the lands were not Mal lands within the Zamindari of Burdwan but had been granted as Lakheraj grantees. Held, that a presumption of lost grant could be made only when there was no person capable of making a grant; and where the right is claimed by a fluctuating body of persons, it must follow that they could have been held on the date of the permanent settlement as Laksheraj grant. The fact that the respondents claimed to hold under a Lakhe Rajgunz Asthal was not sufficient to sustain a presumption that the possession was referable to a grant by the owner entitled to the land but that such grant had been lost. Raja Braja Sundar Deb vs Moni Behara and Others, (1917) L.R. 44 I.A. 147, referred to. Held further, that on the facts found, no presumption of a lost grant can be made in favour of the defendants and that the plaintiff was entitled to assessment of fair and equitable rent on the holdings in their possession. The suit properties formed part of Mauza Nala within the zamindari assessed to revenue and were not shown to relate to the suit lands. The documents relied on by the defendants as containing assertions that they held under a Jhalraj grant are not shown, but a permanent lease because there is neither premium paid nor rent reserved but a Lakharaj grant unsupported by any consideration.

The appellant was the owner of certain agricultural land. The Tenancy Act, 1948, came into force on October 15, 1965. Section 85A provides that when upon a reference a decision is recorded by the competent authority under the Tenancy Act and the order of the competent authori ty is communicated to the civil court, such Court shall proceed to deal with the suit in accordance with the procedure applicable thereto. The appellant filed a suit for specific performance of a contract which was dismissed by the trial court on the ground that he was an agriculturist within the meaning of the Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950. The respondent 's appeal before the High Court was allowed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the jurisdiction of the civil Court to settle, decide or deal with any question which is by or under the tenancy Act required to be settled, decided or dealt with by any authority competent to settle; and (ii) if the court does not take note of the situation where upon a contest an issue arises between the parties which is required to he settled, decide the issue whether the plaintiff is an agriculturist. HELD: (i). The jurisdiction of civil court to settle the, decided, or dealt With by the Tenancy act, is totally ousted. Therefore, it is incumbent upon the Civil Court to refer the issue to the competent au thority under the Act and decide it in accordance therewith. [598F] (ii). The High Court has rightly held that if an issue arose in a properly constituted civil suit which the civil courts are competent to decide, but takes note of it, it will be open to the Civil court to deal only with that issue in some proceeding before him under some specific provision of the Act. [599H] (iii). The expression "any issues which are required tobe settled, deciding or dealt wo with by a competent authority" in section 70(a) of the Bombay Tenancy and Land Reforms Act, 1947 would mean that if upon assertion and denial and consequent contest an issues arise in the context of the provisions of the tenancy law and which is require to be settle, decided and dealt with, the jurisdiction will be barred. [600H] In the instant case, the dispute was not an agriculturist but a question arose as to whether the respondent was an agriculturalist within the definition of the word 'agricultural land ' in section 2(g) of Bombay Tenancy Act. The Mamlatdar had jurisdiction under section 70 to decide or dispose of the contention which stands in the forefront a reference to the Mamlatdar under section 71 read with sections 85 and 85A is enevitable. [698H; 599A B] (iv). The respondent was not entitled to any relief on the basis of the bar imposed by section 70A of the ' Tenancy Act because he was not agriculturist.

The assessee, a heavy engineering concern manufacturing steam, machinery parts and castings from outside the castings manufactured in the steel Foundry Division of the assessee company was started in the assessment year 1958 59 and continued thereafter. The Income tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner on the facts found that out of a total sale of Rs. 28,23,127/ of steel castings goods worth Rs. 18,39,433/ were used in connection with various other concerns, the assessee was purchasing the spare parts, forgings and cast ings from outside. The Tribunal held that it could not be said that the undertakings were formed out of the existing business to come within the mischief of exclusion clause in section 15C(2)(i) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. On reference, the High Court held that even though the manufactured products of the new industrial undertaking were mostly used by the reconstruction of the business already in existence, the benefit of section 15 C was available to the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the two undertakings are distinct and separate from the original business, and (ii) the grant of a special licence for the steel foundry division did not make it an industrial undertaking to qualify for exemption under section 15(C). HELD: The High Court was right in answering the two questions in the negative. [776 D] (i)(a) The new industrial undertakings are independent producing arti cles which may be of aid to the principal business but yet the undertakings are different and not reconstruction out of tho existing business of the assesses. Use by the assessee of the articles produced in its existing business or the concept of expansion are not decisive tests in construing section 15. [764 D] Commissioner of Income tax vs Gangs Sugar Corpora tion Ltd., ; , referred to. (b) The High court was not right in holding that the two undertaking as formed by reconstruction of a new business of heavy engineering were independent producing articles and the undertakings can be carried on separately without complete absorption and losing their identity in the old business, they are not to be treated as being formed by re struction of the old. [774 E] (c) The fact that an assessee by establishment of a newly established industrial undertaking expands his existing business which he certainly does would not, on that score, deprive him of the benefit under section15C(1).

The inamdar of the appellant village made an application to the Revenue Divisional Officer under section 44 B(2)(a)(i) asking for a decree declaring that the inam lands were granted to him as remuneration for services and were not resumable under section 43 B. The Inamdars contended that the inams were personal inams burdened with services and was not resuscitated by adverse possession of the lands by the alienees for over 80 years. The trial court dismissed the suit but the High Court in second appeal held that the Inams comprised both melwaram and melwarar and were personal inam burdened with service and were therefore personal inams. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Section 44 B does not apply to a personal inam governed by section 44B(2) (a)(ii). The inam title, if any, of all persons claiming through the inamdars to any subordinate interest in the inams stood determined. [549 E] (ii) Section 43 B(1) is in its direct operation prospective as it authorises only future resumption after it came into force. It does not authorise resumption of the inam on the ground that the holder of the Inam has made an exchange, gift, sale or mortgage of the land or any portion thereof or has granted a lease of it for a term exceeding five years. [557 F] (iii) The inams in the present case were not personal inams and were inams granted to office holders as remuneration. [550 G] (iv) The inamdars were lessees of the inams under the inamdar. During the continuance of the tenancy, their possession was not adverse to the Government under whom the inamants held the inam properties. They did not acquire any prescriptive title to the kudiwaram rights either against the inamers or against the Government.

The Indore Municipality was governed by the Indore City Municipal Act, 1909. Under section 79(1) of the Act the Municipality had imposed a tax on houses or buildings or lands or both. Section 76(6) provided that where a municipality adopts a previously prepared list for any subsequent year the provisions of sections 75 and 76 shall be applicable as if a new assessment list has been completed at the commencement of that particular official year. The appellant Corporation, which was governed under the Indore Municipal Act,, 1909, filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of the excess amount paid by it on the ground that the tax could not be assessed on the basis of gross annual letting value as such imposition was illegal and ultra vires. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) Section 76 provides expressly that when a municipality adopted a previously framed list for an subsequent year, it can be done subject to the provisions laid down in section 73(6). Sub section 2 of section 79 provides expressly, that when such a previous list is adopted for a particular official years, it could be done under the new Act to the extent that they are consistent with the provisions Of section 73. [131 C D] (2) The saving and the deeming provisions in section 2(c) can only apply if the tax is assessed in the manner consistent with section 73, that is, if it is assessed on a net and not the gross annual tenancy value after deducting 10% statutory allowance in lieu of the costs of repairs or any other account whatsoever. If the construction of section 2 (c) as suggested by counsel were to be accepted it would render section 73 (2), nugatory. [132 E F] (3) The appellant was entitled to impose house tax on the income of the basis that imposition is inconsistent with section 75 under which the annual letting values would be the gross return value less 10% Statutory allowance. But the contention was not accepted by the High court.

The assessee company carried on the business of manufacturing matches till it was wound up and there were several transactions in respect of which a large amount of money had been paid as income derived from carrying on a business. The assessee company sold chemicals and paper for manufacture. The Deputy Commissioner of Income tax, who tried to assess the company for the account year ending April 30, 1944, held that the amount was not liable to income tax because there was no real profit. On appeal by the assessee company the Appellate Tribunal found that the business had not completely ceased to exist since the assessee Company was carrying on manufacturing, on behalf of the purchaser, and the sale could not be regarded as a realisation sale after the company was wound. The High Court held that by the sale of chemicals and raw materials the profit made out of the agreement of sale was distinct from the sale price for which the property was exchanged, but that there was an identifiable profit of Rs. 1,15,259 on the sale, of the chemicals and the raw materials. Held, that the assessee was not a dealer within the meaning of section 2(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, and that the transaction was not one of sale of the chemical and raw material for match manufacture. Doughty vs Commissioner of Taxes, ; , distinguished. The fact that the clause in the Memorandum gave power to the company to Bell chemicals could not make it a sale in the course of business operations which alone would have attracted tax if profit resulted. In the present case, the assessee 's profit was earned by the purchaser till the entire consideration was paid, made no difference because the agreement clearly indicated that the appellant company was keeping the factory going, not on its own behalf but entirely on behalf Of the buyer. The question whether a sale of an chemicals and a raw materials for match manufacturer was anything more than a winding up sale, not with a view to trading in chemicals and manufacturing chemicals, was a mixed question of law and fact. Dictty vs C.I.T., ; , referred to.
